# podssh: manual and documents

The manual is the output of `podssh man --no-pager`.

```text
podssh 1.1.0-beta.3 - no-privilege SSH over a WebSocket relay

SYNOPSIS
  podssh COMMAND [OPTIONS]

  Start here:
    podssh doctor  what works on this host, one line for each check
    podssh ssh user@example.org
                   log in to a host, through the relay
    ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' -o ServerAliveInterval=60 user@example.org
                   use the OpenSSH client, with podssh as its way out

  Connect:
    ssh         the OpenSSH-compatible client, over the relay
    each        one command on many hosts at once: each line with its host, and
                the worst status as the exit
    containers  the containers of a host, of docker, podman or kubectl, each
                with the command that enters it
    proxy       ProxyCommand form: a byte pipe, not an SSH client; node://NAME
                reaches a node, as operator NAME does
    pipe        join two byte streams, as socat does: stdio, fd:N, exec:CMD,
                with no listener unless one side is tcp-listen:, unix-listen:,
                http-listen: or ws-listen:
    ts          the tailnet node and byte pipe, over DERP (not in this build)

  Work on a host:
    run  copy a project to a host, only the files that changed, then run a
         command in it, with its exit status
    job  jobs on a host that outlive the connection, each in its tmux, and a
         queue of them: start, submit, list, log, wait, fetch, stop; an ID is
         the 8 hex digits that start or submit printed

  Copy files:
    cp    copy files to or from a remote host
    mv    move files; across hosts this is a copy and a delete
    scp   copy files with the command line of OpenSSH's scp
    sftp  file commands on a host, from a batch or at a prompt, as OpenSSH's
          sftp
    edit  edit a file of a host in an editor here; it goes back only when the
          host's file did not change meanwhile
    tx    in the shell of a podssh ssh session: a file to or from podssh at its
          other end, through the terminal itself

  Keys:
    keygen  make an SSH key pair, or print a key's public key or fingerprint
    agent   an SSH agent inside podssh, and add, list, remove and lock its keys

  Check this host and the path:
    doctor  what this host allows and whether the relay works: ok, FAIL or ????
            per check
    status  the state of this host as one line of JSON: relays, token, proxy,
            terminal, a host key
    ping    a short check of the path: each step to the relay, pings, and with
            a host the echo and throughput; with node://NAME, each of its roads
            and the one that answered first; with --nodes or --net, those of
            each node
    health  the far host's load, CPUs, memory, uptime, network, disks and
            processes, read over one exec

  The reverse road:
    node      reverse mode: expose a local service to operators
    operator  reverse mode, operator side: raw bytes to a named node
    net       your own nodes as one net: their names and keys, signed by your
              key, kept by each
    exit      a SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT proxy here, whose connections start at
              an exit node of your net
    share     a running node's local services by name, for its net: add, rm and
              ls, each reached as node://NODE/NAME
    funnel    a local HTTP service at a public https:// name, through a quick
              tunnel (TLS ends at Cloudflare's edge) or OpenTunnel (TLS ends
              here)

  An SSH server here:
    serve  an SSH server here: one connection on stdin and stdout, as sshd -i,
           or the node of a pair through the relay; with a host key kept and
           authorized keys

  Runs in the background:
    detached  the runs that --detach and -f sent into the background, by their
              names: list them, the state of one, stop one

  Messages:
    chat  messages and files with another podssh, end to end encrypted

  Recordings:
    play  play a recording of podssh ssh --record again, with its timing

  Settings:
    config  ssh_config blocks from the host list of another tool: import

  Tools for an agent:
    mcp      the commands as tools for an agent: a Model Context Protocol
             server on stdin and stdout
    session  a session that outlives each call, for an agent: start it, send
             keys, wait until the output stops, read the screen

  The relay:
    relay  the relay's hosts, pool and view of a target; the pairs of the
           reverse road; its document

  This manual:
    man  this manual: each command, flag, variable, file and exit code

  This binary:
    update  this binary from the newest release, its signature and its sum
            checked first; only when asked

  Options:
    -h, --help
        Print help; --help COMMAND or help COMMAND prints the help of one
        command.
    -V, --version
        Print the version, and the commit of a release build.

DESCRIPTION
  podssh carries SSH, or another TCP stream, through a WebSocket relay on port
  443. It is one static binary for hosts whose only way out is HTTPS, often
  through an HTTP CONNECT proxy. It needs no installed ssh, no root, no pty, no
  DNS and no user database entry.

  Answers go to stdout. Diagnostics go to stderr, so stdout can carry a
  protocol.

  A question (a host key, a password, a passphrase) goes to the controlling
  terminal or to SSH_ASKPASS. With neither, podssh refuses at once and names
  the remedy. When stdin, stdout and stderr are all redirected, a question on
  the terminal waits 60 s at most.

  With no command, podssh lists the commands on stderr and exits 64. It never
  takes a word as a host: podssh example.org prints the line to type, podssh
  ssh example.org.

  podssh COMMAND --help gives the section of one command, as podssh man COMMAND
  does. This manual is generated from the tables of this binary, so it
  describes this binary and no other version.

COMMANDS

podssh ssh
  the OpenSSH-compatible client, over the relay.

  podssh ssh reaches the host through the relay (see THE RELAY), or over TCP
  with --direct. It needs no installed ssh, no pty and no user database entry.

  The direct road is a fallback of podssh ssh. It goes when no relay host
  opened a session, or one closed a session to an IPv6 target before any byte
  came. It goes only when the user named no relay (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY
  or RelayHost). podssh ssh then tries it once, as the road table gives it, of
  the family of -4 or -6 when one is given: one line says that the relay hosts
  failed and that it tries HOST:PORT directly. It goes through HTTPS_PROXY when
  one is set, whose CONNECT then names the target. The server's version line
  must come within 10 s, as a proxy that takes the CONNECT and carries no SSH
  sends nothing; the proxy is then named. When both fail, the relay's lines
  come first, then one that names both roads with their times, and the exit is
  the relay's. -v gives the relay's lines when the direct road carries the
  session, and says so. --direct is the direct road alone, and a relay that the
  user names is the relay alone: neither falls back. PODSSH_DIRECT=no, or
  Direct no in the settings file, turns the fallback off. The commands that
  reach a server as podssh ssh does (cp, each, job, health, containers, ping,
  pipe ssh:) do the same. So does the first hop of -J.

  Each host that is dialed, the destination after HostName and each hop of -J,
  is checked before anything connects. The check runs on each road, by the rule
  of the relay: letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores, not first a -
  or a ., at most 253 characters, or an IPv4 or IPv6 address; else the exit is
  64. A name beyond ASCII goes in its ASCII form, whose labels begin xn--. An
  IPv6 address with a zone (fe80::1%eth0) is taken where this host dials it
  (--direct) or a jump host does, and refused through the relay.

  node://[user@]NAME reaches the node of the pair under the label NAME (see
  podssh node), through the relay. Its host key is recorded and checked under
  the name node://NAME. --pair-file gives the pair, or its operator's part, in
  a file. The session runs the end-to-end channel, with the node's key pinned
  and this client's key, as podssh operator does: --node-key, --client-key and
  --no-e2e as there; a changed node key, and a key that the node refuses, exit
  255. iroh:TICKET runs the channel too, to the key that the ticket names. A
  node has no port, and -J, -W and --direct cannot go with it as the
  destination. -J node://NAME makes the node the first hop of a chain: its
  roads reach its TARGET, an sshd, whose key is checked under node://NAME. Each
  later hop is inside that connection, and a node cannot be a later hop. podssh
  sends nothing until the node's first bytes (30 s at most), to learn whether
  the node offers the resumable layer; -v says whether it does. With the layer,
  a lost link to the relay is replaced by a new one. That goes on for as long
  as the node keeps the session (10 minutes, or its --resume-deadline; -v says
  it), and the SSH session goes on where it was; one line on stderr tells of
  each loss and each resume. --resume-deadline TIME waits at most TIME, never
  longer than the node keeps the session. --no-resume asks the node to end the
  session with its link: a lost link ends it, with a line, no spare link or
  move goes beside it, and the node keeps nothing of it; -v says that the node
  took the ask. A line says that a node of an earlier podssh does not know it
  and keeps the session as before. When the node forgot the session, as after a
  sleep of this host longer than its deadline, the line says so. It says how
  long this side was away by the wall clock. SIGHUP and SIGTERM end the session
  with its end at the node, which then keeps nothing of it, 2 s at most after
  the signal; Ctrl-C stays the remote command's.

  A spare link: with the resumable layer, podssh watches for a silent node. The
  node is silent when it has not answered a key or a check of the link for
  three round trips. That wait is 1 s at least and 3 s at most. The node is
  silent too when it has said nothing for 20 s. podssh then opens a new link
  beside the silent one, one each 10 s at most, and checks the old one at once.
  When the old link speaks first, the new one closes before its handshake; else
  the new one resumes the session. So a new address of this host costs seconds,
  not the 30 s after which a silent link is dead. -v says each spare link, and
  which link went on; PODSSH_SPARE_LINKS set to no turns them off. The iroh
  road opens none: QUIC carries its session across a new address by itself.

  A notice while the node is silent: with the resumable layer, a key or a check
  of the link may wait 5 s for the node's answer. podssh ssh then says how long
  the node has said nothing, counting up, and how to end the session (~.). With
  a pty, it shows in the window's title. podssh saves the title first on the
  terminal's stack of titles and takes it back before the node's next bytes;
  the screen is not written, and the lines of a loss and a resume are left out
  meanwhile. That is done only on a terminal known to keep such a stack: xterm
  (XTERM_VERSION) and VTE (VTE_VERSION), not inside tmux or screen, or another
  with PODSSH_TITLE_STACK set to yes; elsewhere the lines stay as they are.
  With no pty, it is a line on stderr, and another when the node answers again.
  Never in a pipe, nor with -q. When this host wakes from a sleep, podssh
  checks the link at once. So the spare link and the notice of a link that the
  sleep took count from the wake. On the forward road through the relay, the
  same notice tells the relay's silence: with SSH's bytes up, or at a wake,
  while no question waits, podssh sends a WebSocket Ping. The relay's Pong or
  the target's bytes answer it, so a key that nothing echoes is no silence; a
  link that stays silent ends the session about 30 s after its last frame. With
  --direct, and on a road that tells no silence of its own, the question is
  SSH's: with a key, podssh sends a keepalive that asks for a reply
  (keepalive@openssh.com). The reply, even a failure, or any byte of the
  session answers it; through -J, the target's own, through the hop.

  iroh:TICKET, or user@iroh:TICKET, reaches a node of the iroh road (see podssh
  node), in a build with the feature iroh, as each release binary is. The
  ticket is the address that the node prints, not a credential: the node lets
  in only the client keys of its allowlist. This client's key is made on first
  use, in the cache (client.key, or iroh-client.key of an earlier podssh) or in
  the file of --iroh-key; podssh prints its fingerprint when it is new, and
  when a node refuses it, as the line that the node's operator adds. The host
  key is recorded and checked under the name iroh:KEY, the node's key, which
  stays when the ticket changes. A node has no port, and -J, -W and --direct
  cannot go with it yet. The session runs the resumable layer: a lost link is
  replaced by a new one, for 10 minutes. podssh asks the ticket's relay first,
  then those of --iroh-relay (see THE RELAY). When the ticket's relay does not
  reach the node, podssh asks for the node's record of pkarr. It dials the
  relay that the record names, and says the node's ticket there (see iroh
  record in THE RELAY).

  cf://[user@]HOST reaches a service that Cloudflare's cloudflared publishes
  under HOST, the name of a tunnel's ssh:// or tcp:// rule: over the WebSocket
  that cloudflared access tcp opens, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, with
  no relay and no program of Cloudflare's. A name behind Cloudflare Access
  needs a service token (PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID and
  PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET) or a token made where its login runs
  (PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_TOKEN or PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_TOKEN_FILE); a refusal of Access
  says so. The id and the secret may come from the files of
  PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID_FILE and PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE
  instead. The host key is recorded and checked under HOST. A tunnel has no
  port here, and -J, -4, -6, HostName and --direct cannot go with it. -J
  cf://HOST makes a tunnel the first hop of a chain, the hops after it in its
  channels. So a jump host whose sshd a tunnel publishes reaches the rest; a
  tunnel after the first hop is refused. podssh proxy cf://HOST is the same
  pipe. A podssh node that makes the quick tunnel of HOST itself sends the
  resumable layer's greeting first, where cloudflared's service speaks SSH
  first: the session then runs in the layer, with the end-to-end channel above
  it, and a new WebSocket to HOST carries it after each lost one. The node's
  key is the one of --node-key, the key that the node prints as it starts. Else
  it is pinned under cf://HOST at its first sight; --node-key with a far end
  that greets with no layer is refused. SSH's keepalives are off there unless
  ServerAliveInterval is given. podssh proxy cf://HOST carries the bytes as
  they are, for cloudflared's services.

  iap://[user@]PROJECT/ZONE/INSTANCE[:PORT] reaches a port of a VM of GCP, 22
  by default, through Google's Identity-Aware Proxy for TCP, as gcloud compute
  start-iap-tunnel reaches it: a WebSocket to tunnel.cloudproxy.app through
  HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, with no relay and no program of Google's. It
  needs an account with the role IAP-secured Tunnel User
  (roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor), and a firewall rule that lets TCP in from
  35.235.240.0/20. It needs a token in the file of PODSSH_IAP_TOKEN_FILE or
  GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS (see ENVIRONMENT). The token goes in a header,
  never in a URL. podssh waits 20 s for IAP to open the session, and a refusal
  names its step: the token, the upgrade, or the VM, its port or its name. A
  lost link is taken up on a new one at the bytes that each side had, as gcloud
  takes it up. A new token goes when the old one expired; a line tells of each.
  IAP is not made for bulk transfer, and ends a session after an hour with no
  traffic. The host key is recorded under iap://PROJECT/ZONE/INSTANCE, and the
  blocks of ssh_config are those of INSTANCE. -p and Port give the port;
  --direct, -4, -6 and HostName cannot go with it. -J with it first makes the
  VM the first hop of a chain, as with a Cloudflare tunnel.

  eice://[user@]ENDPOINT/ADDRESS[:PORT] reaches a port of an EC2 instance by
  its private address (an IPv6 one in brackets), 22 by default. It goes through
  an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint by its DNS name, which aws ec2
  describe-instance-connect-endpoints gives. It reaches the port as aws
  ec2-instance-connect open-tunnel reaches it: a WebSocket to the endpoint
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, with no relay and no call to the API of
  EC2. It needs the permission ec2-instance-connect:OpenTunnel and a credential
  of AWS in the file of PODSSH_EICE_CREDENTIALS_FILE or
  AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, else ~/.aws/credentials (see ENVIRONMENT). Each
  connection signs a new URL, good for 60 s, which carries the credential: the
  one URL of podssh that does, by the operator's ruling, and podssh never
  prints it. A tunnel lasts an hour at most, or
  PODSSH_EICE_MAX_TUNNEL_DURATION, and an endpoint takes 20 at once; podssh cp
  goes on in a new tunnel before the end. A refusal gives this host's clock, as
  a signed URL is checked against AWS's. The host key is recorded under
  eice://ID/ADDRESS, ID the endpoint's. -p and Port give the port; --direct,
  -4, -6 and HostName cannot go with it, and -J with it first makes the
  instance the first hop of a chain.

  warp://[user@]HOST[:PORT] reaches a port of any host, 22 by default (an IPv6
  address in brackets), inside WARP's tunnel. It needs a build with the feature
  warp, as each release binary is: MASQUE over HTTP/2 to Cloudflare's endpoint
  162.159.198.2:443 (or PODSSH_WARP_ENDPOINT), through HTTPS_PROXY when one is
  set, with no relay and no account; Cloudflare's network reaches HOST, whose
  name is asked of 1.1.1.1 inside the tunnel. Each endpoint of the device goes
  in turn, one at a time, the dial of each but the last within 3 s: the one
  that last opened, 162.159.198.2:443, then the peers that WARP's API gave, on
  port 443; one that the way out does not reach, or whose edge fails or carries
  nothing, gives way to the next. The device's record keeps the one that
  opened. The first run registers a device with WARP's API
  (api.cloudflareclient.com, else api.devices.cloudflare.com, or
  PODSSH_WARP_API first; a failure names each), once
  PODSSH_WARP_ACCEPT_TERMS=yes accepts Cloudflare's Terms, and keeps its record
  in the cache (see FILES); each run then reads it. The proxy must take a
  CONNECT to that address: one that allows listed names alone refuses it, and
  podssh doctor's line egress takes names the case. A certificate of another
  key than the endpoint's pinned one sends podssh to WARP's API for the
  device's record again: a new key that the API gives is kept in the record and
  tried, and once more a second later; a key that the API never gave is never
  taken. Else the certificate is a proxy's that re-terminates TLS: it is named
  by its issuer, and the road is not tried again in the run. Once the tunnel
  opens, one TCP connection inside it to 1.1.1.1:443 must be answered through
  it, tried twice 700 ms apart: a front door that takes TLS and relays nothing
  is named so (69), not left to time out each stream; PODSSH_WARP_PROBE=no
  skips the probe. Where a probe of UDP to the endpoint answers, the same
  tunnel goes over HTTP/3, each packet in a QUIC datagram: after HTTP/2 failed
  to reach it, or first (PODSSH_WARP_H3). TCP inside the tunnel is smoltcp's,
  in this process, with no TUN device. The host key is recorded under
  warp://HOST. -p and Port give the port; --direct, -4, -6 and HostName cannot
  go with it, and -J with it first makes HOST the first hop of a chain.

  ssh+tls://[user@]HOST[:PORT], as the destination or as any hop of -J, is SSH
  inside TLS, as stunnel serves it, port 443 by default: TLS goes over the
  stream that reaches the hop (the relay's, --direct's through HTTPS_PROXY, or
  the channel of the hop before it). Its certificate is checked for HOST with
  podssh's trust (--ca-file, SSL_CERT_FILE, CaFile, else the system's). SSH
  then runs inside it, the host key checked as for each hop and recorded under
  [HOST]:PORT. A proxy that waits for TLS on port 443 carries it where it ends
  plain SSH. A failure names its step: the connection, TLS (an unknown issuer,
  or a certificate for another name), or SSH. podssh doctor --hop ssh+tls://...
  probes it inside TLS.

  tor://[user@]HOST[:PORT] reaches a port of any host, 22 by default (an IPv6
  address in brackets), through the Tor network. It needs a build with the
  feature tor: Arti in this process, with no relay and no account, and no
  program besides; each of its connections to a Tor relay goes through
  HTTPS_PROXY when one is set. In that case it goes to a relay on port 443
  alone, or on the ports of PODSSH_TOR_PORTS. An exit resolves HOST and
  connects to it; an exit's policy, or the host, may refuse Tor. The first run
  fetches Tor's directory, which can take a minute; Arti keeps it and its
  guards in the cache (see FILES), and later runs start sooner. With
  PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES, the first hops are the bridges of that file alone, plain
  or through meek_lite or WebTunnel. podssh speaks those in this process, and
  they pass where HTTPS passes (see ENVIRONMENT). The host key is recorded
  under tor://HOST. -p and Port give the port; --direct, -4, -6 and HostName
  cannot go with it, and -J with it first makes HOST the first hop of a chain.

  -f, --detach and ForkAfterAuthentication yes send the run into the background
  once its request went (after the login; -L and -D are bound before it), with
  a command or -N, as OpenSSH's -f; a shell or -W is refused (64). A command
  then reads no stdin (-n), and its output goes to the log. podssh does it
  itself, with no other program: it starts this program again (as podssh
  --detach-child ..., a form that podssh alone writes). Its prompts (a
  password, a passphrase, a host key) use this terminal until it is ready; then
  it leaves this terminal and its session (setsid, SIGHUP ignored; on Windows
  its console, and the caller's job where the job allows it). It keeps no
  descriptor that it inherited, so that a caller that reads its pipes to their
  end ends with the parent. The parent prints the child's pid and its log
  (detached/ssh-PID.log in the cache; see FILES) and exits 0; a failure before
  then is its code, its lines on stderr. On Linux, from a login session's
  scope, the run then asks the user's systemd for a scope of its own
  (podssh-detached-PID.scope). It asks over D-Bus on this host. So a logout
  does not end it where logind ends a session's processes. The run says the
  outcome in its log; the user's last logout still ends it where lingering is
  off (loginctl enable-linger), as it ends the user's systemd.
  PODSSH_SYSTEMD=no asks nothing. At ready the run leaves the caller's working
  directory for the root. It keeps the caller's directory when a word of the
  run is a relative path or a command that runs here (exec: of pipe,
  LocalCommand). Where the sandbox has no /dev/null, its stdin is a pipe that
  is closed. As the first process of a namespace it refuses (69); a unit of
  systemd, WSL and Termux, which may end it still, are named first. A CI's job
  ends it at the job's end: podssh touches no variable by which a CI finds its
  processes. --persist keeps the forwards going across a lost relay. With
  --restart a small process stays in the background between the parent and the
  run (the pid printed is its own): once the run is ready, it starts the run
  again whenever it ends (a crash, a kill, an abort), after the relay's
  backoff. It does not start it after 64, 77 or 78, which a new start would
  repeat. Nor does it after its own SIGTERM, which it passes on; a run that
  lasted 30 s starts the count again, and it never gives up. It holds no
  connection, and killed, it leaves the run going. Each run beats each 10 s
  from its runtime (the time of detached/NAME.alive); one that beat, then gave
  no beat for 90 s (a hang, a stopped process), is ended (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL
  after 10 s). It is started again, with a line in the log; one that never beat
  is not ended for it. node and pipe take it too. --detach-name NAME names the
  run (else its verb and its pid): a second start of a name that runs refuses
  (75), and podssh detached lists the runs, says the state of one and stops it.

  --forwarder TEMPLATES reaches the first hop through WebSocket forwarders of
  other products, in place of the relay: services that dial the host and the
  port that a client names and carry its bytes. They are the plumbing of a MUD
  client or of an SSH client in a browser. A template is a ws:// or wss:// URL
  with {host} and {port} once each, in its path or its query. podssh fills them
  with the target, checked as each target of the relay is and then
  percent-encoded, as in wss://web-proxy.mudlet.org/?host={host}&port={port};
  or a URL with neither, and then podssh sends the target in a first text
  frame, {"Host":HOST,"Port":PORT}. It takes the forwarder's answer
  {"status":"ok"} before the target's bytes, as ssheasy's proxy does. A list,
  separated by commas, is tried in order: a forwarder that refuses the upgrade,
  closes within 3 s of it, or answers with a failure gives way to the next. The
  dial is that of a WebSocket by its URL: TLS checked for the forwarder's name,
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, and no relay token, no mint and no pool.
  Binary frames carry the bytes; a forwarder's text frames are its own words,
  shown with -v and never written into the session. A close other than 1000
  names the forwarder, its code and its reason. A forwarder is another
  product's endpoint: it publishes no limit and can stop at any time, so name
  more than one. PODSSH_FORWARDER and Forwarder of the settings file give the
  list too, below the flag. A run has one road: --relay-host, --relay-failover,
  --direct, PODSSH_RELAY beside PODSSH_FORWARDER, -4 and -6 cannot go with it.
  Nor can a destination with a road of its own (node://, iroh:, cf://, iap://,
  eice://). A template may name a forwarder that you run yourself.

  wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ (or wisp+ws://) names a server of the Wisp protocol,
  Mercury Workshop's. It carries TCP streams over one WebSocket and takes the
  target in a CONNECT packet of its own. So its URL has no {host} and no
  {port}, and its path ends with /. podssh opens one stream for each session:
  it offers version 2 of the protocol and speaks version 1 with a server that
  answers so; it sends no data past the credit that the server's CONTINUE
  gives; a stream that the server closes before its first bytes gives way to
  the next forwarder, with the server's reason (0x42, unreachable; 0x48,
  blocked; 0x49, throttled; and the others of the protocol); the server's
  message of the day is shown with -v. A server that requires a password or a
  key is refused, as podssh sends neither.

  Four words name public forwarders, which the binary carries by the operator's
  rulings: three that GitHub's issue 59 measured: mudlet, the Worker of
  Mudlet's web client, wss://web-proxy.mudlet.org/, on Cloudflare, whose
  runtime refuses port 25, private addresses and Cloudflare's own; ssheasy, the
  proxy of ssheasy's SSH client in a browser, wss://ssheasy.com/p, which takes
  the target in a first frame. It slows a connection to 100 KiB/s after 1 GiB
  and takes one connection a second from each address; and mudix, an older copy
  of Mudlet's Worker, wss://mudix.delwing.workers.dev/, on one person's name;
  then wisp, Mercury Workshop's demo server of the Wisp protocol,
  wisp+wss://wisp.mercurywork.shop/, which is for demo and testing. It allows
  500 kB/s for each address and resolves names through a resolver that blocks
  malware and adult names. They serve their own products' users. podssh falls
  back to them when each relay host failed with no word about the target. Such
  a failure is a dial, TLS, a time-out, an upgrade, the relay's own 5xx or a
  refused token. The relay must also be podssh's own choice: no --relay-host,
  PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost, and no -4 or -6. podssh then sends the target to
  them in that order, 10 s at most each, wisp last and never first. They come
  after the direct road when that one is tried (PODSSH_DIRECT), as the direct
  road sends the target to no one else; podssh proxy, which has no direct road,
  tries them at once. The relay's 502 of a target that it could not reach, and
  its refusal of a target by its policy, end the run. The run ends with the
  relay's words, as no forwarder reaches that target better. A line says what
  goes to whom first, and one line gives each one's reason when none carries
  the session; a bad setting ends the run as before, and no relay token goes to
  them. PODSSH_FORWARDER_FALLBACK=no, or ForwarderFallback no, turns this off;
  doctor's line fallback says so, unmeasured, and doctor --forwarder WORDS asks
  them.

  The public services that podssh tries when you named no server of their kind,
  each after podssh's own roads and by the operator's rulings: on the forward
  road, the four forwarders above, wisp last. Then come the public Wisp servers
  that their operators run for the use of others. Each is named in the line
  that says what goes to whom. They come before the ws:// forms (none is named
  in this release: PODSSH_FORWARDER_FALLBACK=no turns them off with the rest);
  on the reverse road, Tailscale's DERP servers for tailcat, then Tailscale's
  main DERP fleet. That fleet serves Tailscale's own clients, and let podssh in
  when it was tried (PODSSH_DERP_MAIN=no keeps to tailcat's). Then come Least
  Authority's transit relay, ppng.io then piping.onrender.com, and n0's server
  of pkarr (see podssh node); last, croc's public relays behind croc-web's
  bridge, Pinggy's free TLS tunnels, then Serveo's private aliases, then
  ssh-j.com's names. Then come localhost.run's tunnels, then localtunnel's
  names, then bore.pub's TCP ports. Each goes where podssh's list of services
  names its server, whose lines say so. PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns each such
  last fallback off. Each is a third party that nobody vouches for: its
  operator sees the target or the two ends, the sizes and the times, may log
  them, and may stop serving podssh at any time; the host key of SSH, and on
  the reverse road the end-to-end channel, keep the bytes from it. podssh names
  no other public server of their kinds: no community DERP server, no Wisp
  server of a web proxy's list and no public proxy node of an aggregator's
  list. None of them names an operator who answers for it. A server that you
  name (--derp-server, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --vless, --via, --wstunnel)
  is yours to trust. podssh never uses, and never names, a domain that looks
  taken over: a school's, a church's or a shop's, or a name made to look like
  one.

  --shadowsocks FILE reaches the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in
  place of the relay: a server that takes the target in an address header and
  dials it, with a key in place of a token. FILE must be yours and closed to
  others (chmod 600), as a pair file is: each line is an ss:// URI of SIP002,
  ss://USERINFO@HOST:PORT#TAG. Its USERINFO is method:password in base64url or
  percent-encoded (the older form, all of it in base64, is read too); or
  subscription https://URL, a list that a provider serves; # starts a comment.
  The methods are the AEAD ones, chacha20-ietf-poly1305, aes-256-gcm and
  aes-128-gcm, whose key is a password; and those of Shadowsocks 2022 (SIP022),
  2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm, 2022-blake3-aes-256-gcm and
  2022-blake3-chacha20-poly1305. Their key is the base64 of 16 or 32 bytes that
  the server's operator gives, and their header holds this host's clock: a
  server more than 30 s off is named, with this host's clock. A key of several
  users (iPSK:uPSK, SIP023) and a key that names a plugin, another program, are
  refused (78). So is a line that cannot be read, named by its number and never
  its text. The servers are tried in the order of the file: TCP to the server,
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then the salt and the target; a server
  gives way to the next when it does not answer with its salt and its first
  chunk within 10 s. So does one that closes, or whose chunk does not open.
  Silence names the proxy as the likely cause when one carried the TCP: a proxy
  that waits for TLS on port 443 carries no Shadowsocks. A subscription is
  fetched over TLS, checked with podssh's trust (--ca-file), at most 1 MiB. It
  is read as lines of ss://, the same lines in base64, or SIP008's JSON; its
  list is kept in the cache (see FILES), read for a day, and fetched again when
  each kept server failed; at most 16 servers of a list are tried. The password
  goes into the key and nowhere else, and a line shows a subscription by its
  host alone. The host key of SSH protects the session, as on each road: the
  server sees the target's name and SSH's encrypted bytes. A published key is
  shared with strangers, has no operator who answers for it, and changes:
  podssh names no server and no list. A run has one road: --relay-host,
  --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder, -4, -6, and a destination with a
  road of its own cannot go with it (64).

  A line of the file of --shadowsocks may also be an Outline access key:
  ssconf://HOST[:PORT]/PATH, which podssh fetches as https://HOST[:PORT]/PATH,
  or key https://URL; a name after # is its server's. It is fetched as a
  subscription is, over TLS through HTTPS_PROXY, and kept in the cache for a
  day (see FILES); its body is one server: an ss:// link, JSON with server,
  server_port, password and method, or the YAML of Outline's configuration.
  That YAML's transport (tcpudp's tcp part, or a shadowsocks one) names cipher,
  secret and an endpoint: HOST:PORT for raw TCP, a websocket with its wss://
  URL, or first-supported with its options, of which podssh takes the first
  that it reads. A server in a WebSocket is reached as Outline's servers serve
  it (outline-ss-server 1.9 and later, behind a TLS front): TLS checked for the
  URL's host with podssh's trust (--ca-file), through HTTPS_PROXY when one is
  set. Then the same Shadowsocks stream goes in binary messages, so a proxy
  that waits for TLS on port 443 carries it. A path that the server does not
  serve (404) is named. So are an upgrade that its front refuses and a key that
  is not the server's; the URL's path, often the server's secret, is never
  shown, nor the key's own path. The UDP part is not read, as podssh carries
  TCP; a salt's prefix, a WebSocket with an endpoint of its own and the other
  types of Outline's configuration are refused by their names. They are refused
  when the key is read. A ws:// URL goes to this host alone. podssh reads the
  subset of YAML that the keys use: mappings and lists by their indentation,
  quoted and plain values, comments and anchors.

  --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] reaches the first hop through a forward
  proxy over TLS that you run (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port, h2o),
  in place of the relay; the port is 443 when none is named. podssh opens TLS
  to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, checked for HOST with podssh's
  trust (--ca-file). It then sends CONNECT HOST:PORT of the first hop inside:
  HTTP/2's CONNECT when the proxy chooses h2 by ALPN, so that the sessions of
  one run (podssh each) are streams of one connection, else HTTP/1.1's; a proxy
  that resets the CONNECT on HTTP/2 gets HTTP/1.1 on a connection of its own,
  and -v says which carried it. PODSSH_VIA_HTTP=1.1 or 2 offers one version
  alone. Basic credentials come from --via-auth-file FILE (or
  PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE), a file of yours that others cannot read: one line,
  USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER. A URL that
  holds a password is refused (64), as argv would show it. A 407 says the
  schemes that the proxy asks for and whether credentials went (77, as a
  refusal of the proxy's, 403 too). PODSSH_VIA names the proxy where the
  command line names no other road; beside PODSSH_RELAY or PODSSH_FORWARDER it
  is refused (78). A run has one road: --relay-host, --relay-failover,
  --direct, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, -4, -6, and a destination with a road
  of its own cannot go with it (64). The host key of SSH protects the session,
  as on each road.

  --vless FILE reaches the first hop through VLESS servers that you run
  (Xray-core, shoes, sing-box), in place of the relay: a server that takes the
  target in a short header and dials it, with a user's ID in place of a token.
  FILE must be yours and closed to others (chmod 600), as a pair file is: each
  line is a share link as panels and Xray-core's clients give it,
  vless://ID@HOST:PORT. Then come ?type=ws or type=xhttp, security=tls, sni=,
  host=, path= and mode=, joined by &, and #TAG; # starts a comment. ID is a
  UUID, or a word of 1 to 30 bytes, which Xray-core maps to one. type=ws
  carries the stream over a WebSocket at the path; type=xhttp carries it over
  XHTTP's plain HTTP requests on HTTP/2, which pass where a proxy or a front
  end refuses the WebSocket upgrade: mode=packet-up (a streamed GET down, and a
  numbered POST for each chunk up, which auto takes, as Xray-core's client does
  with TLS). Or stream-up (a streamed GET down and one streamed POST up), or
  stream-one (one POST, its body up and its answer down). security=tls is TLS
  to HOST:PORT, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, checked for sni (else
  host, else HOST) with podssh's trust (--ca-file); host gives the request's
  Host; with security=none XHTTP speaks HTTP/2 with no TLS. A server may choose
  HTTP/1.1, or refuse HTTP/2 with no TLS, and so may a front end that ends TLS
  on the way. Such a server gets packet-up and stream-up over HTTP/1.1 on two
  connections to it: the GET on one, the upload on a second, opened only then
  (-v says "on two connections"); stream-one is refused there (proxy exits 78;
  ssh 255, as for each first hop that it does not reach), as Go's server reads
  a request's whole body before it answers. A flow (xtls-rprx-vision), REALITY,
  VLESS's encryption, type=tcp, and an extra setting of XHTTP that changes its
  requests are refused by their names (78). So is a line that cannot be read,
  by its number and never its text. The servers are tried in the order of the
  file. Each waits up to 10 s for VLESS's answer, which comes with the server's
  version line: a server that ends the session before it has refused the ID or
  could not reach the target, and gives way to the next; -v says which
  transport carried the session. Xray-core holds a session to a private address
  with no word, unless the finalRules of its freedom outbound allow it. The
  wait then ends with that said. The host key of SSH protects the session, as
  on each road: the server sees the target's name and SSH's encrypted bytes. A
  run has one road: --relay-host, --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder,
  --shadowsocks, --via, --wstunnel, -4, -6, and a destination with a road of
  its own cannot go with it (64). The first write that carries data is one
  write of 3,333 bytes. Over XHTTP it is the request's head and its first data;
  over a WebSocket, the upgrade head alone. Xray-core's gorilla server refuses
  a frame before the handshake, so VLESS's request follows in the first
  message. A short write is padded and said. -v and doctor name the size, the
  short write and which shape applies. --early-data 0rtt|1rtt|off (default:
  PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA, else off) offers early data where the link's ed
  names a size: a nonce used twice in 10 minutes is refused, and the session
  stays at 1-RTT; the nonce goes in no line. Without --vless it is refused
  (64). --h2-shape existing|browser|firefox (default: PODSSH_H2_SHAPE, else
  existing) chooses the shape of podssh-ws's h2 road. The default session road
  is the WebSocket upgrade and does not read it. A word that is not one refuses
  the run (64).

  --trojan FILE reaches the first hop through Trojan servers that you run
  (trojan-gfw, trojan-go, Xray-core, sing-box), in place of the relay: after a
  real TLS handshake the server takes the SHA-224 of a password and the target
  in a short request, and dials it. FILE must be yours and closed to others
  (chmod 600), as a pair file is: each line is a share link as panels and
  clients give it, trojan://PASSWORD@HOST[:PORT] (443 when none). Then come
  ?type=tcp or type=ws, sni=, host= and path=, joined by &, and #TAG; # starts
  a comment. type=tcp, the default, carries Trojan in TLS alone; type=ws in a
  WebSocket over TLS at the path, which passes through a CDN or a front end
  that serves other paths. TLS goes to HOST:PORT, through HTTPS_PROXY when one
  is set, checked for sni (else host, else HOST) with podssh's trust
  (--ca-file); host gives the upgrade's Host. fp and alpn shape a ClientHello
  that a Trojan server does not read, and pass; a flow, REALITY and
  security=none (the password would cross in the clear) are refused by their
  names (78). So are a certificate that is not checked (allowInsecure) and
  another type. So is a line that cannot be read, by its number and never its
  text. Trojan has no answer: the servers are tried in the order of the file,
  and each waits up to 10 s for the target's version line. A server that does
  not take the password hands the bytes to its fallback, an HTTP server. Its
  answer is said with its status line (proxy exits 77; ssh 255, as for each
  first hop that it does not reach); one that ends the session first has no
  fallback, or could not reach the target; each gives way to the next, and -v
  says what carried the session. The host key of SSH protects the session, as
  on each road: the server sees the target's name and SSH's encrypted bytes. A
  run has one road: --relay-host, --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder,
  --shadowsocks, --via, --vless, --wstunnel, --chisel, -4, -6, and a
  destination with a road of its own cannot go with it (64).

  --hysteria FILE reaches the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
  (apernet/hysteria), in place of the relay, where UDP passes: a server of QUIC
  that takes a credential in one HTTP/3 request and dials the target named on a
  stream of its own. To one who has no credential it is a web server. FILE must
  be yours and closed to others (chmod 600), as a pair file is: each line is a
  share link as Hysteria's clients give it, hysteria2://AUTH@HOST[:PORT]/ or
  hy2:// (443 when no port). Then come ?sni=, pinSHA256=, insecure=,
  obfs=salamander and obfs-password=, joined by &, and #NAME; # starts a
  comment. AUTH is the server's password, or USER:PASSWORD for its userpass.
  TLS 1.3 is checked for sni (else HOST) with podssh's trust (--ca-file). With
  pinSHA256 (64 hex digits, as Hysteria prints them), the server's own
  certificate alone passes, by the SHA-256 of its DER. obfs=salamander wraps
  each datagram in Salamander, with its password of 4 bytes or more. insecure=1
  with no pinSHA256, several ports (port hopping), obfs=gecko, ech and a realm
  (hysteria2+realm://) are refused by their names (78). So is a line that
  cannot be read, by its number and never its text. No HTTP proxy carries UDP:
  a server whose host has a proxy of HTTPS_PROXY is not tried (69), and
  NO_PROXY with its host lets UDP go straight to it. The servers are tried in
  the order of the file, each after a probe: one QUIC packet of a reserved
  version to the server's port, sent three times within 1.5 s, which a server
  of QUIC answers at once. With no answer, the road ends with a line that UDP
  does not reach the server, and waits for no QUIC handshake. A server that
  answers the credential with another status than 233 did not take it (proxy
  exits 77; ssh 255, as for each first hop that it does not reach); one that
  could not reach the target says so in its words; each gives way to the next.
  The session's QUIC keeps a keepalive each 10 s and ends after 30 s of
  silence. The host key of SSH protects the session, as on each road: the
  server sees the target's name and SSH's encrypted bytes. A run has one road:
  --relay-host, --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via,
  --vless, --trojan, --wstunnel, --chisel, -4 and -6 cannot go with it (64).
  Nor can a destination with a road of its own.

  --turn turns:HOST[:PORT] reaches the first hop through a TURN server that you
  run, in place of the relay. Such a server is often coturn, as a server of
  calls or chat often has one on 443. The road is a TCP allocation of RFC 6062.
  podssh opens TLS to HOST (port 443 when none is named), through HTTPS_PROXY
  when one is set, checked with podssh's trust (--ca-file); asks an allocation
  for TCP with the credential that the server's 401 asks for; sends Connect
  with the target's address, which podssh resolves in its own order of
  resolvers; then opens a second connection to the same server, binds it to the
  target (ConnectionBind), and carries the session on it. The first connection
  holds the allocation and refreshes it before its lifetime ends. Through a
  proxy, both are CONNECTs to HOST. turn:HOST[:PORT] (port 3478) has no TLS and
  goes to this host alone (64). The credential comes from --turn-auth-file FILE
  (or PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE), never from the URI: see FILES. A server that
  offers no TCP allocation (442 or 508) is refused in those words (69); a
  credential refused twice (401) and a target that the server's policy refuses
  (403, as coturn's denied-peer-ip) are refused (77); a target that the server
  did not reach (447) is said so (69). A proxy that re-terminates TLS stops
  this road. PODSSH_TURN names the server where the command line names no other
  road; beside PODSSH_RELAY, PODSSH_FORWARDER, PODSSH_VIA, PODSSH_WSTUNNEL or
  PODSSH_CHISEL it is refused (78). A run has one road: --relay-host,
  --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless,
  --trojan, --tuic, --hysteria, --wstunnel, --chisel, -4 and -6 cannot go with
  it (64). Nor can a destination with a road of its own. The host key of SSH
  protects the session, as on each road: the server sees the target's address
  and SSH's encrypted bytes.

  devtunnel://[user@]TUNNEL[:PORT] reaches a port of the host of a Microsoft
  Dev Tunnels tunnel, 22 by default, through the service's relay on port 443.
  It needs a build with the feature devtunnel (70 in another build): TUNNEL is
  the tunnel's name, or ID.CLUSTER as the devtunnel tool shows it. podssh asks
  the management API for the tunnel's relay and a connect token; it asks with
  your token, from the private file of PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE (see FILES);
  or with a tunnel's access token, from the private file of
  PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_ACCESS_FILE; or, with neither set, with no token, for a
  tunnel that allows anonymous access; never from argv, and both set is refused
  (78); opens the relay's WebSocket through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set,
  checked with podssh's trust; runs SSH to the tunnel's host inside it, whose
  key must be one that the API names, with no user authentication; and opens a
  direct-tcpip channel to 127.0.0.1:PORT of that host, which carries the
  session. The host of the tunnel must have the port; your own SSH server
  behind it checks you as on each road. The host key is recorded under
  devtunnel://TUNNEL. A failure names its stage: management, websocket, ssh or
  channel. A refusal names the form of what was sent (a user token, a tunnel
  access token, no token), never a token: a token that the API refuses and a
  host key that is not the tunnel's are 77; a tunnel that does not exist or has
  no host connected and a refused port 69; a time limit or the API's 429 75; a
  token file or a setting that cannot be used 78. A relay session that ends is
  opened again with a fresh connect token, a few times at most, and never after
  a refused token. -p and Port give the port; --direct, -4, -6 and HostName
  cannot go with it, and -J with it first makes the tunnel the first hop of a
  chain.

  node://NAME with --iroh-ticket TICKET races the two roads to the node: the
  iroh road starts first, the pair's road 250 ms later, or at once when the
  iroh road fails. The first far end that speaks carries the session; the other
  link ends before it sends anything, so it opens nothing at the node's TARGET.
  Each resume races them again, and -v says which road answered first.

  [user@]derp:TICKET[/ROUTE] reaches a node of the DERP road (see podssh node
  --derp), in each build: the ticket's server first. The rest of the list
  follows in its order, when the list holds that server. The list is that of
  --derp-server, PODSSH_DERP_SERVER or Tailscale's fleets (tailcat's, then the
  main fleet unless PODSSH_DERP_MAIN=no). On that list a node whose home went
  away calls the next server home. This client's key on the servers is new for
  each run; the end-to-end channel runs to the node's key that the ticket
  names. The node lets this client's key (see --client-key) in by its
  allowlist, so --no-e2e is refused (64). The host key is recorded under derp:
  and the node's key, which stays when the ticket changes. -J, -W, -p, -4, -6,
  HostName and --direct cannot go with it. -v says each server tried, and which
  carried the session.

  node://NAME with --derp-ticket TICKET adds the DERP road to the race: the
  iroh road of --iroh-ticket first, the pair's road 250 ms later, the DERP road
  250 ms after that. Each starts at once when the roads before it failed. The
  tickets name one node, or the run is refused (64). The ticket is kept under
  NAME in the cache (derp-NAME.ticket). A later podssh ssh node://NAME that
  gives none dials it only once the roads before it failed. It dials it as the
  only road, too, when no pair is stored under NAME: the fallback that podssh
  takes, which PODSSH_DERP=no turns off. -v says the order of the roads, and
  which answered first.

  node://NAME of a member of the net that the net names by its key races the
  roads of the member's record of pkarr too. That needs a build with the iroh
  road, and comes after the roads of its tickets: once each of them failed (at
  once, with none), the record is asked, and kept 30 s. Then comes the iroh
  road at its home relay, and the DERP road at its DERP home. Then come its
  quick tunnel and its OpenTunnel name (where no name is given or kept). Each
  goes 250 ms after the one before, for each road that no ticket gave; never
  with --no-e2e, as the end-to-end channel checks the member's key on each (see
  iroh record in THE RELAY). -v says what the record named, and which road
  carried the session.

  node://NAME also races the transit road of its pair, last, and only once each
  road before it failed: the magic-wormhole transit relay where the node waits,
  Least Authority's by default. PODSSH_TRANSIT=no turns it off, a ws:// or
  wss:// URL there names another relay, and --no-e2e leaves it out, as the
  relay is a stranger's. Each resume races the roads again, so a session whose
  relay of the pair went away goes on through the transit relay.

  node://NAME also races croc's relay road of its pair, after the transit
  relay's, and only once each road before it failed: the rooms of the pair at
  croc's relay behind croc-web's bridge, where the node waits, a last fallback,
  before the Pinggy, Serveo and ssh-j roads. The client tries the pair's 4
  rooms in order: a room that two members hold sends it to the next, and so
  does one with no one in it, after 3 s; a client of the same pair that it
  meets starts the rooms again, once. Before its first link through the public
  bridge, a line says that croc's relays, a volunteer's service that nobody
  vouches for, carry the session. Each try of a room is a join, which croc's
  relay limits for each source (the bridge is one source for all its users).
  Its answer rate limited is said. PODSSH_CROC=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no
  turns it off, a wss:// URL there names your own bridge, and --no-e2e leaves
  it out; so does a run where a road found the WebSocket upgrade refused on the
  way, as the bridge is a WebSocket too. podssh ping node://NAME does not
  measure it.

  In a build with the feature zerotier, node://NAME also races ZeroTier's road
  of its pair, only once each road before it failed. It comes after croc's
  relay road and the Pinggy road and before Tox's relay road, a last fallback:
  a member of the pair's own ad-hoc network, with the client's own ZeroTier
  identity. That identity is made at its first run and kept in the cache, a
  private file. It goes through ZeroTier Inc.'s roots and TCP relay (or those
  of PODSSH_ZEROTIER and PODSSH_ZEROTIER_PLANET). It reaches the node's
  address, which both ends make of the pair's connect token. It waits 120 s at
  most for the node to answer: the roots check an identity that they do not
  know yet, and that comes through the relay. They check it only in turn with
  the relay's other users, so a first run is the slow one. Before its first
  link through ZeroTier Inc.'s relay, a line says that ZeroTier Inc.'s roots
  and relay carry the session. PODSSH_ZEROTIER=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no
  turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it out. podssh ping node://NAME does not
  measure it.

  In a build with the feature tox, node://NAME also races Tox's relay road of
  its pair, only once each road before it failed. It comes after ZeroTier's
  road and before the Serveo road, the last fallback: a connection with a fresh
  key to the relay of the pair. That relay is the one that the SHA-256 of its
  name picks among the Tox project's public relays of podssh's list of
  services. Or it is the relay of PODSSH_TOX. Then a hello goes to the node's
  key, which both ends make of the pair's connect token, again each 2 s. Last
  comes a routed connection to the key that the node offers. It waits 30 s at
  most for the node's answer. The relay passes no more than a short queue, so
  the stream keeps its own order, window (32 KiB) and resends inside the
  relay's packets. Before its first link through a public relay, a line says
  that the Tox project's relay carries the session. PODSSH_TOX=no or
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no (for the public relays) turns it off, and --no-e2e
  leaves it out. podssh ping node://NAME does not measure it.

  In a build with the feature yggdrasil, node://NAME also races Yggdrasil's
  road of its pair, only once each road before it failed. It comes after the
  Tox road and before the Serveo road, the last fallback: this end joins
  Yggdrasil's network with a fresh key through the pair's peer, once a run.
  That peer is the one that the SHA-256 of its name picks among the public
  wss:// peers of podssh's list of services. Or it is the peer of
  PODSSH_YGGDRASIL. This end then says hello to the node's key, which both ends
  make of the pair's connect token. The hello holds a proof of the token, and
  goes again each 1 s, until the node welcomes it. It waits 45 s at most: the
  first lookup across the network takes some seconds. The network drops what it
  cannot place, so each link keeps its own order, window (256 KiB) and resends
  inside the packets. Before its first link through a public peer, a line says
  that the peer carries the session. It says too that this end routes for the
  network while the road is up. PODSSH_YGGDRASIL=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no
  (for the public peers) turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it out. podssh ping
  node://NAME does not measure it.

  In a build with the feature hyperdht, node://NAME also races HyperDHT's road
  of its pair, where UDP passes. It goes only once each road before it failed,
  after Yggdrasil's road and before Syncthing's relay road: this end joins
  HyperDHT with a fresh key, once a run, through the bootstrap of podssh's list
  of services or of PODSSH_HYPERDHT. It looks up the topic of the node's key,
  which both ends make of the pair's connect token, again each 5 s. Then it
  connects by that key. It waits 45 s at most; where no bootstrap node answers
  within 15 s, UDP does not pass, and the road fails with that word. Before it
  joins the public DHT, a line says that the DHT's nodes see this end's
  address. PODSSH_HYPERDHT=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no (for the public DHT)
  turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it out. podssh ping node://NAME does not
  measure it.

  In a build with the feature strelay, node://NAME also races Syncthing's relay
  road of its pair, only once each road before it failed. It comes after
  HyperDHT's road and before the onion road, the last fallback: a request with
  a fresh certificate to the pair's relay for the node's device ID, which both
  ends make of the pair's connect token. The pair's relay is the one on 443
  that the SHA-256 of its name picks among the pool's relays of podssh's list
  of services. Or it is the relay of PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY. Then the session
  has its own TCP connection to the relay. It waits 30 s at most. Before its
  first link through a relay of the pool, a line says that the relay carries
  the session. PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no (for the
  pool's relays) turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it out. podssh ping
  node://NAME does not measure it.

  In a build with the feature tor, node://NAME also races the onion road of its
  pair, only once each road before it failed. It comes after Syncthing's relay
  road and before the Serveo road, the last fallback: this end bootstraps Arti
  through the Tor road, once a run, and puts the pair's key of restricted
  discovery in its keystore. It then opens a stream to the node's onion
  service. The address is that of PODSSH_ONION (the node's line says it). Else
  it is the one of the node's record of pkarr where the net names the node's
  key, read again at each link. Else it is the one kept under NAME by a node of
  this host or by a run that was given it. It waits 120 s at most. Before its
  first circuit, a line says that the Tor network carries the session.
  PODSSH_ONION=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it
  out. podssh ping node://NAME does not measure it.

  node://NAME also races the smee.io road of its pair, only once each road
  before it failed. It comes after the onion road and before the Serveo road,
  the last fallback: a stream of server-sent events of its way down at
  smee.io's server on 443 (the listed one, or the one of PODSSH_SMEE). A hello
  at the node's door is posted again each 3 s until the node's mark comes, 20 s
  at most. Then a POST goes for each frame up, each one after the answer to the
  one before. A stream that gives no event within 15 s ends the road for the
  run. That happens through a proxy that holds an answer until its end. Before
  its first link through the listed server, a line says that the server carries
  the session. PODSSH_SMEE=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no (for the listed server)
  turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it out. podssh ping node://NAME does not
  measure it.

  node://NAME with --opentunnel-name HOST races the OpenTunnel road too, 250 ms
  after the DERP road: HOST is the name that the node's line name says,
  ROUTE.ID.opentunnel.xyz. Each link is TCP to HOST on port 443 through
  HTTPS_PROXY, then TLS by HOST, checked with the host's trust (SSL_CERT_FILE,
  else the system's stores). There is no WebSocket upgrade, so a proxy that
  refuses the upgrade passes it. So does a proxy that ends TLS itself, whose CA
  the host trusts. The name is kept under NAME in the cache
  (opentunnel-NAME.name). A later run that gives none dials it only once each
  road before it failed. That is the fallback, which PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL=no turns
  off. With neither, a member of the net whose key the net names races the name
  of the node's record of pkarr. It races it among the roads of its record (not
  kept: it is asked again). The end-to-end channel checks the node's key by the
  pins of NAME, or --node-key, so --no-e2e leaves the road out (64 with
  --opentunnel-name).

  node://NAME with --pinggy-name HOST#PIN races the Pinggy road too, 250 ms
  after the road before it: HOST is the name that the node's line name says,
  and PIN the pin of its TLS key that the line says beside it (SHA256:...); a
  name with no pin is refused (64). Each link is TCP to HOST on port 443
  through HTTPS_PROXY, then TLS by HOST with no WebSocket upgrade. So a proxy
  that refuses the upgrade passes it; the node's certificate is its own, which
  no CA signs. So TLS takes only a certificate of the pinned key, and refuses
  another with the key it showed: a stranger at the name, or a proxy that ends
  TLS. The end-to-end channel then checks the node's own key by the pins of
  NAME, or --node-key, so --no-e2e leaves the road out (64 with --pinggy-name).
  The address is kept under NAME in the cache (pinggy-NAME.name). A run that
  gives none dials the address of the node's record of pkarr. It does so where
  the net names NAME by its key and the record is asked. The node puts each
  tunnel's address there. Else the run dials the one kept, last, once each road
  before it failed, the last fallback; the record is signed by the node's key,
  so its pin is the node's word, and -v says where the address came from.
  Before it, a line says that Pinggy, a third party that nobody vouches for,
  carries the session. The line adds that SSH and the end-to-end channel keep
  its bytes. A free tunnel's name changes each hour, and its pin does not: the
  record names the new one, else give the new name that the node says, with the
  same pin. PODSSH_PINGGY=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the road off.

  node://NAME races the Serveo road too, a last fallback. It goes once each
  road before it failed, and before the ssh-j road and the roads after it. It
  goes only where the road has a server (podssh's list of services, or
  PODSSH_SERVEO) and a key of the node is known: --node-key, else the key that
  the net names for NAME, else the pins of NAME, which a first session over
  another road writes. Each link is raw SSH to the server on port 443, then 22,
  through HTTPS_PROXY. Then comes a direct-tcpip channel to the node's alias,
  as ssh -J jumps: the alias is a hash of the key's fingerprint, so no name is
  given or kept. The aliases of the node's series are tried in their order. The
  end-to-end channel then checks the node's key, so a stranger that holds the
  alias is refused, and --no-e2e leaves the road out. Before it, a line says
  that Serveo, a third party that nobody vouches for, carries the session. The
  line adds that SSH and the end-to-end channel keep its bytes; -v says which
  alias it reached. podssh ping node://NAME never measures it. PODSSH_SERVEO=no
  or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the road off.

  node://NAME races the ssh-j road too, last, before the roads that follow it.
  It goes once each road before it failed, the Serveo road's too. It goes only
  where the road has a server (ssh-j.com where podssh's list of services names
  it, or PODSSH_SSH_J). podssh must also hold the node's key: --node-key, else
  the key that the net names for NAME, else the key that the pins of NAME hold
  from an earlier session. The node's name there comes from that key, as the
  node derives it. Each link is SSH to the server on port 22, directly or
  through HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT; where that dial fails, the forwarders that the
  binary names carry it, as when no relay host answers
  (PODSSH_FORWARDER_FALLBACK=no keeps them out); then a channel to the node's
  name, as ssh -J takes it, under the resumable layer and the end-to-end
  channel. That channel checks the node's key, so --no-e2e leaves the road out.
  Before its first link, a line says that the server, a third party that nobody
  vouches for, carries the session over SSH that it ends. The line adds that
  the end-to-end channel keeps its bytes; -v names the server's host key and
  the name. podssh ping never measures it. PODSSH_SSH_J=no or
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the road off.

  node://NAME with --tunnel-url https://HOST races the localhost.run road too,
  250 ms after the road before it: a WebSocket at / of HOST, the name that the
  node prints, on port 443 through HTTPS_PROXY, whose TLS this host's roots
  verify. It runs under the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel, which
  checks the node's key. So --no-e2e leaves the road out (64 with
  --tunnel-url). The name is kept under NAME in the cache; a later run that
  gives none dials it, or the name of the node's record for a member that the
  net names by its key. It dials it last, once each road before it failed, the
  ssh-j road's too. That comes before the localtunnel and bore roads. Before
  its first link, a line says that localhost.run, a third party that nobody
  vouches for, carries the session over HTTPS that it ends. The line adds that
  the end-to-end channel keeps its bytes. A free name changes after a few
  hours. podssh ping measures it only with --tunnel-url.
  PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the road off. A name
  under Sandhole's tunnels' zone is the Sandhole road's: its line names
  Sandhole, and PODSSH_SANDHOLE=no turns it off; so for srv.us's
  (PODSSH_SRV_US) and tunnl.gg's (PODSSH_TUNNL_GG). With no name at all, the
  srv.us road derives the node's name there from its whole key, as srv.us does.
  That key is --node-key, the net's, or the pins of NAME. It races that name
  last, after the names given, kept or recorded; a fingerprint alone derives
  none. Last of all, once each road before it failed, the Bare hop reaches the
  same name through a Bare v3 node. That node is the one of podssh's list of
  services, or of PODSSH_BARE. So a proxy sees the node's name alone; its line
  names the node, which sees the tunnel's name and which nobody vouches for.
  PODSSH_BARE=no turns it off.

  node://NAME races the localtunnel road too, last, before the bore road. It
  goes once each road before it failed, the ssh-j road's and the localhost.run
  road's too. It goes only where the road has a server (localtunnel's where
  podssh's list of services names it, or PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL). podssh must also
  hold the node's key: --node-key, else the key that the net names for NAME,
  else the key that the pins of NAME hold from an earlier session. The node's
  name there comes from that key, as the node derives it. Each link is TLS to
  that name on port 443 through HTTPS_PROXY, checked by this host's roots for
  the hosted server. Then comes a WebSocket with the header
  Bypass-Tunnel-Reminder, which passes the server's page for browsers (a 511,
  which the line names). The link runs under the resumable layer and the
  end-to-end channel, which checks the node's key. So --no-e2e leaves the road
  out. Before its first link, a line says that the server, a third party that
  nobody vouches for, carries the session and ends its TLS. The line adds that
  the end-to-end channel keeps its bytes. A node that serves the relay role
  there is a relay host too: --relay-host with its URL. podssh ping never
  measures the road. PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns it
  off.

  node://NAME races the bore road too, last of all, once each road before it
  failed. That includes the ssh-j, localhost.run and localtunnel roads. It goes
  only where the road has a server (bore.pub where podssh's list of services
  names it, or PODSSH_BORE). podssh must also hold the node's key: --node-key,
  else the key that the net names for NAME, else the key that the pins of NAME
  hold from an earlier session. The node's ports come from that key, as the
  node derives them. Each link is raw TCP to a port of the key, the one that
  answered last first, directly or through HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT; where that
  dial fails, as behind a proxy that allows port 443 alone, the forwarders that
  the binary names carry it. They do so as when no relay host answers
  (PODSSH_FORWARDER_FALLBACK=no keeps them out); a port whose first bytes are
  not the node's hello sends the link to the next. The link runs the resumable
  layer and the end-to-end channel, which checks the node's key, so --no-e2e
  leaves the road out. Before its first link, a line says that the server, a
  third party that nobody vouches for, carries the session over raw TCP. The
  line adds that the end-to-end channel keeps its bytes; -v names the ports.
  podssh ping never measures it. PODSSH_BORE=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns
  the road off.

  In a build with the feature filehost, node://NAME also races the file hosts'
  road of its pair. It goes only once each road before it failed, after every
  other road, the last of the last fallbacks: a hello at the node's door on the
  public MQTT broker of podssh's list. Then each write of a way of at most 16
  KiB is a sealed note at the broker. Each larger piece is one sealed upload to
  a public file host, and its URL a sealed note there. The file hosts are the
  listed ones whose terms allow it, or those of PODSSH_FILEHOSTS. It makes one
  request at a time. A node polls its door each 60 s at most, so the first link
  may wait that long, until the node takes its hello. Before its first link a
  line names the broker, and before each host's first upload a line names the
  host. Both are third parties that nobody vouches for. PODSSH_FILEHOSTS=no,
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no or PODSSH_MQTT=no turns it off, and --no-e2e leaves it
  out. podssh ping node://NAME does not measure it.

  In a build with the feature gsr, node://NAME with --gsr-secret-file FILE or
  PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE also races the GSRN road. It goes last, once each road
  before it failed, and before the file hosts' road: a connection to the relay
  of gsocket at the shard that the secret gives, directly or through
  HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT. Then a CONNECT to the secret's address, and TLS with
  SRP of the secret with the node of podssh node --gsr; it needs no pair here.
  The end-to-end channel checks the node's key by the pins of NAME, or
  --node-key, and the resumable layer resumes a session on a new pairing. A
  line names the relay as a third party before the first link. Never with
  --no-e2e; a file that cannot be used is refused (78) before anything
  connects. A build without the feature refuses --gsr-secret-file (70) and
  passes the variable over.

  node://NAME with PODSSH_FRP=FILE, the node's own frp file, races the frp road
  too, once each road before it failed: a connection of its own to frps for
  each link, by the same TLS. Each link visits the STCP service of NAME, or of
  the file's name line. The visit is signed with the secret as frpc's visitor
  signs it. The end-to-end channel checks the node's key by the pins of NAME,
  or --node-key, and the resumable layer resumes a session on a new visit. With
  a user line, the visitor logs in to frps as USER first, as frpc's visitor
  does. It holds that login with frp's heartbeat while the visit lasts, and
  frps checks USER against the service's allowUsers; with none, it visits with
  no login, as the user that a service of no user allows. owner USER, frpc's
  visitor's serverUser, names the frpc whose service it is: the visit asks for
  OWNER.NAME, else USER.NAME with a user, else NAME. The line plain, with no
  value, names a real frpc's STCP service of a plain TCP service, an sshd: no
  podssh node is behind it, so the frp road is the only one, with no end-to-end
  channel and no resumable layer. SSH runs on the visit itself, its host key
  checked in the known hosts under node://NAME; cp, scp and sftp take it too. A
  route, or --node-key, has nothing to apply to there (64). frps refusing a
  visit, a user that the service does not allow among them, ends the session
  (255) in frps's words. A file that does not read is a configuration error
  (78), which names its line and never its text.

  node://NAME with --carrier ADDR reaches the node at the other end of a stream
  that exists already. That stream is its one road, with no relay and no pair:
  exec:CMD, a program that podssh starts with no shell. It can be the
  platform's own SSH into a host whose every road out is closed: exec:'ssh -T
  sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio NAME TARGET'; or fd:N, a descriptor that
  podssh inherited (Unix). stdio is refused (64), as stdin and stdout are the
  session's. podssh serves the relay's side of the node's socket in its own
  process, as podssh operator --carrier does. It waits up to 60 s for the
  node's first frame. It then runs the session in the resumable layer and the
  end-to-end channel as on the pair's road, and no other road races it. NAME is
  a label alone, under which the node's key is pinned at its first sight, so a
  stream that another key answers is refused; the host key is recorded under
  node://NAME, as on each road. At the end the node hears a Close, and the
  program of exec: is waited for 5 s, then ended. With --exit NAME in place of
  node://NAME, the exit is the node at the other end of the stream. That node
  runs podssh node NAME --exit --carrier stdio, and the stream is its one road:
  the destination, or the first hop of -J, is a host that the exit dials from
  its own host. It dials it by the net's rule of the exit, and the host key is
  the host's, as on each road: podssh ssh --exit gw --carrier 'exec:ssh -T
  gateway podssh node gw --exit --carrier stdio' user@host.example.
  --pair-file, --relay-host, --relay-failover, --relay-addr, --ca-file,
  --direct, --iroh-ticket, --derp-ticket, --derp-server, a server's road in the
  relay's place and --upgrade are refused with it (64). So is --carrier with a
  destination that is no node and no --exit.

  node://NAME with --grant FILE carries a grant used once in the end-to-end
  channel of the session. The grant is an OpenSSH certificate of this client's
  key (client.key, or --client-key). A node lets it in once although no line of
  its allowlist names that key (see podssh node). A URL in its place, and
  --no-e2e beside it, are refused (64); a destination that is no podssh end is
  too. --bearer SIGNER carries a bearer in its place, as podssh operator
  --bearer makes it.

  node://NAME opens each leg after the first with the session's next token of
  one leg, as podssh operator does (see its notes). It does so where the node
  gave them through podssh relay serve.

  Host keys are checked against the known_hosts files. On a terminal, podssh
  asks about an unknown key. With no terminal and no SSH_ASKPASS, it refuses
  the key and names the remedy: -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new records a
  new key with no question. A changed key is always refused, and podssh shows
  both fingerprints. Under accept-new and no, a user known_hosts file that
  exists and cannot be read makes an unknown key a refusal. A key recorded
  there is not seen. A key that cannot be recorded (no HOME, UserKnownHostsFile
  none, a failed write) holds for this connection only, and podssh says so. A
  host that a @cert-authority line names is asked for a host certificate. The
  certificate is accepted with no record when that CA signed it for this host
  and it is valid now. Else it is refused with the check that failed. Each hop
  of -J checks its own key, under its own name, [HOST]:PORT off port 22;
  HostKeyAlias names the destination's key alone, with no port, as OpenSSH
  files it. The settings of host keys and authentication of -o and -i hold for
  each hop, where OpenSSH's command line holds for the destination only.

  Authentication tries the agent and the identity files, then
  keyboard-interactive and password. Prompts go to the terminal or to
  SSH_ASKPASS. With -o BatchMode=yes, each prompt is an error.

  A key file of a security key (ED25519-SK, ECDSA-SK) signs in its device:
  podssh first looks for a device that it may reach. With none it skips the
  key, and says why with -v and in the message of a login that fails. When the
  server takes the key, podssh asks for a touch of the device on stderr, and
  waits 30 s for it, also with BatchMode; BatchMode forbids only the question
  of the device's PIN, which a key made with verify-required needs.

  -t asks for a pty when there is a local terminal. -tt asks for one also when
  there is none, so interactive programs work from a host with no pty.

  What podssh reads from the terminal: in a session with a pty, the escape
  character (~, or that of -e; -e none turns it off) at the start of a line,
  and the key after it: ~. ends the session; ~R asks for a re-key; ~C opens a
  command line that adds and stops forwards (below); ~# lists the forwards of
  the session with the connections, bytes and state word of each (below; with
  -v, the end of a run prints the same lines); ~d leaves the shell to a far end
  that keeps shells (see --attach) and goes as typed elsewhere; ~Z sends a file
  by ZMODEM (below); ~? lists the escapes that this session offers, and ~~
  sends one ~; another key goes with the ~ before it. Each other byte passes
  unchanged, as the remote side reads it: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, Ctrl-D, Escape, the
  sequences of the keys, the mouse and a paste; only a question of ZMODEM, and
  a transfer, take the keys. A resize of the terminal sends the new size. With
  no pty, podssh reads no byte: stdin is the command's data, and Ctrl-C is the
  local terminal's signal to podssh (below). A session through a control master
  has its escapes at the master.

  Ctrl-C in a session with no pty that runs a command or a shell (not -N, -W or
  -s): the first sends signal INT to the command, as OpenSSH's sshd ends the
  command and its process group by it. podssh then waits 2 s for the command's
  end, whose signal or status is the exit code (130 for INT). A second Ctrl-C,
  or the end of the wait with no end, ends podssh with 130; -v says each step.
  A server may ignore the request: Dropbear signals only the process that it
  started. --no-signal keeps OpenSSH's way: no request, and Ctrl-C ends podssh
  at once. A SIGINT that was ignored when podssh started stays ignored. With a
  pty, Ctrl-C is a byte for the remote pty, as before. Ctrl-C ends a run of -N,
  also with --persist, as interrupted with 130; no request goes. --no-signal
  there keeps SIGINT's default, which kills podssh.

  ZMODEM, for a server that gives a shell and nothing else: in a session with a
  pty and a local terminal, podssh watches the output for the start of sz or rz
  of lrzsz. When sz sends, podssh asks where the files go (Enter takes the
  directory of the last answer, at first the current one; Ctrl-C refuses and
  cancels sz). Each file comes to a temporary name beside its own, the CRC of
  each frame and the length checked. Then a rename gives it its name; a name
  that the server sends is one component, and a file that exists is replaced
  only after the answer y. When rz waits, podssh asks which local file to send;
  ~Z asks first, then types rz on the server. Each wait for the other side has
  10 s, and after 4 waits with no answer the transfer ends and the session goes
  on. Ctrl-C during a transfer stops it, and a file that did not end is
```
