  removed. A file of 4 GiB or more cannot cross: the positions of ZMODEM have
  32 bits. A command that the server sends (sz with a command) never runs here.
  With no terminal, through a control master, or with PODSSH_ZMODEM set to off,
  nothing is watched, and the bytes go to stdout as they come. The same watch
  finds podssh tx at the far end, which carries a file where tmux or another
  terminal between breaks ZMODEM (see podssh tx).

  --sudo runs the command as root with sudo -S, with no pty, and --su with su
  -c, in a pty: the password is asked here, on the terminal or through
  SSH_ASKPASS, never taken from the command line. podssh answers one prompt,
  holds its input until the command starts, and asks nothing when sudo asks
  nothing; a second prompt, a wrong password, ends the input. A password that
  cannot be given (a question cancelled, an SSH_ASKPASS that exits non-zero,
  BatchMode or nothing to ask on) is never sent: podssh says why and ends the
  command's input, for su also its line on the pty. That takes the pty's kill
  and end-of-file keys, Ctrl-U and Ctrl-D by default. So sudo or su refuses
  with its own words and status. A command that neither starts nor ends within
  30 s ends podssh with 255. The remote shell must read POSIX quoting.

  --snippet NAME runs the command NAME of the settings file (see FILES): after
  a line [snippets], each line is NAME COMMAND. The placeholders of a command
  get these values: {{host}} the host that podssh connects to, after HostName;
  {{user}} the user; {{port}} the port; {{1}} to {{9}} the words after the
  host, which must be as many as the highest of them. Each value goes in quoted
  for a POSIX shell, as one word that runs nothing. Thus a placeholder must not
  be inside the command's own quotes: the file refuses that, and an unknown
  placeholder, with exit 78. \{{ gives {{ as text. podssh shows the whole
  command, with its values, and asks on the terminal or through SSH_ASKPASS:
  only y or yes runs it. --yes runs it with no question, and shows it on stderr
  (not with -q). podssh exits 64 before anything connects for each other
  answer, and for a name that the file does not have. It exits 64 too when
  nobody can answer, or when BatchMode is on and --yes is not given. A word
  that no placeholder takes, and -N, -s, -W or -O, with --snippet are refused
  (exit 64).

  With no destination, and stdin and stdout both terminals, podssh lists the
  literal Host names of ssh_config, each with a number. Beside each name are
  the user, host, port and jump that it resolves (see --list-hosts). They are
  those of -F, or of ~/.ssh/config and the system's file, with their Include
  lines. podssh logs in to the one picked, as if it were typed. A number picks;
  other text narrows the list to the names whose line holds it; an empty line
  or the end of input picks none (exit 64). The first word after the flags is
  the destination, as in OpenSSH. So the command of several hosts comes by -o
  RemoteCommand=COMMAND or --snippet NAME. Then several numbers (1 3, or 1,3)
  run it on each host picked, as podssh each runs it; with neither, one host is
  picked. A pattern, a negated name, a name of many hosts (a comma, a brace, a
  leading @) and a name of known_hosts are never listed. In each other case,
  and with no name to list, a missing destination is a usage error (exit 64).

  --record FILE keeps what the session showed, with its timing, as asciicast
  v2, for podssh play: never what was typed, and never the command line. The
  file is closed to others and never written over (exit 255); the output can
  hold a secret that a program printed.

  --expect TEXT --send KEYS are given once or more, in this order. Each pair is
  a rule of a session with a pty (-t on a terminal, -tt with none): each rule
  waits for TEXT in the output, as it is written, then sends KEYS, where \r,
  \n, \t, \\ and \xNN are read. The next rule reads only what came after the
  match, and the last 64 KiB at most. Until the last rule sent its keys, podssh
  holds its own input. A rule waits the time of --expect-timeout (30 s); when
  it sees no match, the session ends with 255 and the message names the rule.
  Each process of this host can read the command line: a password comes through
  SSH_ASKPASS, never in KEYS. -T, -N, -W, -s, --sudo, --su and --persist cannot
  go with the rules (64), and a session with no pty runs nothing (255).

  LocalCommand runs a command here after the login and before the session, only
  with PermitLocalCommand=yes, as OpenSSH runs it: SHELL -c COMMAND, else
  /bin/sh -c COMMAND, else exit 78 before anything connects. It takes the %
  tokens, and %T, which is NONE. podssh waits for its end, and its exit status
  changes nothing; its input is none, and with -W its output goes to stderr. It
  runs once, after the first login of --persist; podssh each, podssh
  containers, podssh cp and the other commands run none, as OpenSSH's scp runs
  none.

  --persist runs the shell in tmux on the server, as tmux new-session -A -s
  NAME with a pty. NAME is podssh, or the one of --persist-name. podssh looks
  for tmux after the login and refuses without it (exit 255): a new shell after
  a lost link would look like the old one. The refusal names the command that
  would install it, from the first package manager on the server's PATH, as
  podssh job does; podssh runs none. When the link is lost (no exit status;
  through the relay, a broken link or a close for its limits or its link to the
  server), podssh connects again. It tries 10 times at most in 5 minutes, and
  attaches the same session; one that is gone is not started again. A
  connection that lasted less than 30 s starts no new count. An exit status, a
  detach, ~., a refused host key or login, and Ctrl-C during the wait end the
  run. The logins after the first ask nothing (as BatchMode=yes); a key that a
  passphrase opened and a password that the server took are kept for the run.
  Keys typed meanwhile go to the session after the attach. With a command, -W,
  -s, -T, node:// or iroh:, --persist is refused (exit 64). --persist-forever
  lifts the limit, for a tunnel that must not end: podssh connects again for as
  long as it takes, about 30 s apart at most, and a first connection that
  failed is a loss too; it says each of the first 10 attempts, then one in 10.
  A refused host key or login still ends the run. Without --persist it is
  refused (exit 64).

  --upgrade logs in as each run does, then asks the server for podssh
  --version. When a podssh answers, it runs a temporary podssh node there in
  the same SSH session. The node takes this client's key (client.key in the
  cache, or --client-key): a node in front of the sshd of that session, with a
  pair that no file keeps. The node's one line, the pair's connect token and
  the node's key, comes back in the SSH channel, encrypted, and is on no argv.
  podssh then logs in again through that node, with the resumable layer and the
  end-to-end channel. The host key is the same, so known_hosts needs no change;
  the first connection closes once that login is done. The session then resumes
  after a lost link, as one to a node does. When no podssh answers, it starts
  no node, it offers no layer, or the second login fails, one note says so. The
  session then stays on the first connection. podssh never copies itself to the
  server: install it there, on the PATH of a command that sshd runs. The node
  ends with its last session, or 10 minutes after its start with none.
  --upgrade with node://, iroh:, cf://, --persist, a remote forward or -O is
  refused (exit 64); ControlPath has no effect with it.

  -L [BIND:]PORT:HOST:HOSTPORT listens here, and each connection that it takes
  goes on from the server; HOST:HOSTPORT may be a socket path on the server,
  and the listening side a socket path here (mode 0600). -D [BIND:]PORT, or a
  socket path, is a SOCKS4, SOCKS4a and SOCKS5 proxy, CONNECT only and no
  authentication; podssh answers a SOCKS client once the server opened its
  channel. A port with no address listens on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, or with -g
  (GatewayPorts) on each address; localhost is loopback, and an empty address
  or * each address, as in OpenSSH. Each listener is made before anything
  connects: one that cannot be made ends the run (exit 255), with the system's
  words and -W HOST:PORT, which needs none; PODSSH_LISTEN set to no turns
  listening off (exit 78). ClearAllForwardings yes drops each forward, and -W
  implies it, as in OpenSSH. -W /PATH reaches a Unix socket on the server, as
  OpenSSH's -W does.

  -R [BIND:]PORT:HOST:HOSTPORT asks the server to listen; each connection that
  it takes reaches HOST:HOSTPORT from this host, as one more outbound
  connection, through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set, within 20 s. A port of 0 lets
  the server choose, and podssh prints it. A forward that the server refuses is
  a warning; with -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes it ends the run (exit 255). -R
  takes OpenSSH's other forms too: a socket path on the server (-R
  SERVERPATH:HOST:HOSTPORT), a socket on this host as the target (-R
  [BIND:]PORT:LOCALPATH, -R SERVERPATH:LOCALPATH; on Unix), and a SOCKS proxy
  that the server listens for and podssh serves (-R [BIND:]PORT, or -R
  SERVERPATH alone). Its targets are dialed from this host, the answer after
  the dial.

  --persist -N keeps the forwards: no tmux runs, and after a loss, the server's
  own close too, podssh connects again and asks for each -R again; -L and -D
  keep their listeners. A forward refused after a loss is asked again for 2
  minutes, as the server may hold its port for the old connection. Then it is
  refused as on the first connection (see ExitOnForwardFailure); a port that
  the server chose may change, and the new one is printed. The logins after the
  first ask nothing, unless SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE is force and SSH_ASKPASS names
  a program to ask. With no forward, or --persist-name, -N with --persist is
  refused (exit 64).

  Each forward has a state word. It follows the counts in ~# and in the lines
  of -v, and is state in --result-file. bound: the listener is bound, or the
  remote forward is asked for, and no link carries it yet. waiting: the link
  was lost, and --persist connects again or asks again for a refused remote
  forward. up: it serves on the link. refused: the server's policy refused it,
  as AllowTcpForwarding no does. A refused channel gives the server's reason in
  parentheses; a refused remote forward has none, as SSH sends none. A target
  that is down fails one connection and leaves the word. A forward that ~C
  stopped says closed instead, in --result-file too. With --persist, each
  change of a word is one line on stderr, NAME: WORD; waiting ends with the
  loss that names the hop that broke. At the end of a run each word is the last
  one that the forward had.

  ~C, in a session with a pty, opens the command line of OpenSSH, ssh>, on the
  terminal. -L, -D or -R with a spec of the command line adds that forward to
  the running session: the listeners of -L and -D are made as those of the
  command line are (the probe, -g, PODSSH_LISTEN). -R asks the server and waits
  20 s at most for its answer. -KL, -KD or -KR with [BIND:]PORT, or a socket
  path for -KL and -KD, stops one: a closed listener takes no new connection,
  and the connections that it took go on; the server lets the port of -R go,
  and a channel for that port is refused from then on. help or ? lists the
  commands; an empty line, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D do nothing, and a line that starts
  with ! runs no command (OpenSSH's PermitLocalCommand). After a forward that
  ~C stopped, ~# says closed. The forwards that ~C adds last as long as the
  connection, and those that it stops stay stopped: a new connection of
  --persist asks only for the forwards of the command line that ~C did not
  stop. A session through a control master has no ~C, as with OpenSSH: the key
  goes to the server as typed.

  --attach NAME DEST joins the shell that the far end keeps as NAME. --attach
  DEST with no other word lists the shells kept there, one on each line, then
  exits 0. A far end that keeps shells says so in the resumable layer of
  node://NAME; a podssh node in front of an SSH server keeps none, and then
  --attach ends with 255 before a session opens. In a session with a pty there,
  ~d asks the far end to keep the shell. It prints the name that it keeps it
  as, and exits 0; elsewhere ~d is sent as typed. The far end gives a shell to
  one client at a time: --take takes it from the client that has it, whose
  session ends. A session there counts the shell's output that it got. After a
  lost link, ~., a signal or ~d, podssh keeps that offset in the cache. The
  next --attach NAME from this host gives it, and the far end replays what this
  client missed. With no offset kept, podssh reads the far end's list first.
  Where the far end's ring no longer holds the offset, it says so and gives the
  last output. --reset asks for that last output from a clean boundary in any
  case. The far end refuses an attach from inside the shell itself: it puts
  PODSSH_SHELL_ID in each shell's environment, and podssh sends that value. A
  refusal of the far end comes as its words on stderr and its exit status.
  Another destination, a command, -N, -W, -s, -T or --persist with --attach is
  refused (exit 64). Against a standard sshd, --persist keeps the shell in
  tmux.

  A first relay host may offer the resumable layer in its /relays.json, as
  podssh relay serve does. podssh reads that offer at each run with
  PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER=yes, and keeps it for a day when it is unset (see
  ENVIRONMENT). Where it is offered, podssh ssh carries the session to a
  standard sshd in the resumable layer at the relay: the relay keeps its
  connection to the server while this host's link is lost. A new link resumes
  the session where it was, for as long as the relay keeps it, 10 minutes by
  default. The new link goes to the same relay, or to the process that its
  /relays.json names as forward.host; one line tells of each loss and each
  resume. SSH's keepalives are off unless ServerAliveInterval is given, as the
  layer's heartbeat finds a dead link. -4 and -6 hold for each link. A host
  that offers none takes the contract's road, as podssh proxy does, with one
  line under PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER=yes alone. So does a host that has no room for
  a new resumable session, with one line. So does a host whose first link fails
  for a reason that another host may not share; so does --no-resume. The
  copies, run, each and job log in the same way.

  -A forwards the agent, off by default as in OpenSSH; -a turns it off, and the
  last of the two wins, over the keyword ForwardAgent. podssh asks for it on
  the session, never on a jump host. It joins each agent channel that the
  server opens to the agent that podssh logs in with (IdentityAgent, else
  SSH_AUTH_SOCK); ForwardAgent with a path or $NAME names another agent. While
  the session lasts, the server, and root on it, can use each key of the agent,
  though it cannot read one. podssh binds the agent to the server's host key
  first, as OpenSSH does (session-bind@openssh.com). So an OpenSSH agent keeps
  from the server each key that ssh-add limits to other hosts; an agent that
  refuses the bind serves unbound. An agent channel that a server opens with no
  -A is refused, with a warning.

  -X and -Y forward X11 to the display of DISPLAY; -x turns it off, and the
  last of the three wins. The server is given a spoofed cookie, and podssh puts
  the real one in each X11 channel's first packet. -Y uses the cookie of
  XAUTHORITY or ~/.Xauthority, and gives the server's X clients full access; -X
  an untrusted cookie that xauth makes, for ForwardX11Timeout, and with no
  xauth it is refused. With no DISPLAY, no X server that answers, or no cookie
  that it takes, the run ends with 255 before anything connects.

  -M with -S PATH (or ControlMaster and ControlPath) makes this run the control
  master, on Unix: other runs with -S PATH go through its one connection, as
  with OpenSSH, whose ssh -O check and clients work with it; a second -M asks
  before each request. -O check, forward, cancel, exit and stop speak to the
  master. With no master there, a run connects alone, and ControlMaster auto
  makes it the master. The socket is made mode 0600 before anything connects,
  and goes with the master. ControlPersist keeps a -N master with no client for
  that long; podssh does not go to the background. On Windows, -M, -S and -O
  are refused (exit 64).

  -P on ssh is the Tag of OpenSSH, which Match tagged reads, not a port; a tag
  that is a number gets a note on stderr. On scp and sftp, -P is the port. Use
  -p for the port of ssh.

  -G prints the settings in effect, as ssh -G does: a line of keyword and value
  for each keyword of OpenSSH that podssh applies, defaults included, then
  exits 0 with nothing opened. The defaults that differ from OpenSSH's do on
  purpose: ServerAliveInterval and ConnectTimeout are 60, and no identity file
  of a security key is tried; each list of algorithms is what podssh will
  offer, its own unless a keyword gave one. podssh's own settings, such as the
  relay hosts, print no line, as OpenSSH knows no keyword for them.

  Ciphers, MACs, KexAlgorithms, HostKeyAlgorithms, PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms and
  CASignatureAlgorithms filter what podssh offers, as OpenSSH reads them: a
  list replaces podssh's own, one that starts with + adds to it, with - takes
  from it, and with ^ puts its names first. A name that podssh does not speak
  is left out, and -v says so; a list that leaves nothing is refused before
  anything connects (exit 64, or 78 for a line of a file). The host key
  algorithms that known_hosts records for the host go first within the list.
  RequiredRSASize is the least RSA key: a smaller key of the user is not
  offered. A smaller host key, or key of the CA of a host certificate, ends the
  connection (exit 255). The other keywords of a restriction, which podssh does
  not apply, such as VerifyHostKeyDNS and BindAddress, get one note when you
  give them. They get none for the system's ssh_config and none with -q; the
  keywords that change nothing get a note at -v that names their place.

  Paths in -i and in the IdentityFile, UserKnownHostsFile,
  GlobalKnownHostsFile, IdentityAgent and ForwardAgent keywords take the tokens
  of OpenSSH: %% %C %d %h %i %j %k %L %l %n %p %r %u, with OpenSSH's values. %u
  is the local user and %r the remote one. An unknown token is refused (exit
  64). ${NAME} in them is the variable NAME, which must be set (exit 64); a
  whole $NAME as IdentityAgent or ForwardAgent is the variable that holds the
  path, and no agent when it is not set. -E FILE is opened as typed.

  A repeated value follows OpenSSH: the first -p and -l, the last -e, -E and
  -F, and the first value of each -o keyword. A second -J or -W is refused, and
  so is a second --relay-host, --relay-addr or --ca-file: give several hops,
  hosts or addresses as one comma list.

  ConnectTimeout bounds the SSH handshake and each answer of the server while
  podssh logs in. The time that a question waits for its answer does not count,
  the question of a new host key included, which runs inside the handshake: it
  has its own bound, 60 s when stdin, stdout and stderr are all redirected, on
  a console of Windows too. A handshake that does not finish names what came:
  no byte, a line of another service, or the server's version line and the last
  message of the key exchange each way; through a node, also the bytes that its
  resumable layer and its end-to-end channel carried each way. 10 s in (through
  a node, 10 s after its layer opened), a handshake that has not finished says
  where it is. It says so once, and waits on; a question that nobody can see
  says that it waits, and its remedy.

  The version line that podssh sends is SSH-2.0-podssh_VERSION, each dash of
  the version written as an underscore, as RFC 4253 allows none there: podssh
  names its own software, as each client does. A server or a filter that lets
  in only the version lines of OpenSSH refuses it. podssh does not send
  OpenSSH's line: a server reads the line to choose the quirks that it expects
  of a client (OpenSSH's own server so treats its older versions). podssh is
  not OpenSSH.

  Each later hop of -J is reached on a direct-tcpip channel of the hop before
  it, whose open has that hop's ConnectTimeout. A hop that never answers the
  open is named so. A channel on which no byte of an SSH server came within it,
  or that closed with none, is named so too: the hop, and the target of its
  channel, never a handshake of the destination. With -v, podssh says the open,
  and each 10 s while nothing came.

  podssh sends keepalives (ServerAliveInterval), so the relay does not close an
  idle session. To a node, the resumable layer keeps the link busy and finds a
  dead one, and SSH sends none unless ServerAliveInterval is set: a keepalive
  with no answer would end a session that the layer carries onto a new link.
  Through the relay a session carries 64 MiB at most, both ways together: once
  it has carried 60 MiB (less under a relay's smaller limits, or
  PODSSH_SESSION_BUDGET), podssh says so once (with -q, nothing); podssh cp
  copies more on new sessions. With keepalives off, or slower than the relay's
  idle cut (180 s with no payload), podssh warns once 30 s before the cut. The
  warning shows in the window's title where the notice of a silent far end
  shows, else as a line on stderr. It comes again only after a payload crossed;
  --idle-warn SECONDS sets the lead, and 0, or -q, turns it off. The warning
  sends nothing. With --persist each run that crosses the relay warns too, and
  adds that --persist attaches again after the cut; --upgrade warns while its
  session crosses the relay.

  podssh reads options before and after the host, as OpenSSH does. So a host
  that a script did not write can be read as a flag. Put -- before it: podssh
  ssh -- "$HOST" uptime. A host, or a -o HostName=VALUE, that starts with - is
  refused (exit 64), as OpenSSH refuses it.

  An IPv6 address needs brackets only before a port: user@2001:db8::1 is port
  22, and user@[2001:db8::1]:2222 or -p 2222 gives another port. -4 or -6 with
  an address of the other family is refused. The default relay takes an IPv6
  address, but when this version was measured, its way out reached no IPv6
  host: it opens the session, then closes it at once (1011 target closed before
  sending anything). podssh then tries the direct road once, as after a relay
  that failed, also under -6, whose dial takes the name's IPv6 addresses alone;
  with a relay named, or PODSSH_DIRECT=no, it ends, and the note names the
  roads that carry IPv6: a relay of yours on a host with IPv6 (podssh relay
  serve, then --relay-host), a node with IPv6 egress (-J node://NAME), or
  warp://[ADDR]. podssh relay serve dials an IPv6 target where its host routes
  IPv6 out. Where it does not, it refuses the target before the upgrade (502,
  this relay's host has no IPv6 route out). So the next relay host is tried at
  once. --direct needs no relay.

  --result-file FILE writes one JSON object to FILE at the end of each run,
  also of one that failed before it connected: schema; exit (the code that
  podssh exits with); status (the remote exit status, or null); signal (its
  name and core_dumped, or null); end (status, signal, no-status, lost,
  escaped, terminated, detached, interrupted, failed or shared; interrupted is
  Ctrl-C with no pty and no end of the command, or of -N; shared is a run
  through a control master, which tells the exit code alone; null with no
  session, as with -W); failure (connect, host-key, auth, forward, policy,
  relay, session, usage, config or not-built, or null); bytes (stdin, stdout
  and stderr, as they passed; null through a control master, which carries
  them), duration_ms, and relay (its host, close_code and reason, or null with
  no relay). A run with forwards adds forwards, also one that failed before its
  link. Each object has name as written, state (bound, waiting, up, refused or
  closed) and reason (the server's, or null). It also has closed (stopped by
  ~C), connections, open, failed, bytes_up and bytes_down. A link lost after
  the remote exit status and before the end of the output ends lost, with exit
  255 and the status kept. stdout and stderr stay as they are; the command's
  output never goes into the file. A new file is made for its owner alone; - is
  refused (exit 64). No file is written after a flag that podssh does not know,
  which ends it before it reads the others. Nor is one written when a signal
  kills podssh: only a session on a terminal ends at SIGTERM or SIGHUP, as
  terminated. One with no pty ends at Ctrl-C, by the command's end or as
  interrupted. A run of -N, also with --persist, ends at Ctrl-C as interrupted,
  with 130 and its file.

  --install NAME, with -N, --persist and a forward, makes the tunnel a service
  of this user. The service starts it again whenever it ends, as podssh node
  --install makes a node's, by the same ways: a user unit of systemd
  (podssh-ssh-NAME.service), a LaunchAgent (dev.podssh.ssh.NAME), two lines of
  the crontab, or a task of Windows. A server that only the tunnel reaches is
  locked out while it is down. The service runs this program with the words of
  this command line but --install NAME. It runs in this directory, so that each
  relative path means what it meant; after ssh come BatchMode=yes,
  ForkAfterAuthentication=no, ControlPath=none and ExitOnForwardFailure=yes,
  each after -o. They win over the rest and over ssh_config. Nobody answers a
  prompt there, and a run in the background or through a master would leave the
  service. A refused forward serves nothing until a new start; then --env-file
  with ssh-NAME.env, the private file of the variables that it reads, with no
  token. Last comes --persist-forever, so that an outage of the relay never
  ends the tunnel between two starts. The login needs a key with no passphrase,
  and the host key in known_hosts: run the same command once in the foreground
  first. The command line is resolved first: a shell, a command, -W, -f, -G,
  -O, --attach, --upgrade or --snippet is refused (64). So is a tunnel without
  --persist, or with no forward. --uninstall NAME removes what --install NAME
  wrote, and nothing else. --env-file FILE sets the variables of FILE first and
  holds FILE.lock while the run lasts, as for podssh node: a second start of
  the same service ends at once with 0.

  A key's echo while a download runs: for 2 s after a key on a session with a
  pty, podssh grants each channel of the connection a small window. The
  channels are the session's own, a forward of -L, -R or -D, SFTP, a command,
  and the agent's. The window is what the path moves in its least round trip
  and 40 ms more. A third more is added, as podssh tops a window up once a
  quarter of it is used; 16 KiB at the least, so that a key waits behind little
  of the download; idle, 200 ms more. Each channel takes messages of 8 KiB at
  most from the server, so that a slow path's window holds a few of them.
  podssh measures the rate and the round trip on the connection itself, end to
  end, through any relay or proxy and against any sshd. To time the path and
  not its queue, it lets the windows drain at the first key and each 10 s of a
  download. They drain until a round trip is timed across an empty queue (10 s
  at most). Until it has measured them, a channel has the window of before, 512
  KiB, topped up once half of it is used. Where nobody types, a window grows by
  the same rule, up to the cap of its road. A window is what a road may hold
  for a slow reader: 16 MiB with --direct, on the iroh road and at podssh's
  relay role (podssh relay serve); 1.5 MiB through the default relay; 768 KiB
  on a node's pair road; 512 KiB on each other; the channels that carry bulk
  share it, each with 512 KiB at least, and the requests in flight of cp, scp
  and sftp follow it. podssh's own uploads (cp, sftp, and the local side of
  each forward) wait while a key waits for its echo, a second at most. Each TCP
  socket that podssh dials keeps 16 KiB unsent at most, where the system takes
  that option (Linux and macOS).

  upterm://SESSION@HOST[:PORT] reaches a session of upterm's host
  (owenthereal/upterm) as its guests reach it: a WebSocket to the uptermd at
  HOST, port 443 by default, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its TLS
  checked with podssh's trust. Then SSH runs inside it as the user SESSION, the
  session's ID that its host shows. It logs in with your keys, which uptermd
  checks against the host's list. uptermd's host key is a certificate:
  known_hosts checks it under the @cert-authority line that upterm gives for
  its server, for the name [HOST]:443, as upterm's own client keys it. As the
  destination it is the session, the host's shared terminal. As the first hop
  of -J it carries the next hop in a direct-tcpip channel to the host's
  loopback. upterm host lets a guest forward there (its forwarding allowed to
  loopback). So the host's own sshd checks you end to end: podssh ssh -J
  upterm://SESSION@HOST user@127.0.0.1. A session that uptermd knows not is
  refused in its words (ssh's exit 255, as for any first hop not reached;
  podssh proxy's 77), and a host that lets no forward refuses the channel in
  its own. podssh names no uptermd: give the server's name, the community
  server's too. upterm+ws://SESSION@127.0.0.1:PORT reaches an uptermd of this
  host over ws://. -p gives the port; --direct, -4, -6 and HostName cannot go
  with it.

  --tuic FILE reaches the first hop through TUIC servers that you run
  (sing-box, mihomo, shoes, Itsusinn's tuic), in place of the relay. It goes
  over QUIC where UDP passes: TUIC version 5, a server that takes a user's UUID
  and a token of its password, then the target, and dials it. FILE must be
  yours and closed to others (chmod 600), as a pair file is: each line is a
  share link as panels and clients give it, tuic://UUID:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT,
  then ?sni= (or peer=) and alpn= (a comma list; h3 when none), joined by &,
  and #TAG; # starts a comment. congestion_control, udp_relay_mode, disable_sni
  and reduce_rtt pass: the first is the sender's own and no server reads it,
  and this road carries no UDP of its own. A certificate that is not checked
  (allow_insecure), a version other than 5, and a line that cannot be read are
  refused (78). The line is named by its number and never its text. QUIC is
  UDP, which no HTTP proxy carries, so the road goes beside HTTPS_PROXY, and
  only where a probe found that UDP reaches the server: one QUIC packet of a
  reserved version, which a server of QUIC answers at once; with no answer
  within 1 s the server is not tried, and the line says that UDP does not pass.
  Then TLS 1.3 inside QUIC, checked for sni (else HOST) with podssh's trust
  (--ca-file); the token is 32 bytes of TLS's keying material exporter, the
  UUID its label and the password its context, so neither crosses; and a
  heartbeat each 10 s while the session lives. TUIC has no answer: the servers
  are tried in the order of the file, and each waits up to 10 s for the
  target's version line. A server that closes the connection did not take the
  UUID or the password. Its words are said (ssh 255, as for each first hop that
  it does not reach); one that ends the stream with no byte could not reach the
  target, or its rules refuse it. Itsusinn's tuic refuses a loopback or private
  target unless its experimental drop_loopback and drop_private are off; each
  gives way to the next, and -v says the address that QUIC reached. The host
  key of SSH protects the session, as on each road: the server sees the
  target's name and SSH's encrypted bytes. A run has one road: --relay-host,
  --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless,
  --trojan, --wstunnel, --chisel, -4 and -6 cannot go with it (64). Nor can a
  destination with a road of its own.

  --list-hosts prints a JSON array on stdout and connects to nothing. It holds
  one object for each literal Host alias of the files that the picker reads, in
  their order. The keys are alias, host, port, user, identity_files, proxy_jump
  and error. host is after HostName, in lower case, as -G prints hostname.
  identity_files are the files that the login would try, expanded. proxy_jump
  and error are null when there is none. Each object is what podssh ssh ALIAS
  resolves, with the other flags of the command line, through the same code; an
  alias that resolves nothing has its reason in error and null in the other
  keys, and the list goes on (exit 0). It holds no key and no passphrase. A
  destination or a command exits 64.

  --list-hosts stops at a fault that each alias meets: exit 78, with nothing on
  stdout. It stops for a file of the list that cannot be read, and for an
  Include of any host that others may change. It stops for a bad line outside
  each block or under Host *, and for a bad variable, as PODSSH_RELAY. A fault
  in one alias's own block is that alias's error, and the list goes on (exit
  0). Such faults are a bad value (Port 99999, HostName with no value), an
  Include of that block that others may change, and a usage fault. No name is
  resolved: HostName 300.1.1.1 is listed as written, and fails when podssh ssh
  connects. The file of -F or PODSSH_SSH_CONFIG is your choice: its owner and
  mode are not checked, as OpenSSH does not check them. Each file that it
  includes is checked.

  --predict shows each key that you type at once, underlined, where the far end
  will echo it. When the echo comes, the underline goes. It works only to
  podssh serve with a pty, which tells the client which keys reached the pty
  and whether the pty echoes. A kept shell tells the client that has it now. A
  shell shared by name tells its owner and each seat that types, each of its
  own keys; a seat that watches gets nothing. Another server refuses the ask,
  and -v says so. A Windows console that takes no VT sequences shows no guess
  either, and -v says so. Guesses start to show at a round trip of 120 ms, and
  stop below 80 ms. The guesses are printable characters, Backspace and the
  left and right arrows, on the cursor's row. After each other key, a paste or
  a wrong guess, nothing shows until the far end echoes a new guess. A line
  that the pty reads with no echo, as for a password, shows no guess at all. A
  line of podssh's own on the terminal, an escape, ZMODEM or a far end that
  counts wrong ends the guesses for the session.

  POLICY: with --policy FILE, podssh ssh judges the destination's algorithms by
  an algorithm policy. The verdict falls at the server's host key, before
  known_hosts is read and before any login. A mismatch ends the run with exit
  78, and a KEXINIT that does not read ends it with exit 69. Either way the
  verdict goes to stdout as one JSON object. A pass goes on to the login, and
  -v says the verdict. So does a size that one exchange cannot measure: -v
  names it unmeasured, and only podssh health exits 69 for it. A host of -J is
  not judged. --policy goes with no --persist, --upgrade, -M, -S or -O (64);
  ControlPath of a file has no effect then.

  The file is in the grammar of ssh-audit, whose policy files load unchanged.
  Each line is KEY = VALUE, and a line that starts with # is a comment. name
  and version are required; banner and header are compared whole. compressions,
  host keys, key exchanges, ciphers and macs are lists by commas, expected in
  that order; optional host keys may come beside the host keys.
  allow_algorithm_subset_and_reordering = true takes the key exchanges, ciphers
  and MACs in any order, each one named by the policy.
  allow_hostkey_subset_and_reordering = true does the same for the host keys.
  host_key_sizes is JSON, as {"rsa-sha2-512": {"hostkey_size": 4096}}, with
  ca_key_type and ca_key_size for a certificate. dh_modulus_sizes is JSON too,
  and the older lines hostkey_size_ALG, cakey_size_ALG and dh_modulus_size_KEX
  are read. A size must be equal, or at least as large with allow_larger_keys =
  true. client policy = true judges a client, so it finds a mismatch on a
  server. An unknown key, a key given twice, or a value that does not read is
  refused with its line (78).

  A size is read on the key that came, of the type that the exchange agreed. A
  key of another type is a mismatch, and its size counts for nothing. One
  exchange measures one host key, so the size of another type that the server
  offers is said as unmeasured, never passed. ext-info-s and the name of the
  strict key exchange are judged only by a policy that names one of them. The
  verdict is one JSON object: schema, policy, version, verdict (pass, mismatch,
  unmeasured or no reading), exit, mismatches, unmeasured, and why with no
  reading. Each mismatch has field, expected, optional and actual.

  --exit NAME starts the road to the first hop (the destination, or the first
  host of -J) at NAME, in place of the relay. NAME is a node of your net that
  lends its egress (see podssh node --exit). It works as a Tailscale exit node
  carries a device's traffic: the node dials the host from its own, on each of
  its roads that answers, raced as for node://NAME. The session resumes on any
  of them. The host travels in the end-to-end channel, so the relay sees
  neither the host nor a byte; the node resolves it and checks each address: a
  public one, or one of its ranges, as its net's policy lets this client. It
  dials those addresses alone. The host key is the host's, under its own name,
  as on the relay. NAME is a member of the net, whose key the channel checks,
  and the label of its pair here. A refusal of the node or of its net's policy
  says why, and ssh exits 255. --exit goes with no node://, iroh:, derp:,
  cf://, iap:// or eice:// destination (64). It goes with no --direct, no -4 or
  -6, no --no-e2e and no road of another server (64). With --carrier ADDR, the
  exit is the node at the other end of that stream. The stream is its one road,
  with no relay and no pair (see --carrier). podssh cp, scp and sftp take it
  too.

  node://NAME and --exit NAME refuse --relay-host and --relay-failover (64),
  and PODSSH_RELAY (78), as podssh proxy node://NAME does: the pair names its
  relay. A RelayHost of the settings file is ignored there, with a line at -v.
  --relay-addr and --ca-file reach the pair's relay.

  podssh may try the cleartext road, the relay's last, before the direct road
  and the forwarders. It does so when each relay host failed, and the TLS of
  one failed on the way. That TLS failure is a certificate that is not the
  relay's, as a proxy that intercepts TLS presents its own. It can also be a
  reset or a close in the handshake, or its bound. The road goes to a host of
  each deployment once, on its own port, through HTTPS_PROXY as each road
  dials. podssh asks it with no TLS for a token of one session (POST
  /v1/mint?once=1, signed by this client's key where the relay asks). Then the
  upgrade goes with that token, with no TLS either. Each hop reads the target
  and that token, which lives minutes and which one upgrade spends; SSH inside
  stays end to end, its host key checked as on each road. No other token goes
  there, a token of PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN or of the cache among them; the token is
  never cached, and a relay whose answer does not say "once": true, with an end
  within 10 minutes, gets no upgrade. A line says what goes, and another which
  host carries the session; -v says that the session runs in cleartext. podssh
  relay serve serves the road (see podssh relay); the default relay's edge
  serves TLS alone on its port, and refuses it. After the forwarders that
  podssh names, the road tries their ws:// form, where a probe with no TLS of
  their host's port 80 passed. The probes go one at a time, 5 s each: no relay
  token goes to a forwarder. PODSSH_CLEARTEXT=no turns both off. podssh proxy,
  podssh pipe and each command that reaches its server as podssh ssh does take
  the road too.

  To a relay host that you named (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost), the
  sessions of one run can share one connection. They are streams of one HTTP/2
  connection where the host offers RFC 8441's extended CONNECT, as podssh relay
  serve does: the hosts of podssh each, and each other session of the run to
  that relay host, cost no TLS handshake past the first. -v names the road of
  each session (see THE RELAY, The WebSocket over HTTP/2). Where the host's TLS
  chooses http/1.1, the upgrade goes as before; where its HTTP/2 offers no
  extended CONNECT, the upgrade goes on a new connection. The run then asks
  that host for no HTTP/2 for 10 minutes. PODSSH_H2=no keeps each session on
  its own connection; yes offers the road to the default relay too.

  --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH] reaches the first hop in place of the
  relay. It goes through a server of jpillora/chisel that you run (chisel
  server on port 443 with a user and a password): podssh opens its WebSocket,
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, checked for HOST with podssh's trust
  (--ca-file), with the subprotocol chisel-v3; then SSH inside it as chisel's
  client speaks it (chisel 1.8 and later). SSH carries its configuration of one
  remote, and a channel to the first hop, which the server dials. The sessions
  of one run are channels of one connection. What the server takes and shows
  comes from --chisel-auth-file FILE (or PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE), a file of
  yours that others cannot read: auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's own auth
  option and its authfile's keys; fingerprint BASE64, the fingerprint that
  chisel server prints, which podssh then checks before it logs in. With no
  fingerprint, -v says that the server's key is not checked: TLS names the
  server, and the first hop's own host key protects the session. http:// goes
  to this host alone (64), as the password would cross the network in the
  clear. A wrong password and a key that is not the file's fingerprint are
  refused with their words (77). So is a target that the server's authfile does
  not allow; an answer that is not chisel's is said so (69). Its 404 Not found
  is named as the words of a chisel server that did not take the upgrade.
  PODSSH_CHISEL names the server where the command line names no other road;
  beside PODSSH_RELAY, PODSSH_FORWARDER, PODSSH_VIA or PODSSH_WSTUNNEL it is
  refused (78). A run has one road: --relay-host, --relay-failover, --direct,
  --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless, --wstunnel, -4, -6, and a
  destination with a road of its own cannot go with it (64).

  --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT] reaches the first hop through a server of
  erebe/wstunnel that you run (wstunnel server wss://[::]:443), in place of the
  relay: podssh opens the WebSocket to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set,
  checked for HOST with podssh's trust (--ca-file). Its token names the first
  hop as wstunnel's own client names it; the server dials it and carries the
  bytes. podssh speaks the protocol of wstunnel 9.1 to 11 over its WebSocket,
  which each server serves beside its HTTP/2 on one port: https:// and wts://
  are refused (64), and ws:// has no TLS. What the server checks of a client
  comes from --wstunnel-secret-file FILE (or PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE), a
  file of yours that others cannot read: path-prefix PREFIX, the prefix that
  the server restricts its clients to; credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or
  authorization VALUE, the Authorization that its restrictions match; or one
  line, the prefix alone. With no file, podssh is the client of wstunnel's
  defaults, the prefix v1. Over ws:// a secret goes to this host alone (64).
  The server refuses a tunnel with a 400 that names no cause: podssh says it in
  the words of the version that sent it (a path prefix or an Authorization that
  it does not take; a target that it does not allow; or one that it could not
  reach; its log names which), and exits 77. An answer that is not wstunnel's
  is said so (69). Each frame is masked with a key of zero, which the server
  reads the same whether it applies masks or not. PODSSH_WSTUNNEL names the
  server where the command line names no other road; beside PODSSH_RELAY,
  PODSSH_FORWARDER or PODSSH_VIA it is refused (78). A run has one road:
  --relay-host, --relay-failover, --direct, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via,
  --vless, -4, -6, and a destination with a road of its own cannot go with it
  (64). The host key of SSH protects the session, as on each road.

  -L and -D listen here, and each connection that they take goes on from the
  server. -W HOST:PORT carries one connection, with no listener.

  -R [BIND:]PORT:HOST:HOSTPORT: the server listens, and each connection reaches
  HOST:HOSTPORT from here, through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set. A socket path
  can take the place of either side, or [BIND:]PORT alone for SOCKS.

  -P on ssh is OpenSSH's Tag, which Match tagged reads, not a port. On scp and
  sftp, -P is the port. The meaning is per-verb.

  Other names: podssh connect

  Usage: podssh ssh [OPTIONS] [--] [user@]host [COMMAND...]

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host]
        the host to log in to: [user@]host, host:PORT, [user@][IPV6]:PORT or
        ssh://[user@]host[:PORT].
    [COMMAND]...
        the command to run on the host, its words joined with spaces as OpenSSH
        joins them; without one, the host starts a shell.

  Options:
    -p, --port PORT
        port to connect to; never a proxy port.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...];
        ssh+tls://[user@]host[:port] is SSH inside TLS.
    -N, --no-remote-command
        run nothing; stay connected until the server closes.
    -n, --stdin-null
        do not read stdin; the remote side sees end of input at once.
    -s, --subsystem
        the command is a subsystem name, such as sftp.
    -t, --force-tty
        request a pty; twice to request one even without a local tty.
    -T, --disable-tty
        disable tty allocation.
    -e, --escape-char CHAR
        escape character for sessions with a pty, or none (default ~).
    -C, --compress
        ask the server for compression.
    -4, --ipv4-only
        use IPv4 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=4.
    -6, --ipv6-only
        use IPv6 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=6.
    -W, --stdio-forward HOST:PORT
        stdin and stdout become a connection the server opens to HOST:PORT, or
        to the Unix socket /PATH on it.
    -E, --log-file LOGFILE
        append podssh's own messages to a file instead of stderr.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    -V, --version
        print the version and exit.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    --StrictHostKeyChecking yes|accept-new|no|ask
        host key policy, as -o StrictHostKeyChecking; there is no --insecure.
    --UserKnownHostsFile FILE
        known-hosts file to consult, as -o UserKnownHostsFile.
    --host-key-fingerprint SHA256:B64[,...]
        accept only a host key of these fingerprints, also under accept-new,
        and record none; -J hops keep known_hosts.
    --policy FILE
        before the login, judge the server's KEXINIT by the algorithm policy in
        FILE; a mismatch exits 78 with the verdict as JSON on stdout.
    --LogLevel LEVEL
        quiet, fatal, error, info, verbose, debug.
    --ConnectTimeout SECONDS
        bound on the SSH handshake and on each answer while logging in, as -o
        ConnectTimeout.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the next starts after 2 s or
        a failure; the default), parallel or serial; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS); a HOST pinned to loopback
        addresses alone goes with no proxy.
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set; a
        proxy that takes the CONNECT and sends nothing back is named as the
        cause; with no relay named, this road is tried once after each relay
        host failed (env PODSSH_DIRECT=no turns that off).
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --early-data WORD
        the VLESS road's early data: 0rtt, 1rtt or off (default: env
        PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA, else off); a nonce repeated inside ten minutes
        is a replay, and the session continues at 1-RTT on the same connection.
    --h2-shape WORD
        the shape of the HTTP/2 road that podssh builds: existing (the
        default), browser or firefox (default: env PODSSH_H2_SHAPE); SETTINGS
        and their order and the connection's window are sent, while PRIORITY
        frames and padded DATA are recorded and not sent through h2 0.4. The
        default session road is the WebSocket upgrade of HTTP/1.1 and does not
        read it.
    --cover-credential
        ask the relay for a cover name's application-layer credential after the
        TLS handshake, check it, and upgrade on that connection. It checks the
        issuer, chain, window, subject key and exporter. Off by default, and
        refused with --h2-shape because that road has no credential step.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET and a node's cf://HOST: this client's key in
        FILE, made when missing (default: client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME and a node's cf://HOST: the node's key, or its fingerprint
        SHA256:..., in place of the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --iroh-key FILE
        the same as --client-key, by its earlier name.
    --iroh-relay URLS
        iroh:TICKET: the iroh relays to try after the ticket's,
        https://HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env PODSSH_IROH_RELAY, else the
        net's relay members' own, then n0's).
    --iroh-ticket TICKET
        node://NAME: race the iroh road to TICKET, first, with the pair's road;
        the first that answers carries the session; a build with the feature
        iroh.
    --derp-ticket TICKET
        node://NAME: race the DERP road to TICKET, after the iroh road and the
        pair's road; the ticket is kept under NAME, and a later run that gives
        none dials it when the roads before it fail.
    --opentunnel-name HOST
        node://NAME: race the OpenTunnel road to HOST, the name that the node
        prints (ROUTE.ID.opentunnel.xyz), 250 ms after the road before it; the
        name is kept under NAME, and a later run that gives none dials it when
        each road before it failed.
    --pinggy-name HOST#PIN
        node://NAME: race the Pinggy road to HOST, the tunnel's name that the
        node prints, 250 ms after the road before it; its TLS takes only a
        certificate of the key of PIN (SHA256:..., which the node prints with
        the name); a name with no pin is refused (64); the address is kept
        under NAME, and a later run that gives none dials it last, when each
        road before it failed; a free tunnel's name changes each hour, its pin
        does not.
    --tunnel-url URL
        node://NAME: race the road of a tunnel of HTTP made by ssh -R
        (localhost.run's, Sandhole's, srv.us's or tunnl.gg's) to https://HOST,
        the name that the node prints; it starts 250 ms after the road before
        it: a WebSocket at / of HOST, whose TLS this host's roots verify; the
        name is kept under NAME; a later run that gives none dials it, or the
        one of the node's record, last, when each road before it failed; a free
        name changes after a few hours.
    --derp-server SERVERS
        derp:TICKET and node://NAME: the DERP servers to try after the
        ticket's, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env PODSSH_DERP_SERVER, else
        Tailscale's tailcat fleet).
    --exit NAME
        start the road at NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit): it dials the destination, or the first hop of -J,
        from its own host; on each road between the two, or with --carrier ADDR
        on that stream alone; the host key is the destination's; NAME auto: the
        exit whose route of the net holds the first hop's address.
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, as its one road, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a
        program started with no shell, as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node
        --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's
        bucket of the S3 API; or dns:FILE, the node's DNS road; NAME is then
        the label under which the node's key is pinned; with --exit NAME, the
        exit at the other end of ADDR dials the host.
    --gsr-secret-file FILE
        node://NAME: race the GSRN road last, to the node that serves it with
        the secret of FILE, a private file of yours (default: env
        PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE); never with --no-e2e; a build with the feature
        gsr.
    --persist
        run the shell in the server's tmux, and after a lost link connect again
        and attach it again; tmux is probed.
    --resume-deadline TIME
        node://NAME and iroh:TICKET: wait at most TIME for a new link after a
        loss, though the node keeps the session longer: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d,
        from 1 minute to 72 h (default: as long as the node keeps it).
    --no-resume
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET, derp:TICKET, a node's cf://HOST and --exit
        NAME: no resume; the session ends with its link, and the node, asked
        so, keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --grant FILE
        node://NAME: a grant used once, an OpenSSH certificate of this client's
        key, which the end-to-end channel carries to the node for this session
        alone; a URL is refused.
    --bearer SIGNER
        node://NAME: a bearer of 30 s for this session's channel alone, in the
        place of --grant, which SIGNER signs: a podssh key file, agent for the
        SSH agent's first Ed25519 key, or agent:SHA256:...
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the remote status or
        signal, the end, the failure, the bytes and the relay.
    --idle-warn SECONDS
        through the relay: warn this long before its idle cut, once nothing
        crossed for the rest of it (default 30; 0: no warning; none with -q).
    --persist-name NAME
        the tmux session of --persist: letters, digits, _ and -, 32 at most
        (default podssh).
    --persist-forever
        with --persist: connect again after each loss, and after a first
        connection that failed, with no limit of attempts or of time.
    --install NAME
        make this tunnel, with -N and --persist, a service of this user named
        NAME, which starts it again whenever it ends: the ways of podssh node
        --install, with these words but --install NAME.
    --uninstall NAME
        remove the service that --install NAME made, its file of variables and
        its lock, and nothing else.
    --env-file FILE
        read the variables of FILE, a private file of NAME=VALUE lines, before
        anything else; hold FILE.lock while it runs, so that a second start
        ends at once: the file that --install writes.
    --attach NAME
        node://NAME: join the shell that the far end keeps as NAME, which ~d
        left; --attach DEST alone lists the kept shells.
    --take
        with --attach NAME: take the shell from the client that has it, whose
        session ends.
    --reset
        with --attach NAME: the shell's last output from a clean boundary, not
        the output from where this client left.
    --predict
        show each typed key at once, underlined, before its echo; only to
        podssh serve with a pty, above a round trip of 120 ms.
    --access-host HOST
        the relay's roads to HOST carry the credentials of Cloudflare Access in
        their headers, in the place of AccessHost of the settings; HOST[,...],
        repeatable; no other host gets them.
    --expect TEXT
        with a pty: wait for TEXT in the output, then send the --send after it;
        repeatable, the rules in order.
    --send TEXT
        the keys of the --expect before it: \r, \n, \t, \\ and \xNN are read;
        no secret, as each process reads argv.
    --expect-timeout TIME
        how long each --expect waits, as 30s, 2m or 500ms (default 30s); a miss
        ends the session with 255.
    --upgrade
        log in, then move the session to a temporary node that the server's
        podssh starts, which resumes after a lost link; with no podssh there,
        the session stays.
    --no-signal
        with no pty, Ctrl-C ends podssh at once, as OpenSSH's ssh; by default
        it sends signal INT to the command first.
    --sudo
        run the command as root with sudo -S, with no pty; the password is
        asked here (terminal or SSH_ASKPASS).
    --record FILE
        keep the session's output, with its timing, in FILE as asciicast v2
        (mode 0600, never over a file); podssh play shows it again.
    --su
        run the command as root with su -c, in a pty; the password is asked
        here (terminal or SSH_ASKPASS).
    --snippet NAME
        run the command NAME of the settings file's [snippets]: the words after
        the host fill its {{1}} to {{9}}, each value quoted; it is shown, and
        asked, before it runs.
    --yes
        run the --snippet with no question; its command is still shown on
        stderr, but with -q.
    -x, --no-x11
        no X11 forwarding (the default); the last of -X, -Y and -x wins.
    -A, --forward-agent
        forward the agent: while the session lasts, the server may use its keys
        (ForwardAgent=yes).
    -a, --no-agent-forwarding
        no agent forwarding (the default; the last of -A and -a wins).
    -k, --no-gssapi-delegation
        no GSSAPI delegation (podssh never delegates credentials).
    -g, --gateway-ports
        remote hosts may connect to local forwarded ports: -L and -D with no
        address listen on each address.
    -P, --tag TAG
        the Tag that Match tagged reads, as OpenSSH's -P; not a port, which is
        -p.
    -L, --forward-local SPEC
        [BIND:]PORT:HOST:HOSTPORT or PATH:HOST:HOSTPORT: listen here; each
        connection goes on from the server.
    -R, --forward-remote SPEC
        [BIND:]PORT:HOST:HOSTPORT, a socket path in place of either side, or
        [BIND:]PORT alone for SOCKS: the server listens; each connection goes
        on from here, through the proxy.
    -D, --dynamic-forward SPEC
        [BIND:]PORT or PATH: a SOCKS4 and SOCKS5 proxy here; each connection
        goes on from the server.
    -B, --bind-interface IFACE
        podssh chooses no source address: the relay does, or the system with
        --direct. Refused.
    -b, --bind-address ADDR
        podssh chooses no source address: the relay does, or the system with
        --direct. Refused.
    -c, --cipher CIPHERS
        the ciphers are a list of the keyword Ciphers, which podssh applies.
        Refused. Use -o Ciphers=LIST.
    -m, --mac MACS
        the MACs are a list of the keyword MACs, which podssh applies. Refused.
        Use -o MACs=LIST.
    -f, --detach
        go to the background once logged in and the request went, with a
        command or -N (see --detach).
    --restart
        with -f or --detach: a small process in the background starts the run
        again whenever it ends, but after 64, 77 or 78 or a stop of that
        process; it never gives up.
    --detach-name NAME
        with --detach: the run's name, letters, digits, _ and -, 64 at most; a
        second start of a name that runs refuses (75), and podssh detached
        shows and stops it (default: the verb and the pid).
    -G, --print-config
        print the settings in effect, as ssh -G does, and connect to nothing.
    --list-hosts
        print a JSON array on stdout, one record for each literal Host alias of
        ssh_config as a connection to it resolves, and connect to nothing.
    -I, --pkcs11 LIBRARY
        PKCS#11 keys are not supported. Refused. Use -i FILE.
    -K, --gssapi
        GSSAPI authentication is not supported. Refused. Use -i FILE or a
        password.
    -M, --control-master
        be the control master of -S: other runs share this connection (a second
        -M asks first).
    -O, --control-command CMD
        ask the control master of -S: check, forward, cancel, exit or stop.
    -S, --control-path PATH
        the control socket: use its master, or be it with -M (ControlPath);
        none shares nothing.
    -Q, --query QUERY
        -G prints the lists of algorithms that podssh will offer. Refused. Use
        -G.
    -w, --tunnel TUN
        a tunnel device needs privileges that podssh never assumes. Refused.
        Use -W HOST:PORT.
    -X, --forward-x11
        X11 forwarding to DISPLAY, untrusted: a cookie that xauth makes;
        refused before the connection when the probe fails.
    -Y, --forward-x11-trusted
        X11 forwarding to DISPLAY, trusted: the X server's own cookie, never
        sent to the server.
    -y, --syslog
        podssh does not write to syslog; where stderr is the journal's stream,
        an error or a warning reaches it at its priority (JOURNAL_STREAM).
        Refused. Use -E LOGFILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Keywords for -o NAME=VALUE:
    The name is not case-sensitive. NAME=VALUE, NAME VALUE and NAME = VALUE are
    the same. For a single value, the first one given wins, as in OpenSSH. An
    unknown keyword is an error before podssh connects.

    AddressFamily=any|inet|inet6
        inet is -4 and inet6 is -6
    BatchMode=yes|no
        yes: never prompt; a prompt becomes an error
    CASignatureAlgorithms=LIST
        the signatures with which a CA that a @cert-authority line names may
        sign a host certificate; another refuses it with 255
    ChallengeResponseAuthentication=yes|no
        the old name of KbdInteractiveAuthentication
    Ciphers=LIST
        the ciphers to offer, in order
    ClearAllForwardings=yes|no
        yes: no -L, -D or -R, from the command line or a file (default no)
    Compression=yes|no
        the same as -C
    ControlMaster=yes|no|ask|auto|autoask
        be the master of ControlPath (yes is -M, ask is -MM; auto: when none
        answers); Unix only (default no)
    ControlPath=PATH|none
        the control socket: a run goes through its master when one answers (the
        same as -S); it takes the tokens
    ControlPersist=yes|no|TIME
        how long a -N master stays with no client (default no)
    ConnectTimeout=SECONDS
        the limit on the SSH handshake, and on each answer of the server while
        podssh logs in, a question's time left out (default 60)
    ConnectionAttempts=1-100
        rounds over the relay hosts, or dials with --direct (default 1)
    DynamicForward=[BIND:]PORT|PATH
        the same as -D; repeatable
    EscapeChar=CHAR|^X|none
        the same as -e
    ExitOnForwardFailure=yes|no
        yes: a forward of -R that the server refuses ends the run with 255
    ForkAfterAuthentication=yes|no
        yes is -f: the run goes to the background once its request went, with a
        command or -N
    ForwardAgent=yes|no|PATH|$NAME
        yes is -A: while the session lasts, the server may use the agent that
        podssh logs in with; PATH, or the variable NAME, names another agent
        (default no)
    ForwardX11=yes|no
        yes is -X: the server may open X11 channels to DISPLAY (default no)
    ForwardX11Timeout=TIME
        -X: no new X11 channel after this time; 0 for none (default 20m)
    ForwardX11Trusted=yes|no
        yes: -X gives the X server's own cookie, as -Y does (default no)
    GatewayPorts=yes|no
        the same as -g (default no)
    GlobalKnownHostsFile=FILE...|none
        the system known_hosts files
    HostKeyAlgorithms=LIST
        the host key algorithms to ask for; those that known_hosts records for
        the host go first within it
    HostKeyAlias=NAME
        look up and record the host key under this name, in lowercase
    HostName=HOST
        the host to connect to, in place of the destination; %h is the host as
        typed
    IdentitiesOnly=yes|no
        yes: use only the identity files, not the other keys of the agent
    IdentityAgent=PATH|$NAME|SSH_AUTH_SOCK|none
        the agent socket (a named pipe on Windows), or the variable NAME that
        holds its path; none: no agent
    IdentityFile=FILE
        the same as -i; repeatable
    IgnoreUnknown=PATTERN,...
        unknown keywords to accept with no effect, when they come after it
    KbdInteractiveAuthentication=yes|no
        allow keyboard-interactive authentication
    KexAlgorithms=LIST
        the key exchanges to offer, in order
    LocalCommand=COMMAND
        with PermitLocalCommand yes: run COMMAND here after the login, as SHELL
        -c COMMAND; it takes the % tokens, and %T
    LocalForward=[BIND:]PORT HOST:HOSTPORT
        the same as -L, with a space between the two sides; repeatable
    LogLevel=QUIET|FATAL|ERROR|INFO|VERBOSE|DEBUG|DEBUG2|DEBUG3
        how much podssh says on stderr (default INFO)
    MACs=LIST
        the MACs to offer, in order; a cipher with its own, such as AES-GCM,
        uses none
    NumberOfPasswordPrompts=N
        password attempts (default 3)
    PasswordAuthentication=yes|no
        allow password authentication
    PermitLocalCommand=yes|no
        yes: run LocalCommand (default no)
    Port=PORT
        the same as -p
    PreferredAuthentications=LIST
        publickey, keyboard-interactive and password, in the order to try them
    ProxyJump=HOSTS|none
        the same as -J
    PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=LIST
        the algorithms that podssh signs a login with: a key of another is not
        offered; an RSA key signs with the list's first of RSA when the
        server's best is not in it
    PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes=LIST
        the old name of PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms
    PubkeyAuthentication=yes|no
        allow key authentication
    RemoteCommand=COMMAND
        the command to run when the command line gives none; it takes the %
        tokens
    RemoteForward=LISTEN [TARGET]
        the same as -R: a port or a socket path, then HOST:PORT or a socket
        here, or none for SOCKS; repeatable
    RequestTTY=auto|yes|force|no
        yes is -t, force is -tt, no is -T
    RequiredRSASize=BITS
        the least RSA key: a smaller key of the user is not offered; a smaller
        host key, or key of the CA of a host certificate, ends the connection
        with 255; under 1024 it changes nothing (default 1024)
    SendEnv=NAME...
        send these local variables; the server decides which to accept
    ServerAliveCountMax=N
        keepalives with no answer before podssh ends the session (default 3)
    ServerAliveInterval=SECONDS
        seconds between keepalives (default 60; 0 turns them off)
    SessionType=none|subsystem|default
        none is -N and subsystem is -s
    SetEnv=NAME=VALUE...
        set these variables on the server
    StdinNull=yes|no
        the same as -n
    Tag=NAME
        the tag that Match tagged reads; the same as -P
    StrictHostKeyChecking=yes|accept-new|no|ask
        what to do with an unknown host key (default ask); a changed key is
        refused with each value
    User=USER
        the same as -l, but it takes the % tokens, not %C or %r
    UserKnownHostsFile=FILE...|none
        the user's known_hosts files; a new host key goes to the first
    XAuthLocation=PATH
        the xauth that makes the untrusted cookie of -X (default: xauth in
        PATH)

    A LIST of Ciphers, MACs, KexAlgorithms, HostKeyAlgorithms,
    PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms or CASignatureAlgorithms is read as OpenSSH reads
    it: a comma list replaces podssh's own, one that starts with + adds to it,
    with - takes from it, and with ^ puts its names first; a name may be a
    pattern of * and ?. A name that podssh does not speak is left out, and -v
    says so; a list that leaves nothing is refused before anything connects
    (64; 78 in a file), and names what podssh speaks. -G prints each list as
    podssh will offer it.

    ProxyCommand
        refused: podssh ssh reaches the host through the relay itself: none,
        and podssh proxy %h %p, are accepted, and the first value holds, as in
        OpenSSH, so -o ProxyCommand=none goes past a file's; a command of a
        file is refused (exit 78), and its line names that flag; to use
        OpenSSH, give it ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p'
    RevokedHostKeys
        refused: mark the keys @revoked in a known_hosts file
    KnownHostsCommand
        refused: list the keys in a known_hosts file
    Include
        refused: a keyword of ssh_config files, not an option
    Match
        refused: a keyword of ssh_config files, not an option
    Host
        refused: a keyword of ssh_config files, not an option

    Accepted and not applied. podssh gives one note at the default level for a
    value that you gave, on the command line or in your own ssh_config. It
    gives none for the system's file, which says it at -v, and none with -q:

    BindAddress
        not applied: podssh binds no socket of its own: the relay dials, or the
        system chooses the address with --direct
    BindInterface
        not applied: podssh binds no socket of its own: the relay dials, or the
        system chooses the interface with --direct
    CertificateFile
        not applied: podssh offers no certificate of the user, only keys
    ChannelTimeout
        not applied: podssh closes no channel for being idle
    IPQoS
        not applied: podssh leaves the type of service of its connection to the
        system
    RekeyLimit
        not applied: podssh rekeys at russh's limits, after 1 GiB each way or
        an hour
    SecurityKeyProvider
        not applied: podssh speaks to a security key itself, with no provider
        library
    TCPKeepAlive
        not applied: podssh leaves TCP keepalives to the system;
        ServerAliveInterval finds a dead link
    Tunnel
        not applied: podssh opens no tun device; -W and -D carry a stream
    TunnelDevice
        not applied: podssh opens no tun device
    UpdateHostKeys
        not applied: podssh records no host key that the server sends after the
        login
    VerifyHostKeyDNS
        not applied: podssh checks host keys against known_hosts alone
    WarnWeakCrypto
        not applied: podssh says nothing of the algorithms that it negotiated

    Accepted with no effect, because they change nothing that podssh does; -v
    names the place of each: AddKeysToAgent, CanonicalDomains,
    CanonicalizeFallbackLocal, CanonicalizeHostname, CanonicalizeMaxDots,
    CanonicalizePermittedCNAMEs, CheckHostIP, EnableEscapeCommandline,
    EnableSSHKeysign, FingerprintHash; GSSAPIAuthentication,
    GSSAPIClientIdentity, GSSAPIDelegateCredentials, GSSAPIKeyExchange,
    GSSAPIKexAlgorithms, GSSAPIRenewalForcesRekey, GSSAPIServerIdentity,
    GSSAPITrustDns, HashKnownHosts, HostbasedAcceptedAlgorithms;
    HostbasedAuthentication, LogVerbose, NoHostAuthenticationForLocalhost,
    ObscureKeystrokeTiming, StreamLocalBindMask, StreamLocalBindUnlink,
    SyslogFacility, VersionAddendum, VisualHostKey.

  Examples:
    log in to a host, through the relay
        $ podssh ssh user@example.org

    run one command; podssh exits with its exit status
        $ podssh ssh user@example.org 'uname -a'

    keys for a menu after the login, then the session; with no match in 30 s,
    exit 255
        $ podssh ssh -tt --expect 'Choice: ' --send '2\r' user@example.org

    the command logs of the settings file, nginx as its {{1}}: shown, quoted,
    and asked first
        $ podssh ssh --snippet logs user@example.org nginx

    a Unix socket on the server, on stdin and stdout
        $ podssh ssh -W /run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432 user@db.example.org

    keep what a session showed, with its timing, and show it again twice as
    fast
        $ podssh ssh -tt --record top.cast user@example.org top && podssh play --speed 2 top.cast

    SSH to a host from the exit gw, then a local SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy whose
    connections start there
        $ podssh ssh --exit gw git@github.com && podssh exit gw --listen 127.0.0.1:1080

    a port, a key, and a new host key recorded with no question
        $ podssh ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new user@example.org

    an interactive program, from a host with no terminal
        $ podssh ssh -tt user@example.org top

    a host whose key fingerprint the operator gave: that key only, and no
    known_hosts
        $ podssh ssh --host-key-fingerprint SHA256:JfDOvc6FaJOB34ANs+ou385/Kh+mMQhnUx0gHXVAfUI user@example.org

    a shell in the server's tmux, attached again after a lost link
        $ podssh ssh --persist user@example.org

    through a jump host
        $ podssh ssh -J user@bastion.example.org user@inner.example.org

    a host from a script: -- before it, so it is never read as a flag
        $ podssh ssh -- user@example.org uptime

    an IPv6 address with a port, with no relay
        $ podssh ssh --direct 'user@[2001:db8::1]:2222'

    send a file with no scp
        $ podssh ssh user@example.org 'cat > notes.txt' < notes.txt

    on a host with no DNS: give the address of the relay
        $ podssh ssh --relay-addr tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev=ADDRESS user@example.org

    try these relay hosts, in this order
        $ podssh ssh --relay-host tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev,tcp-us-east-1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev user@example.org

    no relay: other products' public forwarders, in this order; they publish no
    limit
        $ podssh ssh --forwarder mudlet,ssheasy user@example.org
