    from outside, log in to the node's SSH server with the operator's file
        $ podssh ssh --pair-file lab-operator.json node://user@lab

    log in, then move the session to a node that the server's own podssh
    starts: it resumes after a lost link
        $ podssh ssh --upgrade user@example.org

    from anywhere, a session through that relay, with this client's key on its
    list
        $ podssh ssh --relay-host https://NAME.trycloudflare.com user@example.org

podssh each
  one command on many hosts at once: each line with its host, and the worst
  status as the exit.

  podssh each HOSTS -- COMMAND runs one command on each host of a comma list,
  [user@]host[:port],..., through the relay or with --direct. It takes the
  connection flags of podssh ssh: -p and -l for each host that names none, -i,
  -o, -F and -J; the Host blocks of ssh_config apply to each host as podssh ssh
  applies them. A host can be a node, node://[user@]NAME or a name of the net.
  It is reached over the roads that podssh ssh races to it, one connection for
  each node. A host can also be the node of an iroh: or derp: ticket, over its
  road (the client's key of the cache; PODSSH_DERP_SERVER names DERP's servers,
  and in a build with the iroh road its variable names the relays). Each host
  is checked before anything connects: a bad one exits 64, and nothing has run
  anywhere. A host named twice runs once. Commas part the hosts of the command
  line, and a blank parts none: 'a b', or a tab, is refused (64), and the
  refusal gives a,b; a blank beside a comma is dropped.

  An item of the list takes the braces of bash: web{1..3} is web1, web2 and
  web3, {01..12} keeps its zero padding, {a..c} gives letters, {1..9..2} a
  step, a{b,c}d is abd and acd, and braces nest. @NAME is the group NAME of the
  settings file (see FILES): after a line [groups], each line is NAME HOSTS.
  Its hosts are a list of the same kind, parted by commas or blanks, and can
  name groups. 1000 hosts at most; more, none, an empty host, a range that runs
  backwards or a group that is not there is a usage error (64). A group that
  names itself, through others or not, is refused with the file (78). Square
  brackets stay an IPv6 address. podssh ssh takes a pattern of one host, and
  refuses one of more, naming podssh each.

  At most --parallel hosts run at once (8; 1 to 64), each on a connection of
  its own. No host gets a terminal or stdin: each session is as podssh ssh -T
  -n makes it. Nothing asks a question: BatchMode is on, and an unknown host
  key refuses its host and names its fingerprint and -o
  StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new, which records each new key. Through the
  relay, one token serves each host.

  Each line of a host's output starts with HOST: , on stdout or stderr as the
  host wrote it, and podssh's own messages about a host start with podssh:
  HOST: . A line is never cut by another host's; one longer than 64 KiB comes
  in pieces, each with its host. With --output-dir DIR, the bytes go unchanged
  into DIR/HOST.out and DIR/HOST.err, and the exit status into DIR/HOST.status
  at the host's end; each byte of HOST but a letter, a digit, a dot, an
  underscore, a hyphen and @ is written %XX. The files are made before anything
  connects (73 when they cannot be), and a host with no status file did not
  run.

  --snippet NAME runs the command NAME of the settings file on each host, as
  podssh ssh --snippet runs it (see podssh ssh): the words after HOSTS fill
  {{1}} to {{9}}, and {{host}}, {{user}} and {{port}} are those of each host.
  podssh shows each host and its command once, before anything connects and
  before a file of --output-dir is made. It asks once for all the hosts; --yes
  runs them with no question.

  -o RemoteCommand=COMMAND gives the command in place of -- COMMAND, as OpenSSH
  reads it. A command after HOSTS wins over it, and RemoteCommand none is no
  command (exit 64).

  At the end a summary on stderr gives each host and its status; -q leaves it
  out. The exit status is the largest of the hosts': 0 only when each host gave
  0, and 255 when one could not connect or log in. With --fail-fast no host
  starts after one failed, and the hosts that run end as they end.

  For a program: --result-file FILE writes one JSON object to FILE at the end,
  a new file for its owner alone, and the lines stay as they are; - is refused
  (64). --json writes the same object on stdout once each host ended, with each
  host's stdout and stderr in its record in place of the lines: 1 MiB of each
  at most, and truncated when more came. Each is text when it is UTF-8 and else
  base64, as stdout_encoding and stderr_encoding say; podssh's own lines stay
  on stderr. With --output-dir the bytes go to the files, and the record names
  them (files). The object has schema, podssh (the version), exit, counts
  (hosts, ok, failed and not_started) and hosts, in the order of the list. Each
  host has host, destination (user@host:port) and exit (its part, null when it
  did not start). It has status, signal, end, failure, bytes and relay as
  podssh ssh --result-file gives them. It also has error (the words of its
  failure), duration_ms and files. Each host's facts are its own session's,
  also when hosts fail at once. With --interactive, --json and --result-file
  are refused (64).

  podssh each --interactive HOSTS opens a shell with no pty on each host, 64
  hosts at most. Each line typed goes to the hosts of the selection, at first
  each host; the output of each comes as HOST: LINE. The terminal keeps its
  normal mode, so that its own line discipline edits the line. A line that
  starts with : is for podssh: :all, :none, :only HOST..., :list, :intr and
  :help. In :only, braces and @GROUP are as in HOSTS, and USER@ may be left
  out. :intr signals INT to each selected host, which a server may ignore; a
  line that starts with :: goes to the hosts with one : less. With --confirm, a
  line for more than one host waits for a second Enter, and another line drops
  it. A COMMAND, --parallel, --fail-fast and --output-dir are refused (64).

  The emergency stop is Ctrl-\ (SIGQUIT) on Unix and Ctrl-Break on Windows: at
  once, also while a line is half typed, no host is selected, and each byte
  that waits for a host is dropped; podssh says broadcast stopped; :all starts
  it again. On Unix, --stop-key ^X makes another control key the stop for the
  run, as the terminal's QUIT character. It puts the old one back at the end; a
  key that the terminal keeps for INTR, EOF, SUSP, ERASE, KILL or the end of a
  line is refused (64). So is the flag on Windows. It is armed before anything
  connects, and where it cannot be, podssh exits 78. Each host has a queue of
  64 KiB, what its shell has not read yet: a line that does not fit does not go
  to that host, which leaves the selection, and podssh names it. Ctrl-C goes to
  no host. At the end of the input (Ctrl-D, or Ctrl-Z on Windows), each shell
  reads what waits for it, then its end; Ctrl-C then cuts the hosts whose shell
  still runs, each with 130.

  Usage: podssh each [OPTIONS] HOSTS [--] COMMAND...

  Arguments:
    [HOSTS]
        the hosts, a comma list of [user@]host[:port], each named as it is
        written here; braces as in bash, web{01..12} and {a,b}, and @GROUP of
        the settings file.
    [COMMAND]...
        the command to run on each host, its words joined with spaces as
        OpenSSH joins them; none with --interactive.

  Options:
    --parallel N
        at most N hosts at once, 1 to 64 (default 8).
    --fail-fast
        start no new host after one failed; the hosts that run end as they end.
    --output-dir DIR
        each host's output, unchanged, in DIR/HOST.out and DIR/HOST.err, and
        its status in DIR/HOST.status.
    --json
        at the end, one JSON object on stdout: each host's exit, status,
        failure and its stdout and stderr (1 MiB each at most), and no line
        with a label.
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: each host's exit, status or
        signal, end, failure, bytes and relay; the lines stay as they are.
    --snippet NAME
        run the command NAME of the settings file's [snippets]: the words after
        the host fill its {{1}} to {{9}}, each value quoted; it is shown, and
        asked, before it runs.
    --yes
        run the --snippet with no question; its command is still shown on
        stderr, but with -q.
    --interactive
        a shell with no pty on each host, and each line typed goes to the
        selected hosts; Ctrl-\ (Ctrl-Break on Windows) stops it at once.
    --confirm
        with --interactive: a line for more than one host waits for a second
        Enter.
    --stop-key KEY
        with --interactive: the emergency stop is the control key KEY, as ^X,
        in place of Ctrl-\ (Unix).
    -p, --port PORT
        port to connect to, for each host that names none.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as, for each host; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors and the summary included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    the same command on three hosts, two at once: each line starts with its
    host; the exit is the worst
        $ podssh each --parallel 2 web1.example.org,web2.example.org,user@db.example.org -- uptime

    twelve hosts in one word, and the group db of the settings file; each host
    once
        $ podssh each 'web{01..12}.example.org,@db' -- 'df -h /'

    each line typed to the shells of three hosts; Ctrl-\ (Ctrl-Break on
    Windows) stops it at once
        $ podssh each --interactive 'web{1..3}.example.org'

podssh containers
  the containers of a host, of docker, podman or kubectl, each with the command
  that enters it.

  podssh containers HOST logs in to HOST as podssh ssh does, through the relay
  or with --direct, with the connection flags of podssh ssh: -p, -l, -i, -o, -F
  and -J. One command, with no pty, runs sh there: sh looks for docker, podman
  and kubectl on its PATH, and lists the containers that each one has: the
  names of docker ps and of podman ps, and the pods of kubectl in its current
  context and namespace. kubectl waits 20 s at most for them. --tool asks one
  of them alone. No program runs here, and none runs there that sh did not
  find. The list waits 60 s at most.

  Each line on stdout gives the tool, the name, and the podssh ssh command that
  enters that container with its sh and a pty. The command has the connection
  flags that were given. A name has letters, digits, underscores, dots and
  hyphens alone, with a letter or a digit first (and pod/ first for kubectl).
  So each shell reads it as one word: a name of another form is left out and
  named on stderr. A tool that fails (no access to the socket of docker, a
  cluster that does not answer) gives its lines on stderr. The other tools go
  on.

  --exec NAME enters NAME on the same connection after the list, so that a
  password is asked once: the tool that lists it runs its exec there, with the
  program of --shell (sh by default). The session has a pty when this side has
  a terminal, or with -tt, and the tool then gets -i and -t; with no pty, -i
  alone. When docker and podman each list NAME, the first in the order docker,
  podman, kubectl is entered, and --tool enters another. For kubectl, NAME may
  leave out pod/.

  The exit status: 0 when each tool gave its whole list; 65 when a tool listed
  a name that is left out; 69 when the host has none of the tools, or one of
  them failed. 69 also when sh did not run the list to its end, or --exec names
  no container that a list has; 255 when the connection or the login failed.
  With --exec, the status of the session, as podssh ssh gives it. A node:// or
  iroh: destination is for podssh ssh (64), and the forwards, X11 and the
  control socket of ssh_config are not used.

  Usage: podssh containers [OPTIONS] [user@]host

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host]
        the host whose containers are listed: [user@]host, host:PORT,
        [user@][IPV6]:PORT or ssh://[user@]host[:PORT].

  Options:
    --exec NAME
        enter the container NAME, as the list names it (pod/ may be left out),
        on the same connection.
    --shell PROG
        with --exec: the program to start in the container (default sh).
    --tool TOOL
        ask docker, podman or kubectl alone (default: each of them that the
        host has).
    -t, --force-tty
        with --exec: twice (-tt), a pty also when this side has no terminal.
    -p, --port PORT
        port to connect to; never a proxy port.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    the containers of a host, of docker, podman and kubectl, each with the
    command that enters it
        $ podssh containers user@example.org

    enter one of them on the same connection, with bash
        $ podssh containers --exec web --shell bash user@example.org

podssh run
  copy a project to a host, only the files that changed, then run a command in
  it, with its exit status.

  podssh run HOST -- COMMAND copies the project here (the working directory, or
  --from DIR) to the host. It then runs the command in its far directory, on
  the same connection, and exits with the command's status. The far directory
  is DIR of HOST:DIR, under the home directory when it is relative; with none,
  ~/.podssh/run/NAME, NAME the name of the project here. A parent that is not
  there is made, with mode 0700. The connection flags are those of podssh ssh,
  and the Host blocks of ssh_config apply. HOST can be a node,
  node://[user@]NAME, a name of the net, or an iroh: or derp: ticket.

  The copy is that of podssh cp for a directory, over SFTP, with the times
  kept: each file to a temporary name, verified by its digest, then renamed,
  several files at once, as podssh cp sends them by default. So the next run
  sends only the files whose size or time of change differs from the far
  file's. target/, node_modules/ and .git/ never go, at any depth. Nor does
  what the project's .podsshignore, --exclude and --exclude-from leave out.
  .podsshignore has a pattern a line, as the file of --exclude-from;
  --no-ignore sends the first four too, and --exclude and --exclude-from still
  apply. Before the command starts, one line on stderr says what the copy did,
  as podssh cp says it at its end: the files copied, those left as they were,
  the paths that the excludes left out, and how long it took; -q silences it,
  and -v names each path left out with its pattern.

  Nothing on the host is removed: an exclude leaves a path out of the copy, and
  what an earlier run sent stays on the host. podssh run removes no path there.
  podssh cp -r has no default excludes and reads no .podsshignore: it copies
  what its command line names, and only --exclude and --exclude-from leave
  paths out.

  --dry-run connects and makes the copy's looks, which only read. Then it says
  on stdout each action that the copy would take, as podssh cp -r --dry-run
  says it, but only for what changed: a mkdir for each directory that is not
  there; a copy for each file whose size or time differs; a link for each link
  that is not there as it is here; then the line run cd DIR && COMMAND. Nothing
  changes on either side and nothing runs; stderr counts the paths that the
  excludes left out. It exits 0, or 255 when the far side cannot be read, with
  no plan.

  The command runs as cd DIR && COMMAND in the login shell, with stdin, as
  podssh ssh runs one. When the copy used most of what the relay carries in one
  session, the command runs on a new session. A copy that failed exits 255 and
  runs nothing; else the exit status is the command's, with the rules of podssh
  ssh.

  --result-file FILE writes one JSON object to FILE at the end, also of a run
  refused before it connected: the keys of podssh cp, its verb run, files and
  transferred of the copy (up alone); and the status, signal, end and bytes of
  the command as podssh ssh --result-file gives them; bytes is null when the
  command did not run, as after a copy that failed. - is refused (exit 64), as
  stdout is the command's.

  target/, node_modules/ and .git/ never go, at any depth, nor what the
  project's .podsshignore names (a pattern a line). --no-ignore sends them. The
  summary counts what they left out, and -v names each.

  An exclude removes nothing on the host. What an earlier run sent stays.

  podssh cp -r has no default excludes, and reads no .podsshignore.

  Usage: podssh run [OPTIONS] [user@]host[:DIR] [--] COMMAND...

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host[:DIR]]
        the host, and the far directory of the project: under the home
        directory when it is relative, ~/.podssh/run/NAME when none is named;
        scp://[user@]host[:port][/DIR] too.
    [COMMAND]...
        the command to run in the far directory, its words joined with spaces
        as OpenSSH joins them.

  Options:
    --from DIR
        the project to copy (default: the working directory); the far directory
        takes its name.
    --exclude PATTERN
        leave out one more path, beside target/, node_modules/, .git/ and the
        patterns of the project's .podsshignore, which never go: * and ? within
        a name; with a /, from the root of the project; repeatable; it removes
        nothing on the host, so what an earlier run sent stays.
    --exclude-from FILE
        the --exclude patterns of FILE, one a line; # starts a comment.
    --no-ignore
        send target/, node_modules/, .git/ and what .podsshignore names too;
        --exclude and --exclude-from still apply.
    --dry-run
        say on stdout what the copy would change (mkdir, copy, link, skip),
        then the command as run cd DIR && COMMAND; change nothing on either
        side, and run nothing.
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the command's status or
        signal, end and bytes, the files of the copy and their bytes, the
        failure and the relay.
    -p, --port PORT
        port to connect to.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    copy the project here to a stronger host, only what changed, then run its
    tests there
        $ podssh run user@build.example.org -- cargo test

    what that run would copy, only what changed, and the command; nothing
    changes there, and nothing runs
        $ podssh run --dry-run user@build.example.org -- cargo test

podssh job
  jobs on a host that outlive the connection, each in its tmux, and a queue of
  them: start, submit, list, log, wait, fetch, stop; an ID is the 8 hex digits
  that start or submit printed.

  podssh job start HOST -- COMMAND starts the command on the host in a tmux
  session of its own, podssh-job-ID, and prints the ID on stdout: 8 hex digits.
  The job runs on after the connection ends. The command runs in sh, in the
  home directory, with no input; its output and its errors go to a file. The
  host is reached as podssh ssh reaches it, with its connection flags and the
  Host blocks of ssh_config. It is reached through the relay or with --direct,
  or as a node: node://[user@]NAME or a name of the net, whose TARGET has sh
  (an sshd, or podssh serve), or the node of an iroh: or derp: ticket.

  Nothing of podssh runs on the host but a POSIX sh script, which each call
  sends and keeps as ~/.podssh/jobs/jobs.sh. Each job is a directory beside it,
  of mode 0700, with its command, its state, its output and its exit status.
  tmux is probed, never assumed: with no tmux on PATH, start and submit exit
  255, name it, and start nothing. The refusal names the command that would
  install it, from the first package manager on the host's PATH. It looks for
  apk, apt-get, dnf, yum, zypper, pacman, brew or pkg. The command has sudo
  first for a login that is not root and has it, such as sudo apt-get install
  -y tmux; podssh runs no such command. ssh --persist says the same.

  --no-tmux, the user's choice and never the default, runs a job of start or
  submit with no tmux. It is for a host that has none and cannot get it: a
  runner of the far script, under nohup and in a session of its own where
  setsid is there, is the parent of the command. stop writes a file that asks
  the runner, which alone signals its own command: TERM to its process group
  where setsid made it the leader of one (on Linux, as /proc shows it), else to
  the command alone. KILL follows 10 s later; no call signals a process ID read
  from a file, which the system may have given to another process. stop waits
  15 s for the end, and a job that still runs keeps its directory (255). Such a
  job ends with the login where systemd's KillUserProcesses is on, as a tmux
  built without systemd does; and a stop does not reach a command that puts a
  process in a group of its own. Nor does it reach one started in the
  background where setsid is missing. list, log, wait and fetch work as for a
  job in tmux; a job whose runner is gone is lost. With --no-tmux, submit
  starts a runner of the queue in the same way, whose lock is the directory
  runner.lock.

  podssh job list HOST prints a line for each job, in the order of their
  starts: the ID, the state (queued; running; done; or lost, when neither the
  job's session nor its status is there, as after a restart of the host). Then
  the exit status (a dash while there is none) and the command. podssh job log
  HOST ID writes the job's output to stdout, also after its end. podssh job
  stop HOST ID ends the tmux session of that exact name, never another, and
  removes the job's directory with its output.

  podssh job log --follow HOST ID writes the job's output as it comes, on one
  connection, and exits with the job's status once it ended: 255 for a job that
  is lost, and 75 at --timeout DURATION, the job running on. Each call of the
  far script gives the new bytes each second, from the count of the bytes that
  came, for 20 s at most. A read of the state follows it; so a quiet job costs
  one call each 20 s. A call that broke goes on where the output stopped, with
  no byte twice. A dead link is found within 30 s, as for each call. --from-end
  starts at the size of the output then. --jsonl writes one JSON object for
  each line, {"event":"line","text":...}, or "base64" for bytes that are not
  UTF-8, then {"event":"end","state":...,"status":...}. A reader that went (|
  head) ends it, with 0.

  podssh job submit HOST -- COMMAND queues the command on the host and prints
  its ID; a runner in the host's tmux, podssh-runner, starts the oldest queued
  job while fewer jobs run there than the slots. --slots N sets the slots, 1 to
  64; they stay for the next submits, and are 1 until one sets them. The name
  of the runner's session is its lock, so that no second runner starts; with
  nothing queued and nothing running it ends, and the next submit starts one.
  HOST may be a list, with the braces and the groups of podssh each: one list
  of each host gives its jobs queued or running. The host with the fewest gets
  the job (the first of the list on a tie), and stdout gives HOST ID. There is
  no logic of GPUs and no list of devices: the slots are the only limit.

  podssh job wait HOST ID reads the job's state every 5 s, each read a call of
  its own, and exits with the job's status; after a lost connection it connects
  again, 5 times in a row at most. With --timeout DURATION, it exits 75 when
  the job has not ended within DURATION, and the job runs on. podssh job fetch
  HOST ID [DIR] copies the job's output to DIR/out, as podssh cp copies a file.
  With --files GLOB it also copies each file of that pattern of sh in the
  host's home directory to DIR/files, by its path; DIR is ./podssh-job-ID by
  default. A job that is queued or running is not fetched, as its output is not
  whole yet (75). podssh job list HOST --json gives one JSON object: the host,
  and each job with its id, state, status, started_ms and command.

  The exit status is that of podssh ssh: 0; 64 for a usage error and 78 for a
  setting, before anything connects; 255 when the host cannot be reached or
  logged in to, has no tmux, has no such job, or gives no answer. 255 also when
  a job of --no-tmux runs on after its stop. wait and log --follow give the
  job's status, or 75 at their --timeout.

  ID is the 8 hex digits that start or submit printed, as list shows it.

  fetch of a job that is queued or running exits 75, as its output is not
  whole. Run podssh job wait HOST ID first.

  Usage: podssh job [OPTIONS] SUBCOMMAND HOST [ID [DIR]] [-- COMMAND...]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        start, submit, list, log, wait, fetch or stop.
    [HOST]
        the host, [user@]host[:port], as podssh ssh takes it, with its Host
        blocks of ssh_config; for submit, a list of hosts as podssh each takes
        it, of which the one with the fewest jobs queued or running gets the
        job.
    [ID|COMMAND]...
        log, wait and stop: the job's ID; fetch: the ID, then the directory
        here (default ./podssh-job-ID); start and submit: the command after --,
        its words joined with spaces as OpenSSH joins them, for sh on the host.

  Options:
    --slots N
        submit: the jobs of the host's queue that run at once, 1 to 64; it
        stays for the next submits (default 1).
    --timeout DURATION
        wait, log --follow: exit 75 when the job has not ended within DURATION,
        such as 30s, 10m or 2h.
    --follow
        log: the output as it comes, on one connection, until the job ends; its
        status is then the exit.
    --from-end
        log --follow: only what the job writes from now on.
    --jsonl
        log --follow: one JSON object for each line of the output, then one
        with the state and the status.
    --files GLOB
        fetch: also the files of this pattern of sh in the host's home
        directory, under DIR/files.
    --json
        list: one JSON object on stdout: the host, and each job with its id,
        state, status, start and command.
    --no-tmux
        start, submit: run the job with no tmux, under nohup, for a host that
        has none and cannot get it.
    -p, --port PORT
        port to connect to.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    a long build that goes on after the connection, in the host's tmux: its ID,
    then each job of the host
        $ podssh job start user@build.example.org -- make all && podssh job list user@build.example.org

    the same on a host that has no tmux and cannot get it: the job runs under
    nohup
        $ podssh job start --no-tmux user@build.example.org -- make all

    a job's output as it comes, on one connection; the exit is the job's status
        $ podssh job log --follow user@build.example.org 0123abcd

    queue a build on the least busy of three hosts, wait 2 h at most for its
    status, then fetch its output
        $ podssh job submit 'build{1..3}.example.org' -- make all && podssh job wait --timeout 2h build2.example.org 0123abcd && podssh job fetch build2.example.org 0123abcd

podssh proxy
  ProxyCommand form: a byte pipe, not an SSH client; node://NAME reaches a
  node, as operator NAME does.

  podssh proxy sends stdin to the target through the relay, and the target's
  bytes to stdout. It is not an SSH client. Its main use is as the ProxyCommand
  of OpenSSH: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' user@host. It also
  carries each TCP protocol that a program can speak over stdin and stdout.

  podssh proxy has no direct road: it reaches the target through the relay, or
  through a road in the relay's place. For the direct road, from this host
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, the ProxyCommand of OpenSSH is podssh
  pipe: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh pipe - tcp:%h:%p' user@host (see podssh
  pipe).

  With OpenSSH, set -o ServerAliveInterval=60: the relay closes a session with
  no traffic (see THE RELAY). Once nothing crossed for all but 30 s of the
  relay's idle cut, podssh proxy says so on stderr, which OpenSSH shows;
  --idle-warn SECONDS sets that lead, and 0 turns it off.

  Where a first relay host offers it in its /relays.json (podssh relay serve
  does), podssh proxy carries the session in the resumable layer. The offer is
  read at each run with PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER=yes, and kept for a day when it is
  unset (see ENVIRONMENT). The session goes to that host alone, or to the
  process that its /relays.json names as forward.host, of the same deployment:
  the relay keeps its connection to the target while this host's link is lost.
  A new link resumes the session where it was. So an OpenSSH session outlives a
  drop of this host's network, for as long as the relay keeps it, 10 minutes by
  default. Each loss and resume is a line on stderr. The end of stdin is the
  end of the target's input there (the layer's END, a half-close of the relay's
  connection to the target). So a target that reads to the end of its input
  still answers, and the target's end ends the session; with a relay that takes
  no END, the end of stdin stops sending and keeps receiving until the target
  closes, as on the contract's road. OpenSSH's SIGHUP at its exit ends the
  session at the relay at once. A host that offers none, or that has no room
  for a new resumable session, takes the contract's road, with one line. For a
  host that offers none, that line comes with PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER=yes alone.
  Where podssh can run on the server's side, a roost in front of its sshd gives
  the same (podssh node --sshd, see podssh node). The roost needs no relay that
  keeps the session; this road is for an sshd where nothing else runs.

  The session ends when the target closes the connection or when stdout closes;
  both are a success. An error is one line on stderr; the codes are in EXIT
  STATUS.

  HOST can be an IPv6 address, bare (as OpenSSH gives %h) or in brackets. In
  one word, the form is [ADDRESS]:PORT. Through the relay, see the IPv6 note of
  ssh.

  Put -- before a HOST that a script did not write: podssh proxy -- "$HOST" 22.
  Else a HOST that starts with - is read as a flag.

  podssh proxy iap://PROJECT/ZONE/INSTANCE:PORT and podssh proxy
  eice://ENDPOINT/ADDRESS:PORT carry the pipe through a cloud's own tunnel to a
  VM, as podssh ssh does (see its notes). They take no relay and no relay flag;
  the port goes in the destination, 22 when none is given, and the destination
  takes no user. As the ProxyCommand of OpenSSH: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh
  proxy iap://my-project/us-central1-a/%h:%p' user@my-vm. On IAP the end of
  stdin ends the session once its bytes went, as IAP has no half-close.

  podssh proxy warp://HOST:PORT carries the pipe inside WARP's tunnel, as
  podssh ssh does (see its notes). It needs a build with the feature warp, as
  each release binary is: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy warp://%h:%p'
  user@host.

  podssh proxy tor://HOST:PORT carries the pipe through the Tor network, in a
  build with the feature tor, as podssh ssh does (see its notes): ssh -o
  ProxyCommand='podssh proxy tor://%h:%p' user@host.

  podssh proxy upterm://SESSION@HOST carries uptermd's SSH of that session, as
  upterm's own proxy carries it, for OpenSSH's ProxyCommand: ssh -o
  ProxyCommand='podssh proxy upterm://ID@HOST' ID@HOST. The SSH client logs in
  as SESSION; podssh ssh upterm://SESSION@HOST does it in one.

  podssh proxy --forwarder TEMPLATES carries the pipe through other products'
  WebSocket forwarders and Wisp servers, in order. It takes no relay, as podssh
  ssh does (see its notes); PODSSH_FORWARDER gives them too. The end of stdin
  sends no Close (nor Wisp's CLOSE), as a close is no half-close: the target's
  bytes come until it closes. When each relay host failed, the forwarders that
  podssh names follow, as for podssh ssh.

  podssh proxy --shadowsocks FILE carries the pipe through the Shadowsocks
  servers of FILE, in order, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes).
  A pipe's client may speak first, so a server that says nothing for 3 s is
  taken; one that closes, resets or answers with a chunk that does not open
  within them gives way to the next. The end of stdin is TCP's half-close,
  which the server passes on: the target's bytes come until it closes.

  podssh proxy --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] carries the pipe through a
  forward proxy over TLS, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes);
  PODSSH_VIA names it too. The end of stdin is the tunnel's half-close (the end
  of the stream, on HTTP/2): the target's bytes come until it closes.

  podssh proxy --vless FILE carries the pipe through the VLESS servers of FILE,
  in order, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes). A pipe's client
  may speak first, so a server that says nothing for 3 s is taken; one that
  ends the session, or answers in another protocol, within them gives way to
  the next. A WebSocket and packet-up have no half-close: the end of stdin ends
  nothing, and the target's bytes come until the server ends; stream-up and
  stream-one end their upload. It takes --early-data and --h2-shape as podssh
  ssh does (see its notes).

  podssh proxy --trojan FILE carries the pipe through the Trojan servers of
  FILE, in order, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes). A pipe's
  client may speak first, so a server that says nothing for 3 s is taken; one
  whose fallback answers, or that ends the session, within them gives way to
  the next. In TLS alone the end of stdin closes the stream's way up; a
  WebSocket has no half-close, and the target's bytes come until the server
  ends.

  podssh proxy --hysteria FILE carries the pipe through the Hysteria 2 servers
  of FILE, in order, where UDP passes. It takes no relay, as podssh ssh does
  (see its notes); the flag wins over PODSSH_CHISEL, PODSSH_WSTUNNEL and
  PODSSH_VIA. The server answers once it reached the target, so a pipe whose
  client speaks first waits for no silence. The end of stdin closes the
  stream's way up, which the server passes on to the target.

  podssh proxy --tuic FILE carries the pipe through the TUIC servers of FILE,
  in order, where UDP passes. It takes no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its
  notes); the flag wins over PODSSH_CHISEL, PODSSH_WSTUNNEL and PODSSH_VIA. A
  TUIC server never answers the request, so a pipe whose client speaks first
  takes the stream after 3 s of silence. The end of stdin closes the stream's
  way up, which the server passes on to the target.

  podssh proxy --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT] carries the pipe through a wstunnel
  server that you run, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes);
  PODSSH_WSTUNNEL names it too. The end of stdin sends no Close, as a Close is
  no half-close: the target's bytes come until it closes.

  podssh proxy --chisel https://HOST[:PORT] carries the pipe through a chisel
  server that you run, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes). It
  serves it as chisel client URL stdio:HOST:PORT does; PODSSH_CHISEL names it
  too. The end of stdin ends the channel's way up alone: the target's bytes
  come until it closes.

  podssh proxy --turn turns:HOST[:PORT] carries the pipe through a TURN
  server's TCP allocation, with no relay, as podssh ssh does (see its notes);
  PODSSH_TURN names it too. The bytes go as they are on the second connection,
  so the end of stdin is its half-close: the target's bytes come until it
  closes.

  podssh proxy devtunnel://TUNNEL:PORT carries the pipe to a port of a Dev
  Tunnels host, as podssh ssh does (see its notes). It needs a build with the
  feature devtunnel: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy devtunnel://TUNNEL:%p'
  user@host.

  podssh proxy tries the cleartext road last too, as podssh ssh does (see its
  notes). It does so when each relay host failed and the TLS of one failed on
  the way; PODSSH_CLEARTEXT=no turns it off.

  podssh proxy node://NAME[/ROUTE] is the pipe of podssh operator NAME[/ROUTE]
  (see its notes): stdin goes to the node of the pair under the label NAME, and
  the bytes of its TARGET, or of its ROUTE, to stdout. It takes the pair stored
  under NAME or that of --pair-file, and the end-to-end channel and its flags
  --client-key, --node-key and --no-e2e. It takes --resume-deadline and
  --no-resume too, and gives the same exit codes. As the ProxyCommand of
  OpenSSH: ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy node://NAME' user@NAME. The node
  names the service, so a PORT is refused (64). So are the relay's flags
  (--relay-host, --relay-failover), --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless,
  --wstunnel, --exit and --idle-warn: each takes the relay's place or speaks of
  it; --relay-addr and --ca-file reach the pair's relay. The flags of a node
  with another target are refused (64). A word that starts with node: and is no
  node://NAME is refused with the three forms of a node's ProxyCommand: podssh
  proxy node://NAME, podssh operator NAME and podssh pipe - node:NAME;
  node:PORT stays the host node and its port. With --carrier ADDR the node is
  at the other end of a stream that exists already, with no relay and no pair.
  It is reached as podssh operator --carrier reaches it (see its notes), with
  its checks and codes: ssh -o ProxyCommand="podssh proxy --carrier 'exec:ssh
  -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' node://box"
  user@box.

  --ConnectTimeout SECONDS, 1 to 86400, bounds the time from the start to the
  session's open, on each road: the relay's answer (each host's dial, its TLS,
  the upgrade, and its dial of HOST), or the answer of the road in the relay's
  place. For node://NAME it bounds the steps of podssh operator. Each step
  keeps its own limit too, and the first limit to pass ends the wait. Past the
  bound one line names the step that waited, as: no relay host answered within
  25 s (--ConnectTimeout), and the exit is 69. The bytes after the open are
  never bounded: a pipe may wait. proxy takes no -o, so -o ConnectTimeout=N is
  refused (64); 0 is refused too. --timeout DURATION is another name of the
  same bound, as a duration (30s, 2m, 1h) rounded up to whole seconds, a day at
  most. PODSSH_TIMEOUT gives it its default, held to a day, as for podssh
  operator: the line past the bound names the one that set it, and
  --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given.

  podssh proxy --exit NAME HOST PORT carries the pipe from NAME in place of the
  relay. NAME is a node of your net that lends its egress (see podssh node
  --exit and podssh exit): the node resolves HOST, checks each of its addresses
  and dials HOST PORT from its own host. The pipe goes over the pair kept under
  NAME, in the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel. A refusal of the
  node, or of its net's policy, is one line on stderr; no byte of stdout comes
  before the node reached the target. With --carrier ADDR, the exit is the node
  at the other end of a stream that exists already. That road has no relay and
  no pair (podssh node NAME --exit --carrier stdio): exec:CMD, a program
  started with no shell, or fd:N (Unix); the net's rule of the exit holds as on
  each road, and at the end the node hears a Close. stdio, --relay-addr and
  --ca-file are refused with it (64), as stdin and stdout carry the pipe's
  bytes and the stream has no relay. With --exit cf://HOST, the exit is the
  node behind that quick tunnel, over a WebSocket of the tunnel (see podssh
  exit); --pair-file and --carrier are refused with it (64).

  node://NAME takes --grant FILE as podssh operator does: a grant used once, in
  the end-to-end channel of the one session. It takes --bearer SIGNER as podssh
  operator does too.

  Usage: podssh proxy [OPTIONS] [--] HOST PORT | node://NAME[/ROUTE]

  Arguments:
    [HOST]
        the host that the relay connects to, or an IPv6 address; HOST:PORT or
        [IPV6]:PORT in one word also works; node://NAME[/ROUTE], with no PORT,
        is the node of a pair, as podssh operator NAME reaches it.
    [PORT]
        the TCP port on that host; none after node://NAME.

  Options:
    --stdin-stdout
        a byte pipe on stdin/stdout; not an SSH client.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the next starts after 2 s or
        a failure; the default), parallel or serial; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the target through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the target through the Shadowsocks servers of FILE, in order, in
        place of the relay: ss:// lines, subscription https://URL lines and
        Outline access keys (ssconf://URL), in a private file.
    --vless FILE
        reach the target through the VLESS servers of FILE, in order, in place
        of the relay: vless:// share links in a private file.
    --early-data WORD
        the VLESS road's early data: 0rtt, 1rtt or off (default: env
        PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA, else off); a nonce repeated inside ten minutes
        is a replay, and the session continues at 1-RTT on the same connection.
    --h2-shape WORD
        the shape of the HTTP/2 road that podssh builds: existing (the
        default), browser or firefox (default: env PODSSH_H2_SHAPE); SETTINGS
        and their order and the connection's window are sent, while PRIORITY
        frames and padded DATA are recorded and not sent through h2 0.4. The
        default session road is the WebSocket upgrade of HTTP/1.1 and does not
        read it.
    --cover-credential
        ask the relay for a cover name's application-layer credential after the
        TLS handshake, check it, and upgrade on that connection. It checks the
        issuer, chain, window, subject key and exporter. Off by default, and
        refused with --h2-shape because that road has no credential step.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the target through the Trojan servers of FILE, in order, in place
        of the relay: trojan:// share links in a private file.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the target through the Hysteria 2 servers of FILE, in order, in
        place of the relay, where UDP passes: hysteria2:// share links in a
        private file.
    --tuic FILE
        reach the target through the TUIC servers of FILE, in order, in place
        of the relay, where UDP passes: tuic:// share links in a private file.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --exit NAME
        carry the pipe from NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit), in place of the relay: it dials HOST PORT from
        its own host; with --carrier ADDR, NAME is the node at the other end of
        that stream; NAME auto: the exit whose route of the net holds HOST, an
        address.
    --client-key FILE
        with --exit, and node://NAME: this client's key in FILE, made when
        missing (default: client.key in the cache).
    --idle-warn SECONDS
        warn on stderr this long before the relay's idle cut, once nothing
        crossed for the rest of it (default 30; 0: no warning).
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME: the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of
        the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --resume-deadline TIME
        node://NAME: wait at most TIME for a new link after a loss, though the
        node keeps the session longer: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d, from 1 minute to 72
        h (default: as long as the node keeps it).
    --no-resume
        node://NAME: no resume, as with operator's: the session ends with its
        link, and the node keeps nothing of it after a loss.
    --grant FILE
        node://NAME: a grant used once, as operator --grant takes it: one
        session, once, in the end-to-end channel.
    --bearer SIGNER
        node://NAME: a bearer of 30 s for this channel alone, as operator
        --bearer takes it: a podssh key file, agent or agent:SHA256:...
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, with no relay and no pair, as podssh operator --carrier
        does: exec:CMD, a program started with no shell, fd:N (Unix), s3:FILE
        or dns:FILE; NAME is then the label under which the node's key is
        pinned; with --exit NAME HOST PORT, the exit at the other end of ADDR
        dials HOST PORT.
    --ConnectTimeout SECONDS
        the bound on the time to the session's open, 1 to 86400: the relay's
        answer (each host's dial, TLS, the upgrade, its dial of HOST), or that
        of the road in its place; or the steps of node://NAME as operator has
        them; past it one line names the step that waited, and the exit is 69;
        never the bytes after the open.
    --timeout DURATION
        another name of --ConnectTimeout, as a duration (30s, 2m, 1h) rounded
        up to whole seconds, a day at most; it bounds the session's open and
        never its bytes; --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given; never
        required (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh pipe
  join two byte streams, as socat does: stdio, fd:N, exec:CMD, with no listener
  unless one side is tcp-listen:, unix-listen:, http-listen: or ws-listen:

  podssh pipe A B joins two byte streams, as socat does, with no listener
  unless one side asks for one: what A gives goes to B, and what B gives goes
  to A. Each address is KIND:REST: - or stdio (stdin and stdout), fd:N (a
  descriptor that podssh inherited, 3 or more, on Unix), or exec:CMD (a
  program). relay:HOST:PORT is TCP through the relay on the contract's road,
  with no half-close (see below). tcp:HOST:PORT is TCP from this host, through
  HTTPS_PROXY when it is set. ssh:[USER@]HOP[,HOP...],HOST:PORT is TCP that the
  last SSH hop opens, as -W asks. node:NAME is the TARGET of the node of a
  pair, and udp:node:NAME is UDP through a node; see below. The others are
  iroh:TICKET (the TARGET of a node of the iroh road), unix-connect:PATH (a
  local socket; @NAME in Linux's abstract namespace; on Windows a Unix socket
  or a named pipe, \\.\pipe\NAME), or serial:PATH[,BAUD] (a serial line, on
  Unix). Both are checked before anything starts, and stdio on both sides is
  refused.

  unix-listen:PATH (by the names of unix-connect:) and tcp-listen:[ADDR:]PORT
  (on 127.0.0.1, or on ADDR, an address of this host; port 0 asks for a free
  one) listen, one side at most. The bind is the probe: a host that refuses it
  gives 77, and the line names the error. A Unix socket is made mode 0600 and
  takes only this user's programs: a client of another user is closed. A TCP
  port takes each user of this host, and other hosts too when ADDR is not
  loopback; podssh says which. The first client is joined to a new instance of
  the other side, then the listener closes and its file goes; --keep-listening
  takes each client in turn, 8 at once, until SIGINT or SIGTERM, after which
  the file goes too. A path that is a file and not a socket is kept (64), and a
  socket that answers is another program's (69). PODSSH_LISTEN set to no turns
  listening off (78).

  --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT] carries tcp:HOST:PORT and the first hop of
  ssh: through a forward proxy over TLS, as podssh ssh --via does (see its
  notes), with the credentials of --via-auth-file; tcp: takes the flag alone,
  as PODSSH_VIA names a road in place of the relay.

  --detach sends a listening pipe into the background once it listens, as
  podssh ssh -f does (see its notes): this program again, its log
  detached/pipe-PID.log in the cache; its other side may not be stdio (64), as
  the background has neither stdin nor stdout. --detach-name NAME names it, and
  a second start of a name that runs refuses (75); see podssh detached.

  http-listen:[ADDR:]PORT, as tcp-listen: takes it, or http-listen:PATH, a
  socket by the names of unix-listen:, is an HTTP CONNECT proxy, for a program
  that knows only HTTPS_PROXY: set it to http://127.0.0.1:PORT. Each CONNECT
  HOST:PORT opens the other side with that target, which the other side names
  as %h:%p: relay:%h:%p, tcp:%h:%p or ssh:[USER@]HOP[,HOP...],%h:%p. A side
  with no %h and no %p is read with its target, and podssh says the reading
  before it listens: ssh:HOPS alone takes ,%h:%p at its end, each of its words
  a hop, and relay and tcp take :%h:%p. Another kind, as exec:, stdio or node:,
  is refused (64): each CONNECT names its own target, which it does not take. A
  client on a socket of http-listen:PATH needs one that speaks to a proxy
  there; curl's --unix-socket goes past its --proxy. Each request is a road of
  its own, 32 at once, until SIGINT or SIGTERM; podssh's line names the value
  of HTTPS_PROXY. The client hears 200 once its road is open, so that it learns
  whether its target was reached; 403 when a policy refuses the target, with
  its words (the relay's, an upstream proxy's, or an SSH server's
  administratively prohibited); 502 with the reason of a dial that failed; 504
  for one past its limit.

  A proxy takes CONNECT alone, in HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/1.0, as many clients send
  it. Another method gets 405, another version of HTTP (HTTP/2) 505, and a
  request line with no version 400. A head over 16 KiB gets 431. Nothing is
  dialed for them. With --proxy-auth-file FILE, a private file of lines
  USER:PASSWORD, each client gives one of them in Proxy-Authorization (Basic),
  which podssh checks first, in constant time: a request with none, or with a
  wrong one, gets 407 and a challenge, and nothing is dialed. A port on an ADDR
  that is not loopback needs the file (64): other hosts reach it, and each
  request spends this host's road. The bytes that a client sends after its
  CONNECT, before the 200, go to the road once it is open.

  ws://HOST[:PORT]/PATH and wss://HOST[:PORT]/PATH are a WebSocket by the URL
  that a user copies, reached through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set: wss: checks
  the certificate for HOST with the trust of --ca-file, and ws: is in the
  clear, as tcp: is. No token goes on them, but for --access-host; the path and
  its query are the user's, and podssh's lines show the URL without its query.
  Bytes go out in binary frames, and text and binary frames come in as bytes.
  At the end of this side's input podssh sends a Close, and what the other end
  sends before its own Close still comes; the other end's Close ends the pipe,
  and a code other than 1000 is on stderr with its reason (69). A refused
  upgrade gives its status: 77 for 401 and 403, else 69.

  --access-host HOST, repeatable, or AccessHost in the settings, names a host
  for the credentials of Cloudflare Access. A ws: or wss: side to HOST then
  sends them in the headers that cloudflared sends. Those are the service token
  of PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID and PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET, or of their
  files, and the token of PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_TOKEN. No other host gets them. ws:
  takes them to this host's loopback alone (64 else), and a flag that names no
  side is refused (64). With no credential set, the run is refused (78). A
  refusal of Access (401 or 403) gives 77 and names the variables; a value that
  the far end quotes is not shown.

  ws-listen:[ADDR:]PORT or ws-listen:PATH is a WebSocket server, by the rules
  of tcp-listen: and unix-listen:, whose clients are joined to the other side
  as given. A client's upgrade is checked as RFC 6455 asks (GET, Upgrade,
  Connection, version 13, a key of 16 bytes). A bad one is refused with its
  status (405, 400, 426); a request with an Origin is a browser's, and is
  refused (403), so that no page that the user opens reaches the other side.
  The other side opens before the client hears 101, and 502 when it does not.
  podssh's frames are a server's, unmasked, and a client's unmasked frame
  closes the session with 1002. One client by default, the first whose upgrade
  is good; --keep-listening takes each in turn.

  --cover DIR gives ws-listen: a page for a visit. A GET or HEAD that asks for
  no upgrade, as a browser's, gets the file of DIR that its path names, typed
  by its name. It gets index.html for / and for a directory, which is never
  listed; 404 when there is none. A path with .., a name that starts with a dot
  (.git, .env), or an escape that hides a separator gets 404. So does a link
  whose file is out of DIR, a file over 1 MiB, or one that is not a regular
  file. Another method gets 405, and a request of HTTP/1.1 with no Host 400. A
  page is no session: the connection closes after it, and the other side opens
  for an upgrade alone, with the refusals above. DIR must be a directory, and
  the flag is for ws-listen: alone (64).

  --raw-upgrade lets ws-listen: answer an upgrade with no Sec-WebSocket-Key,
  the request of a client of WebTunnel's shape, as podssh's own: GET with a
  Host, Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade, and no key or version. It
  hears 101 with those two headers and no Sec-WebSocket-Accept, and then its
  bytes go both ways as tcp-listen: carries them, the ones it sent after its
  request first: no frames, so no close code and no Ping, and no idle bound;
  TCP alone finds a path that died. A request with a key is framed as above,
  its version and its key checked (a key that is not 16 bytes 400). An Origin
  is 403 with or without a key, so no page reaches the other side. Without the
  flag a request with no key gets 426. What it admits: each program that sends
  such a GET reaches the other side, as at tcp-listen:, which has no check at
