  all; ws-listen: has no authentication either way. There is no TLS on
  ws-listen:: a client of https:// needs a front that ends TLS before it. The
  flag is for ws-listen: alone (64).

  The hops of ssh: log in as podssh ssh logs in: through the relay, or with
  --direct, with -i and -o; an -o of a session (RequestTTY, RemoteCommand) is
  refused. node: takes the pair stored under NAME, or the one of --pair-file.
  iroh: takes this client's key of --iroh-key, and the relays of --iroh-relay
  after the ticket's.

  With --carrier ADDR, node:NAME and udp:node:NAME take the node at the other
  end of a stream that exists already. That road has no relay and no pair, as
  with podssh operator --carrier (see its notes): exec:CMD, a program that
  podssh starts with no shell, or fd:N (Unix); NAME is the label under which
  the node's key is pinned. stdio is refused (64), as the pipe's own stdin and
  stdout are a side or none. --pair-file is refused too, and so is a pipe with
  no node side and no --exit. Each node side, and each client of a listening
  side, is a session of its own on the one stream, which ends with the pipe:
  the node hears a Close, and the program of exec: ends. The other side keeps
  its road. podssh pipe tcp-listen:2222 node:box --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox
  podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' --keep-listening gives a port
  here for the node's sshd.

  exec:CMD starts the program with no shell: its words split at blanks, with
  single and double quotes, and no variables, globs or escapes; exec:sh -c
  'CMD' names a shell. The program gets one end of a socketpair as its stdin
  and stdout, or two pipes where a socketpair is refused and on Windows. Its
  stderr is podssh's. In a pipe that does not listen, SIGINT, SIGTERM and
  SIGHUP end the pipe: the program gets the same signal, and 10 s to exit. A
  program still there then is killed (SIGKILL). podssh says so in one line and
  exits 128 + N: 130, 143 or 129. On Windows, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break reach the
  program from the console; podssh ends it after 10 s, and exits 130.

  udp:node:NAME carries UDP through the node of the pair under NAME, whose
  TARGET is udp:HOST:PORT (see podssh node): the relay carries TCP only, and
  this host sends no UDP. Each datagram is its length in two bytes, big-endian,
  then its bytes, 65,507 at most; the other side gives and takes that framing
  on stdin and stdout, a descriptor or a socket. A program of exec: beside it
  gets one end of a Unix datagram socketpair as its stdin and stdout on Unix,
  which needs no bind: each send is one datagram at the target, each receive
  one answer; where that is refused, and on Windows, its stdin and stdout carry
  the framing. The node's session has no half-close: after the end of this
  side's input it waits for answers until none came for 5 s. A datagram socket
  has no end of input either: when the other side ends, the program gets 10 s
  to exit, then SIGTERM. A length over 65,507 in the stream exits 65; a longer
  datagram of the program is counted and dropped. Over the relay, datagrams
  wait for each other: a lost segment delays each later one.

  When one side's input ends, the other side gets the end of its input. The
  other direction goes on, so that a reply still comes back: tcp:, ssh: and
  unix-connect: pass it on as a half-close. The relay has no half-close, so a
  relay: side sends nothing at the end of input. The target's bytes come until
  it closes, as a named pipe's do, whose listening side closes it at its end of
  input; node: and iroh: end their session. With a node: side, SIGHUP, SIGTERM
  and SIGINT end the node's session as an end of input does, so that the node
  keeps nothing of it. The road's status is then 0 when the node took the
  session (see podssh operator). --no-resume ends the session of each node:,
  udp:node: and iroh: side with its link, as podssh operator --no-resume does,
  and a pipe with none of them refuses it (64). The pipe ends when both have
  ended, or when a side's reader is gone. It also ends when a program has
  exited and its output has ended, or when a road has ended. podssh waits for
  each program, as a shell does.

  A road that failed gives the exit status, as podssh proxy gives it: 69 for a
  road out of reach, and 77 for a refusal (of the relay, a proxy, a host key or
  a login). It is 78 for a setting that cannot be used. A read of a side that
  failed (a socket that was reset) is no end of its input: one line names the
  side and the bytes carried before it, and the status is 69. Else the status
  is the program's (B's when both are programs), or 128 + N for a signal. It is
  127 for a program that is not found and 126 for one that cannot run; with
  neither, 0. 65 for a stream of udp: that is not its framing.

  serial:PATH[,BAUD] opens a serial device of this host, such as /dev/ttyUSB0,
  at BAUD (115200 when none is given). The line has 8 data bits, no parity, 1
  stop bit and no flow control, in raw mode. A PATH with a comma takes a BAUD
  after it. BAUD is one of the rates that Linux has a code for: 1200, 1800,
  2400, 4800, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600, 115200, 230400, 460800, 500000,
  576000, 921600, 1000000, 1152000, 1500000, 2000000, 2500000, 3000000, 3500000
  or 4000000. Another rate is refused (64). The path must be a character device
  that is a terminal (else 64), and one that this user may open: a refusal is
  77 and says whose the device is, as podssh assumes no group; another failure
  is 69. podssh holds the line alone while the pipe runs, and puts its settings
  back at the end. It does so at SIGINT and SIGTERM too, which then exit 130
  and 143. The line has no end: the end of the other side's input leaves it
  open. The pipe ends when the other side ends it, at a signal, or when the
  device fails (69). On Windows, serial: is refused (64).

  --ConnectTimeout SECONDS bounds the open of a node: or relay: side as podssh
  operator and podssh proxy bound theirs, the other side's open with it, and
  never the bytes after it; past it one line names the step that waited, and
  the exit is 69. Each hop of an ssh: side takes it as its own ConnectTimeout
  too (the SSH handshake, and each answer while logging in), and alone where no
  side is node: or relay:. A listening side refuses it (64), as each client
  opens a road long after the start, and so does a pipe with no node:, relay:
  or ssh: side. --timeout DURATION is another name of it, a duration (30s, 2m,
  1h) rounded up to whole seconds, with the same refusals, and each ssh: hop's
  ConnectTimeout too; --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given. PODSSH_TIMEOUT
  gives the bound of a node: or relay: side its default where no side listens;
  it refuses no pipe, as it bounds whole runs of other commands, and is no
  hop's ConnectTimeout.

  --exit NAME starts relay:HOST:PORT, and each relay:%h:%p of http-listen:, at
  NAME in place of the relay. NAME is a node of your net that lends its egress
  (see podssh node --exit and podssh exit). It is reached over the pair kept
  under NAME: the node resolves HOST and dials it from its own host. A pipe
  with --exit and no relay: address is refused (64). With --carrier ADDR, the
  exit is the node at the other end of that stream, with no pair (podssh node
  NAME --exit --carrier stdio). Each relay: session is then a session of the
  one stream; a node: side beside it is refused (64), as one node is at the
  other end of a stream. With --exit cf://HOST, the exit is the node behind
  that quick tunnel, each relay: session a WebSocket of the tunnel (see podssh
  exit); --pair-file and --carrier are refused with it (64).

  --grant FILE gives the first session of a node: side a grant used once, as
  podssh operator --grant takes it; a pipe with no node: side refuses it (64),
  and a listening side's later clients carry none. --bearer SIGNER is taken the
  same way, as podssh operator --bearer takes it.

  An HTTP CONNECT proxy whose connections go on from an SSH server, and a
  client:
  podssh pipe http-listen:3128 ssh:user@bastion.example.org
  curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:3128 https://example.org/

  ssh:HOPS with no target takes each CONNECT's %h:%p. A program that reads
  HTTPS_PROXY takes HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3128.

  Usage: podssh pipe [OPTIONS] A B

  Arguments:
    [A]
        the first address, KIND:REST, one of: -, stdio, fd:N, exec:CMD,
        relay:HOST:PORT, tcp:HOST:PORT, ssh:[USER@]HOP[,HOP...],HOST:PORT,
        node:NAME, udp:node:NAME, iroh:TICKET, unix-connect:PATH,
        unix-listen:PATH, tcp-listen:[ADDR:]PORT, http-listen:[ADDR:]PORT,
        http-listen:PATH, ws://HOST[:PORT]/PATH, wss://HOST[:PORT]/PATH,
        ws-listen:[ADDR:]PORT, ws-listen:PATH, serial:PATH[,BAUD]; exec:CMD
        takes the program's words in one argument.
    [B]
        the second address, of the same kinds; one side at most listens.

  Options:
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        ssh: the identity file of each hop, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        ssh: an OpenSSH option of the hops, as -o Name=Value; repeatable; one
        of a session (RequestTTY, RemoteCommand) is refused.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        ssh: reach the first hop without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY
        when one is set.
    --pair-file FILE
        node: the pair in FILE, a private file, not the one stored under NAME;
        its operator's part will do.
    --client-key FILE
        node:, iroh: and the exit of --exit: this client's key in FILE, made
        when missing (default: client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node: the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of the
        pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either; the relay
        then sees each byte.
    --iroh-key FILE
        the same as --client-key, by its earlier name.
    --iroh-relay URLS
        iroh: the relays, https://HOST[:PORT][,...], after the ticket's
        (default: env PODSSH_IROH_RELAY, else the net's relay members' own,
        then n0's).
    --keep-listening
        unix-listen:, tcp-listen:, ws-listen: take each client in turn, 8 at
        once, each with a new instance of the other side, until SIGINT or
        SIGTERM; http-listen: always does, 32 at once.
    --detach
        a listening side: go to the background once it listens, as podssh
        itself; the other side may not be stdio.
    --restart
        with --detach: a small process in the background starts the run again
        whenever it ends, but after 64, 77 or 78 or a stop of that process; it
        never gives up.
    --access-host HOST
        ws: and wss: to HOST carry the credentials of Cloudflare Access in
        their headers; repeatable.
    --detach-name NAME
        with --detach: the run's name, letters, digits, _ and -, 64 at most; a
        second start of a name that runs refuses (75), and podssh detached
        shows and stops it (default: the verb and the pid).
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --exit NAME
        relay:HOST:PORT and relay:%h:%p start at NAME, a node of your net that
        lends its egress (podssh node --exit), in place of the relay; with
        --carrier ADDR, NAME is the node at the other end of that stream; NAME
        auto: for each, the exit whose route of the net holds HOST, an address.
    --proxy-auth-file FILE
        http-listen: each client gives a USER:PASSWORD of FILE, a private file,
        one a line, in Proxy-Authorization; needed off loopback.
    --cover DIR
        ws-listen: a GET or HEAD that asks for no upgrade gets a file of DIR,
        index.html for / and a directory; 1 MiB at most, else 404.
    --raw-upgrade
        ws-listen: an upgrade with no Sec-WebSocket-Key gets 101 with no
        accept, then raw bytes both ways: no frames, close code or idle bound.
    --ConnectTimeout SECONDS
        node: and relay:: the bound on the time to the session's open, as
        operator and proxy take it, with no listening side; ssh:: each hop's
        ConnectTimeout too, and with no node: or relay: side the hops' alone.
    --timeout DURATION
        node:, relay: and ssh:: another name of --ConnectTimeout, as a duration
        (30s, 2m, 1h) rounded up to whole seconds, a day at most;
        --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given; never required (default: env
        PODSSH_TIMEOUT, for a node: or relay: side of a pipe that does not
        listen).
    --carrier ADDR
        node: and udp:node:: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream
        that exists already, with no relay and no pair, as podssh operator
        --carrier does: exec:CMD, a program started with no shell, fd:N (Unix),
        s3:FILE or dns:FILE; each client of a listening side is a session of
        the one stream; with --exit NAME, relay: starts at the exit at the
        other end of ADDR, with no node: side.
    --no-resume
        node:, udp:node: and iroh:: no resume, as with operator's: each session
        ends with its link, and the node keeps nothing of it after a loss.
    --grant FILE
        node:: a grant used once, as operator --grant takes it, for the first
        session of the side alone.
    --bearer SIGNER
        node:: a bearer of 30 s, as operator --bearer takes it, for the first
        session of the side alone.
    --install NAME
        make this pipe a service of this user named NAME, which starts it again
        whenever it ends: the ways of podssh node --install, with these words
        but --install NAME. A side of stdio or fd: is refused, and so is a URL
        with a user and a password.
    --uninstall NAME
        remove the service that --install NAME made, its file of variables and
        its lock, and nothing else.
    --env-file FILE
        read the variables of FILE, a private file of NAME=VALUE lines, before
        anything else; hold FILE.lock while it runs, so that a second start
        ends at once: the file that --install writes.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    a program at the other end of stdin and stdout, as socat joins them; its
    exit status is the pipe's
        $ podssh pipe stdio "exec:sh -c 'tr a-z A-Z'"

    a descriptor that the calling program opened for podssh, on Unix
        $ podssh pipe fd:3 stdio

    a board's serial console on stdin and stdout, at 115200 baud, on Unix;
    Ctrl-C ends it
        $ podssh pipe serial:/dev/ttyUSB0,115200 stdio

    a TCP service behind an SSH server, on stdin and stdout, as -W reaches it
        $ podssh pipe stdio ssh:user@bastion.example.org,db.internal:5432

    the same service on a local port, for a client that connects: one client,
    then the port closes
        $ podssh pipe tcp-listen:5432 ssh:user@bastion.example.org,db.internal:5432

    an HTTP CONNECT proxy for pip, npm, cargo or git, with HTTPS_PROXY set to
    http://127.0.0.1:3128: each CONNECT goes through the relay
        $ podssh pipe http-listen:3128 relay:%h:%p

    the same proxy whose CONNECTs go on from an SSH server: ssh: with no target
    takes each one's %h:%p; a client: curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:3128 URL
        $ podssh pipe http-listen:3128 ssh:user@bastion.example.org

    a WebSocket of another service on stdin and stdout, by its URL, as websocat
    joins one
        $ podssh pipe stdio wss://ws.example.org/socket

    from outside, a program whose stdin and stdout are a datagram socket (Unix)
    sends each query
        $ podssh pipe 'exec:python3 query.py' udp:node:dns --pair-file dns-operator.json

podssh node
  reverse mode: expose a local service to operators.

  podssh node serves TARGET, a TCP service, to the operators of the pair stored
  under NAME (see podssh relay). Each session that an operator opens is one
  connection to TARGET, from this host, through HTTPS_PROXY unless TARGET is on
  the loopback. podssh dials TARGET once at the start, and exits when it
  cannot. It says online once the relay has its socket, and online again after
  a loss: an operator reaches it from that line on.

  Each session runs the resumable layer: an operator that loses its link to the
  relay resumes the session on a new link. The node keeps the session and its
  connection to TARGET for 10 minutes after a loss, on each road. Or it keeps
  them for the TIME of --resume-deadline, from 1 minute to 72 h: a laptop that
  sleeps for a night needs 8h or more. The node names that time to each
  operator, which waits as long, and its first line says it. A session kept
  longer keeps its replay buffers longer, and the bound below holds. TARGET is
  dialled only once the operator's handshake is done. The node keeps at most 64
  MiB of replay buffers: a whole buffer for each session that can still fill
  one, linked or waiting for its operator (16 sessions with the default of
  PODSSH_REPLAY_BUFFER); for a session whose TARGET ended and whose end went
  out, the bytes that the operator has not acknowledged; nothing for a session
  that ended, whose operator had each byte but lost the link before it
  answered: its id alone waits as long, and a resume of it hears the end. A new
  session past the 64 MiB ends at once with the reason. The reason counts the
  sessions with a link and those waiting for their operator, and says when the
  first of those is forgotten; the node says the same on stderr, once a minute
  at most, and once when its buffers pass three quarters of the 64 MiB. An
  operator may ask for no resume: podssh operator --no-resume, and the same
  flag of ssh, cp, scp, sftp, proxy and pipe. It then gets a session that the
  node forgets as its link ends, which holds nothing after. podssh ssh node://
  and podssh operator speak the layer. For an operator that does not, --plain
  carries each session's bytes as they are, TARGET dialled at the start of the
  session: a lost link then ends the session. The default relay closes the
  node's whole socket with 1003 for a frame of a session whose operator's link
  it lost. podssh relay serve drops such a frame. On the default relay, one
  operator's lost link can thus end each --plain session of the node. Where the
  layer runs, it resumes each of its sessions; the node connects again at once
  after such a close. The node's first line names its mode.

  A roost: with --sshd, the node serves a standard sshd, TARGET, or
  127.0.0.1:22 when no TARGET is given. A normal server gets the resumable
  layer, and with --iroh the iroh road, this way: the roost owns the TCP
  connection to sshd. Before the node goes online, it dials each TARGET and
  reads its first lines. They must hold SSH's version line (SSH-2.0-...) within
  10 s and 4 KiB; lines before it, which RFC 4253 lets a server send, are
  skipped, as podssh ssh skips them. Else it exits, and names TARGET and what
  came back: 78 for another service, 69 for no line or a close. The node's
  first line gives the version line. Each session's connection to sshd, made
  after the layer's handshake, is checked the same way. A session whose TARGET
  does not answer as sshd ends at once with the reason. The check takes no byte
  of the session: the client still reads sshd's line. podssh ssh node://NAME
  keeps sshd's host key under node://NAME, the name that the user gives, as
  OpenSSH does for a host behind a ProxyCommand.

  A roost's sshd must run already: podssh brings none. When nothing listens at
  a TARGET on the loopback, the roost exits 69. After the dial's words, it says
  whether this host has an sshd, looked for on PATH, then in /usr/sbin,
  /usr/local/sbin and /sbin. On Windows it looks in the OpenSSH folder of
  System32. It says where the sshd is, and that nothing listens at TARGET
  (start it, or give the port that it listens on). Or it says that none is
  installed, with the command that installs one. The command is of the first
  package manager on PATH (apk, apt-get, dnf, yum, zypper, pacman, brew, pkg).
  It puts sudo first where the user is not root and does not own the package
  manager's file, and sudo is on PATH. Else the command says as root; Homebrew
  never takes sudo. podssh names the command and runs none. A TARGET off the
  loopback keeps the dial's words alone. podssh doctor's line sshd says the
  same before a roost starts.

  --temporary KEY is the node that podssh ssh --upgrade starts on its server
  (see podssh ssh): a roost in front of the sshd that its SSH session came
  through (SSH_CONNECTION: on the loopback first, then at the server's
  address), or of TARGET. It has a pair that it makes on the relay of
  PODSSH_RELAY (else the default) and that no file keeps. It has a key for this
  run only. It lets in the client key KEY alone. Once the relay takes the
  pair's sessions, it writes one line to stdout: the pair's connect token and
  its own key. On Unix it then leaves that SSH session: SIGHUP is ignored, and
  stdin, stdout and stderr become /dev/null. It ends with its last session, or
  10 minutes after its start with none, and stops its pair. With it, --iroh,
  --derp, --pair-file, --plain, --no-e2e, the flags of the node's key, and a
  route are refused (exit 64).

  Each session runs the end-to-end channel above the layer (Noise XX): the
  relay sees ciphertext only, and the operator's key and the node's prove
  themselves in it. The node's key is a private file in the cache
  (node-NAME.key, or iroh-node-NAME.key of an earlier podssh). Or it is the
  file of --key, made when it is missing; --ephemeral-key makes one for this
  run only. The node says its fingerprint as it starts, and an operator pins it
  at the first sight. With --allow FILE, only the operator keys of FILE come
  in, on each road: one key or fingerprint on each line, read again for each
  session; a refused operator gets no byte of TARGET, and its key is said on
  stderr, as the line to add. With no allowlist, each operator with the pair's
  connect token comes in, and its key is said. TARGET is dialled only once the
  operator's key is let in. --no-e2e carries the bytes with no channel, to
  operators run with --no-e2e too: the relay then sees them.

  Routes: podssh node lab 127.0.0.1:22 web=127.0.0.1:8080 db=127.0.0.1:5432
  offers each TARGET under its route, here web and db. A route is a name of the
  form of a pair's, with one pair and one node for all; the TARGET with no
  route is the one of an operator that names none. An operator names a route as
  NAME/ROUTE (podssh operator NAME/ROUTE, podssh ssh node://NAME/ROUTE,
  iroh:TICKET/ROUTE). The name goes in the end-to-end channel, so the relay
  never sees it and --no-e2e offers none. With --allow, a key reaches a route
  only when its line says so: KEY routes=web,db, or routes=* for each; a key
  with no routes= reaches the TARGET with no route alone. A route that the node
  does not have, or that the key may not use, is refused with the same words,
  before any dial. With no allowlist, each operator may use each route. Each
  TARGET is dialled once at the start. A node of the channel serves its shares
  too: routes that podssh share adds and removes while it runs. It reads them
  again for each session from node-NAME.shares in the cache or the file of
  --shares FILE. Each is dialled at its session alone (see podssh share).

  TARGET udp:HOST:PORT offers a UDP service, for a host that allows UDP: each
  session is one flow, a UDP socket from this host to HOST:PORT. Each datagram
  goes after its length in two bytes in the session's bytes, as podssh pipe
  udp:node:NAME carries them. The flow ends with its session, or after 60 s
  with no datagram either way. Before it registers, the node opens a UDP socket
  to TARGET and closes it, with nothing sent: a host that refuses UDP, as a
  sandbox does, exits 78, and a name with no address 69. A UDP TARGET is the
  node's only one, with no route, and not on the iroh road. A datagram of the
  target over 65,507 bytes is dropped, and the node says how many when the flow
  ends.

  The node runs until Ctrl-C or SIGTERM (exit 0), or until the relay ends the
  pair: stopped, expired, refused, or served by another node; each has its code
  in EXIT STATUS. A pair lives 72 hours at most: the node says its expiry 24
  hours, 6 hours and 1 hour before it, with the command that makes the next
  pair. That command is podssh relay pair NAME (see podssh relay). At the
  expiry the node goes on with the pair stored under NAME since, if one expires
  later; else it exits 77. A node of --pair-file needs a new FILE and a new
  start. Where its relay renews pairs (podssh relay serve), the node renews its
  own at the start of its last 24 hours instead. Then it tries each hour until
  a renewal took, with its tokens the same, and says each renewal; the store
  keeps the new expiry, and the lines above are said only where the relay
  renews none. A stopped node deletes the stored pair only while it is the
  node's own. A broken connection to the relay is made again, and a line says
  how it ended: the relay is restarting (1012, as podssh relay serve closes
  each socket before it stops), or the link ended with no Close. The line may
  also name a fault of the node's bytes, or another close. The first try after
  a connection that served goes at once, as none of these is an overload, and
  once each 10 s at most; each other try after a growing wait, which the line
  names. After a loss the relay can still hold the old connection, and answer
  409: the node then connects again for the time that it keeps a session (10
  minutes, or --resume-deadline), with a line for each 409. A 409 at the start
  means that another node serves the pair. It can also mean that the relay
  still holds the connection of the node that ran just before: the node
  connects again for 30 s, with a line for each 409, then exits 69. stdout
  stays empty; notes go to stderr.

  With --pair-file, the pair comes from FILE, in the form of the store, and the
  store is not used. FILE must be a regular file of the user that nobody else
  can read.

  --detach sends the node into the background once it is online (a quick
  tunnel's, once registered; the iroh road's, once its ticket is said), as
  podssh ssh -f does (see its notes): this program again, its log
  detached/node-PID.log in the cache. For a node that must outlive a logout or
  a reboot, --install; --detach goes with no --install, --uninstall or
  --temporary (64). --detach-name NAME names the run. A second start of a name
  that runs refuses (75), where a second node of the pair would meet the
  relay's 409; see podssh detached.

  --install makes the node a service of this user, with no privilege. The
  service starts it again whenever it ends, by the first way that a probe
  finds. A user unit of systemd (podssh-node-NAME.service, enabled and started)
  when systemctl answers for this user: it restarts 5 s after each end with no
  limit of starts, but not after 64 or 78, a refused command line or setting;
  77, an expired pair, is started again, so that a new pair is taken at the
  next start. Else a LaunchAgent
  (~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.podssh.node.NAME.plist, with KeepAlive and
  RunAtLoad), loaded with launchctl bootstrap in the user's login session, when
  launchctl has one: it starts now, at each login and 5 s after each end, and
  its lines go to node-NAME.log in the cache. Else two lines of the crontab
  when crontab answers: one at boot, and one each 5 minutes that starts the
  node when it is not running. On Windows a task (schtasks) at the user's logon
  and each 5 minutes while the user is logged on. The task also starts again a
  minute after a failure; never a Windows service, and no task at boot, which
  need an administrator: after a reboot the task waits for the logon. The
  service runs this binary by its absolute path with the node's own TARGET and
  flags, each file by its absolute path, and --env-file: the variables that the
  node reads (the proxy's, SSL_CERT_FILE, PODSSH_RELAY and the places of
  podssh's files) go into node-NAME.env. It is a private file beside the pair,
  as a service has none of the shell's. No token goes in it, nor on a command
  line: PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN and the secrets of Cloudflare Access are not
  carried, and the pair's tokens stay in the pair's file. A user unit runs
  while the user has a session unless lingering is on, which podssh says and
  never changes. With no way, the command to run at login is printed on stdout,
  and the exit is 69. With --temporary, --ephemeral-key or --iroh-ephemeral,
  --install is refused (64). So is a pair that is not stored with neither
  --iroh nor --derp, which serve with none (78). A new --install replaces what
  an earlier one made for NAME, by any way, so that two never start the node.
  --uninstall removes what --install wrote for NAME, and nothing else: the
  unit, stopped first, the LaunchAgent, booted out first, the lines of the
  crontab, or the task. It removes the files of its variables, its lock and its
  log too; a node that the crontab started goes on until it ends.

  --env-file FILE sets the variables of FILE before anything else: lines of the
  form name=value, and # comments, each name a variable that podssh reads. FILE
  must be a private file of the user; a token in it is refused (78), with its
  line. The run then holds a lock on FILE.lock, with its pid in it, for as long
  as it runs: a second run with the same FILE (the crontab's each 5 minutes, or
  a person's) ends at once with 0. It says so only on a terminal. A lock that
  this file system cannot take is said, and the run goes on without one.

  With --iroh, in a build with the feature iroh, as each release binary is, the
  node serves TARGET over the iroh road, with no pair: QUIC between keys,
  through an iroh relay and HTTPS_PROXY, and directly when UDP works. The
  relays are n0's public ones, or those of --iroh-relay, and the first that
  answers is the node's (see THE RELAY). The node's key is the same on both
  roads (see above); --iroh-key and --iroh-ephemeral are --key and
  --ephemeral-key by their earlier names. When it starts, the node prints its
  key's fingerprint and its ticket (iroh:...) on stderr, and a new ticket when
  its home relay changes; a client dials the ticket with podssh ssh
  iroh:TICKET. On n0's relays, the node also keeps a record of its roads at
  n0's server of pkarr: its home relay and, with --derp, its DERP home. A
  client with an older ticket, or with the node's key alone, finds them there
  (see iroh record in THE RELAY). When the pair NAME is stored and good, or
  --pair-file gives one, the node serves the pair's road too. One keeper of
  sessions serves both: a session resumes on either road, and podssh ssh
  node://NAME --iroh-ticket TICKET races them. When the pair's road ends, the
  node says why, and the iroh road goes on.

  A client of the iroh road gets in only when its key, or the key's
  fingerprint, is a line of the file of --allow. --iroh-allow is its earlier
  name. The node reads the file again for each connection, so a key added
  counts at once. With no such file, no client gets in. Each refused key is
  said on stderr: it is the line to add. A session reaches TARGET only after
  the layer's handshake, and resumes on a new link for 10 minutes, as on the
  relay.

  With --derp, the node serves TARGET over the DERP road, in each build: DERP's
  packets over a WebSocket at wss://SERVER/derp, through HTTPS_PROXY. The
  servers are Tailscale's free servers for tailcat first (tc301a.ipn.dev to
  tc304a.ipn.dev). These need no account and are rate-limited, and Tailscale
  may withdraw them at any time. Then comes Tailscale's main fleet, which
  serves Tailscale's own clients and which PODSSH_DERP_MAIN=no leaves out (see
  the public services in the notes of podssh ssh). Or they are the servers of
  --derp-server or PODSSH_DERP_SERVER. The road runs under the resumable layer,
  with an adapter that sends again what a server drops. The node's home is the
  first server whose /derp/probe answers within 5 s and whose DERP handshake
  takes the node's key. Where a server closes after the handshake, the node
  goes on to the next. Its key there is derived from the node's key. Its ticket
  (derp:...), which it prints on stderr, thus stays while its home does. After
  3 failed connections in a row to its home, the node calls the next server of
  its list home that takes a connection. It then prints the new ticket. A
  client dials the ticket with podssh ssh derp:TICKET, or races it with podssh
  ssh node://NAME --derp-ticket TICKET. A DERP server lets any key send, so the
  road needs the end-to-end channel and a door for it: --allow, or a node key
  that is a member of the net held here and in force (see podssh net). The
  net's members are then the door alone, on each road of the node, and the
  first line says so. --no-e2e, --plain and a udp: TARGET are refused with it
  (64), and so is --derp with neither door, before the node's key is made. A
  node with no --allow that leaves its net lets nobody in. With the pair NAME
  stored and good, or --pair-file, the node serves the pair's road too, and
  with --iroh the iroh road. One keeper of sessions serves each road. A server
  sees each end's key on it, the sizes and the times; the channel keeps the
  bytes from it. With --iroh, the node's record of pkarr names its DERP home;
  with no --iroh, in a build with the iroh road, it does too. That record is at
  n0's server unless its variable names another or off (see iroh record in THE
  RELAY).

  A node may have no pair stored under NAME (or one that expired), no --iroh
  and no --plain, and a door. The door is an allowlist, or a key that the net
  held here names. Such a node serves the DERP road unasked, and its first line
  says so; PODSSH_DERP=no turns that off, and the node refuses as before (78).
  With neither door, it refuses as before too, as no client could come in.

  A node of the pair's road with a TCP TARGET also waits for the pair's
  operators at a magic-wormhole transit relay. It does so only with the
  resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no --no-e2e). The
  relay is Least Authority's wss://relay.mw.leastauthority.com, which needs no
  account, or the relay of PODSSH_TRANSIT; PODSSH_TRANSIT=no turns it off. The
  token by which the relay pairs the two ends comes from the pair's connect
  token. So does a proof of the pair that each end gives the other. A side that
  knows the token alone, as the relay does, is thus refused before the
  resumable layer. The node keeps one connection waiting there, and opens the
  next at each meeting. It keeps the sessions of both roads with one keeper, so
  that a session resumes on either; its line names the relay. The relay sees
  the token, the sizes and the times; the channel keeps the bytes from it. A
  node of --derp with a pair waits there too.

  A node of the pair's road with a TCP TARGET also waits for the pair's
  operators at croc's public relays, a last fallback. It does so only with the
  resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no --no-e2e). Its way
  there is croc-web's WebSocket bridge at the address that podssh's list of
  services names (wss://getcroc.com/ws, while the list names it; none in this
  release), or the bridge of PODSSH_CROC (wss://HOST/ws, croc-web of your own
  before croc relay), through HTTPS_PROXY. The bridge pipes the WebSocket to
  one of croc's relays, which the pair's secret picks. The node passes croc's
  own handshake: a PAKE on the curve SIEC with croc's public key, then the
  relay's password and a room, in AES-GCM. It then waits in the first of the
  pair's 4 rooms that no link of its own holds; the relay sends it a frame each
  second while it waits. A client of the pair meets it there, and each proves
  the pair's secret to the other before the resumable layer. This way a peer
  that knows a room alone, as the relay does, is refused. The rooms and the
  proof come from the pair's connect token. The node opens its next wait at
  each meeting. It keeps the sessions of each road with one keeper, so that a
  session resumes on any; its line names the bridge and, for the public one,
  says that a volunteer's service that nobody vouches for carries the sessions
  of this road. croc's relay keeps a room 3 h at most, and a waiting room only
  while it has fewer than 128: the layer moves a session to a new room, and the
  node waits again at once. PODSSH_CROC=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the
  road off. The bridge and the relay see the room, the sizes and the times; the
  channel keeps the bytes from them.

  In a build with the feature zerotier, a node of the pair's road also waits
  for the pair's operators on ZeroTier. It does so only with a TCP TARGET, the
  resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no --no-e2e). This is
  the last fallback after croc's relay. ZeroTierOne's own core, linked into
  podssh, joins an ad-hoc network of the pair's own (no controller, no
  account). It joins through ZeroTier Inc.'s roots and its TCP relay, which
  podssh's list of services names. Or the relay is the one of PODSSH_ZEROTIER
  (IP:PORT, ZeroTierOne's tcp-proxy of your own). It uses one TCP connection
  through HTTPS_PROXY. The node's ZeroTier identity, its address and the
  network's one port come from the pair's name and connect token. Its operators
  thus know them with no word between the two ends; the node waits at its
  6plane address there. It serves each connection with the resumable layer
  under the keeper of its other roads. It dials the relay again, after 1 s,
  doubled to 32 s, when it goes. Its line names the relay. It says that
  ZeroTier Inc.'s roots and relay carry the sessions of this road and see the
  two ZeroTier addresses, the times and the sizes; the channel keeps the bytes
  from them. PODSSH_ZEROTIER_PLANET names a planet of your own roots in the
  place of ZeroTier Inc.'s. PODSSH_ZEROTIER=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns
  the road off.

  In a build with the feature tox, a node of the pair's road also waits on a
  TCP relay of the Tox project's public nodes. There it waits for the pair's
  operators, the last fallback after ZeroTier's. It does so only with a TCP
  TARGET, the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no
  --no-e2e). The relay is the one that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks
  among those that podssh's list of services names. There is none while the
  list names none. Or it is the relay of PODSSH_TOX (IP:PORT=KEY, c-toxcore's
  tox-bootstrapd of your own with its TCP relay). The node reaches it by one
  TCP connection through HTTPS_PROXY. The node's key on the relay comes from
  the pair's name and connect token. Its operators thus know it with no word
  between the two ends; each session has a connection with a fresh key of its
  own, offered to the client out of band. This way one session's pace never
  holds another's. The node serves each with the resumable layer under the
  keeper of its other roads. It dials the relay again, after 1 s, doubled to 32
  s, when it goes. Its line names the relay. For a public one, it says that the
  relay carries the sessions of this road. That relay sees the two ends' keys,
  the times and the sizes; the channel keeps the bytes from it. PODSSH_TOX=no
  turns the road off, and PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns off the public relays.

  In a build with the feature yggdrasil, a node of the pair's road also waits
  for the pair's operators in Yggdrasil's network. It does so only with a TCP
  TARGET, the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no
  --no-e2e). This is the last fallback after the Tox road. It takes one
  WebSocket (ygg-ws) through HTTPS_PROXY to a public wss:// peer. The peer is
  the one that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks among those that podssh's
  list of services names. There is none while the list names none. Or the peer
  is the one of PODSSH_YGGDRASIL (a wss:// or ws:// URL, yggdrasil-go of your
  own with that Listen). Its handshake is signed, and Ironwood, Yggdrasil's
  router, runs over it. The node's key in the network comes from the pair's
  name and connect token. Its operators thus know it with no word between the
  two ends; a client's hello proves the token. Each session is a stream of its
  own, served with the resumable layer under the keeper of its other roads.
  While the road is up the node is a router of the network too, as each node of
  Yggdrasil is. It dials its peer again, after 1 s, doubled to 32 s, when the
  link goes. Its line names the peer. For a public one, it says that the peer
  carries the sessions of this road. It says too that the peers on the path see
  the two ends' keys, the times and the sizes; the channel keeps the bytes from
  them. PODSSH_YGGDRASIL=no turns the road off, and PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns
  off the public peers.

  In a build with the feature hyperdht, a node of the pair's road also waits
  for the pair's operators in HyperDHT where UDP passes. It does so only with a
  TCP TARGET, the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no
  --no-e2e). It comes after Yggdrasil's road. It joins the DHT through the
  bootstrap nodes that podssh's list of services names (none while it names
  none). Or it joins through those of PODSSH_HYPERDHT
  (HOST:PORT[,HOST:PORT...], a DHT of your own). It joins under a key that the
  pair's name and connect token make, and announces a topic of that key. Its
  operators thus find it with no word between the two ends. Each connection is
  a hole punched through both NATs and a Noise channel over UDX. It is served
  with the resumable layer under the keeper of its other roads. Where no
  bootstrap node answers within 15 s, UDP does not pass: the node says so and
  serves its other roads. Its line says that the DHT's nodes see the node's
  address and topic; the channel keeps the bytes from them. PODSSH_HYPERDHT=no
  turns the road off, and PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns off the public DHT.

  In a build with the feature strelay, a node of the pair's road also waits for
  the pair's operators on a relay of Syncthing's pool. It does so only with a
  TCP TARGET, the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no
  --no-e2e). This is the last fallback after HyperDHT's road. The relay is the
  one on 443 that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks among those that
  podssh's list of services names. There is none while the list names none. Or
  it is the relay of PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY (a relay:// URL in the pool's form,
  with the relay's device ID: Syncthing's strelaysrv of your own). The node
  reaches it by one TLS connection through HTTPS_PROXY. Its certificate, whose
  SHA-256 is its device ID, comes from the pair's name and connect token. Its
  operators thus find it with no word between the two ends; each session is a
  TCP connection of its own to the relay, served with the resumable layer under
  the keeper of its other roads. It joins again, after 1 s, doubled to 32 s,
  when its connection goes. Its line names the relay. For one of the pool, it
  says that the relay carries the sessions of this road. That relay sees the
  two ends' certificates, the times and the sizes; the channel keeps the bytes
  from it. PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY=no turns the road off, and
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns off the pool's relays.

  In a build with the feature tor, a node of the pair's road waits as an onion
  service of the Tor network too. There it waits for the pair's operators, the
  last fallback after Syncthing's relay road. It does so only with a TCP
  TARGET, the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no
  --no-e2e). Arti bootstraps in podssh's process through the Tor road
  (HTTPS_PROXY, PODSSH_TOR_PORTS, PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES and PODSSH_TOR_NETWORK
  hold). It keeps a directory of the cache of the node's own, where Arti keeps
  the service's key. The service's address thus stays from one start to the
  next. Every circuit of the service is a connection out to a Tor relay: the
  node listens on nothing. Its descriptor is of restricted discovery, readable
  only with a key that both ends make of the pair's name and connect token.
  Each stream to its virtual port is served with the resumable layer under the
  keeper of its other roads. Its line says its address, which a node of this
  host keeps under NAME. A node of DERP puts the address in its record of pkarr
  (onion=), where it keeps one. The line says too that the Tor network's
  volunteer relays carry the sessions of this road; the channel keeps the bytes
  from them. PODSSH_ONION=no or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns the road off.

  A node of the pair's road with a TCP TARGET also waits for the pair's
  operators at smee.io's server. It does so only with the resumable layer and
  the end-to-end channel (no --plain, no --no-e2e). This is the last fallback
  after the onion road, for a proxy that refuses the WebSocket upgrade. Its
  server is podssh's listed one (none while the list names none), or the one of
  PODSSH_SMEE (https://HOST[:PORT][/PREFIX], smee.io's server of your own). It
  is reached over HTTPS by name on 443 through HTTPS_PROXY, with no account and
  no upgrade. It reads its door, a channel whose name comes from the pair's
  name and connect token, as a stream of server-sent events; a client's hello
  there names a link. Each end then posts its way to a channel of that way, one
  numbered frame of base64 in JSON at a time. Each reads the other's. While a
  link runs the door waits, so the node holds two connections at most. Its line
  names the server. For the listed one, it says that the server carries the
  sessions of this road. It says too that anyone who knows a channel's name
  sees the times and the sizes; the channel keeps the bytes. PODSSH_SMEE=no or
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no (for the listed server) turns the road off.

  In a build with the feature filehost (none of a release yet), a node of the
  pair's road waits at public file hosts too. There it waits for the pair's
  operators, the last of the last fallbacks, for a proxy that refuses every
  other road. It does so only with a TCP TARGET, the resumable layer and the
  end-to-end channel (no --plain, no --no-e2e). The hosts are those of podssh's
  list of services whose terms let a program upload unasked and that the list
  has on by default. Or they are those that PODSSH_FILEHOSTS names. The road
  goes over HTTPS by name on 443 through HTTPS_PROXY, with no account. Its door
  is a topic of the first public MQTT broker of the list (PODSSH_MQTT). The
  topic's name comes from the pair's name and connect token. The node polls it
  each 2 s at first and each 60 s at most; a client's hello there names a link.
  Each write of a way of at most 16 KiB is then a note sealed under the pair's
  key. The note goes to a topic of the broker that only the pair can name, with
  no host. This way the handshakes do not wait for a host; each larger piece,
  up to 4 MiB, is one upload sealed under that key, at the host's shortest
  life. Its host, URL and delete token are such a note. The reader takes the
  note, downloads a piece, deletes it where the host lets it, and clears the
  note. One request of the road at a time, never two connections; uploads at
  four fifths of a host's published rate, one each 30 s where it publishes
  none. A host that answers 429 rests while the next takes the piece. Its lines
  name each host and the broker as third parties that nobody vouches for before
  their first byte. Slow: for output and files, not for typing.
  PODSSH_FILEHOSTS=no, PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no or PODSSH_MQTT=no turns the road
  off.

  A node of a pair has a road for a proxy that refuses the WebSocket upgrade:
  the Piping Server road, through https://ppng.io, which needs no account, then
  https://piping.onrender.com where ppng.io fails, or the server of
  PODSSH_PIPING alone. Once TARGET answered, the node asks the relay for its
  socket with no token; where something on the way refuses the upgrade, the
  node says so and serves the Piping Server road alone, unasked, until the pair
  expires (77). It waits there with a GET at a door whose path comes from the
  pair's secret; a client of the pair posts a hello there. Each end then sends
  its way of the link as a POST and reads the other's as a GET. This goes over
  HTTP/2 on one connection where the server offers it, else over HTTP/1.1,
  through HTTPS_PROXY. Where a proxy holds a streamed body until its end, the
  link goes in numbered pieces, a whole POST for each. PODSSH_PIPING=yes, or a
  server's https:// URL, serves the road beside the pair's, with one keeper of
  sessions for both; PODSSH_PIPING=no turns it off. The road runs the resumable
  layer and the end-to-end channel, so --plain, --no-e2e and a udp: TARGET keep
  the node on the pair's road alone. The server sees the paths, the sizes and
  the times; the channel keeps the bytes from it.

  With --opentunnel, the node serves TARGET over the OpenTunnel road: a blind
  TLS tunnel of https://opentunnel.xyz, which needs no account, or of the
  service of PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL. The node makes one tunnel, ID.opentunnel.xyz,
  with a P-256 key and the CSR of its name that it makes itself. It keeps the
  tunnel, its token and its key in a private file of the cache before the
  service orders its certificate. This way each start keeps the same name and
  asks for no new certificate, of the 5 a day that the service gives a tunnel.
  Its route is 26 random letters, so its name is ROUTE.ID.opentunnel.xyz, which
  the line name says, with the command of a client; the node keeps a bridge to
  the service, a WebSocket through HTTPS_PROXY, again after each loss. TLS ends
  at the node with the tunnel's certificate: the service sees the name, the
  times and the sizes, never the bytes. Anyone may connect to a tunnel's name,
  so the road needs the end-to-end channel and a door: --allow, or the members
  of the net held here when the node's key is one; never --plain, --no-e2e,
  --exit or a udp: TARGET (64). With the pair NAME, or --pair-file, the node
  serves the pair's road beside it, with one keeper of sessions. A node with no
  pair, a door, and the DERP road turned off (PODSSH_DERP=no) serves the road
  unasked, and its first line says so; PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL=no turns the road off.
  In a build with the iroh road, the node names its tunnel in its record of
  pkarr (opentunnel=), signed by its key. It does so once its tunnel is ready,
  at n0's server unless its variable names another or off (see iroh record in
  THE RELAY). The service's refusals are named: a token that it no longer takes
  (a new tunnel is made, and said), and a route that an earlier run holds
  (tried again). Its limit of 30 tunnels an hour from one address is named too,
  with its wait.

  With --pinggy, the node serves TARGET over the Pinggy road: a TLS tunnel of
  Pinggy's free tier, which needs no account, or of the server of PODSSH_PINGGY
  (HOST[:PORT]). The node's leg is SSH to Pinggy's server on port 443, through
  HTTPS_PROXY, as user tls, with one remote forward: raw SSH first; where that
  fails before SSH's version line, as behind a proxy that passes TLS alone, SSH
  inside TLS. The trust of --ca-file, SSL_CERT_FILE or podssh's roots verifies
  that TLS, as for a relay host; a line says which way carries. Pinggy gives
  the tunnel a name, which the node reads from Pinggy's list of the tunnel's
  addresses, or from the session's text. The node says the name in its line
  name, with the pin of its TLS key (SHA256:...) and the command of a client
  (--pinggy-name NAME#PIN). It keeps the name under NAME in the cache
  (pinggy-NAME.name). Pinggy routes each visitor's TLS by its name and never
  ends it: TLS ends at the node, with a certificate of its own key, which no CA
  signs. Pinggy thus sees the name, the times and the sizes, never the bytes.
  The node keeps that key in a private file beside its own key
  (KEY.pinggy-tls.pem), so the pin stays across its names and its starts; with
  --ephemeral-key, or a file that cannot be used, the key is for the run, and
  the line says so. The host key of Pinggy's server is checked against the one
  that podssh's list of services names, where it names one; else any key
  passes, and the line says so. A free tunnel ends at 60 minutes: the node
  opens the next, which has a new name, and says it; the sessions that the
  layer keeps go on when their client dials the new name. In a build with the
  iroh road, the node puts each tunnel's address (NAME#PIN) in its record of
  pkarr, signed by its key. The record is at the server of pkarr that the iroh
  road names, and the new address takes the place of the last. Its line says
  so; a client whose net names the node by its key finds the new name there
  with no --pinggy-name. Each visitor's end has a line, with why it ended and
  its bytes each way; PODSSH_PINGGY_TRACE=1 adds one each 5 s while it lives.
  Anyone may connect to a tunnel's name, and Pinggy is a third party that
  nobody vouches for. The road thus needs the end-to-end channel and a door:
  --allow, or the members of the net held here when the node's key is one;
  never --plain, --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, or --opentunnel, --iroh or
  --derp (64). With the pair NAME, or --pair-file, the node serves the pair's
  road beside it, with one keeper of sessions. A node with no pair, a door, and
  the DERP road turned off (PODSSH_DERP=no) serves the road unasked, the last.
  It does so when the OpenTunnel road is turned off too (PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL=no),
  or reached no service. Its lines say so and name the third party.
  PODSSH_PINGGY=no turns the road off, and so does PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, the
  switch of each last fallback.

  With --serveo, the node serves TARGET over the Serveo road: a private alias
  at Serveo, which needs no account, at the server that podssh's list of
  services names, or at the one of PODSSH_SERVEO (HOST[:PORT]); where the list
  names none, only PODSSH_SERVEO gives the road a server (64 without it). The
  node's leg is raw SSH to the server on port 443, then 22, through
  HTTPS_PROXY, as user anonymous. It asks one remote forward of an alias on
  port 22, as ssh -R ALIAS:22:localhost:22 asks it; Serveo documents no SSH
  inside TLS, so a proxy that passes TLS alone leaves the road out. The alias
  is derived from the node's key, a hash of its fingerprint. A client that
  holds the key computes it, and the node's line alias says it. Another tunnel
  may hold the alias, as Serveo may hold the node's last one a while after an
  abrupt end. The node then takes the next of its series of four, and says so.
  Each client's channel carries the resumable layer with no TLS of the node's:
  Serveo sees the alias, the times and the sizes, and the end-to-end channel
  keeps the bytes. The host key of the server is checked against the one that
  podssh's list of services names, where it names one; else any key passes, and
  the line says so. A tunnel that ends is opened again, with the first alias
  first. The sessions that the layer keeps go on when their client links again.
  Anyone who knows the alias may connect to it, and Serveo is a third party
  that nobody vouches for. The road thus needs the end-to-end channel and a
  door: --allow, or the members of the net held here when the node's key is
  one; never --plain, --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, or --opentunnel,
  --pinggy, --ssh-j, --iroh or --derp (64). With the pair NAME, or --pair-file,
  the node serves the pair's road beside it, with one keeper of sessions. A
  node that would serve the Pinggy road unasked serves this one unasked after
  the Pinggy road reached no server. It serves it in the Pinggy road's place
  where PODSSH_PINGGY=no. This road comes before the ssh-j road and the roads
  after it. Its lines say so and name the third party. PODSSH_SERVEO=no turns
  the road off, and so does PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, the switch of each last
  fallback.

  With --ssh-j, the node serves TARGET over the ssh-j road: ssh-j.com, a public
  SSH jump and forwarding server with no account, where podssh's list of
  services names it, or the server of PODSSH_SSH_J (HOST[:PORT]); with neither,
  --ssh-j is a configuration error (78). The node's leg is SSH to the server on
  port 22, directly or through HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT. It logs in as a user that
  its key gives (podssh-, then 16 hex digits). It asks one remote forward of a
  name that its key gives too (n, then 16 hex digits), on port 22, as ssh -R
  NAME:22:... asks it there; its line ssh-j name says USER@NAME and the command
  of a client. A client that holds the node's key derives the same name, so
  neither says it to the other and no record is needed; the name stays across
  the node's starts. The server ends that SSH: it sees the times, the sizes and
  the layer's bytes, which the end-to-end channel keeps from it. Its host key
  is checked against the one that podssh's list of services names, where it
  names one; else any key passes, and the line says so. Anyone may take any
  name there, so the road needs the end-to-end channel and a door: --allow, or
  the members of the net held here when the node's key is one; never --plain,
  --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, or --opentunnel, --pinggy, --serveo, --iroh
  or --derp (64). The server keeps a name for the session that holds it: a leg
  that ends is opened again, with a wait that doubles from 1 s to 60 s. The
  sessions that the layer keeps go on over the next; a name that a stranger
  holds first is refused to the node, which tries again. A client that reaches
  the stranger is refused by the end-to-end channel. The road is served alone:
  a pair of NAME is not served beside it, and a line says so. A node that would
  serve the OpenTunnel, Pinggy or Serveo road unasked serves this one, before
  the last roads that follow it. It does so when none of them reached a
  service, or when each is turned off. Its lines say so and name the third
  party, which nobody vouches for. PODSSH_SSH_J=no turns the road off, and so
  does PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, the switch of each last fallback.

  With --localhost-run, the node serves TARGET over the localhost.run road: a
  tunnel of HTTP made by ssh -R with no account. It is at localhost.run where
  podssh's list of services names it, or at the server of PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN
  (HOST[:PORT]); with neither, --localhost-run is a configuration error (78).
  The node's leg is SSH to the server on port 22, directly or through
  HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT, as the user nokey. It asks the remote forward of port
  80, as ssh -R 80:localhost:PORT nokey@localhost.run asks it; the server's
  line that says tunneled names the tunnel's HTTPS name. The node says it in
  its line tunnel https://NAME with the command of a client. It keeps the name
  under NAME in the cache and puts it in its record. The service ends each
  visitor's TLS and sends its HTTP down the tunnel: a WebSocket at / is a link
  of the resumable layer, under the end-to-end channel, which keeps the bytes
  from the service; it sees the name, the times and the sizes. A free name
  changes after a few hours: the node says each new one, and puts it in the
  record and the cache in the place of the last. With --relay, the relay's
  forward and reverse roads are served behind the tunnel too, as behind a quick
  tunnel, and TARGET may be left out; each other path gets 404. Its host key is
  checked against the one that podssh's list of services names, where it names
  one; else any key passes, and the line says so. Anyone may visit the name, so
  the road needs the end-to-end channel and a door: --allow, or the members of
  the net held here when the node's key is one; never --plain, --no-e2e,
  --exit, a udp: TARGET, or --opentunnel, --pinggy, --serveo, --ssh-j,
  --localtunnel, --bore, --iroh, --derp, --quick-tunnel or --frp (64). A tunnel
  that ends is opened again, with a wait that doubles from 1 s to 60 s. The
  sessions that the layer keeps go on over the next. The road is served alone:
  a pair of NAME is not served beside it, and a line says so. A node that would
  serve the ssh-j road unasked serves this one, before the localtunnel and bore
  roads. It does so when the ssh-j road reached no service, or when it is
  turned off. Its lines say so and name the third party, which nobody vouches
  for. PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN=no turns the road off, and so does
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, the switch of each last fallback. With --sandhole, the
  node serves the same road at Sandhole's public server (demo.sandhole.com.br
  where podssh's list of services names it, or the server of PODSSH_SANDHOLE):
  its leg is SSH on port 443, then 22, as the user tunnel with a key made for
  the login alone, never the node's; the server's line that says Starting HTTPS
  names a random name under its own, new at each connection. A node that would
  serve the localhost.run road unasked serves this one after it when it reached
  no server; PODSSH_SANDHOLE=no turns it off. With --srv-us, the node serves
  the same road at srv.us (where podssh's list of services names it, or the
  server of PODSSH_SRV_US): its leg is SSH on port 22 as the user nomatch, with
  the remote forward of port 1. It logs in with the node's own key, so srv.us
  sees that public key; srv.us names the tunnel by that key and port, the same
  at each connection. The node says when the name it gave is not the one that a
  client derives. With --tunnl-gg, the node serves it at tunnl.gg (where
  podssh's list of services names it, or the server of PODSSH_TUNNL_GG): SSH on
  port 22 with no key, the forward of port 80 and the command output=json. The
  command's first line names a random name, new at each connection. A node that
  would serve the Sandhole road unasked serves srv.us's after it, then
  tunnl.gg's; PODSSH_SRV_US=no and PODSSH_TUNNL_GG=no turn them off.

  With --localtunnel, the node serves TARGET over the localtunnel road:
  localtunnel's public server, with no account, where podssh's list of services
  names it. Or the server of PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL (an https:// URL, or http:// on
  this host's loopback); with neither, --localtunnel is a configuration error
  (78). The node asks the server over HTTPS, through HTTPS_PROXY, for a tunnel
  under a name that its key gives (podssh-, then 16 hex digits). Then it keeps
  the TCP connections that the server names, up to 10, to a port that the
  server's system chose. It dials them directly or through HTTPS_PROXY's
  CONNECT. A proxy that lets CONNECT reach port 443 alone refuses that port.
  The node then needs an egress that reaches it, while its clients need port
  443 alone. A connection that ends is opened again at once; three refused
  dials in a row mean the server forgot the tunnel. The node then asks for it
  again, with a wait that doubles from 1 s to 60 s. The tunnel's URL is the one
  line on stdout. Each visitor's WebSocket is a link of the resumable layer,
  with the end-to-end channel above it; with --relay, the relay role of podssh
  relay serve answers its own paths on the same connections, as behind
  --quick-tunnel. It mints for the node's door unless --mint says otherwise,
  and TARGET may be left out; its relay host is the URL. The server ends the
  visitors' TLS: it sees the times, the sizes and the layer's bytes, which the
  end-to-end channel keeps from it; and nothing proves who connects to a
  tunnel's port there, so a stranger may serve its visitors, whom the channel
  refuses. Where a stranger holds the name first, the server gives another,
  which the node says; a client that derives the name then reaches the
  stranger, and is refused. The road needs the end-to-end channel and a door:
  --allow, or the members of the net held here when the node's key is one;
  never --plain, --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, or another road's flag (64).
  The road is served alone: a pair of NAME is not served beside it, and a line
  says so. A node that would serve the OpenTunnel, Pinggy, Serveo, ssh-j or
  localhost.run road unasked serves this one, before the bore road. It does so
  when none of them reached a service, or when each is off or has no server.
  Its lines say so and name the third party, which nobody vouches for.
  PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL=no turns the road off, and so does PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no,
  the switch of each last fallback.

  With --bore, the node serves TARGET over the bore road: bore.pub, a public
  server of bore's protocol that gives a TCP port with no account, where
  podssh's list of services names it. Or the server of PODSSH_BORE
  (HOST[:PORT], its control port, 7835 where none is named); with neither,
  --bore is a configuration error (78). Its control connection is raw TCP to
  the server's port 7835, directly or through HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT: no TLS and
  no HTTP, so a proxy that allows port 443 alone leaves the road out. On it,
  the node asks a public port that its key gives. It asks the next of a series
  of four where the server refuses one (another holds it, or it is outside the
  server's range); its line bore port says HOST:PORT and the command of a
  client. A client that holds the node's key derives the same ports, so neither
  says them to the other and no record is needed. Each visitor comes as a
  Connection on the control connection. The node takes it on a new connection
  to port 7835 with Accept, then a hello of its key. This way a client passes
  over a port that another holds. The server sees the times, the sizes and the
  layer's bytes, which the end-to-end channel keeps from it. Anyone may take
  any port there, so the road needs the end-to-end channel and a door: --allow,
  or the members of the net held here when the node's key is one; never
  --plain, --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, or another road's flag (64).
  bore.pub restarts on purpose and ends a tunnel at 24 hours: a registration
  that ends is made again: at once after one that lived a minute, else with a
  wait that grows from 1 s to 30 s. The sessions that the layer keeps go on
  over the next; a client that reaches a stranger at a port is refused by the
  end-to-end channel. The road is served alone: a pair of NAME is not served
  beside it, and a line says so. A node that would serve the OpenTunnel,
  Pinggy, Serveo, ssh-j, localhost.run or localtunnel road unasked serves this
  one, the last of all. It does so when none of them reached a service, or when
  each is turned off. Its lines say so and name the third party, which nobody
  vouches for. PODSSH_BORE=no turns the road off, and so does
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, the switch of each last fallback.

  In a build with the feature gsr, --gsr serves TARGET over the GSRN road. It
  is the relay of gsocket (hackerschoice's Global Socket Relay Network, where
  podssh's list of services names it). It needs no account and no token: the
  node and its clients share one secret, the first line of the private file of
  --gsr-secret-file or PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE, never argv. The secret gives an
  address and a shard of the relay; the node keeps one registration there, by
  one TCP connection to port 443, directly or through HTTPS_PROXY's CONNECT. It
  sends a ping each 5 s, under the 15 s at which a proxy was seen to cut an
  idle tunnel; each client that connects with the same secret is paired with
  it, and the node registers again at once. TLS with SRP of the secret
  (OpenSSL, built in and linked static, as rustls has no SRP) keeps the bytes
  from the relay; the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel run above it,
  as on each road. Whoever holds the secret reaches the door, so the road needs
  one: --allow, or the members of the net held here when the node's key is one;
  never --plain, --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET, --spares or another road's
  flag (64). A first registration that fails within 10 s ends the node (69) in
  the relay's words; a later one is made again after a pause that grows to 30
  s. A line names the relay's host and its party as a third party that nobody
  vouches for. --gsr-secret-file without --gsr is 64; a secret file that cannot
  be used, or a secret longer than the relay takes (32 bytes), refused (78), in
  words that never hold it. A build without the feature refuses --gsr and
  --gsr-secret-file (70).

  --carrier s3:FILE carries the node's stream through a bucket of the S3 API,
  for a host whose one way out is an object store. FILE says where the bucket
  is and where the keys are (see FILES). Each end writes its objects under one
  prefix and reads the other's. So a key needs a write right on one prefix and
  a read right on the other. Each object is sealed under a key of FILE's
  secret, its name a MAC of it: the bucket holds no byte in clear. The node
  waits until a client's hello comes, then serves that one stream. Each request
  goes on one connection, through HTTPS_PROXY, one at a time. The road is slow:
  each end polls each 2 to 3 s, and each request is billed at most providers.
  podssh names no provider; the endpoint is yours.

  --carrier dns:FILE carries the node's stream in DNS, for a host that reaches
  a resolver and nothing else. The client's bytes go up in names under a zone
  of your own; the node's come down in TXT records. The road is pod-link's: an
  ARQ, and TLS 1.3 with each end's key pinned by the other. The node needs a
  public address and UDP, and the zone delegated to it by an NS record. It
  answers at FILE's listen, a listener that you ask for; PODSSH_LISTEN=no
  refuses it (78). A bind that the host refuses gives 77, as pipe's listeners
  do. An address in use, or not of this host, gives 69. The node says that it
  serves only once it is bound and its key is read. It takes the first client
  whose key is a peer of FILE, then serves that one stream. The client sends to
  its resolver: resolver of FILE, else the first nameserver of
  /etc/resolv.conf. A UDP socket toward it, which sends nothing, comes first.
  Where the host refuses UDP, the run ends with one line (69), and nothing is
  sent. A resolver of FILE that is https://NAME[:PORT]/PATH takes the queries
  as DNS over HTTPS instead, through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set: no UDP, so no
  probe, and a 429 pauses the next query. At most 20 queries a second and 8 in
  flight; FILE may lower them, never raise them (78). The road is slow: about
  2.6 KB/s up and 18 KB/s down at best. A resolver's operator sees about 2,000
  queries an hour while it is idle, and can block the zone. It is a last
  resort; podssh doctor --dns-zone says whether a resolver passes the zone.

  With --frp FILE, the node serves TARGET through the user's own frps, as an
  frpc of it does, with no relay and no pair: it logs in with frps's token, and
  registers an STCP service of NAME (or of the file's name line) with the
  file's secret. The service opens no public port, and the node sends a
  heartbeat each 30 s. FILE is a private file of the user's, a line each:
  server frp://HOST[:PORT] (frp's own TCP with TLS, port 7000 by default); or
  server wss://HOST[:PORT][/PATH] (frp's WebSocket behind the user's TLS front
  end, path /~!frp by default, with frpc's Origin); token, frps's token;
  secret, the STCP service's secret; user USER, frpc's user, optional: the node
  logs in as USER and its service on frps is USER.NAME, as frpc names its
  proxies, which frps lets that user alone visit; # starts a comment. A
  visitor's lines, owner and plain, are refused in a node's file (78). Neither
  the token nor the secret goes on argv or in a line. TLS is checked with the
  host's trust, or --ca-file; there is no frp road in the clear. Each visitor's
  work connection is a link of the resumable layer, with the end-to-end channel
  above it. frps thus sees the service's name, the times and the sizes, never
  the bytes. frp's own encryption of the service stays off. The holder of the
  secret reaches the node through frps, so the road needs a door: --allow, or
  the members of the net held here when the node's key is one; never --plain,
  --no-e2e, --exit, a udp: TARGET or another road's flag (64). A lost
  connection is made again, after 1 s and up to 30 s apart; a token that frps
  refuses ends the node (69), in frps's words. With no --frp, PODSSH_FRP names
  the file.

  A node lets in an operator with a grant used once, also one whose key no
  --allow names: an OpenSSH user certificate of the operator's key, which the
  end-to-end channel carries from it, encrypted, so no relay sees it. Its
  issuer is the node's own key, or a key of --allow (or a member of the net)
  for what that key may reach itself. Its principal is node: and the node's
  fingerprint (node:SHA256:...), with /ROUTE for a route; it has a window, and
  the critical option once@podssh. Before it dials, the node checks that the
  channel proved the certificate's key. It checks the issuer's signature, a
  user certificate, the principal, the window (5 minutes of skew), each
  critical option, and the serials of --revoked FILE. Then it records the grant
  as used, in grants-NAME of the cache, synced, and only then lets the session
  in. A second use of it is thus refused, also after a restart, and a crash
  between the two spends it. A grant that leaks is worth nothing without its
  key. The resumable layer carries the session on with no new check. podssh
  node NAME --grant-to KEY prints one on stdout and serves nothing: the node's
  key signs it for KEY (ssh-ed25519 BASE64, or its 64 hex digits), for its
  TARGET or for --grant-route ROUTE. --grant-route +exit names the node's exit:
  its caller goes out to public addresses alone, never to a range of --routes.
  Port 25, private, loopback and metadata addresses are refused as podssh relay
  serve refuses them. Its issuer is the node's key, or a member that may go out
  through the exit itself. It is for --grant-for TIME (1h by default), with a
  random serial; the operator gives it with podssh operator --grant FILE. An
  issuer of --allow makes one with OpenSSH: ssh-keygen -s ISSUER -I ID -n
  node:SHA256:... -O clear -O critical:once@podssh -V +1h KEY.pub. With
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR=none no use can be recorded, and each grant is refused. A
  node with no --allow and no net says that the pair's token alone is its door.
  A TARGET that is not SSH has no other gate behind it. The same door takes a
  bearer of an operator's --bearer: a token of 30 s that a key signs for one
  channel. Its signer is one that may issue a grant, for what that key may
  reach itself. The node checks the bearer's signer, signature, life (10 s of
  skew), operator key and channel. It keeps each bearer in memory for its life,
  and refuses a second use. A bearer copied to another channel is refused: it
  names the channel's binding. The node's log names the check that refused it.

  With --ask, a person at the node's terminal lets each operator key in, after
  the node's door, on each road of the node: for each key that --allow, the net
  or a grant lets through, the node asks on stderr and reads y or n on stdin.
  The question names the key's fingerprint and its name in the net held here.
  It names what the key asks (the target, a route, or an exit's target) and
  whether a grant brought it; no answer within 100 s is a no. One question for
  each key at a time: each session of that key that comes meanwhile waits for
  its answer; one question shows at a time, and a line typed before it showed
  is no answer to it. A yes lets the key in while one of its sessions is open
  and 120 s after its last, with no question; a no stands 15 s, in which the
  key is refused with no question and with its grant unspent. A key that the
  door refuses raises no question, and a yes lets in nothing that the door
  refused; a grant meets the question after its check, which spends it. The
  node's line of each session that came in says by what: the door or a grant,
  and a yes or its cover. The operator hears only that its key is not let in
  (77). An operator waits 130 s for the node's verdict, and one of an earlier
  podssh 30 s. A yes that comes later lets its next session in. stdin and
  stderr must each be a terminal, else --ask is refused (78); --detach,
  --install, --uninstall, --temporary, --no-e2e and --carrier stdio are refused
  with it (64), as nobody could answer there. Nothing is kept: a node that
  starts again asks again.

  Its relay may be podssh relay serve, whose hello on the node's socket says
  so. Then each session that the node lets in gets the seed of its tokens of
  one leg in the node's verdict. The seed goes inside the end-to-end channel,
  where no relay sees it. The tokens are one connect token for each leg after
  the first, which only that leg takes. This way a token that a proxy logged
  from a leg's headers is spent already. The node registers the SHA-256 of the
  next four at the relay, on its socket, never a token; the relay says which
  one each upgrade took, and the node registers the four after it; a session's
  end withdraws them, and a new socket registers each session's again. A
  session of --plain or --no-e2e gets none. At its first socket that heard it,
  and each day after, the node rotates the pair's stop token there too: it
  draws the next one, and names its SHA-256 to the relay by the token now. It
  keeps it in the store in the place of the one before, then uses it once. That
  makes it the pair's and ends the one before; a stop at any step leaves a
  token that the relay takes. podssh relay revoke, and the renewal of podssh
  relay pair, on the node's host read the store, so they take the new one; a
  copy of the pair on another host can no longer stop or renew it. A pair of
  --pair-file keeps its stop token, as its file is the user's and is never
  rewritten, and the node says so. The next pair that the node goes on with at
  an expiry is rotated so too, from its own first socket that hears the offer.
  It is renewed in its last 24 hours where its relay renews, also when the pair
  before it was on a relay that does neither. A relay of the contract (the
  default relay) offers neither, and the pair's tokens stay as they were.

  With --spares N, 0 to 16, the node asks its relay to keep up to N sessions
  open and readied ahead for its operators. This works where the relay is
  podssh relay serve, whose hello offers it: an operator's leg then takes one,
  with no open and ready to wait for and no open of the node's local side. A
