  run of short connections to the node (a copy of many files, a loop of
  commands) thus waits for none. The relay keeps N while they are taken, and
  one after a minute in which no operator took one. It keeps one more for each
  operator that found none. It never keeps them past the node's 64 sessions
  with its operators' counted, and never one that an operator's session needs.
  Each spare is a session at rest on the node, drawn again each 15 to 20 s. The
  node's resumable layer and its end-to-end channel give a client 30 s from the
  session's open: with them it costs a pipe and a task here, and TARGET sees
  nothing of it; with --plain --no-e2e it is a connection to TARGET with nobody
  on it. An sshd counts it among those that have not logged in (its
  MaxStartups, 10 by default), so keep N under that bound. A spare that TARGET
  refuses stops them until the next minute. The node's line says once whether
  its relay keeps them; a relay of the contract (the default relay) keeps none,
  and the node goes on as without the flag. --spares is for the pair's road,
  and is refused with --iroh, --derp, --opentunnel, --quick-tunnel, --carrier
  and --temporary. --install writes it into the service.

  --print-unit prints the unit that --install would write, on stdout, and
  writes nothing. It does so on any system, so that the unit is read before it
  is installed. With --system --run-as USER, it is the system unit. --install
  --system --run-as USER writes /etc/systemd/system/podssh-node-NAME.service,
  then runs systemctl daemon-reload, enable and restart. It probes first, in
  this order: root (else 77), systemd as the service manager
  (/run/systemd/system, else 69), USER in /etc/passwd (else 69), and USER's
  cache of podssh (else 69). USER is no root (64). The unit runs as USER, with
  HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME in USER's home. So the node reads
  the pair and the keys that USER's own runs keep: podssh relay pair NAME, run
  as USER, makes them. The file of its variables is
  /var/lib/podssh-node-NAME/node-NAME.env, of mode 0600 and USER's, in the
  unit's state directory. Each user may read a unit, so no token goes in it.
  The unit is hardened. It sets NoNewPrivileges, an empty
  CapabilityBoundingSet, ProtectSystem strict, and ProtectHome tmpfs with
  USER's cache bound in. It sets PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ProtectKernel*,
  and RestrictAddressFamilies to inet, inet6 and unix sockets. It sets
  SystemCallFilter to the set of a system service, LockPersonality and
  MemoryDenyWriteExecute. --exit, --routes and --iroh add netlink sockets, by
  which the kernel gives this host's own addresses. A comment of the unit names
  that line. A roost (--sshd) relaxes nothing. --uninstall --system, as root,
  removes the unit, stopped first, and the file of the variables with its lock.

  A route may name unix-connect:PATH as its service, as a route of TCP names
  its own (see TARGET). It offers a service that listens on a Unix socket, with
  no bridge of TCP. On Linux, @NAME is a name in the abstract namespace. On
  Windows, PATH is a socket of the Unix family; a named pipe is refused, as an
  upgrade moves a socket alone. The node connects to PATH for each session of
  the route, and only then; a connect is no listener. A failure names PATH and
  its cause, and the operator gets it. Such a TARGET always has a route, as an
  operator names it with NAME/ROUTE. It is refused with --sshd, whose sshd is
  on TCP, and with --exit, which lends TCP. --no-e2e refuses it too, as a route
  travels in the end-to-end channel. --caller-line ROUTES, by commas, names
  routes to a Unix socket. Before each session's first byte, the node writes
  one line to that socket: podssh-caller v1, the operator's key as SHA256:...,
  the route's name, and a newline. The service reads that line, and the rest is
  the session. The node writes it once its door let the key in: its allowlist,
  the net's policy, a grant, or the person of --ask. So the line is a fact of
  the door, and no claim of the caller. A key that the door refuses never
  reaches the socket. Without --caller-line, the node writes nothing of its
  own: a plain bridge. Under --install, PATH is absolute or @NAME, as a service
  starts in another directory (64 else). A system unit lets through the
  directory of a socket that ProtectHome hides, read-only.

  With --net-url URL --net-owner KEY, the node takes its net from the signed
  document at URL. A change of the net then needs no copy of a file to each
  node. URL is https:// alone; an http:// URL, or one with a user or a
  password, is refused (64). TLS alone is not the trust. Each document must be
  signed by the owner of --net-owner, its fingerprint SHA256:... or its public
  key. One of another owner, with a bad signature, or with a serial not higher
  than the one held is refused; the copy held stays. A document that is taken
  goes where podssh net take puts one, and each door of the node reads it at
  the next session. The node fetches it once before it goes online. A fetch
  that fails stops the start (78) when no copy from the URL is held; else the
  copy of before is read. Then it fetches it again each --net-ttl seconds (300,
  at least 60), one fetch at a time. Each fetch is one GET through the proxy,
  with the trust of --ca-file, 64 KiB at most, with no redirect. A fetch that
  fails is a line, and the copy ages. Past --net-ttl and --net-stale (3600 s)
  the net lets nobody in, and a line says so. Sessions that live go on, and the
  keys of --allow still come in. A fetch that works opens the door again. The
  record of the last fetch, net-url.json in the cache, names the URL by its
  host alone. podssh status --net shows it. NetUrl and NetOwner of the settings
  file stand in for the flags. --install writes them into the service, and
  --temporary refuses them (64).

  SIGUSR2 asks a node to take the binary now at its path, as podssh update
  leaves it, with its sessions: a node of the pair's road, with or without the
  transit road beside it. It holds too for a node of --iroh, --derp,
  --quick-tunnel, the Piping Server road or the OpenTunnel road. Where such a
  node has the pair's road beside it, that road goes too. The node first runs
  that binary once, as podssh --version with PODSSH_HANDOVER=probe, for 10 s at
  most: a binary that does not start, or does not say that it takes a node's
  sessions of this version, leaves the node as it is. A line says why. Else the
  node stops its socket as a stop does, each session's close saying that the
  node upgrades; each link of the resumable layer stops at a record's end, each
  end-to-end channel between two messages; and the node becomes the new binary
  in the same process (execve). It keeps the same pid, words, environment and
  scope of systemd, so a supervisor of --restart or a service manager sees no
  end. The new binary keeps each session as one whose link was lost, with its
  offsets and its replay buffer. The session keeps its channel's keys and
  nonces, its tokens of one leg, and the very TCP connection to TARGET. The new
  binary then goes online; each client resumes on a new leg as after any loss,
  and an sshd behind a roost never sees its connection end. The sessions' state
  passes in anonymous memory, never a path: memfd on Linux, a POSIX shared
  object unlinked at once on macOS, else a private file of the cache unlinked
  at once. Their sockets stay open across the exec alone. Some sessions cannot
  move: a UDP flow, a target in this process, a channel that does not stop
  within 10 s. Such a session waits as an ended one. Its client's resume hears
  the session's end with why; a session of --plain, which has no layer, ends at
  the stop. A binary that does not start after the probe gives the sessions
  back to this one, which serves on. Its lines say how many sessions went, and
  the new binary's first lines how many it took. Each road's own connection is
  made again by the new binary, as the same, so that each client finds the node
  where it was: the iroh road's endpoint and the DERP road's home under the
  same key, so the ticket stays; this holds also for a key of --ephemeral-key,
  which passes with the sessions; the same door of the Piping Server, as its
  path is the pair's; the OpenTunnel road's tunnel kept in the cache, under the
  same name; a tunnel that no directory of the cache took gets a new name, and
  the node says so as it starts; and the quick tunnel's same name, as its
  credentials pass with the sessions. The new binary registers it again with no
  request to Cloudflare's API. Should the edge refuse it, the node asks for a
  new tunnel, under a new name. The clients of the sessions that came over do
  not hold that name. A session of --iroh with --no-e2e, a pipe in this
  process, ends at its resume. A node of --carrier and one of --temporary
  ignore the signal and go on with their binary. So does a node of
  --quick-tunnel with --relay, whose relay role's tokens and pairs live in its
  process. Windows has no such signal and no exec: a node there waits for its
  event of an upgrade (podssh-node-upgrade-PID, PID the one of its run's
  record). It probes the binary as above, and starts it as its child with the
  same words. It hands it each target's socket and the sessions' state, and
  waits for it, ending with its code: the pid and the locks of the run stay the
  first binary's, and a job ends the child should the first one be ended. A
  route's Unix socket goes to the child as a TCP one does. A session whose
  socket Windows does not duplicate for the child ends at its resume: the first
  binary serves nothing once the child runs. A line names the socket's family
  and the error of Windows.

  The node reads the dialect of the reverse road that its relay speaks, the
  version of the relay's hello. It states its own on each upgrade, in the
  header X-Podssh-Proto; a hello with no version is the dialect of before, 1,
  which the default relay and each podssh before it speak. A relay may speak a
  dialect that this node does not read, by its hello or by its answer 426 to
  the node's upgrade. That ends the node with exit 78 and one line. The line
  names both and the side to update: podssh update, where this node is the
  older one. The node does not connect again, as each new socket would meet the
  same; --restart does not start it again either. This podssh and its relay
  role speak 1 alone, so nothing is refused until the dialect changes.

  With --publish-tls TARGET, the pair's sessions are a site that podssh relay
  serve publishes by its name (see its notes): the relay sends each TLS
  connection whose ClientHello names it here, before any handshake and with
  each byte untouched. Each session is one connection to TARGET, a TLS service
  of this host whose own certificate answers. It is carried as it came, with no
  resumable layer and no end-to-end channel, as a visitor speaks neither; a
  connection that ends is a visitor that left, and no session resumes. The
  first line names the pair's name for the relay's table. It says that the
  relay reads the name of each connection and never its bytes. With --acme
  NAME, the published name, the node ends TLS itself and TARGET gets the
  cleartext: its certificate comes from an ACME CA: Let's Encrypt, or the
  directory of --acme-directory, reached with the trust of --ca-file. It is
  proven by TLS-ALPN-01, whose validation the relay sends here too, so the node
  needs no port of its own. The order starts once the node is online. The
  certificate is kept in the cache and renewed while the node runs, and a first
  order that fails stops the node (69). TARGET is the flag's own: a TARGET
  beside it, and each flag of another road, of the channel or of the layer, are
  refused (64). A visitor that reads more slowly than TARGET sends meets the
  relay's bound of 1 MiB, as an operator of a node with --plain does.

  With --quick-tunnel, the node serves TARGET at
  https://NAME.trycloudflare.com, a quick tunnel of Cloudflare's that podssh
  makes itself, with no pair, no account and no cloudflared. The name is new
  each run, and is the one line on stdout. The node needs port 7844 of
  Cloudflare's edge, and races its roads there: QUIC where no proxy is set, as
  cloudflared does, after a probe of UDP (one QUIC packet, whose answer it
  waits 300 ms for); HTTP/2 on TCP, directly or through a proxy that allows it;
  and HTTP/2 inside WARP's tunnel, in a build with the feature warp (see
  warp:// in the notes of ssh: its device, and PODSSH_WARP_ACCEPT_TERMS), as a
  cage whose proxy allows port 443 alone reaches the edge so; --warp puts
  WARP's tunnel first. Each road starts 2 s after the one before, or at once
  when that one failed; the first that the edge registers is kept, and the
  others are closed. The road that won goes first at the next connection, and
  the node exits 69 when no road reaches the edge. Its line of the registration
  names the road and how long the race took, after a line for each road that
  gave way. A client in a cage reaches the name on port 443. The name is
  public, so the node needs a door: --allow FILE, and only an operator whose
  key is a line of FILE reaches TARGET, through the end-to-end channel above
  the resumable layer; or, with no --allow, a key of the node's that the net
  held here names. Then only the net's members come in, and its first line says
  so. With neither, it is refused (64). The node keeps two connections to the
  edge, each to its own region first, so that one stays while the other is made
  again. On the edge's GOAWAY its visitors go on for up to 90 s while a new
  connection, at once, takes the new ones. A connection to the edge that is
  lost is made again, with the same name; at Ctrl-C the node unregisters each.
  --iroh, --derp, --plain, --no-e2e, --pair-file, a route and a udp: TARGET are
  refused with it (64). In a build with the iroh road, the node's record of
  pkarr names the tunnel, for a client with the node's key. The record is at
  n0's server unless its variable names another or off (see iroh record in THE
  RELAY).

  With --quick-tunnel --relay, the node is its owner's relay too, with no
  listener: behind its tunnel it serves the relay's forward and reverse roads,
  those of podssh relay serve. Without the role, a request of another path than
  a visitor's would get 404: /health, /v1/mint, /connect/HOST/PORT,
  /relays.json, /trace, /llms-full.txt and each path under /v1/. Its one line
  on stdout is the relay host: a client reaches the relay with --relay-host
  https://NAME.trycloudflare.com, as it reaches another relay. With no TARGET,
  the node is the relay alone, and each path is the relay's. It mints tokens,
  and makes pairs, for the keys of --allow by default (the net's members, with
  no --allow). Each key signs the relay's challenge, and a signed request must
  name the tunnel. --mint keys:FILE names another list. --mint net names the
  members of the node's net, as its policy lets them reach relay:NAME (NAME the
  node's name in the net) or relay:*. --mint anyone mints for each client, and
  --mint nobody for none. --pairs FILE keeps its pairs across a restart, though
  the tunnel's name is new each run; --allow-private dials non-public targets
  too, and --routes RANGES those inside its ranges alone, as podssh relay serve
  --routes. The relay dials each target from this host, as podssh relay serve
  does: through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set, the proxy that the node's dial of
  the edge takes too. Each mint, upgrade and step of the reverse road is a line
  on stderr. Ctrl-C or SIGTERM first closes each socket of the reverse road
  with 1012.

  The name is asked of api.trycloudflare.com, which limits a host that made a
  few tunnels: when it refuses for now (429, or a 5xx), the node asks again for
  up to 5 minutes. Each try comes after its Retry-After (seconds, or a date) or
  a growing wait, with a line for each wait. Ctrl-C ends the wait (0). A
  Retry-After past those 5 minutes, or a refusal that lasts them, ends the node
  at once with exit 75. The line says until when the API asks to wait; any
  other refusal exits 69. A text of Cloudflare's API or edge is shown on one
  line, with no control character.

  podssh node NAME [TARGET] --exit lends this host's egress to the members of
  its net, as a Tailscale exit node does: an operator names a target of its own
  (podssh ssh --exit NAME, podssh proxy --exit NAME, podssh exit --listen). The
  target travels in the end-to-end channel. The node resolves its name here,
  checks each address, and dials those addresses alone, never the name again.
  This way a name that resolves anew elsewhere reaches nothing that was not
  checked. A public address needs a rule to exit:NAME (or exit:* or *) of the
  net's policy; a private one, loopback, link-local or another that the relay
  refuses needs a rule to its address. It also needs one of podssh node
  --routes RANGES, ADDR/BITS or one address apart by commas. A prefix that sets
  bits past it, as 10.0.0.5/8, is refused with the network that it names. A
  name with one address that fails is refused whole. The net must give the node
  the role exit, signed by its owner, else the node does not start (78); a key
  of --allow, or an operator of the connect token alone, never reaches the
  exit. TARGET is then optional. It goes on the pair's, the iroh, the DERP, the
  transit and the Piping Server roads, and on a carrier (--carrier). It goes
  behind a quick tunnel (--quick-tunnel) too, whose visitors are the keys of
  --allow or, with none, the net's members: podssh ssh --exit cf://HOST and the
  copies reach it by the tunnel's name, which the node prints. So do podssh
  exit, proxy --exit and pipe --exit, each session a WebSocket of the tunnel.
  --no-e2e, --temporary and a udp: TARGET are refused with it (64).

  With --carrier ADDR, the node's one road is a stream that exists already. It
  is for a host whose every road out is closed but that grants one channel.
  Such is the exec channel of a platform's own SSH: stdio (or -), the stdin and
  stdout that such a channel gives the program that it starts; fd:N, a
  descriptor that the node inherited (Unix); or exec:CMD, a program that the
  node starts with no shell, as podssh pipe reads these. The stream carries the
  node's socket of the reverse road, its WebSocket frames with no HTTP before
  them. Its other end serves the relay's side of that socket in its own
  process. That end is podssh operator --carrier, or podssh proxy, ssh, cp, scp
  and sftp with --carrier to node://NAME. No relay, no pair and no token:
  whoever holds the stream reached the node through what carries it. NAME is
  thus a label alone, for the node's key, and each operator comes in unless
  --allow names its keys. The resumable layer, the end-to-end channel, the
  routes, a roost and a udp: TARGET are as on the pair's road; the relay's
  limits (64 MiB a session, a pair's 72 hours) do not hold. The node dials
  TARGET first, then sends one Ping, its first frame, and says online: the
  other end opens no session before it. One stream is the node's life: at its
  end the sessions end, and the node exits 0 after the other end's Close, or 69
  for a stream that failed; a program of exec: is waited for 2 s, then ended.
  --carrier stdio refuses a terminal on stdin (64), whose keys the node would
  read as frames. --pair-file, --relay-addr, --ca-file, --iroh, --derp,
  --quick-tunnel, --relay, --temporary, --install, --detach and the flags that
  go with them are refused with --carrier (64): the stream is the node's
  parent's. --exit goes with it: the client at the other end is podssh exit
  --listen ADDR:PORT --carrier ADDR NAME. Or it is podssh ssh, podssh proxy or
  podssh pipe with --exit NAME and --carrier. The net's rule of the exit holds
  as on each road. This way a host whose one channel is a platform's exec
  channel gets egress through its other end.

  Usage: podssh node [OPTIONS] NAME [TARGET] [ROUTE=TARGET]...

  Arguments:
    [NAME]
        the label of a stored pair (podssh relay pair NAME); with --iroh, the
        node's name, which labels its key; with --temporary, the label of its
        lines (default upgrade).
    [TARGET]...
        the TCP service that each session reaches: HOST:PORT, or [IPV6]:PORT;
        ROUTE=HOST:PORT offers one more under ROUTE, which an operator names as
        NAME/ROUTE; ROUTE=unix-connect:PATH, a Unix socket (@NAME, abstract, on
        Linux); udp:HOST:PORT, alone, a UDP service; with --sshd and none,
        127.0.0.1:22; with --quick-tunnel --relay and none, the relay alone;
        with --exit, none is needed.

  Options:
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --pair-file FILE
        use the pair in FILE, a private file, not the one stored under NAME
        (operator: its operator's part will do).
    --plain
        carry each session's bytes as they are, with no resumable layer, for an
        operator that does not speak it; a lost link ends the session.
    --resume-deadline TIME
        keep a session whose link is lost for TIME, on each road, and tell its
        operator so: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d, from 1 minute to 72 h (default 10m).
    --spares N
        ask the pair's relay to keep up to N sessions, 0 to 16, open and
        readied ahead for this node's operators; this way, a run of short
        connections waits for no open and ready; each is a session at rest
        here, drawn again each 15 to 20 s, and with --plain --no-e2e a
        connection to TARGET; podssh relay serve keeps them, a relay of the
        contract none (default 0, none).
    --sshd
        a roost: each TARGET (default 127.0.0.1:22) is a standard sshd that
        runs already; it must send its SSH version line, after any lines of a
        greeting, at the start and on each session's connection; podssh brings
        no sshd (podssh doctor's line sshd says whether this host has one).
    --temporary KEY
        the far end that podssh ssh --upgrade starts on its server: a roost in
        front of the session's sshd, with a pair and a key that no file keeps,
        for the client key KEY alone; one line on stdout gives the offer; it
        ends with its last session, or after 10 minutes with none.
    --key FILE
        the node's key in FILE, on each road, made when missing (default:
        node-NAME.key in the cache); its fingerprint is said as the node
        starts.
    --ephemeral-key
        a new key for this run only, kept in no file; an operator that pinned
        the node's key refuses it.
    --allow FILE
        the operator keys that may come in, on each road: one key or
        fingerprint on each line, read again for each session (default: on the
        pair's road, each operator with the connect token; on the iroh road,
        none).
    --no-e2e
        carry each session's bytes with no end-to-end channel, to operators
        that run none either; the relay then sees them.
    --exit
        lend this host's egress to the members of its net: a session may name a
        target of its own, which the node resolves; the node then dials it at a
        public address alone, or in a range of --routes; needs a net that gives
        this node the role exit; TARGET is then optional.
    --routes RANGES
        with --exit: the private ranges that the exit dials too, ADDR/BITS or
        one address, separated by commas; each for the members that the net's
        policy lets reach the address; a loopback address or one of this host's
        own is dialled only when a range names it alone (ADDR, or ADDR/32 and
        ADDR/128); with --relay: the private ranges that the relay role dials
        too, as podssh relay serve --routes; a prefix that sets bits past it is
        refused.
    --carrier ADDR
        serve TARGET over ADDR, a stream that exists already, with no relay and
        no pair: stdio (or -), as the exec channel of a platform's own SSH
        gives it, fd:N (Unix), or exec:CMD, a program started with no shell; or
        s3:FILE, a bucket of the S3 API that FILE describes (see FILES); or
        dns:FILE, names and TXT answers of DNS under a zone of your own (see
        FILES); the other end runs podssh operator --carrier, or proxy, ssh,
        cp, scp or sftp --carrier to node://NAME; or for --exit, podssh exit
        NAME --listen ADDR:PORT --carrier, or ssh, proxy or pipe with --exit
        NAME --carrier; stdin may not be a terminal.
    --iroh
        serve TARGET over the iroh road, with no pair: a client dials the
        ticket that the node prints; a build with the feature iroh.
    --derp
        serve TARGET over the DERP road, through Tailscale's tailcat fleet: a
        client dials the ticket that the node prints; beside the pair's road
        and the iroh road; needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key
        that the net held here names, whose members are then the door.
    --opentunnel
        serve TARGET over the OpenTunnel road, a blind TLS tunnel of
        opentunnel.xyz with no account (or the service of env
        PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL): one tunnel for the node, kept in the cache; a
        client dials the name that the node prints, by TLS with no upgrade;
        beside the pair's road; needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a
        key that the net held here names, whose members are then the door.
    --pinggy
        serve TARGET over the Pinggy road, a TLS tunnel of Pinggy's free tier
        with no account (or the server of env PODSSH_PINGGY): SSH on port 443
        through the proxy, raw, else inside TLS that --ca-file or this host's
        roots verify; a new name each hour, which the node prints with the pin
        of its TLS key, kept beside its key; a client dials it by TLS with no
        upgrade, which takes that key alone; a third party that nobody vouches
        for, so a last fallback; beside the pair's road; needs the end-to-end
        channel, and --allow or a key that the net held here names, whose
        members are then the door.
    --frp FILE
        serve TARGET through your own frps, as an STCP service of NAME with no
        public port: FILE, a private file, names frps (frp://HOST[:PORT] or
        wss://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]), its token and the service's secret, a line
        each; a client names the same file in env PODSSH_FRP; the road alone,
        with no pair; needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that
        the net held here names, whose members are then the door.
    --serveo
        serve TARGET over the Serveo road; a private alias at Serveo with no
        account (the server that podssh's list of services names, or the one of
        env PODSSH_SERVEO): raw SSH on port 443, then 22, through the proxy;
        the alias is derived from the node's key, the next of its series where
        another holds it; so a client that holds the key (its pins, --node-key,
        the net) jumps to it with no name given; it does so last, when each
        road before it failed; a third party that nobody vouches for, so a last
        fallback; beside the pair's road; needs the end-to-end channel, and
        --allow or a key that the net held here names, whose members are then
        the door.
    --ssh-j
        serve TARGET over the ssh-j road; a public SSH jump and forwarding
        server with no account (ssh-j.com where podssh's list of services names
        it, or the server of env PODSSH_SSH_J): SSH on port 22, directly or
        through the proxy's CONNECT; as a user and with a remote forward of a
        name that the node's key gives; a client that holds the key
        (--node-key, the net, or the pins of NAME) derives the name and races
        the road last; a third party that nobody vouches for, which ends that
        SSH, so a last fallback; the road alone, with no pair's road beside it;
        needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that the net held
        here names, whose members are then the door.
    --localhost-run
        serve TARGET over the localhost.run road; a tunnel of HTTP made by ssh
        -R with no account (localhost.run where podssh's list of services names
        it, or the server of env PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN): SSH on port 22,
        directly or through the proxy's CONNECT, as the user nokey, with the
        remote forward of port 80; the service ends each visitor's TLS at an
        HTTPS name, new after a few hours; the node prints the name, keeps it
        under NAME in the cache and puts it in its record; a client takes a
        WebSocket at / of that name; with --relay, the relay role behind it
        too, and TARGET may be left out; a third party that nobody vouches for,
        so a last fallback; the road alone, with no pair's road beside it;
        needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that the net held
        here names, whose members are then the door.
    --sandhole
        serve TARGET over the same road at Sandhole's public server
        (demo.sandhole.com.br where podssh's list of services names it, or the
        server of env PODSSH_SANDHOLE): SSH on port 443, then 22, directly or
        through the proxy's CONNECT; with a key made for the login alone and
        the remote forward of port 80; the service ends each visitor's TLS at a
        random HTTPS name under its own, new at each connection; the node
        prints the name, keeps it under NAME in the cache and puts it in its
        record; with --relay, the relay role behind it too; a third party that
        nobody vouches for, so a last fallback, after localhost.run's; the road
        alone; needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that the net
        held here names.
    --srv-us
        serve TARGET over the same road at srv.us (where podssh's list of
        services names it, or the server of env PODSSH_SRV_US): SSH on port 22,
        directly or through the proxy's CONNECT; as the user nomatch, logged in
        with the node's own key, and the remote forward of port 1; srv.us
        derives the tunnel's HTTPS name from that key and port; so a client
        that holds the node's key (--node-key, the net, or the pins of NAME)
        derives the name; it races the road last, with no record; the node
        prints the name, keeps it under NAME and puts it in its record; with
        --relay, the relay role behind it too; a third party that nobody
        vouches for, which sees the node's public key, so a last fallback,
        after Sandhole's; the road alone; needs the end-to-end channel, and
        --allow or a key that the net held here names.
    --tunnl-gg
        serve TARGET over the same road at tunnl.gg (where podssh's list of
        services names it, or the server of env PODSSH_TUNNL_GG): SSH on port
        22, directly or through the proxy's CONNECT; with no key and the remote
        forward of port 80, and the command output=json; its first line names a
        random HTTPS name, new at each connection; the node prints the name,
        keeps it under NAME in the cache and puts it in its record; with
        --relay, the relay role behind it too; a third party that nobody
        vouches for, so a last fallback, after srv.us's; the road alone; needs
        the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that the net held here
        names.
    --hostc
        serve TARGET over the hostc road; an HTTPS name at hostc's public
        server with no account (where podssh's list of services names it, or
        the server of env PODSSH_HOSTC): the node asks the server over HTTPS
        for a tunnel, then keeps one WebSocket to it on port 443, both through
        the proxy; so it passes where a WebSocket does; each visitor's request
        or WebSocket comes down that socket; the name is random: the node says
        it, keeps it under NAME and puts it in its record; a client takes it as
        a tunnel of ssh -R's (--tunnel-url https://NAME, or the record), last;
        with --relay, the relay role answers its paths there too, and TARGET
        may be left out; the URL is the line on stdout; a third party that
        nobody vouches for, which ends the visitors' TLS, so a last fallback;
        the road alone, with no pair's road beside it; needs the end-to-end
        channel, and --allow or a key that the net held here names, whose
        members are then the door.
    --localtunnel
        serve TARGET over the localtunnel road; an HTTPS name at localtunnel's
        public server with no account (where podssh's list of services names
        it, or the server of env PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL): the node asks the server
        over HTTPS for a name that its key gives; then it keeps TCP connections
        to a port that the server names, directly or through the proxy's
        CONNECT; so its egress must reach that port; a client that holds the
        key (--node-key, the net, or the pins of NAME) derives the name and
        races the road last; it uses TLS and a WebSocket on port 443; with
        --relay, the relay role answers its paths there too, and TARGET may be
        left out; the URL is the line on stdout; a third party that nobody
        vouches for, which ends the visitors' TLS, so a last fallback; the road
        alone, with no pair's road beside it; needs the end-to-end channel, and
        --allow or a key that the net held here names, whose members are then
        the door.
    --bore
        serve TARGET over the bore road; a public TCP port with no account
        (bore.pub where podssh's list of services names it, or the server of
        env PODSSH_BORE): raw TCP to the server's control port 7835, directly
        or through the proxy's CONNECT; it asks a port that the node's key
        gives, the next of a series of four where another holds it; a client
        that holds the key (--node-key, the net, or the pins of NAME) derives
        the ports and races the road last of all; it reaches the port directly,
        by CONNECT, or through the forwarders that the binary names; a third
        party that nobody vouches for, so a last fallback; the road alone, with
        no pair's road beside it; needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or
        a key that the net held here names, whose members are then the door.
    --gsr
        serve TARGET over the GSRN road, the relay of gsocket with no account
        (where podssh's list of services names it): one TCP connection to the
        relay's port 443, directly or through the proxy's CONNECT, at the
        address that a shared secret gives; the secret comes from the private
        file that the flag of the secret's file, or env PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE,
        names; a client with the same secret races the road last; TLS with SRP
        of that secret keeps the bytes from the relay, a third party that
        nobody vouches for; the road alone, with no pair's road beside it;
        needs the end-to-end channel, and --allow or a key that the net held
        here names, whose members are then the door; a build with the feature
        gsr.
    --gsr-secret-file FILE
        with --gsr: the shared secret, the first line of FILE, a private file
        of yours, never argv (default: env PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE); a build
        with the feature gsr.
    --quick-tunnel
        serve TARGET at https://NAME.trycloudflare.com, a quick tunnel of
        Cloudflare's that podssh makes itself, with no pair and no account; the
        name, new each run, is the line on stdout; needs --allow, or a key that
        the net held here names; and TCP port 7844 of Cloudflare's edge,
        directly or through a proxy that allows it.
    --warp
        with --quick-tunnel: reach the edge's TCP port 7844 inside WARP's
        tunnel first, over HTTP/2 to Cloudflare on port 443; without it, WARP's
        tunnel is tried after QUIC and TCP fail; a build with the feature warp.
    --relay
        with --quick-tunnel or --localhost-run: serve the relay's forward and
        reverse roads too, those of podssh relay serve, at the tunnel's name,
        with no listener; a client names https://NAME.trycloudflare.com, or the
        name of localhost.run's tunnel, as its relay host; with no TARGET, the
        relay alone.
    --mint WHO
        with --relay: who may mint a token and make a pair: keys:FILE, the keys
        of FILE, a file or an https:// URL whose list is fetched again each 5
        minutes with the trust of --ca-file; each key by its signature of the
        relay's challenge; net, the members of this node's net, as its policy
        lets them reach relay:NAME (this node) or relay:*; net,keys:FILE, both;
        anyone; or nobody (default: the keys of --allow).
    --pairs FILE
        with --relay: keep the pairs of its reverse road in FILE, of mode 0600;
        this way, they outlive a restart (the digests of their tokens, never a
        token).
    --allow-private
        with --relay: dial private, loopback and other non-public addresses too
        (by default only public targets, as the default relay).
    --iroh-key FILE
        the same as --key, by its earlier name.
    --iroh-allow FILE
        the same as --allow, by its earlier name.
    --iroh-ephemeral
        the same as --ephemeral-key, by its earlier name; with --iroh, the
        ticket lasts as long as the run.
    --detach
        go to the background once the node is online, as podssh itself; for a
        node that must outlive a logout, --install.
    --restart
        with --detach: a small process in the background starts the run again
        whenever it ends, but after 64, 77 or 78 or a stop of that process; it
        never gives up.
    --detach-name NAME
        with --detach: the run's name, letters, digits, _ and -, 64 at most; a
        second start of a name that runs refuses (75), and podssh detached
        shows and stops it (default: the verb and the pid).
    --install
        make this node a service of this user, which starts it again whenever
        it ends, as a probe finds one: a user unit of systemd, else a
        LaunchAgent, else a line of the crontab at boot and one each 5 minutes;
        on Windows a task at logon; no privilege is asked for, and no token is
        written into it; with --system, a system unit.
    --uninstall
        remove the service that --install made for NAME, its file of variables
        and its lock, and nothing else.
    --print-unit
        print the unit of systemd that --install would write, on stdout, and
        write nothing: a user unit, or with --system --run-as USER the system
        unit; on any system.
    --system
        with --install, --uninstall or --print-unit: a system unit of systemd,
        /etc/systemd/system/podssh-node-NAME.service, hardened, that runs as
        the user of --run-as; --install and --uninstall need root.
    --run-as USER
        with --system: the user that the node runs as, a user of /etc/passwd
        other than root; the unit names its HOME and its cache, which hold the
        pair and the keys.
    --env-file FILE
        read the node's variables from FILE, a private file of NAME=VALUE
        lines, before anything else; hold FILE.lock while it runs, so that a
        second start ends at once: the file that --install writes beside the
        pair.
    --iroh-relay URLS
        with --iroh: the relays, https://HOST[:PORT][,...]; the first that
        answers is the home relay (default: env PODSSH_IROH_RELAY, else the
        net's relay members' own, then n0's).
    --derp-server SERVERS
        with --derp: the DERP servers, HOST[:PORT][,...]; the first whose
        /derp/probe answers is the home, and after 3 failed connections the
        next that takes one (default: env PODSSH_DERP_SERVER, else tailcat's).
    --grant-to KEY
        print a grant used once for KEY on stdout, an OpenSSH user certificate
        that the node's own key signs, and serve nothing: KEY is the operator's
        key, ssh-ed25519 BASE64, its 64 hex digits, or a file of one line; the
        node's key is read, never made.
    --grant-route ROUTE
        with --grant-to: the grant names ROUTE of the node, node://NAME/ROUTE,
        in place of its TARGET with no route; +exit names the node's exit, to
        public addresses alone.
    --grant-for TIME
        with --grant-to: the grant's window, from now: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d, from
        1 minute to 30 days (default 1h).
    --revoked FILE
        the grants that the node refuses: a serial on each line, or a
        fingerprint and a serial, read again for each grant; a file that is
        missing lets no grant in.
    --shares FILE
        the node's shares in FILE, NAME=HOST:PORT on each line, read again for
        each session; this way, podssh share adds and removes one while the
        node runs; an operator reaches one as node://NAME/SHARE, as a route
        (default: node-NAME.shares in the cache); not with --no-e2e,
        --temporary, --quick-tunnel or a udp: TARGET.
    --caller-line ROUTES
        ROUTES, by commas, are routes to a Unix socket
        (ROUTE=unix-connect:PATH); before each session's first byte, the node
        writes podssh-caller v1 SHA256:KEY ROUTE and a newline to it.
    --ask
        ask at this terminal of each operator key that the door or a grant lets
        in: y or n within 100 s, no answer a no; a yes lets the key in while
        one of its sessions is open and 120 s after its last, a no stands 15 s;
        stdin and stderr must be a terminal (else 78).
    --publish-tls TARGET
        serve the pair's sessions as a site that podssh relay serve --publish
        NAME=PAIR sends here by the name in each ClientHello, before any
        handshake: each session is one connection to TARGET, a TLS service of
        this host that answers with its own certificate; the bytes as they
        came, with no resumable layer and no end-to-end channel; the relay
        reads the name, never the bytes; with --acme NAME, TARGET serves in
        cleartext and the node ends TLS itself; the first line names the pair
        for --publish.
    --acme NAME
        with --publish-tls: end each session's TLS at this node with a
        certificate for NAME, the published name, from an ACME CA (Let's
        Encrypt by default); it is proven by TLS-ALPN-01, whose validation the
        relay that publishes NAME sends here too; asked once the node is
        online, kept in the cache and renewed while the node runs.
    --acme-directory URL
        with --acme: the directory of another ACME CA, reached with the trust
        of --ca-file.
    --net-url URL
        take the net that each door reads from the signed document at URL, an
        https:// URL; it is fetched through the proxy with the trust of
        --ca-file; it needs --net-owner (default: NetUrl of the settings file).
    --net-owner KEY
        with --net-url: the owner that each document must have, its fingerprint
        SHA256:... or its public key; another is refused (default: NetOwner of
        the settings file).
    --net-ttl SECONDS
        with --net-url: fetch the document again each SECONDS, 60 to 86400
        (default 300).
    --net-stale SECONDS
        with --net-url: read the copy for SECONDS more past --net-ttl while its
        server fails, 0 to 604800 (default 3600); past that, the net lets
        nobody in.
    --access-host HOST
        the relay's roads to HOST carry the credentials of Cloudflare Access in
        their headers, in the place of AccessHost of the settings; HOST[,...],
        repeatable; no other host gets them.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    lend this host's egress to the members of its net, as an exit node: its
    owner gave it the role exit
        $ podssh node gw --exit

    then the node, a roost in front of this host's sshd at 127.0.0.1:22: each
    operator's session reaches it
        $ podssh node lab --sshd

    or the other way: that host's programs reach the internet through this one,
    an exit of your net, by HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1080 in the sandbox
        $ podssh node gw --exit --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh exit gw --listen 127.0.0.1:1080 --carrier stdio'

    the node in the background under a name, started again whenever it ends; a
    second start of the name refuses
        $ podssh node lab --sshd --detach --restart --detach-name lab

    a node of a DNS server, on a host that allows UDP: each session is one flow
    of datagrams
        $ podssh node dns udp:10.0.0.2:53

    the relay itself on a host where nothing may listen: behind a quick tunnel,
    minting for the keys of owners.txt; its one line on stdout is the relay
    host
        $ podssh node relay --quick-tunnel --relay --allow owners.txt

podssh operator
  reverse mode, operator side: raw bytes to a named node.

  podssh operator NAME carries stdin to the node of the pair under the label
  NAME, and the bytes of the node's TARGET to stdout. It is as podssh proxy
  carries a forward session. It is the ProxyCommand of OpenSSH for a node: ssh
  -o ProxyCommand='podssh operator NAME' user@NAME. podssh proxy node://NAME is
  the same pipe, with the same flags and codes, by the form of a node that
  podssh ssh takes.

  Before the node takes the session, up to 1 MiB of stdin is kept, and sent
  then. The session ends when stdin ends or the node's TARGET closes; it exits
  0 only when the node took the session. A session cut before its end, as when
  the TARGET's connection was reset, exits 69: the last bytes can be missing.
  An error is one line on stderr; the codes are in EXIT STATUS.

  SIGHUP, SIGTERM and SIGINT (on Windows, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break and the close of
  the console) end the session as the end of stdin does: OpenSSH ends its
  ProxyCommand with SIGHUP as it exits, and does not wait for it. The node
  hears the session's end after the bytes on their way, and keeps nothing of
  it; podssh waits 2 s at most for the node's answer, then exits, 0 when the
  node took the session. A signal before the node took it ends the wait at
  once. A signal that podssh was started to ignore (nohup, a detached run's
  SIGHUP) stays ignored.

  With a node that offers the resumable layer, a lost link to the relay is
  replaced by a new one. This holds for as long as the node keeps the session
  (10 minutes, or its --resume-deadline), and the session goes on where it was;
  one line on stderr tells of each loss and each resume. --resume-deadline TIME
  waits at most TIME, never longer than the node keeps the session. A close
  that a new link would only get again (a stopped or expired pair) ends the
  session. When the node forgot the session, as after a sleep of this host
  longer than its deadline, the line says so. It says how long this side was
  away by the wall clock.

  --no-resume asks the node, in the layer's handshake, to end the session with
  its link: no new link replaces a lost one, and none goes beside it. The node
  forgets the session and closes its connection to TARGET as the link ends. So
  its budget of replay buffers is free at once. A lost link then ends the
  session, as on a node of podssh node --plain, with a line that says so. The
  relay's limits of a session end it too. A node of an earlier podssh, which
  does not know the ask, keeps the session for its deadline as before, and a
  line says so; this side still does not resume it.

  With --pair-file, the pair comes from FILE, or its operator's part alone, as
  podssh relay pair writes it for the operator. The store is not used.

  --ConnectTimeout SECONDS, 1 to 86400, bounds the time from the start to the
  session's open: the relay's answer, the node's ready, its first bytes, and
  the handshakes of the layer and of the end-to-end channel. Each step keeps
  its own limit too (30 s for the relay, 20 s for ready), and the first limit
  to pass ends the wait. Past the bound one line names the step that waited,
  as: the node did not answer ready within 25 s (--ConnectTimeout), and the
  exit is 69. The bytes after the open are never bounded. A node run as podssh
  node --plain sends its TARGET's first bytes as they come, and the bound waits
  for them too: with a TARGET that speaks second, give none. operator takes no
  -o, so -o ConnectTimeout=N is refused (64); 0 is refused too. --timeout
  DURATION is another name of the same bound, as a duration (30s, 2m, 1h)
  rounded up to whole seconds, a day at most. PODSSH_TIMEOUT gives it its
  default, held to a day: the line past the bound names the one that set it, as
  within 25 s (--timeout). --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given; none of
  them is ever required.

  The session runs the end-to-end channel (see podssh node). This operator's
  key is a private file in the cache (client.key, or iroh-client.key of an
  earlier podssh), or the file of --client-key. It is made when it is missing,
  and its fingerprint is said when it is new. The node's key is pinned at its
  first sight in known-nodes, in the cache, one line for each label; a node
  whose key changed is refused, with both fingerprints, the file and the line,
  and exit 77, and the pin is never replaced. --node-key KEY expects that key,
  or fingerprint, instead, and reads and writes no pin. A node that refuses
  this operator's key ends the session with exit 77, and the line names the key
  to add to its allowlist. --no-e2e carries the bytes with no channel, to a
  node run with --no-e2e.

  NAME/ROUTE names a route of the node (see podssh node): the route travels in
  the end-to-end channel, encrypted. The node refuses one that it does not
  have, or that this operator's key may not use, before it dials anything.

  With --carrier ADDR, the node is at the other end of a stream that exists
  already, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a program that podssh starts
  with no shell. It can be the platform's own SSH into a host whose every road
  out is closed: exec:'ssh -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio NAME TARGET';
  or fd:N, a descriptor that podssh inherited (Unix). stdio is refused (64):
  stdin and stdout carry the session's bytes. This end serves the relay's side
  of the node's socket in its own process, and waits up to 60 s for the node's
  first frame. It then carries the session as on the pair's road. So OpenSSH
  reaches the node's sshd with ssh -o ProxyCommand="podssh operator --carrier
  'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' box"
  user@box. NAME is a label alone, under which the node's key is pinned at its
  first sight. So a stream that another key answers is refused (77). A stream
  of exec: that is lost is started again for the next link of a resume; the
  node that it starts is a new one, which knows no session of the one before,
  and the session ends with its reason. A stream of fd: has one life. At the
  end the node hears a Close, and the program of exec: is waited for 5 s, then
  ended. --ConnectTimeout bounds the open here too: the node's read of the
  stream, its ready, then the layer and the channel. podssh proxy --carrier
  ADDR node://NAME is the same pipe. --pair-file, --relay-addr and --ca-file
  are refused with --carrier (64).

  --grant FILE gives a grant used once, KEY-cert.pub of ssh-keygen -s or the
  line of podssh node --grant-to, for this session: the end-to-end channel
  carries it to the node once its key was checked, never a relay or a URL. A
  URL in its place is refused (64), as is --no-e2e beside it. A file that is no
  Ed25519 certificate is 78. The grant must name this operator's key
  (client.key, or --client-key); a line says so when it names another, with
  this key in the form that the issuer signs. A node that refuses the grant
  (used already, out of its window, or for another key, node or route) is 77.
  Its reasons are in the node's log. A node of an earlier podssh reads no
  grant, and ends the session in its handshake. Each grant lets in one session:
  a run that opens more sends it in the first. --bearer SIGNER gives a bearer
  in the place of a grant, for a key that no podssh node --allow names. SIGNER
  is a podssh key file, read and never made. agent is the first Ed25519 key of
  the SSH agent at SSH_AUTH_SOCK; agent:SHA256:... names one. On Windows the
  agent is also OpenSSH's pipe, or Pageant. The bearer is made once the node's
  key was checked, for that channel alone, and lives 30 s. Its signer must be
  the node's key, a key of the node's podssh node --allow, or a member of its
  net. A URL, --grant or --no-e2e beside it is refused (64). A key file that
  cannot be read, or an agent with no such key, is 78. A node that refuses the
  bearer is 77. An agent that does not sign in 20 s is said, and the channel
  then carries no bearer. Like a grant, it goes in the first session of a run.

  A node through podssh relay serve gives the seed of the session's tokens of
  one leg. Where it did, each leg after the first carries the session's next
  token in the place of the pair's connect token. Such a leg is one that a
  resume, a move to a new link or a spare link opens. The first leg alone
  carries the pair's connect token; the relay takes each once. So a session of
  a pair whose connect token takes one upgrade alone (see podssh relay) resumes
  too. A token that leaks from a leg's headers is spent already. A token that
  the relay refuses is tried once more, then the next one. After eight refusals
  in a row the legs take the pair's token, as with a node that gives no seed.

  A relay can answer the operator's upgrade with 426. podssh relay serve
  answers so an upgrade of a dialect of the reverse road that it does not read.
  That ends the run with exit 78 and the relay's line, which names the side to
  update; a session of the resumable layer ends so at its next link, and does
  not wait out the node's deadline.

  Usage: podssh operator [OPTIONS] NAME

  Arguments:
    [NAME]
        the label of a pair: stored here, or named for the --pair-file;
        NAME/ROUTE names a route of its node.

  Options:
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --pair-file FILE
        use the pair in FILE, a private file, not the one stored under NAME
        (operator: its operator's part will do).
    --client-key FILE
        this operator's key in FILE, made when missing (default: client.key in
        the cache), which a node's allowlist may name.
    --node-key KEY
        the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of the pins of
        known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        carry the bytes with no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none
        either; the relay then sees them.
    --resume-deadline TIME
        node://NAME and iroh:TICKET: wait at most TIME for a new link after a
        loss, though the node keeps the session longer: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d,
        from 1 minute to 72 h (default: as long as the node keeps it).
    --no-resume
        no resume: the session ends with its link, and the node, asked so,
        keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --grant FILE
        a grant used once, an OpenSSH certificate of this operator's key
        (KEY-cert.pub of ssh-keygen -s, or of podssh node --grant-to); the
        end-to-end channel carries it to the node, never a relay; it lets in
        one session, once, of the node or route that it names; a URL is
        refused.
    --bearer SIGNER
        a bearer in the place of a grant: a token of 30 s for this channel
        alone, which SIGNER signs; SIGNER is a podssh key file, or agent for
        the first Ed25519 key of the SSH agent, or agent:SHA256:... for one of
        them; the node takes it once, when SIGNER is its own key, a key of its
        --allow or a member of its net; never beside --grant.
    --access-host HOST
        the relay's roads to HOST carry the credentials of Cloudflare Access in
        their headers, in the place of AccessHost of the settings; HOST[,...],
        repeatable; no other host gets them.
    --ConnectTimeout SECONDS
        the bound on the time to the session's open, 1 to 86400: the relay's
        answer, the node's ready, and the handshakes of the layer and of the
        channel, each within its own limit too; past it one line names the step
        that waited, and the exit is 69; never the bytes after the open.
    --timeout DURATION
        another name of --ConnectTimeout, as a duration (30s, 2m, 1h) rounded
        up to whole seconds, a day at most; it bounds the session's open and
        never its bytes; --ConnectTimeout wins when both are given; never
        required (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    --carrier ADDR
        reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that exists already,
        with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a program started with no shell,
        as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N
        (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's bucket of the S3 API (see FILES); or
        dns:FILE, the node's DNS road (see FILES); NAME is then the label under
        which the node's key is pinned.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh net
  your own nodes as one net: their names and keys, signed by your key, kept by
  each.

  podssh net keeps a net of the user's own nodes, as a tailnet does but with no
  server to trust: one document of JSON that names the net and each member. A
  member has its name and its Ed25519 key (the key that the node says as it
  starts, or its fingerprint). It has its roles (node, exit, relay, share) and
  its tickets. The document has a serial and an end. The owner's key signs it
  with SSHSIG in the namespace podssh-net, as ssh-keygen -Y sign does. So
  ssh-keygen -Y verify -n podssh-net checks it too. The owner's key is an
  OpenSSH key, which podssh keygen makes, and which can stay on one host.

  The owner's subcommands each sign a new document, its serial one higher: init
  NAME (the first, with --owner-key or ~/.ssh/id_ed25519); add NAME KEY (a
  member, or a new key, roles or tickets of one); rm NAME; and renew (the same
  members, a new end). add takes --roles, --iroh-ticket, --derp-ticket, an
  exit's --routes and a node's --shares. Those are the names of its shares,
  which podssh share --net lists with ls. --days sets how long a document
  lasts, a year by default: no end takes it after its end, and a node no longer
  lets in by it. Each end's: ls, one line for each member on stdout (its name,
  roles, fingerprint and tickets, apart by tabs); show, the document's bytes as
  signed, or with --signature its signature; take FILE, a document from its
  owner, as FILE alone or as FILE and FILE.sig, as ssh-keygen -Y sign writes
  them.

  podssh net invite NAME, on the owner's host, adds a new device by a short
  code, as podssh relay pair gives a pair by one: the code, such as
  7-crossover-clockwork-adroitness, shows on this run's terminal alone, beside
  the owner's fingerprint. It never shows on stdout, in a log or in argv, and a
  run with no terminal is refused (64). The owner's key is found, and its
  passphrase asked, before the code is made. On the device, podssh net join
  takes the code; the two ends meet at a mailbox and run the exchange of the
  pairing, SPAKE2 keyed by the whole code. So the mailbox learns nothing and
  changes nothing; the code lives 10 minutes and its first exchange spends it.
  So a wrong code, or a guess, gets one try and adds no member (77 at both
  ends). The owner's host offers the net's name, its owner's key, NAME and its
  roles (--roles, node by default); the device answers with its key; the
  owner's host adds the member NAME with that key, signs and keeps the next
  serial as add does, and gives the signed document back. A NAME that is a
  member already goes to its own key alone, with the document held, as after a
  last word that was lost: another key is refused (77), so no code hands a
  member's name to a new key, and --roles is refused with it (64). stdout has
  one line at each end.

  podssh net join takes the code at a prompt on the terminal, or as one line of
  stdin from a pipe, never from argv. It checks the net's owner before it keeps
  anything: the owner that --owner KEY names, by its public key or its
  fingerprint SHA256:...; else the owner of the net that this host holds; else
  the person at the terminal. That person sees the owner key's fingerprint,
  made here from the key, and answers yes; the owner's host shows it beside the
  code and in each line of its podssh net ls. With the code on a pipe and
  neither, the run is refused (64) before the code is read. A stranger's code
  would make this host a member of the stranger's net. A refusal is said to the
  owner's host, which signs nothing (77 at each end). The device's key is --key
  FILE, else node-NAME.key in the cache, the key of podssh node NAME, made when
  missing; with --client-key and that file, a client of this host reaches the
  other members as NAME. The document that comes is checked: the owner's
  signature, the owner and the net of the offer, and this key as NAME. Then it
  is taken by the rule of take. The mailboxes are the pairing's:
  magic-wormhole's public one, then Least Authority's, or --pair-mailbox URLS
  and PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX, such as podssh relay serve's wss://HOST/v1/mailbox;
  no turns the code off (78), and add and take are the way left.

  Each end keeps the newest document that it was given, in net.doc of the cache
  (or the file of PODSSH_NET). It takes another only with the owner's
  signature, a serial higher than the one held, and an end still to come; its
  first is the one that the user takes, whose owner --owner can name. Two ends
  of the net give each other the newer one inside the end-to-end channel, on
  any road, and only to a member: the operator's before the node's verdict, so
  that it counts for that session, and the node's after it. A node of the net
  says each document that it takes. A field that this podssh does not know
  stays when the owner signs a change; a document that requires a part that it
  does not read is refused, with podssh update as the remedy. An end that
  offers its document to a node that gives none (it holds none, or its podssh
  is older) goes on without it. Such a node lets it in by its own door, and
  podssh ssh says so once among its verbose lines.

  A node whose key is a member lets in each member of the document held, beside
  the keys of podssh node --allow. It reads the document again for each
  session; a member removed by a newer document is refused at its next session.
  A node of no net keeps its door as before. A document that ended, or one that
  is there and fails its check, lets nobody in by the net. So a node that must
  not be locked out keeps an allowlist too. A node of the DERP road (podssh
  node --derp, or unasked with no pair) whose key is a member needs no podssh
  node --allow: the net's members are then its door alone, on each of its
  roads, as a DERP server lets any key send; its first line says so.

  The net's policy says who may reach what, as Tailscale's ACLs do; with none,
  each member reaches each other. Its owner writes it as a file of JSON,
  {"tags": {"dev": ["phone"]}, "rules": [{"from": ["laptop", "tag:dev"], "to":
  ["lab/web"], "note": "..."}]}, and signs it into the net with policy set FILE
  (policy clear removes it); policy show gives it back. A rule is from *, a
  member's name or tag:TAG. It is to * (each node, route, exit and range), or
  to NODE (its TARGET with no route and each route). It can be to NODE/ROUTE
  (one route, as node://NODE/ROUTE reaches it), or to tag:TAG. It can be to
  exit:NODE or exit:* (an exit node's egress), or to ADDR/BITS (a range of
  routes). It can be to relay:NODE or relay:* (the tokens and pairs of a relay
  role that mints for the net). That role is the node's own behind its quick
  tunnel or each one, podssh relay serve's too: see podssh relay. A rule only
  allows, and once a policy is there nothing else is allowed. The node that is
  reached checks it, for each session, against the newest document that it
  holds. It refuses the rest with the policy's words on its own lines; the keys
  of podssh node --allow are not narrowed by it. policy check FROM TO says what
  the policy lets, with no connection: FROM a member's name or key, TO NODE,
  NODE/ROUTE, exit:NODE, relay:NODE, relay:* (a relay that is no member) or an
  address; on stdout allowed or refused, a tab and the rule or the reason, and
  0 or 77. policy test FILE runs the cases of FILE, {"expect": [{"from": "ci",
  "to": "lab/db", "want": "allow", "note": "..."}]} (want allow or refuse),
  through the same check: a line each, ok or FAIL with the rule or the reason,
  and 65 when one is false. policy diff POLICY asks each question of the net
  under the policy held and under POLICY. The questions are each member to each
  node, route of a share, exit, relay role, the first address of each range,
  and relay:*. It prints each answer that changes, + widened and - narrowed,
  then the counts; by the answers, so a reordered policy changes nothing;
  --exit-code makes a widened pair 65. policy set FILE prints the same before
  it signs; --expect FILE signs nothing (65) when a case is false under the new
  policy, and --dry-run signs nothing at all. A document with a policy requires
  it, so a podssh that cannot read the rules refuses the document and keeps the
  one before.

  The document also holds the routes of a gateway, which podssh serve --gateway
  net:NAME reads. podssh net gateway set NAME FILE signs them in: FILE is a
  route file of podssh serve --gateway FILE. Each ca-key in it is the CA's
  public key, TYPE BASE64, as the private key stays on the gateway's host. set
  refuses FILE (65) as the gateway would refuse it, with its line. gateway show
  NAME prints the routes, as a file that set takes again. gateway rm NAME
  removes them, and the gateway then lets nobody in by them. A podssh that does
  not run the gateway keeps them unread, so the document does not require them.

  podssh ssh [user@]tag:NAME names each member of the net held that the
  policy's tag NAME holds with the role node. They come in a shuffled order, a
  member that no road reached in the last 30 s put last: each is tried as
  node://[user@]MEMBER until a race reaches one, and a line names each tried
  and the one used; the run ends at the first member reached, so a command
  never runs on two. When none is reached, a line names each, and the exit is
  the last one's; a tag that no member has is 64 before any connection.

  A member's name is a destination: podssh ssh node://NAME, and podssh ssh NAME
  alone when NAME is a member with the role node, as MagicDNS names a host of
  its tailnet; so is [user@]NAME:path of podssh cp, mv, scp and edit, and NAME
  of podssh sftp, each read as podssh ssh reads it. A name has no dot, so no
  DNS name is a member's. The net names the member's key, which the end-to-end
  channel checks in place of the pins of known-nodes. It names its tickets too,
  which race beside the pair kept under NAME when the command line names none;
  a copy races them as podssh ssh does. In a build with the iroh road, podssh
  ssh asks the member's record of pkarr by that key. It asks once each road
  with a ticket failed, or at once with none. It races each road that the
  record names and no ticket gave (see iroh record in THE RELAY); so does a
  copy. PODSSH_NET=no turns the net off: no name, no door and no document of
  the channel comes from it.

  An exit reaches the private networks of its host for the net, as a Tailscale
  subnet router does: inside the ranges of its own --routes (see podssh node),
  for a member that the policy lets reach the address (a rule to ADDR/BITS). A
  loopback address, or one of the exit's own host, is dialled only where a
  range names it alone (127.0.0.1, or ADDR/32). So 10.0.0.0/8 does not hand the
  node's own services to the net. add NAME KEY --roles node,exit --routes
  RANGES lists an exit's routes in the document, which --exit auto reads (see
  podssh exit); the node says at its start when the document lists other routes
  than its own.

  A member with the role relay is a podssh relay serve of yours, whose key the
  net names: the key that signs its list of deployments, which its first line
  names (see podssh relay). add NAME KEY --roles relay --relay-host HOST[:PORT]
  names where it serves that list, one host, written as relay.example.org or
  relay.example.org:8443; --relay-host with no role relay is refused (64). Each
  end that holds the net then asks that host's /relays.json before the race of
  a session on the default list. It asks once a day whatever the answer, within
  5 s. It takes the list there only when the member's key signed it. So a
  client with no --relay-host and no key of its own learns its role's
  deployments; the host itself joins no list by it, as the role's list names
  where sessions go. podssh relay status names each relay member, its host, and
  whether its list was taken.

  Usage: podssh net [OPTIONS] SUBCOMMAND [NAME [KEY] | FILE | FROM TO]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        init, add, rm, renew, invite, policy set or clear and gateway set or
        rm, the owner's, each signing a new document; join, ls, show, take,
        policy check or show and gateway show, each end's.
    [NAME|KEY|FILE]...
        init NAME, the net's; add NAME KEY, a member and its key or
        fingerprint; rm NAME; invite NAME, a code for a new device, which join
        takes; take FILE, a document that its owner signed; policy check FROM
        TO, policy show, policy set FILE, policy clear; gateway set NAME FILE,
        a gateway's routes; gateway show NAME; gateway rm NAME.

  Options:
    --owner-key FILE
        init, add, rm, renew, invite, policy set, policy clear, gateway set and
        gateway rm: the owner's key that signs, a private key or a public one
        that the agent holds (default: the agent's key or the key of ~/.ssh
        that owns the net; for init, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
    --roles LIST
        add and invite: what the member offers the net, of node, exit, relay
        and share, separated by commas (default node).
    --iroh-ticket TICKET
        add: the member's iroh ticket, which a client races for node://NAME
        when it names none.
    --derp-ticket TICKET
        add: the member's DERP ticket, which a client dials for node://NAME
        when each road before it failed.
    --routes RANGES
        add: the private ranges that the member routes for the net, ADDR/BITS
        or one address, separated by commas, as its podssh node --exit --routes
        dials them; with the role exit; podssh ssh, proxy, pipe and exit find
        the node of an address by them with --exit auto.
    --relay-host HOST[:PORT]
        add: where the member's relay role (podssh relay serve --deployment)
        serves its signed list, one host; with the role relay; each run on the
        default list asks it once a day, and takes the list there only by the
        member's key.
    --shares NAMES
        add: the names of the member's shares, separated by commas, which
        podssh share ls --net lists and an operator reaches as
        node://NAME/SHARE; with the role share; the node serves what its own
        share file holds.
    --days N
        init, add, rm, renew, invite, policy set, policy clear, gateway set and
        gateway rm: the days that the signed document lasts, 1 to 3650 (default
        365); no end takes it after.
    --owner KEY
        take and join: the owner that a first document must have, its
        fingerprint SHA256:... or its public key; later ones must have the
        owner held; join with its code on a pipe needs it, as no question can
        show the owner.
    --signature
        show: the owner's signature, as ssh-keygen -Y sign writes it, in place
        of the document.
    --pair-mailbox URLS
        invite and join: where the two ends meet, wss://HOST[:PORT]/PATH or
        ws://, by commas, in order, such as podssh relay serve's
        wss://HOST/v1/mailbox (default: env PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX, else
        magic-wormhole's public mailbox, then Least Authority's); no turns the
        code off.
    --dry-run
        policy set: check FILE, print what it changes and run --expect, and
        sign nothing: the document and its serial stay.
    --expect FILE
        policy set: the cases of FILE ({"expect": [{"from", "to", "want": allow
        or refuse, "note"}]}) must hold under the new policy, else nothing is
        signed (65).
    --exit-code
        policy diff: exit 65 when the policy widens a pair, for a check of CI.
    --key FILE
        join: this device's key in FILE, made when missing, the member's key
        that the owner signs in (default: node-NAME.key in the cache, the key
        of podssh node NAME).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    a net of your own: sign it with your key, name a node in it, then reach the
    node by its name alone
        $ podssh net init home --owner-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 && podssh net add lab SHA256:JfDOvc6FaJOB34ANs+ou385/Kh+mMQhnUx0gHXVAfUI && podssh ssh user@lab

    the net's policy: who may reach which node and route, signed by its owner,
    then asked with no connection
        $ podssh net policy set policy.json && podssh net policy check laptop lab/web

podssh exit
  a SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT proxy here, whose connections start at an exit node
  of your net.

  podssh exit NAME --listen ADDR:PORT is a local proxy for the programs of this
  host. Each of its connections starts at NAME, a node of your net that lends
  its egress (podssh node --exit). This is as a Tailscale exit node carries a
  device's traffic. One port takes SOCKS5, SOCKS4a and HTTP CONNECT: a program
  reaches it with ALL_PROXY=socks5h://ADDR:PORT, or
  HTTPS_PROXY=http://ADDR:PORT; through socks5h://, a program sends the name of
  its target, which the exit resolves. NAME is the label of the exit's pair
  here (or --pair-file), and a member of the net, whose key the end-to-end
  channel checks.

  Each connection is one session to the exit, over its pair's road, in the
  resumable layer and the end-to-end channel, which carries the target: the
  relay sees neither the target nor a byte. A client hears its success only
  once the exit reached the target; a refusal of the exit, of its net's policy,
  or of an address that is not public, is the refusal of its protocol. That is
  SOCKS 2 or HTTP 403, and for a target out of reach SOCKS 5 or HTTP 502. It
  comes with one line on stderr. 32 connections go at once; -q says no line for
  each one.

  The listener is one that you ask for, on a loopback address alone
  (127.0.0.1:0 takes a free port, which the first line names): SOCKS here takes
  no credentials, and each host that found the port would spend the exit's
  egress. PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses it before anything binds (78), and a refused
  bind is 77. The proxy runs until Ctrl-C or SIGTERM (0).

  With --carrier ADDR, the exit is the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream
  that exists already, with no relay and no pair. podssh node NAME --exit
  --carrier serves it so: stdio (or -), the stdin and stdout that the exec
  channel of a platform's own SSH gives the program that it starts; fd:N
  (Unix); or exec:CMD, a program started with no shell. So a host whose every
  road out is closed, but that such a channel reaches, gets egress through the
  channel's other end: there, podssh node gw --exit --carrier "exec:ssh -T
  sandbox podssh exit gw --listen 127.0.0.1:1080 --carrier stdio"; in the
  sandbox, HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1080. Each connection is a session of
  the one stream; NAME is a member of the net, whose key the channel checks,
  and the net's rule of the exit holds as on each road. The stream starts with
  the proxy; one of stdio or fd:N has one life, and when its node leaves, the
  proxy ends (0); a program of exec: is started again for the next connection.
  Ctrl-C ends the stream with a Close, which ends the node (0). --pair-file,
  --relay-addr and --ca-file are refused with it (64), and so is --carrier
  stdio on a terminal. podssh ssh, podssh proxy and podssh pipe take --exit
  NAME beside --carrier ADDR too, on a stream of their own, exec:CMD or fd:N.
  This is because their stdin and stdout are their own (see their notes).

  --exit auto works in place of NAME here and for podssh ssh, proxy, pipe and
  doctor. It takes the exit whose route of the net holds the target's address:
  the routes that the net's owner lists for each exit (see podssh net), the
  narrowest first, then the first by name; a line says which, for each
  connection here. podssh ssh --exit auto user@10.1.2.3 reaches a host of a lab
  whose exit routes 10.1.0.0/16. It takes an address, not a name, as the exit
  resolves a name itself and may resolve it otherwise; an address that no route
  holds is refused (78), and so are --pair-file and --carrier beside it (64),
  as each names one exit. auto is no member's name.

  cf://HOST, in place of NAME here and for podssh proxy and pipe, names the
  exit behind that quick tunnel. It is the quick tunnel of a node that lends
  its egress, whose line prints HOST. Each connection is a WebSocket of the
  tunnel, through HTTPS_PROXY, in the resumable layer and the end-to-end
  channel. A new WebSocket carries the session after each lost one, as for
  podssh ssh --exit cf://HOST. The node's key is pinned under cf://HOST at its
  first sight, or named by --node-key; a far end that greets with no layer is
  no podssh node (77). The tunnel is its one road: --pair-file, --carrier and a
  user name are refused with it (64).

  Usage: podssh exit [OPTIONS] NAME --listen ADDR:PORT

  Arguments:
    [NAME]
        the exit: a node of your net that runs with --exit, and the label of
        its pair here.

  Options:
    --listen ADDR:PORT
        serve SOCKS5, SOCKS4a and HTTP CONNECT on ADDR:PORT, a loopback
        address, a listener that you ask for (127.0.0.1:0 takes a free port);
        PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses it.
    --pair-file FILE
        the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one stored under
        NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        this client's key in FILE, made when missing (default: client.key in
        the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of the net's or
        the pins of known-nodes.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --carrier ADDR
        the exit is the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that exists
