        already; with no relay and no pair (podssh node NAME --exit --carrier):
        stdio (or -), as the exec channel of a platform's own SSH gives it,
        fd:N (Unix), or exec:CMD, a program started with no shell; or s3:FILE,
        a bucket of the S3 API (see FILES); or dns:FILE, names and TXT answers
        of DNS under a zone of your own (see FILES); each connection is a
        session of the one stream; a stream of stdio or fd:N ends the proxy
        when its node leaves; stdin may not be a terminal.
    -q, --quiet
        no line for each connection; errors still go to stderr.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh share
  a running node's local services by name, for its net: add, rm and ls, each
  reached as node://NODE/NAME.

  podssh share offers a running node's local services by name to its net, as
  Tailscale's serve offers a node's: on the host of the node lab, podssh share
  add web=127.0.0.1:8080 shares that TCP service as node://lab/web. An operator
  reaches it as a route (podssh ssh node://lab/web, podssh operator lab/web,
  podssh proxy node://lab/web) from the node's next session, with no restart;
  podssh share rm web takes it away, and the node refuses it from its next
  session; podssh share ls lists the shares on stdout, each name and its
  HOST:PORT apart by a tab. A share's name has the form of a route's, and its
  service is TCP; a route of the node's command line wins over a share of its
  name.

  The node keeps its shares in a file, one name=HOST:PORT on each line and #
  before a comment: node-NAME.shares in the cache, beside its key, or the file
  of podssh node --shares FILE, which podssh share names with --shares FILE
  too. The node reads it again for each session that names a route, on each of
  its roads but the quick tunnel's. That one serves one TARGET with no route;
  it says where at its start. It says once a line that is no share, or a file
  that it refuses, as one that others may change. A change is made under the
  lock of FILE.lock beside the file, on the file read again there, and kept
  whole by a rename. So two changes at once both count, and a node never reads
  half of one; a lock that another change keeps for 5 s fails this one (75).
  The lines that a change does not touch stay as they are. --node NAME names
  the node of this host; with none, the one node whose key or shares are in the
  cache. A node whose sessions carry no route has no share (podssh node
  --no-e2e, podssh node --temporary, or a udp: TARGET), and
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR=none keeps no file of them: --shares FILE names one (78 with
  neither).

  A share is a route of the node, so each door that holds a route holds a
  share: an allowlist's routes=web, and the net's policy, whose rule to
  NODE/ROUTE names a share as node://NODE/ROUTE reaches it (see podssh net).
  With no allowlist and no net, each operator with the pair's connect token
  reaches each share, as each route. podssh share ls --net lists the shares
  that the net held here names for each member: the member, the name and
  node://NODE/NAME apart by tabs. The net's owner lists them with podssh net
  --shares NAMES of add, for a member with the role share. The list is the
  net's; each node serves what its own file holds.

  Usage: podssh share [OPTIONS] SUBCOMMAND [NAME=TARGET | NAME]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        add, rm or ls, of a running node's shares.
    [NAME=TARGET|NAME]...
        add NAME=HOST:PORT, a TCP service of the node, which an operator
        reaches as node://NODE/NAME; rm NAME.

  Options:
    --node NAME
        add, rm and ls: the node of this host whose shares, as podssh node NAME
        names it (default: the one node of this host whose key or shares are in
        the cache).
    --shares FILE
        add, rm and ls: the share file that a node reads when its own flag of
        this name names it, in place of node-NAME.shares in the cache.
    --net
        ls: the shares that the net held here lists for each member, in place
        of this host's; as its owner wrote them with podssh net add NAME KEY
        --shares NAMES.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh funnel
  a local HTTP service at a public https:// name, through a quick tunnel (TLS
  ends at Cloudflare's edge) or OpenTunnel (TLS ends here).

  podssh funnel TARGET publishes a local HTTP service at a public https://
  name, as Tailscale's funnel does. It goes through a quick tunnel that podssh
  makes itself, with no cloudflared, no relay and no listener: the name is a
  new NAME.trycloudflare.com for each run, and the one line on stdout once the
  edge registered the tunnel. TARGET is HOST:PORT or tcp:HOST:PORT, dialed from
  this host as podssh pipe dials one; unix-connect:PATH, a service on a Unix
  socket; or exec:CMD, a program started for each request, its stdin the
  request and its stdout the answer, as inetd starts one. A host whose sandbox
  refuses a connection to the loopback still serves a socket or a program.

  Each visitor's request goes to a new connection of TARGET as HTTP/1.1, with
  Connection: close, so that the answer ends with the connection: its status
  and its headers go to the edge, and its body as it comes; a body in chunks is
  decoded as it comes, as the edge takes a body's bytes alone. A request's body
  goes to TARGET as it comes too, of any size, with its length, or in chunks
  where the visitor named none; an answer that TARGET gives before the body's
  end goes to the visitor at once. An interim answer (100 Continue) is dropped.
  A WebSocket passes through: TARGET answers its upgrade, and after its 101 the
  frames pass both ways untouched. podssh reads the heads and never a body. A
  TARGET that does not answer a request's dial gets the visitor a 502 in
  podssh's words, and a line on stderr.

  TLS ends at Cloudflare's edge, so Cloudflare can read each byte of this
  traffic, and the first lines say so. The name is public: anyone who learns it
  reaches TARGET, with no key and no allowlist, so publish only what may be
  public, and stop the funnel with Ctrl-C. For a channel that only your keys
  open, use the quick tunnel of podssh node NAME TARGET (its notes say how).
  Its visitors are SSH clients of your net.

  --tunnel-token-file FILE serves a named tunnel of your own Cloudflare account
  in place of a quick tunnel. It uses the token that the account's dashboard
  gives for it: the name is then the one that the account routes to the tunnel,
  which podssh does not know. So stdout stays empty, and the first line names
  the tunnel's id. The token is a credential: podssh reads it from FILE only,
  and says it in no line. The funnel reaches the edge as the quick tunnel of
  podssh node does: QUIC on UDP port 7844 where no proxy is set, else HTTP/2 on
  TCP port 7844, directly or through HTTPS_PROXY. With --warp it goes inside
  WARP's tunnel first; it keeps two connections, and connects again after a
  loss with the same name, until Ctrl-C.

  --opentunnel publishes through OpenTunnel, a blind TLS tunnel with no account
  (https://opentunnel.xyz, or the service of PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL), in place of a
  quick tunnel. Its TLS ends at this host: the funnel makes one tunnel for this
  host's funnels, with a key that never leaves it. The service gets a
  certificate of the tunnel's own name for it. The funnel keeps both in the
  cache, and serves the name https://ID.opentunnel.xyz/. That name is the one
  line on stdout once its bridge attached, and the same at each run. The first
  lines say: "TLS ends at this host; OpenTunnel sees the names, the times and
  the sizes." Each visitor's connection comes over the funnel's bridge, a
  WebSocket through HTTPS_PROXY. So it leaves a cage of an HTTPS proxy with no
  WARP. The funnel offers HTTP/1.1 alone; each request goes to TARGET as above,
  and its answer as TARGET framed it, with Connection: close; a WebSocket
  passes through. The name is public, as a quick tunnel's is: each visitor who
  knows it comes in. A funnel with no token file that the quick tunnel cannot
  carry takes this road unasked: no answer of its API, or no road to port 7844
  of the edge. It says why, and tries for 20 s at most; PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL=no
  turns that off. --opentunnel takes neither --tunnel-token-file nor --warp
  (64). Two funnels of one host at once share the tunnel's name, which one
  bridge holds: the second says so, and tries again until the first stops.

  Usage: podssh funnel [OPTIONS] TARGET

  Arguments:
    [TARGET]
        the HTTP service: HOST:PORT, tcp:HOST:PORT, unix-connect:PATH or
        exec:CMD.

  Options:
    --tunnel-token-file FILE
        a named tunnel of your own Cloudflare account, by the token in FILE; at
        the names that the account routes to it, in place of a new
        NAME.trycloudflare.com; the token goes in no line.
    --warp
        reach Cloudflare's edge inside WARP's tunnel first, for a host whose
        way out does not reach port 7844 (a build with WARP's road).
    --opentunnel
        publish through OpenTunnel, a blind TLS tunnel with no account
        (opentunnel.xyz, or the service of env PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL), in place of
        a quick tunnel: TLS ends at this host, with the tunnel's own
        certificate, so OpenTunnel sees the names, the times and the sizes,
        never the traffic; one tunnel for this host's funnels, kept in the
        cache, at https://ID.opentunnel.xyz/; a funnel that the quick tunnel
        cannot carry takes it unasked (PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL=no turns that off);
        not with --tunnel-token-file or --warp.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh chat
  messages and files with another podssh, end to end encrypted.

  podssh chat carries messages and files between two podssh ends, over the
  end-to-end channel of a road (see podssh node): the relay sees ciphertext
  only. One side waits: podssh chat --listen NAME serves the pair NAME as its
  node (see podssh relay). The other side reaches it: podssh chat NAME, with
  the pair stored under NAME, or the operator's part of it in --pair-file. One
  peer talks at a time; another is told that the chat is busy.

  In a build with the feature iroh, as each release binary is, --listen NAME
  --iroh serves the iroh road too. It needs no pair for it, and says its ticket
  on stderr; the other side reaches it as podssh chat iroh:TICKET, and the
  ticket names the key that the channel checks. On the iroh road, only the keys
  of --allow come in, as on each node of that road. --iroh-relay gives the
  relays.

  Each line of stdin is a message, and each message of the peer is a line of
  stdout, NICK: TEXT, made safe for a terminal. A line that starts with / is a
  command: /file PATH offers a file; /accept ID [PATH] takes the file ID, into
  PATH (a directory, or the path of a new file) or else the working directory;
  /decline ID refuses it; /quit ends. A line that starts with // is a message
  that starts with /. Notes go to stderr; with --jsonl, each message and each
  event is one JSON object on stdout. Nothing that the peer sends is run.

  A file is written only once the user accepts it, with /accept, or each file
  with --accept-dir DIR: under a temporary name in its directory, checked
  against the SHA-256 that the peer offered, and only then given its name;
  never over a file that is there, and never out of the directory, as the name
  is the last part of the offered one. The peer hears whether each file was
  kept.

  The peer acknowledges each message, and a message with no acknowledgement
  when a conversation ends is said, as not delivered. A run ends once stdin
  ended and each message and file went; with --accept-dir, once the peer
  leaves, as its files can come after stdin ended. --send MESSAGE sends one
  message and ends once it is acknowledged; --file PATH offers one file and
  ends once it arrived whole; --sendfile FILE sends each line of FILE in place
  of stdin. The exit is 0 only when each message was acknowledged; the other
  codes are in EXIT STATUS.

  With --listen, the end of stdin ends the listener once each line went: a
  listener that a service, an entrypoint or an agent starts with stdin at
  /dev/null leaves as its first peer comes. It says that stdin ended (in
  --jsonl, the end input-ended). --linger keeps it: the end of stdin ends no
  conversation, and each conversation ends when the peer leaves. The listener
  then waits for the next peer, until --timeout, a signal or /quit. With
  --linger the --timeout is the run's planned end, and the exit is 0 when each
  message was acknowledged, as at SIGTERM. The lines of stdin or of --sendfile
  that came before go to the first peer. The listener connects out to the
  relay, as each node does: --linger opens no socket.

  While no peer is there, the lines wait in memory, 1000 lines or 1 MiB at
  most; podssh then reads no more until some go, and says so. Nothing goes to
  disk. When the peer leaves, the side that waits takes the next one. The side
  that reaches tries again each 5 s, as it does while the node is not there. It
  tries until stdin ended and each line went. --timeout bounds the run, and is
  required when stdin or stdout is not a terminal.

  With --irc SERVER[:PORT], podssh chat talks in the channel PEER (#name) of an
  IRC network, through the relay: TLS inside the relay stream, port 6697 by
  default, the certificate checked against SERVER; a failed handshake ends the
  run, and never falls back to plain text. --irc-plaintext takes port 6667 and
  plain text, which the relay and each server read, and podssh says so;
  --irc-ca-file gives the CAs of the server's TLS. The nick follows the grammar
  of IRC. Each line is a message to the channel; a message of the channel comes
  out as NICK: TEXT, and one to this client as NICK (to you): TEXT. With
  echo-message, a message is delivered once the server echoes it; a server with
  none gives no proof, which podssh says. The server and each user of the
  channel read the messages: IRC has no end-to-end channel. A lost connection
  is made again each 5 s, and the channel joined again; a server's ERROR before
  the channel ends the run with its words. With --direct, podssh connects to
  SERVER over TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set, not through the relay.

  Over IRC, /file PATH offers the file to the channel; the transfer then runs
  between the two nicks alone, in chunks that each server can relay. Each line
  goes in its turn, so that a server's rate limit does not close the link. The
  SHA-256 of the file comes at the end. One file goes at a time: another accept
  meanwhile is told that this side is busy. A file is written only once
  accepted, under a temporary name, and kept only whole, as on the roads.

  The channel is always on: chat has no --no-e2e. The side that waits proves
  its key, the file of --key (default node-NAME.key in the cache) or a key of
  --ephemeral-key. It lets in the keys of --allow FILE, else each peer with the
  pair's connect token. The side that reaches proves the key of --client-key
  (default client.key in the cache). It checks the other side's key against the
  pins of known-nodes, or against --node-key. A changed key, or a key that the
  allowlist refuses, ends the run with exit 77.

  Other names: podssh irc

  Usage: podssh chat [OPTIONS] PEER

  Arguments:
    [PEER]
        the peer: NAME, node:NAME or node://NAME, the node of a pair;
        iroh:TICKET; with --listen, the label of the pair that this side
        serves.

  Options:
    --listen
        wait for the peer: serve the pair PEER as its node, one peer at a time;
        the end of stdin ends the run once each line went (see --linger).
    --linger
        with --listen: the end of stdin ends no conversation; stay for each
        next peer until --timeout (then exit 0), a signal or /quit.
    --send MESSAGE
        send one message, and exit once the peer acknowledged it; never
        prompts.
    --sendfile FILE
        send each line of FILE as a message, in place of stdin, and exit once
        each is acknowledged.
    --file PATH
        offer the file at PATH, and exit once it arrived whole.
    --accept-dir DIR
        accept each file that the peer offers, into DIR, for a script (default:
        each file waits for /accept).
    --nick NICK
        the name that the peer sees, 64 bytes at most, an IRC nick with --irc
        (default: env PODSSH_NICK, else the login name, else podssh).
    --jsonl
        one JSON object per event on stdout.
    --timeout DURATION
        bound the run; required when stdin is not a TTY (default: env
        PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    --key FILE
        with --listen: this side's key in FILE, made when missing (default:
        node-NAME.key in the cache); its fingerprint is said as it starts.
    --ephemeral-key
        with --listen: a new key for this run only, kept in no file; a peer
        that pinned the old key refuses it.
    --allow FILE
        with --listen: the keys that may come in, one key or fingerprint on
        each line, read again for each peer (default: each peer with the pair's
        connect token).
    --client-key FILE
        this side's key in FILE when it reaches the peer, made when missing
        (default: client.key in the cache), which the peer's allowlist may
        name.
    --node-key KEY
        the key of the side that waits, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place
        of the pins of known-nodes.
    --pair-file FILE
        use the pair in FILE, a private file, not the one stored under NAME (to
        reach the peer, its operator's part will do).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --iroh
        with --listen: serve the iroh road too, and print its ticket, which the
        peer reaches as iroh:TICKET; a build with the feature iroh.
    --irc SERVER
        chat in the channel PEER of the IRC network at SERVER[:PORT], through
        the relay, with TLS inside the relay stream (default port 6697).
    --irc-plaintext
        with --irc: plain text, port 6667 by default, which the relay and each
        server read; podssh says so.
    --direct
        with --irc: connect to SERVER over TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when it is
        set, not through the relay.
    --irc-ca-file FILE
        with --irc: trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the server's TLS
        (default: the system and built-in roots).
    --iroh-relay URLS
        the iroh relays, https://HOST[:PORT][,...]; the first that answers is
        the home relay (default: env PODSSH_IROH_RELAY, else the net's relay
        members' own, then n0's).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh cp
  copy files to or from a remote host.

  podssh cp copies files between this host and a server over SFTP, or by exec
  when the server has no SFTP. It goes through the relay (see THE RELAY) or
  over TCP with --direct, with the connection flags of podssh ssh: -o, -J, -i,
  -v and -q, and -P for the port, as scp has it. An operand names a server when
  a : comes before any /: [user@]host:path or [user@][IPV6]:path. ./a:b is a
  local file, and on Windows so is C:\x. An empty path, host:, is the login
  directory. A remote source whose last name holds * or ? names the files of
  its directory that it matches, in order, over SFTP; a name that starts with .
  only by a pattern that does. A pattern that matches nothing exits 66.

  node://[user@]NAME[/ROUTE]:path is the node of the pair under the label NAME
  (see podssh node). It is reached as podssh ssh node://NAME reaches it, on the
  same roads in the same order: its pair's, and those that race beside it,
  again at each resume. Beside it race a ticket of the net, a ticket or a name
  kept under NAME, and the transit relay. The Piping Server road and the
  member's record race too. -v names the road that answered; ROUTE is its
  route. The path comes after the first : after the name, and with none it is
  the login directory. A member of the net (see podssh net) is [user@]NAME:path
  by its name alone, read as podssh ssh NAME reads it, the net first.
  --pair-file, --client-key, --node-key and --no-e2e are those of podssh ssh. A
  port, -J or --direct cannot reach a node (exit 64). With --carrier ADDR, as
  for podssh ssh, the node is at the other end of a stream that exists already.
  There is no relay and no pair: each connection of the copy is a session of
  its own on that one stream, which ends with the copy; each operand that is
  remote is then a node. With --exit NAME, it is a host that the exit at the
  other end of the stream dials. --no-resume, as for podssh ssh, ends each
  session with its link, and the node keeps nothing of it: a copy cut so goes
  on over a new connection, at the offset of the copy, as after any broken
  connection.

  The destination's name never holds a file that was not verified. The bytes go
  to .NAME.podssh-RANDOM.part beside the destination, a new file of mode 0600.
  The SHA-256 of what was sent is compared with the far side's; then the file
  takes the source's permission bits and is renamed onto the destination, at
  once where the server has posix-rename. A failure removes the temporary file
  and leaves the destination as it was.

  The far side's digest comes first from podssh's own SFTP request, when the
  server is podssh serve. Else it comes from sha256sum, shasum or openssl dgst
  on the server, when one runs there. Else podssh reads the file again over
  SFTP, which counts again against the relay's limits. With --jsonl each file
  gives one JSON object: done, with the bytes, the SHA-256 and how the far side
  was checked, or error, with the exit code.

  At its end a run of podssh cp or mv says on one line what it did: the files
  copied and their bytes; those that podssh run left as they were; those
  skipped; the paths that an exclude left out (each named at -v with its
  pattern); those that failed; how long it took and its rate; also after a
  failure, before its error. -q silences it, and --jsonl gives a summary object
  in its place. On a terminal one line shows the progress of the run: the file
  in flight, and with several files their count. Where stderr is no terminal, a
  plain line comes each 10 s once the run has passed 10 s, with no carriage
  return; PODSSH_PROGRESS=off and -q silence it.

  Several sources go into a directory. A copy from server to server goes
  through a temporary file on this host, one connection at a time. -r copies a
  directory and what it holds, each link as a link (scp -r follows links); it
  has no default excludes and reads no .podsshignore, where podssh run leaves
  out target/, node_modules/, .git/ and what the project's .podsshignore names.
  A device, a FIFO or a socket is not copied: one line says so, with --jsonl a
  skipped object, and it is no failure, as OpenSSH's scp and sftp skip one.
  Each failure is said once, when it comes; the rest goes on, and the exit code
  is the first failure's.

  Several files go at once, each over an SFTP session of its own in the one
  connection. So do the files of a tree with -r: as many as the row of
  --parallel says, or K with --parallel K, and one at a time with --parallel 1.
  Through the relay each small file waits for its own round trips, so one at a
  time takes their sum. A file of more than 8 MiB goes after them, alone: in
  one stream, or as chunks, K at once, with --parallel K. Each file keeps its
  own side file, so after a broken connection each goes on where it was. The
  report keeps the order of the sources, and the exit code is that of the first
  failure in that order. The copy by exec goes one file at a time.

  --delta sends only the blocks of 1 MiB that changed, over an older version of
  the file on the other side: one command on the server gives the digest of
  each of its blocks (dd and a digest tool). The temporary file is made from
  the old one there (copy-data, else cat). Where that cannot be, the copy goes
  in full, and a line says why once for each file, without -v (-q silences it);
  a first copy, with no older version, says it at -v. The copy by exec sends no
  delta, and says so. With --jsonl the done object holds delta: the blocks,
  those sent and their bytes, or full and the reason.

  A copy keeps the source's permission bits. -p keeps the access and the
  modification times too, and with -r each directory's, set after its files;
  --owner keeps the owner and the group by number where the side that writes
  may give a file away (root). It says where it could not. A block of 64 KiB of
  zeros is a hole, never sent: up when the source has holes, both ways with
  --sparse. Within one -r upload, two names of one file arrive as one file with
  two names (hardlink@openssh.com). SFTP version 3 carries the times in whole
  seconds from 1970 to 2106, and no inode, extended attribute or ACL: those,
  and a far source's hard links, are not kept.

  --inplace writes into the destination itself, with no temporary name and no
  rename: it keeps its inode and hard links, and needs no room for a second
  copy. podssh says first that a copy that fails leaves its destination
  damaged, and a failure says so. A destination that is a link or a directory
  is refused (exit 64).

  -n (--no-clobber) leaves a destination that is there as it is: the copy looks
  before any byte goes, says DST: there, so not replaced, and counts a skip,
  with exit 0. A name that comes during the copy stays too: the verified file
  takes its name by a hard link (hardlink@openssh.com, or ln by exec), which
  never takes a name that is there; with no hard link the look is the guard,
  and -v says so. -u (--update) copies a file only when its destination is
  missing, older, or of the same second and another size, as rsync's -u does; a
  file that stays is said at -v. -b (--backup) keeps the old destination at its
  name with the suffix ~, or that of --suffix. It does so by a hard link before
  the rename, so that the name is never missing. Else it renames first, which
  -v says; an older backup there is replaced, and --delete never deletes a name
  with the suffix. -n with -b, and -b with --inplace, are refused (exit 64).
  With --jsonl a file left out is a skipped object, its why exists or not
  newer, and a done object holds backup; --dry-run says skip and backup.

  A server with no SFTP subsystem gets a copy by exec, and podssh says so. Each
  step is one command with no pty, sh -c 'SCRIPT' sh PATH..., so the login
  shell only starts sh. Each path is one quoted word; a path with a newline or
  a NUL is refused. A probe finds the far tools: cat, wc, mv and rm are needed.
  The bytes go raw through cat when the 256 byte values come back unchanged,
  else through base64. Each answer comes after a random marker, so text that a
  login prints first is never data. The temporary name, the digests and the
  rename are as above; a copy down keeps mode 0600, or with -p or --owner what
  stat says of the far file; up, chmod, touch -t and chown set what a copy
  keeps, where the server has them. With no POSIX sh, or a needed tool missing,
  the copy exits 69 and names it.

  Each SFTP reply that carries no file data is waited for 30 s at most, and
  each read or write 60 s. --timeout bounds the whole copy, the login included
  (exit 75). With no terminal it is required, or PODSSH_TIMEOUT in its place
  (exit 64 with neither): nobody may be there to stop a run that waits. podssh
  scp and podssh sftp take it as a bound and need none, as OpenSSH's run in
  pipes with no such flag. ConnectTimeout bounds their login. The exit codes
  are the sysexits of EXIT STATUS, as for podssh proxy.

  A copy goes on after a broken connection: the temporary file stays, and a new
  connection writes on at the offset below which each byte is in it. It tries 5
  times in a row at most with no new byte, with a backoff between them. A
  refused login, or a host key other than the first connection's, ends it. The
  same command run again goes on too while the source is as it was: a private
  side file in the cache directories, podssh-cp-*.resume (see FILES), keeps the
  offset, never a byte of the file. The digest covers the whole file.

  --result-file FILE writes one JSON object to FILE at the end of each run,
  also of one refused before it connected. It is a new file for its owner
  alone; - is refused (exit 64). Its keys are those of podssh ssh --result-file
  in their meaning, with verb and error: schema, verb, exit, failure (connect,
  relay, host-key or auth where the connection failed; copy for a source, a
  destination or a step that the server refused; verify for digests that
  differ; session, timeout, interrupted, usage or config; or null), error (its
  words), duration_ms, relay (host, close_code, reason, and sessions, the relay
  sessions that the run opened); files (sent, unchanged, skipped, deleted and
  failed) and transferred (up and down: the bytes of the files through this
  host, with --delta the blocks that went, none for a rename or a hard link). A
  copy that goes on from an earlier run's partial file counts only the bytes
  that this run moved. bytes is null, as in podssh ssh it counts a command's
  streams. After the --timeout, files and transferred are null. --jsonl keeps
  its events on stdout.

  -P here is the port, as on scp and sftp. On ssh it is a Tag.

  A copy that broke goes on when the same command runs again, while the source
  is as it was. A side file in the cache, podssh-cp-*.resume, keeps the offset,
  never a byte of the file (podssh man files).

  Usage: podssh cp [OPTIONS] SRC... DST

  Arguments:
    [PATH]...
        SRC... DST.

  Options:
    -P, --port PORT
        port to connect to; this is scp's -P.
    -p, --preserve
        keep the access and the modification times too (the mode is kept
        always), with -r each directory's.
    --owner
        keep the owner and the group, by number, where the side that writes may
        give a file away (root); else a note.
    --inplace
        write into the destination itself: its inode and hard links stay, and
        no second copy needs room; a failure leaves it damaged, which is said
        first; a link is refused.
    --sparse
        a hole for each block of 64 KiB of zeros, whatever the source; without
        it only a copy up of a sparse file makes holes.
    -n, --no-clobber
        leave a destination that is there as it is, also one that comes during
        the copy; said once, and a skip, not a failure.
    -u, --update
        copy a file only when its destination is missing, older, or of the same
        second and another size, as rsync's -u.
    -b, --backup
        keep the old destination at its name with a suffix (~), an older backup
        there replaced; --delete never deletes such a name.
    --suffix SUFFIX
        with --backup, the suffix of the old file's name, in place of ~.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    --parallel K
        copy several files K at once, and a file of more than 8 MiB as chunks,
        K at once; each over a channel of its own in the one connection (1 to
        16); with none, 4 files at once and a large file in one stream; 1
        copies one at a time.
    --delta
        over an older version of the file, send only the blocks of 1 MiB that
        changed; a full copy when the server cannot, or when the digests then
        differ, which a line says without -v.
    -r, --recursive
        copy a directory and what it holds, depth first; each link as a link,
        and a device, FIFO or socket skipped with a note, which is no failure.
    --exclude PATTERN
        with -r, leave out a path: * and ? within a name; with a /, from the
        root of the copy; repeatable.
    --exclude-from FILE
        with -r, the --exclude patterns of FILE, one a line; # starts a
        comment.
    -l, --limit KBITS
        at most KBITS Kbit/s, as OpenSSH's scp -l: a token bucket before each
        request.
    --delete
        with -r, delete what the target has and the source lacks, once each
        copy succeeded; never an excluded name, the file that a link names, the
        root or the home directory.
    --dry-run
        with -r, say each action (mkdir, copy, link, skip) on stdout, and
        change nothing.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    --jsonl
        one JSON object per event on stdout.
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the failure and its
        words, the files sent, unchanged, skipped, deleted and failed, their
        bytes each way, and the relay.
    --timeout DURATION
        bound the transfer; required with no TTY (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        node://NAME and a node's cf://HOST: this client's key in FILE, made
        when missing (default: client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME and a node's cf://HOST: the node's key, or its fingerprint
        SHA256:..., in place of the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --exit NAME
        start the road at NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit): it dials the destination, or the first hop of -J,
        from its own host; on each road between the two, or with --carrier ADDR
        on that stream alone; the host key is the destination's; NAME auto: the
        exit whose route of the net holds the first hop's address.
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, as its one road, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a
        program started with no shell, as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node
        --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's
        bucket of the S3 API; or dns:FILE, the node's DNS road; NAME is then
        the label under which the node's key is pinned; with --exit NAME, the
        exit at the other end of ADDR dials the host.
    --no-resume
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET, derp:TICKET, a node's cf://HOST and --exit
        NAME: no resume; the session ends with its link, and the node, asked
        so, keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    or podssh itself on that channel: a copy to the node's sshd, each
    connection a session of the one stream
        $ podssh cp --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' notes.txt node://user@box:notes.txt

podssh scp
  copy files with the command line of OpenSSH's scp.

  podssh scp takes the command line of OpenSSH's scp, and copies as podssh cp
  does: over SFTP, or by exec when the server has no SFTP; under a temporary
  name, verified by its digest, then renamed. -p keeps the times, as podssh cp
  -p does. As OpenSSH's scp, it gives no summary at its end, and no progress
  where stderr is no terminal.

  Each letter of OpenSSH's usage parses: -B is BatchMode=yes, -3, -s and -T are
  accepted and change nothing, and the others that podssh does not carry are
  refused by name. An operand can be a URI, scp://[user@]host[:port][/path]:
  its path is under the login directory, and // makes it absolute. An operand
  can name a node as podssh cp does: node://[user@]NAME[/ROUTE]:path, or a
  member's NAME:path, and with --carrier ADDR a node at the other end of a
  stream that exists already; --no-resume ends each session with its link, as
  for podssh cp.

  --timeout DURATION, or PODSSH_TIMEOUT, bounds the whole run, the login
  included (exit 75), and is never required, with no terminal either: a script
  runs OpenSSH's scp in a pipe with no such flag, and each wait of a copy has
  its own limit. ConnectTimeout is the login's (60 s by default). podssh cp and
  podssh mv need it with no terminal, where nothing else bounds the whole run.

  --result-file FILE writes the object of podssh cp at the end, its verb scp;
  stdout and stderr stay those of OpenSSH's scp.

  -P here is the port, as on scp and sftp. On ssh it is a Tag.

  A copy that broke goes on when the same command runs again, while the source
  is as it was. A side file in the cache, podssh-cp-*.resume, keeps the offset,
  never a byte of the file (podssh man files).

  Usage: podssh scp [OPTIONS] SRC... DST

  Arguments:
    [PATH]...
        SRC... DST.

  Options:
    -3, --through-this-host
        a copy between two hosts goes through this host; podssh always does so.
        Accepted and ignored.
    -4, --ipv4-only
        use IPv4 addresses only.
    -6, --ipv6-only
        use IPv6 addresses only.
    -A, --forward-agent
        agent forwarding: a copy runs nothing on the server that would use the
        agent, so podssh forwards none. Accepted and ignored.
    -B, --batch-mode
        batch mode: never ask for a password or a passphrase (BatchMode=yes).
    -C, --compress
        compress the connection.
    -O, --legacy-scp
        the legacy SCP protocol: podssh copies over SFTP, or by exec. Refused.
    -p, --preserve
        keep the access and the modification times too; the mode is kept
        always.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    -R, --remote-copy
        a copy that the first host makes with its own scp. Refused. Use no
        flag: the copy goes through this host.
    -r, --recursive
        copy a directory and what it holds; links are followed, as OpenSSH's
        scp does, and a loop is refused.
    -s, --sftp-protocol
        the SFTP protocol; podssh uses it already. Accepted and ignored.
    -T, --no-name-check
        no check of the names that a server sends; podssh names each file
        itself. Accepted and ignored.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -c, --cipher CIPHERS
        the ciphers are a list of the keyword Ciphers, which podssh applies.
        Refused. Use -o Ciphers=LIST.
    -D, --sftp-server-path PATH
        a local SFTP server program in place of a host. Refused.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -l, --limit KBITS
        at most KBITS Kbit/s: a token bucket before each request.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -P, --port PORT
        port to connect to; this is scp's -P.
    -S, --program PROGRAM
        another program for the connection: podssh is the connection. Refused.
    -X, --sftp-option OPTION
        an SFTP option, repeatable: buffer=BYTES (each read or write, at most
        256K) or nrequests=COUNT (in flight at once).
    --jsonl
        one JSON object per event on stdout.
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the failure and its
        words, the files sent, unchanged, skipped, deleted and failed, their
        bytes each way, and the relay.
    --timeout DURATION
        bound the whole run, the login included (exit 75); never required, with
        no TTY either (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        node://NAME: this client's key in FILE, made when missing (default:
        client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME: the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of
        the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --exit NAME
        start the road at NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit): it dials the destination, or the first hop of -J,
        from its own host; on each road between the two, or with --carrier ADDR
        on that stream alone; the host key is the destination's; NAME auto: the
        exit whose route of the net holds the first hop's address.
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, as its one road, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a
        program started with no shell, as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node
        --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's
        bucket of the S3 API; or dns:FILE, the node's DNS road; NAME is then
        the label under which the node's key is pinned; with --exit NAME, the
        exit at the other end of ADDR dials the host.
    --no-resume
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET, derp:TICKET, a node's cf://HOST and --exit
        NAME: no resume; the session ends with its link, and the node, asked
        so, keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    copy a file to the node's SSH server with the same file; the path comes
    after the first : after the name
        $ podssh scp --pair-file lab-operator.json notes.txt node://user@lab:notes.txt

podssh sftp
  file commands on a host, from a batch or at a prompt, as OpenSSH's sftp.

  podssh sftp takes the command line of OpenSSH's sftp. With -b FILE, or -b -
  for stdin, it runs the commands of FILE in order and prints each line first;
  a line that starts with @ is not printed, and one that starts with - does not
  end the batch when it fails. Else, on a terminal, it asks at a prompt; with
  no terminal and no -b it refuses (exit 64). A destination with the path of a
  file fetches that file and ends; one with a directory starts there. The
  destination can be the node of a pair, node://[user@]NAME[/ROUTE][:path], or
  a member of the net by its name alone, as for podssh cp. With --carrier ADDR
  it can be a node at the other end of a stream that exists already;
  --no-resume ends the session with its link, as podssh ssh does. --timeout
  DURATION, or PODSSH_TIMEOUT, bounds the whole run, the login and the batch
  included (exit 75), and is never required, as for podssh scp.

  The commands: get and put (with reget and reput, which are the same), rename,
  rm (with * and ? in the last name), mkdir [-p], rmdir, ls [-1afhlnrSt], cd,
  lcd, pwd, lpwd, chmod, df [-hi], help, version, and bye, exit or quit. get
  and put copy as podssh cp does; get -p and put -p, or each of them after sftp
  -p, keep the times. get -r and put -r (or -R), or each of them after sftp -r,
  copy a directory and what it holds. They copy as podssh cp -r does, each link
  as a link; an item that fails is said, the rest goes on, and the command
  fails at its end. The exit code is that of the first command that ends the
  batch, as for podssh cp; a usage error is 64 where OpenSSH gives 1.

  ls lists as OpenSSH's sftp does, with its switches [-1afhlnrSt]. With neither
  l nor 1 the names go in columns of the terminal's width, else 80; 1 puts one
  name a line. l gives OpenSSH's long form: the mode, ? for the link count, the
  owner and the group, and the size. Then the time of change in the local zone
  (the hour within half a year, else the year), then the name; for a directory,
  the server's own line of each entry. Where the server names owners by number
  (users-groups-by-id@openssh.com), podssh makes the line with their names. n
  shows the numbers, h the sizes in K, M and G; t sorts the newest first, S the
  largest first, and r turns the order round. f keeps the server's, and a shows
  the names that start with a dot.

  --result-file FILE writes one JSON object to FILE at the end, as podssh cp
  does, its verb sftp. It has commands (run and failed) and failed_command, the
  line of the batch whose failure ended it, as written, or null; a fetch of the
  destination's file is one command. It has no files and no transferred, and
  bytes is null.

  -P here is the port, as on scp and sftp. On ssh it is a Tag.

  Usage: podssh sftp [OPTIONS] DESTINATION

  Arguments:
    [DESTINATION]
        [user@]host[:path], sftp://[user@]host[:port][/path], or
        node://[user@]NAME[/ROUTE][:path], the node of a pair.

  Options:
    -4, --ipv4-only
        use IPv4 addresses only.
    -6, --ipv6-only
        use IPv6 addresses only.
    -A, --forward-agent
        agent forwarding: a copy runs nothing on the server that would use the
        agent, so podssh forwards none. Accepted and ignored.
    -a, --append
        go on with an interrupted transfer; podssh does so by itself, from its
        side file. Accepted and ignored.
    -C, --compress
        compress the connection.
    -f, --fsync
        flush each file to the server's disk; podssh always does, where the
        server can. Accepted and ignored.
    -N, --not-quiet
        not quiet in batch mode; podssh's batch mode is not quiet. Accepted and
        ignored.
    -p, --preserve
        keep the access and the modification times of each get and put, as get
        -p and put -p; the mode is kept always.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    -r, --recursive
        each get and put of a directory copies it and what it holds, as get -R
        and put -R; each link as a link.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -B, --buffer-size BYTES
        the bytes of each read or write, at most 256K and the server's limit
        (default: the server's limit).
    -b, --batch-file FILE
        read the commands from FILE, - for stdin; a failed command ends the
        batch unless it starts with -.
    -c, --cipher CIPHERS
        the ciphers are a list of the keyword Ciphers, which podssh applies.
        Refused. Use -o Ciphers=LIST.
    -D, --sftp-server-path PATH
        a local SFTP server program in place of a host. Refused.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -l, --limit KBITS
        at most KBITS Kbit/s: a token bucket before each request.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -P, --port PORT
        port to connect to; this is sftp's -P.
    -R, --requests COUNT
        the reads or writes in flight at once (default 64), never more bytes
        than the road's window.
    -S, --program PROGRAM
        another program for the connection: podssh is the connection. Refused.
    -s, --subsystem-name NAME
        the subsystem of the SFTP server (default: sftp).
    -X, --sftp-option OPTION
        an SFTP option, repeatable: buffer=BYTES (as -B) or nrequests=COUNT (as
        -R).
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the failure and its
        words, the commands run and failed, the command that ended the batch,
        and the relay.
    --timeout DURATION
        bound the whole run, the login included (exit 75); never required, with
        no TTY either (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE

        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,

    --vless FILE

        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        node://NAME: this client's key in FILE, made when missing (default:
        client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME: the node's key, or its fingerprint SHA256:..., in place of
        the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --exit NAME
        start the road at NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit): it dials the destination, or the first hop of -J,
        from its own host; on each road between the two, or with --carrier ADDR
        on that stream alone; the host key is the destination's; NAME auto: the
        exit whose route of the net holds the first hop's address.
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, as its one road, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a
        program started with no shell, as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node
        --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's
        bucket of the S3 API; or dns:FILE, the node's DNS road; NAME is then
        the label under which the node's key is pinned; with --exit NAME, the
        exit at the other end of ADDR dials the host.
    --no-resume
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET, derp:TICKET, a node's cf://HOST and --exit
        NAME: no resume; the session ends with its link, and the node, asked
        so, keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh mv
  move files; across hosts this is a copy and a delete.

  podssh mv moves files, with the operands and the flags of podssh cp; with no
  terminal it needs --timeout, as podssh cp does. Within one server the server
  renames, with posix-rename or by exec with mv -f, and no byte moves; a rename
  that the server fails for a reason of its own, such as two file systems,
  becomes a copy and a delete, said first.

  Between hosts a move is not atomic, and podssh says so on stderr before any
  byte moves: the copy of podssh cp, its digest check, then a delete of the
  source; between two servers a third connection removes it. The source goes
  last, and only while it is still the file that was copied: the same size and
  time of change, the same file, and the same bytes where a digest command runs
  there.

  A source that changed stays (exit 66). A delete that fails exits 70 and says
  that the copy is complete and verified: the data is then in two places, never
  in none. One file named twice is refused (exit 64). With --jsonl each done
  object says whether the source is gone: source_removed.

  With -n or -u a source whose destination stays is not moved, and stays where
  it is; mv -r leaves it with the directories that hold it. Within one server,
  -n moves by a hard link and the removal of the source's name, so a name that
  came since the look stays; -b keeps the old destination as for podssh cp.

  --result-file FILE writes the object of podssh cp at the end, its verb mv,
  with removed: the sources that the move removed once their copy was verified.

  -P here is the port, as on scp and sftp. On ssh it is a Tag.

  A copy that broke goes on when the same command runs again, while the source
  is as it was. A side file in the cache, podssh-cp-*.resume, keeps the offset,
  never a byte of the file (podssh man files).

  Usage: podssh mv [OPTIONS] SRC... DST

  Arguments:
    [PATH]...
        SRC... DST.

  Options:
    -P, --port PORT
        port to connect to; this is scp's -P.
    -p, --preserve
        keep the access and the modification times too (the mode is kept
        always), with -r each directory's.
    --owner
        keep the owner and the group, by number, where the side that writes may
        give a file away (root); else a note.
    --inplace
        write into the destination itself: its inode and hard links stay, and
        no second copy needs room; a failure leaves it damaged, which is said
        first; a link is refused.
    --sparse
        a hole for each block of 64 KiB of zeros, whatever the source; without
        it only a copy up of a sparse file makes holes.
    -n, --no-clobber
        leave a destination that is there as it is, also one that comes during
        the copy; said once, and a skip, not a failure.
    -u, --update
        copy a file only when its destination is missing, older, or of the same
        second and another size, as rsync's -u.
    -b, --backup
        keep the old destination at its name with a suffix (~), an older backup
        there replaced; --delete never deletes such a name.
    --suffix SUFFIX
        with --backup, the suffix of the old file's name, in place of ~.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    --parallel K
        copy several files K at once, and a file of more than 8 MiB as chunks,
        K at once; each over a channel of its own in the one connection (1 to
        16); with none, 4 files at once and a large file in one stream; 1
        copies one at a time.
    --delta
        over an older version of the file, send only the blocks of 1 MiB that
        changed; a full copy when the server cannot, or when the digests then
        differ, which a line says without -v.
    -r, --recursive
        copy a directory and what it holds, depth first; each link as a link,
        and a device, FIFO or socket skipped with a note, which is no failure.
    --exclude PATTERN
        with -r, leave out a path: * and ? within a name; with a /, from the
        root of the copy; repeatable.
    --exclude-from FILE
        with -r, the --exclude patterns of FILE, one a line; # starts a
        comment.
    -l, --limit KBITS
        at most KBITS Kbit/s, as OpenSSH's scp -l: a token bucket before each
        request.
    --delete
        with -r, delete what the target has and the source lacks, once each
        copy succeeded; never an excluded name, the file that a link names, the
        root or the home directory.
    --dry-run
        with -r, say each action (mkdir, copy, link, skip) on stdout, and
        change nothing.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    --jsonl
        one JSON object per event on stdout.
    --result-file FILE
        at the end, one JSON object in FILE: the exit, the failure and its
        words, the files sent, unchanged, skipped, deleted and failed, their
        bytes each way, and the relay.
    --timeout DURATION
        bound the transfer; required with no TTY (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --pair-file FILE
        node://NAME: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, not the one
        stored under NAME.
    --client-key FILE
        node://NAME and a node's cf://HOST: this client's key in FILE, made
        when missing (default: client.key in the cache).
    --node-key KEY
        node://NAME and a node's cf://HOST: the node's key, or its fingerprint
        SHA256:..., in place of the pins of known-nodes.
    --no-e2e
        node://NAME: no end-to-end channel, to a node that runs none either;
        the relay then sees each byte.
    --exit NAME
        start the road at NAME, a node of your net that lends its egress
        (podssh node --exit): it dials the destination, or the first hop of -J,
        from its own host; on each road between the two, or with --carrier ADDR
        on that stream alone; the host key is the destination's; NAME auto: the
        exit whose route of the net holds the first hop's address.
    --carrier ADDR
        node://NAME: reach the node at the other end of ADDR, a stream that
        exists already, as its one road, with no relay and no pair: exec:CMD, a
        program started with no shell, as exec:'ssh -T HOST podssh node
        --carrier stdio NAME TARGET', or fd:N (Unix); or s3:FILE, the node's
        bucket of the S3 API; or dns:FILE, the node's DNS road; NAME is then
        the label under which the node's key is pinned; with --exit NAME, the
        exit at the other end of ADDR dials the host.
    --no-resume
        node://NAME, iroh:TICKET, derp:TICKET, a node's cf://HOST and --exit
        NAME: no resume; the session ends with its link, and the node, asked
        so, keeps nothing of it after a loss; a node that does not know the ask
        keeps it as before, which a line says.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh edit
  edit a file of a host in an editor here; it goes back only when the host's
  file did not change meanwhile.

  podssh edit [user@]host:path fetches one file of a server as podssh cp copies
  one down: over SFTP, or by exec when the server has no SFTP, through the
  relay or with --direct. It takes the connection flags of podssh ssh, and -P
  for the port. The copy goes into a new directory of mode 0700 in the cache
  (see FILES). It is a file of mode 0600 with the far file's name, so that the
  editor knows its kind. Then the connection closes, and the editor runs here,
  with no time limit: no relay session waits while a person edits.

  The editor is VISUAL, else EDITOR, else vi when PATH has it; with none,
  podssh edit exits 78 and names EDITOR. A value is a program and its words,
  split at blanks with no shell, or one program whose path has a blank. podssh
  edit needs a terminal on stdin and stdout (else 64, and the refusal names
  --no-terminal). While the editor runs, SIGINT and SIGQUIT are the editor's,
  and on Windows so is Ctrl-C.

  --no-terminal runs an editor that needs no terminal, a script that changes
  the file in place: its stdin is empty, and what it prints goes to stderr, so
  stdout stays empty. The check of the far file before the send is the same, so
  a change made on the server is never lost. With no terminal it needs
  --timeout, or PODSSH_TIMEOUT (else 64), as podssh cp does: a program that
  waits for a terminal would wait for ever. The bound covers the editor's run:
  when it passes, podssh ends the editor, sends nothing, and exits 75; the
  first SIGINT or SIGTERM ends it too (130). podssh cannot tell an editor that
  needs a terminal from one that needs none, so the flag says it; --timeout
  goes with it alone (else 64).

  A copy with no change sends nothing (exit 0). Else a new connection, which
  logs in as the first did with no second question, compares the far file with
  what came: its size and its time of change, and its SHA-256. When the far
  file changed, nothing is sent, and the exit is 73. Else the copy goes up as
  podssh cp sends one: a temporary name, the digests, the far file's mode, then
  the rename.

  After a success the copy here goes. After a failure it stays, and podssh
  names it and the directory to remove once the change is merged, when it holds
  a change; a copy with no change goes. A later run says once which kept copies
  are more than 7 days old, with their directories, and removes none: each
  holds a change of the user's. An editor that ends with a status other than 0
  sends nothing, and podssh edit exits with that status. A symbolic link stays
