  a link: over SFTP podssh edits the file that it names; by exec, where no
  portable command names that file, a link is refused (66). The first SIGINT or
  SIGTERM while a file moves ends the run with 130: during the fetch nothing
  stays here; during the send the copy here stays, named.

  -P here is the port, as on scp and sftp. On ssh it is a Tag.

  Usage: podssh edit [OPTIONS] [user@]host:PATH

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host:PATH]
        the file to edit, on a server: [user@]host:path, [user@][IPV6]:path or
        scp://[user@]host[:port]/path.

  Options:
    --no-terminal
        run the editor with no terminal: no input, its output on stderr, for an
        editor that is a script; with no TTY it needs --timeout.
    --timeout DURATION
        with --no-terminal, bound the editor's run (exit 75); required with no
        TTY (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT).
    -P, --port PORT
        port to connect to; this is scp's -P.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh tx
  in the shell of a podssh ssh session: a file to or from podssh at its other
  end, through the terminal itself.

  podssh tx moves one file through the terminal of a podssh ssh session, for a
  path where ZMODEM breaks. tmux and other programs that draw a terminal of
  their own sit between the shell and the session's pty. They repaint what
  passes, and drop the bytes of ZMODEM's frames. Type it in the shell at the
  far end of the session; it needs podssh there too, the same static binary.
  podssh tx send FILE sends FILE to podssh ssh at the near end, which asks
  where it goes, as it asks for sz. podssh tx receive [DIR] waits for a file
  from the near end, which asks which file to send, as it asks for rz; the file
  comes into DIR, the current directory with none. podssh tx receive never
  replaces a name that DIR has: it skips that file and exits 75. At the near
  end, a name that exists asks Replace it? [y/N], and only y replaces it.

  Each byte that crosses is printable ASCII, CR or LF. A first line starts the
  transfer, and the near end removes it from its screen. Then come frames of
  base64 with a CRC-32 each. The near end reads them back from what the
  terminal draws, also wrapped, repainted or cut by escape sequences. One frame
  waits for its answer at a time, and goes again after a silence; a frame that
  comes damaged is dropped and sent again. The file comes as podssh cp writes a
  copy: to .NAME.podssh-RANDOM.part beside its name, then the SHA-256 and the
  size are compared with the sender's, then a rename gives it its name. Nothing
  listens and nothing connects: the session's own terminal carries it all.

  podssh tx sets its terminal raw while it runs, and needs one of 48 columns at
  least. Each wait for the other end has 20 s, and the first one 120 s, for the
  question at the near end. Ctrl-C at the near end, or five Ctrl-X typed in a
  row, stops the transfer at both ends. No file that did not end is kept. A
  question at the near end has no limit: the near end tells the far end that it
  waits. A transfer that the near end never took, or that Ctrl-C stopped,
  leaves its lines on the screen; clear it with clear or Ctrl-L. After the file
  is kept, podssh tx receive waits 25 s more for a confirmation that the
  terminal lost; Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D ends that wait. It exits 0 when the file was
  kept, with one line on stderr. It also exits 0 when podssh tx send sent the
  file and its SHA-256 and no confirmation came, which the line says. It exits
  64 with no terminal, one too narrow, or a word wrong; 65 when the size or the
  SHA-256 differs, or the other end broke the protocol; 66 when FILE or DIR
  cannot be read; 73 when the file that came cannot be created in DIR, written
  or kept; 75 when it was refused, skipped, cancelled or got no answer in time.
  The near end is podssh ssh with a pty and a local terminal; with
  PODSSH_ZMODEM set to off, or through a control master, it watches for neither
  ZMODEM nor this.

  Usage: podssh tx send FILE | receive [DIR]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        send or receive.
    [FILE | DIR]
        send: the file that the near end receives; receive: the directory that
        the file comes into, the current one with none.

  Options:
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh man
  this manual: each command, flag, variable, file and exit code.

  On a terminal, podssh man shows the manual through the program in PAGER; else
  through less, when PATH has it and TERM names a terminal (not on Windows);
  else through its own pager (Enter: the next page, q: quit). With --no-pager
  or --roff, or when stdin or stdout is not a terminal, the manual goes to
  stdout with no pager.

  podssh man --roff > podssh.1 makes a man page; man -l podssh.1 shows it.

  podssh man --json writes the tables as one JSON object, for a program: the
  options, each command (its availability, arguments and flags, each flag with
  its kind: supported, accepted, refused, and what to type instead), the -o
  keywords, the variables, the files and the exit codes. --json SECTION gives
  one command, or the table of environment, files or exit-status. It is never
  paged.

  The manual is the same in each environment: it shows no setting of this host.

  Usage: podssh man [OPTIONS] [SECTION]

  Arguments:
    [SECTION]
        one section only: a command, or relay-facts, retired-variables,
        environment, files, exit-status, examples or see-also; keywords selects
        ssh.

  Options:
    --no-pager
        write the whole manual to stdout; never page, even on a terminal.
    --roff
        write the manual as a man(7) page instead of text, for man -l; never
        paged.
    --json
        write the tables (commands, flags, keywords, variables, files, exit
        codes) as JSON; never paged.
    --llms WHICH
        write llms.txt (index) or llms-full.txt (full) of this binary's manual
        to stdout; never paged.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    this manual with no pager
        $ podssh man --no-pager

    one section of this manual
        $ podssh man environment

    this manual as a man page
        $ podssh man --roff > podssh.1 && man -l podssh.1

podssh relay
  the relay's hosts, pool and view of a target; the pairs of the reverse road;
  its document.

  The relay that podssh uses (hosts, failover, tokens, limits) is in THE RELAY:
  podssh man relay-facts.

  podssh relay pair NAME makes a pair on the relay. It keeps it under the label
  NAME, in a private file of the cache (see FILES). It prints the label and
  when the pair expires, 72 hours later, and never a token. With
  --operator-file, the operator's part of the pair, its connect token alone,
  goes to FILE, a new file that only its owner can read: give it to the
  operator by a channel that you trust. On stderr it says the way past the
  expiry: in its last 24 hours, podssh relay pair NAME --operator-file NEW
  makes the next pair, which the node takes at the expiry. NEW goes to each
  operator; stdout keeps its one line.

  A pair under NAME with more than 24 hours left is not replaced: stop it first
  with podssh relay revoke NAME. In its last 24 hours, the next pair is made
  and takes its place in the store. A node of NAME that runs takes it at the
  expiry, with no new start (see podssh node); the old pair can no longer be
  stopped, and ends at its expiry. The default relay renews no pair, so each
  node of a pair needs the next one every 72 hours. revoke stops the pair on
  the relay and deletes the stored copy; when the relay cannot be reached, the
  copy is kept, because its stop token is the one way to stop the pair before
  it expires.

  podssh relay pair --renew NAME renews the pair stored under NAME at the relay
  that made it. The pair then has 72 hours from now, and never less than it
  had. It keeps the same three tokens, so that each operator's file keeps
  working and the node goes on with no next pair; podssh relay serve renews, by
  the stop token, which the pair's owner alone holds, as often as asked. It
  prints the label and the new expiry, and the store keeps it. A relay that
  renews none (the default relay's contract has no such request: its answer is
  404 or 405) is said so, and the exit is 69. The message gives the next pair
  of the last 24 hours as the way; a refused stop token (403) is a pair that
  was stopped or ended (77). --operator-file and --relay-host are refused with
  it (64): the operator's file is never touched, and its end is asked of the
  relay once the file's has passed.

  podssh relay halt NAME keeps the operators of the pair stored under NAME out
  for a while. It works at podssh relay serve, by the pair's stop token: each
  of its sessions ends once, with 1011 the pair's owner halted it. Each
  operator's upgrade then hears 503 with the words of --reason TEXT and no
  Retry-After, until podssh relay resume NAME. TEXT is one line of 200 bytes at
  most. That refusal spends no connect token of --once and no token of one leg.
  The node keeps its socket, and so the pair's name: it hears that the pair is
  halted, a frame that a node of before skips. It takes the next operator after
  the resume on the same socket, with no new registration. podssh relay status
  NAME says halted, with the words, and its --json halted and halt_reason. A
  second halt changes nothing (stdout: halted already, since when); resume,
  then halt, for new words. The halt lives in the relay's memory alone: a
  restart of the relay serves the pair again. stdout has one line, the label
  and halted, with the sessions that it closed, or resumed, or not halted. A
  relay that halts none (the default relay's contract has no such request: 404
  or 405) is said so, with podssh relay revoke as the way to end the pair, and
  the exit is 69; a refused stop token (403) is a pair that was stopped or
  ended (77); --relay-host is refused with them (64).

  podssh relay status NAME says whether the pair's node is online, its
  sessions, and when the pair expires. The expiry is the relay's where it names
  one (podssh relay serve, whose renewal moves it), else the file's; in its
  last 24 hours, how long is left too (expires in 5 h, at ...). On an
  operator's host, which stores no pair, podssh relay status --pair-file FILE
  [NAME] asks the same of the pair in FILE. FILE may also be the operator's
  part, which podssh relay pair --operator-file writes: the relay answers the
  status to its connect token. NAME is then only the label shown (else FILE).
  With --json, the pair's state is one object: schema (1), podssh, label,
  online, sessions, expires (RFC 3339), seconds_left and halted, for a check.
  It has halt_reason where the pair's owner halted it with words (podssh relay
  halt).

  podssh relay pair NAME --code gives the operator's part by a short code in
  place of a file: the pair stored under NAME while it has 10 minutes left,
  else the next pair, made first. It gives the node's key too (node-NAME.key,
  made when it is missing). The code, such as 7-crossover-clockwork-adroitness,
  shows on this run's terminal alone: on stderr when it is a terminal, else on
  the process's terminal, and with neither it is refused (64) before anything
  is asked. It is never on stdout, in a log or in argv. Read it to the
  operator, who runs podssh relay join NAME and types it: the two ends meet at
  a mailbox and run SPAKE2 keyed by the whole code over it. They seal each
  later message with the key that it gave, so the mailbox learns nothing of the
  code and changes nothing. The code lives 10 minutes and is used once: the
  first exchange spends it, whatever its end, so a wrong code, or a guess, gets
  one try of its 24 bits. The operator's key comes back: --allow FILE adds its
  line to the node's allowlist, which podssh node NAME --allow FILE reads again
  for each session; with none, the pair's connect token is the node's door, and
  the key is said. stdout has one line, the label, the operator's fingerprint
  and the pair's expiry; nobody within 10 minutes is 69, a wrong code 77.

  podssh relay join NAME takes the code at a prompt on the terminal, or as one
  line of stdin from a pipe, never from argv. It finds the node's host at the
  first mailbox that lists the code's number. It checks the pair that comes as
  a pair of the relay is checked. It pins the node's key under NAME in
  known-nodes: a key that differs from the pin is refused (77), and nothing is
  kept. It gives this operator's key (client.key, or --client-key FILE). It
  keeps the operator's part under NAME (operator-NAME.json, see FILES). podssh
  operator NAME, podssh ssh node://NAME and podssh relay status NAME find it
  there, as they find a pair. stdout has one line, the label, the node's label
  and fingerprint and the expiry. A code that nobody holds (it expired, it was
  used, or it was typed wrong at its number) and a wrong code are 77; no
  mailbox reached is 69. The mailboxes: magic-wormhole's public one,
  wss://relay.magic-wormhole.io/v1, then Least Authority's,
  wss://mailbox.mw.leastauthority.com/v1, which podssh may use unasked;
  --pair-mailbox URLS or PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX names others, such as podssh relay
  serve's, and no turns the pairing by code off. Both ends name the same ones.
  Where no mailbox answers, the ends meet at the next place, in this order: a
  public ntfy server's topic of the code (PODSSH_PAIR_NTFY), then a public
  Nostr relay's ephemeral events (PODSSH_PAIR_NOSTR). Then a public WebTorrent
  tracker's peers (PODSSH_PAIR_TRACKER), then a public MQTT broker's topic
  (PODSSH_MQTT); a line names each third party before its first byte, and the
  pairing's proof keeps the messages secret from it.

  podssh relay spec reads the relay's /health and its published document,
  /llms-full.txt. It checks the document against the facts that podssh was
  built with (see RELAY FACTS). It prints ok, with the document's lines, its
  digest and the version that the relay serves. Else it prints a FAIL line for
  each fact that disagrees, and exits 1: the relay changed something that
  podssh depends on. With --document FILE, it checks FILE and reads nothing
  from the network.

  podssh relay conform --relay-host HOST[:PORT] checks whether one relay host
  keeps the contract, by using it. It never checks the default relay unless you
  name it, as it mints tokens there. Each check is one line: pass, fail or
  skip, its id, the section of the contract, its time and its words. With
  --json, one object holds checks, each with id, clause, verdict, detail and
  ms, and passed, failed, skipped and exit. The forward checks: /health and
  /relays.json, a minted token and its form, and an upgrade with no token or a
  wrong one, each refused with 403. Then ?dial=lazy, a Ping and its Pong, the
  Close of a session that dialed nothing (1000), and the refusal of a
  link-local target. A token of one session, where the relay mints one, checks
  that a token in the query string is refused; then an upgrade spends it. With
  --target HOST:PORT, best an echo server of yours: bytes each way, the Close
  after them, the keepalive, and the idle cut that /relays.json publishes, up
  to 300 s. With --reverse: a pair of the check's own, its node's hello, an
  operator's leg opened and readied, a byte each way and the leg's close. Then
  the status, a wrong stop token refused, the renewal and the halt where the
  relay offers them, and the pair's stop. The stop comes also after a failure;
  the pair's tokens must be refused after it. No token is printed. The exit is
  0 with no fail, 1 with one, and 69 when the host did not answer.

  podssh relay status with no NAME asks each relay host for its /health, one
  after the other. It prints a line for each as it answers: the relay's
  version, the edge that answered, the time, the TLS version and how the
  connection was made, or why it failed. It needs one host that answers.

  podssh relay info reads /relays.json from the first relay host: the edge that
  this host reaches, and the pool in the relay's order with its rank and its
  estimate of each round trip. It reads the limits of a session too. The relay
  makes that order from the edge that served the request, so two calls can
  disagree, and neither measures this host's path: podssh relay rank measures
  each host of the pool, and podssh relay status times the hosts that podssh
  tries. podssh ping --relay-host HOST times one. Each measures from this host.
  A relay that names no edge and scores no host above 0, as podssh relay serve,
  is said to give no estimate. The next line says which order a run from this
  host takes, with the list in that order, read from the cache with no
  connection. It uses the words of podssh doctor's line rank: the rank kept for
  this egress, the times of earlier races, the relay's order, RelayRank no, or
  the order that you named. With --json, the relay's fields are unchanged, and
  pool_order says whose order the pool is in and from which edge. relay_order
  gives the order of a run in podssh status's word (rank, samples, pool or
  off), or named for a list that you named. relay_list gives its hosts (host,
  port), in that order. With HOST PORT, also the URL that the relay chooses for
  that target.

  podssh relay rank measures each relay host from this host, one at a time, and
  keeps the rank: the default host and each host of its pool (the pool read
  first when none is cached), or the hosts of --relay-host. Each round probes
  each host in a new random order, 250 ms apart. A probe is a session to
  github.com:22 (--target HOST:PORT for another) that sends no byte. It times
  the dial, TLS and the upgrade, the token's time left out, then --count pings;
  --rounds rounds, 3 by default, within 10 minutes. The hosts go in the order
  of the share of probes that failed, then the median time to open, then its
  p95; two medians within 50 ms or 10 % keep the order that the hosts came in.
  A line for each probe goes to stderr, and the rank to stdout, best first, or
  as one object with --json. The rank is a private file of the cache,
  relay-rank.json, with no token and no name of the proxy: the egress is a
  digest of the proxy's host and port, or direct, and the rank holds 24 h for
  it. --cached prints the rank kept, its age and whether it holds here, and
  --forget removes it; neither connects. Exit 0 when a host opened, 69 when
  none did or PODSSH_OFFLINE is set, 64 for a bad flag. podssh probes no host
  that the user did not ask it to, unless RelayRank auto asks (below).

  The default list of relay hosts takes the rank: while a rank of podssh relay
  rank holds for this egress, the default list takes it. The list is then the
  default host and the best three other hosts of the pool, in the rank's order.
  A run tries the default host at its place among them; the record of failures
  still moves a host that failed lately to the end. Each run also keeps the
  time to open of each host that opened in its race, the last 8 of each. It
  makes no connection of its own for them; where no rank holds, those times
  order the pool. A list that the user names (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY,
  RelayHost) keeps its order. PODSSH_RELAY_RANK=no, or RelayRank no in the
  settings file, gives the relay's order of the pool, as before; podssh status
  says which order a run takes (relay_order), and podssh doctor's line rank and
  podssh relay info name it with the list.

  A rank in a session's background comes only when the user asks for it, never
  by default. RelayRank auto in the settings file asks, or
  PODSSH_RELAY_RANK=auto. Then, when no rank holds for this egress, a session
  of podssh ssh that the default list carries makes one. It probes the default
  host and the hosts of its pool, 8 at most in a day, in its own process, one
  at a time: the first after the session ran 60 s, then one each 10 s at most.
  None runs while a race of relay hosts runs, and none with PODSSH_OFFLINE.
  None runs past the session's end, which drops a probe in flight. Each probe
  is a session to github.com:22 with ?dial=lazy that sends no byte and three
  pings. So the relay dials no target, and the time to open is this host's leg
  alone. The rank is kept after each probe, source background, and the default
  list takes it as it takes one of podssh relay rank; a session that ended
  first leaves it partial, and the next session of the day goes on with the
  hosts that it lacks. A rank that holds, of either source, makes no new one
  for 24 h. podssh proxy, pipe, cp and the other commands make none. podssh
  status gives relay_rank_auto (asked, by, last_ms, last_age_s, partial), and
  podssh doctor's line rank names the setting and when the last background rank
  was made.

  podssh relay trace HOST PORT asks the first relay host to dial the target and
  to read its first line. It sends a forward token in a header, never in the
  URL. It shows: the relay's verdict (live, or silent-or-unreachable for a
  target that sent nothing) and the address that it dialed. It also shows the
  times of the connection and of the first byte, and the banner. A target that
  the relay will not dial (a blocked range, a name with no address) gives the
  relay's reason. It tells a target that is down from a relay that cannot be
  reached. The relay's view of this host's address and place, which it sends
  too, is never shown.

  With --json, status, info and trace write one JSON object on stdout when the
  run ends: schema (1), podssh, and the answer: each host for status with no
  NAME, and the pair's state for status NAME or --pair-file. For info it is the
  relay's /relays.json as it came, and for trace the relay's view of the
  target. The exit codes are in EXIT STATUS.

  podssh relay serve is the relay itself, as a role of podssh: it serves the
  relay's forward road, the contract that podssh speaks (version
  2026-10-03-r2), on --listen ADDR:PORT. Its TLS is from --cert FILE and --key
  FILE (a P-256 key in PEM), or from --acme NAME. So each podssh reaches it
  with --relay-host and the CA that signed its certificate. It serves /health,
  /v1/mint, /connect/HOST/PORT, /relays.json, /trace and /llms-full.txt, dials
  a target only once its name resolves to public addresses (--allow-private
  dials the others too; --routes RANGES, those inside its ranges alone,
  ADDR/BITS or one address, separated by commas, each address of a name
  checked, and never beside --allow-private; a prefix that sets bits past it,
  as 10.0.0.5/8, is refused with the network that it names). It refuses port 25
  in each case. It answers a name that does not resolve, or not to a public
  address, with one 403 that names no address. The cause is a line on stdout.
  It keeps the default relay's limits unless told: 180 s with no payload
  (--idle SECONDS, 1 to 86400) and 12 hours (--session-hours H, 1 to 168). Also
  64 MiB a session (--max-session-mib M, 1 to 4096) and 10 s to dial a target
  (--connect SECONDS, 1 to 120). Also an empty frame each 25 s (--keepalive
  SECONDS, 1 to 3600). /relays.json publishes the first four as they are, never
  the keepalive. A value above the default moves this role's cut only: a client
  keeps its own lower budgets and its own warning, as it only lowers them to
  what /relays.json says. --mint anyone mints a token for each client; by
  default it mints for no one (503), as its tokens are given another way. A
  token lives until the relay stops. Each mint, upgrade and refusal is a line
  on stdout, and so is each session's end: end client, end gone, or end close
  CODE REASON. It listens because you ask it to, and PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses
  it; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM stops it.

  --cover DIR answers the role's own TLS name as a static site from DIR while
  the tunnel keeps the same name: index.html for /, each asset with its type,
  robots.txt, the site's own 404.html, and a Server header of --cover-server
  VALUE (default nginx). A request that is no route of the contract, an unknown
  Host and a path that leaves DIR get the site's own 404; a body and a header
  of an unauthenticated path never name this project, its version or its
  contract. The documents leave the public listener under --cover: /health,
  /trace, /llms-full.txt, /relays.json and /v1/probe/* answer the site's 404
  there. --control-socket PATH (required with --cover, mode 0600) serves them
  on a Unix socket of the owner's instead. A socket's address holds 103 bytes
  on macOS and 107 on Linux. A longer PATH is bound through a short way to it:
  /proc/self/fd on Linux, else a link under /tmp or /var/tmp. The first line
  then says that a client needs a shorter way to it. A PATH that no short way
  serves is refused (78). /v1/mint stays public, and a POST with a body alone:
  another method is 405 with Allow: POST, an empty body 400. A client that
  authenticated with a token at POST /v1/delegate gets a temporary credential
  of the same name and chain. It is bound to the TLS exporter of the
  connection. podssh-ws checks its issuer, name, window and binding, and
  refuses another issuer, a lapsed window or another chain by name. This is an
  application-layer credential, not RFC 9345 and not a TLS delegated
  credential: no CertificateVerify, no certificate extension, and the TLS stack
  still authenticates the certificate. One name for each deployment: a
  certificate whose leaf names a wildcard, or not the name that --acme asked
  for, is refused (78) in both modes. A leaf of more than one name is a
  warning. Under --cover each name that the role terminates must be given by
  --cover-name (repeatable, the first is the role's name). A --cover-name that
  the certificate does not hold is refused (78), and one that is also a
  --publish name is refused (64). --cover-name without --cover, and
  --cover-script without --cover, are refused (64). --cover-script FILE loads a
  TOML measurement and refuses a missing script or one with no date (78); it is
  checked at the start, and the tunnel's records are not shaped by it yet,
  which the record layer's own work covers. A --control-socket or
  --cover-server without --cover is refused. A published name whose node is
  gone still closes before any TLS of the role answers.

  On Linux the relay gives up each capability that it started with, once its
  listener is bound and before it serves. A port below 1024 needs one for its
  bind alone (a start as root, or the file capability cap_net_bind_service on
  the binary). It gives up: no new privileges on an exec, the bounding set
  where the capability to change it is held, and the effective, permitted and
  inheritable sets. It gives them up on each of its threads, which are then
  read again. Its first line on stderr says so; a start that held none says
  nothing. A step that fails, or a thread that keeps a capability, stops the
  start (78). The uid stays: a start as root stays uid 0, which may still write
  each file that root owns, and its first line says so; a user of its own with
  the file capability binds the port with none of root's. The role reads some
  files again: its certificate on SIGHUP, the file of --pairs, the cache of
  ACME. Such a file of another owner must then let it read by its mode. Other
  systems have no such sets, and nothing is dropped there.

  Where HTTPS_PROXY (or https_proxy, all_proxy, ALL_PROXY) is set, the relay
  dials each target through that proxy. It does so as each client of podssh
  reaches its relay, by HTTP CONNECT or SOCKS5; the loopback, and what NO_PROXY
  names, go directly. Its policy checks each address of a name as it resolves
  on this host. The proxy is asked for each checked address, never for the
  name. So a proxy that resolves the name otherwise reaches nothing unchecked;
  with --allow-private, which checks nothing, the name goes to the proxy as it
  came. So a host with no DNS reaches each target that its proxy reaches. A
  proxy's refusal is the relay's 502, with the proxy's status, in words that
  never say where the proxy is; the relay's own line on stdout names it, and
  never its credentials. /trace names the road proxy and its kind. The first
  line on stderr names the proxy by its host and port, and a proxy that cannot
  be read stops the start (78).

  The relay dials an IPv6 target where its host routes IPv6 out. It learns this
  from the table of routes that Linux gives as a file (/proc/net/ipv6_route).
  Else it learns it from a dial that met no route in the last minute. Where it
  does not route IPv6 out, the target gets 502 before the upgrade, also with
  ?dial=lazy: this relay's host has no IPv6 route out, and a client tries its
  next relay host. A name of both families keeps its IPv4 addresses; the
  loopback is the relay's own; through HTTPS_PROXY the proxy decides.
  /relays.json says what the relay knows, as egress.ipv6: true, false, or null.

  Beside the contract it serves /v1/layer/HOST/PORT, the forward road in the
  resumable layer, for a target that speaks no layer, a standard sshd among
  them: each WebSocket is one link. Where a way refuses the upgrade, a session
  of its HTTP road carries a link instead, with the same checks:
  /v1/http/open-layer/HOST/PORT or /v1/http/one-layer/HOST/PORT. The relay
  dials the target once, after the layer's handshake of a new session. It keeps
  the target while the client's link is lost, until a resume on a new link to
  this relay carries the session on. Else 10 minutes pass and the target is
  shut. The token, the upgrade and the policy are checked as on /connect/, with
  the same refusals; the layer's secret never crosses the relay, as each resume
  proves it, and the path names the target alone. Each link keeps the limits of
  a session, and the client moves the session to a new link before them. The
  sessions hold 256 MiB of replay buffers at most, 4 MiB each (--resume-budget
  MIB; 0 serves none), and one whose link is lost is kept 10 minutes
  (--resume-deadline TIME). A new session past the budget is refused in the
  layer's handshake, before its client sent a byte of it. The refusal says what
  holds the budget, and a line on stdout says so once a minute; podssh's client
  then takes /connect/, with no resume. /relays.json offers it as
  forward.layer: true, and podssh proxy and podssh ssh take it, with
  PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER unset or yes. Where several processes serve one name, each
  gives --resume-host HOST[:PORT], a name of its own that its certificate
  holds: /relays.json names it as forward.host. podssh's client sends each link
  of a session there, so that a resume reaches the process that holds the
  session; a name that is not of the deployment of the host that the client
  asked is not taken. A restart forgets each session.

  It serves the reverse road too: /v1/pair, for whom it mints, /v1/node/NAME,
  /v1/connect/NAME, /v1/status/NAME and /v1/stop/NAME. So podssh relay pair
  --relay-host, podssh node and podssh ssh node:// work through it with no
  other relay. A pair lives 72 hours. /v1/renew/NAME, with the stop token,
  gives it 72 hours from then with its tokens, as often as its owner asks.
  podssh relay pair --renew asks so, and its node does in its last day;
  /v1/status/NAME names the expiry beside the contract's fields. /v1/halt/NAME,
  with the stop token, keeps a pair's operators out while its node keeps its
  socket (podssh relay halt). /v1/resume/NAME, with the stop token, lets them
  in again (podssh relay resume); the status says halted. --pairs FILE keeps
  the pairs in FILE, so that they outlive a restart. FILE is of mode 0600, and
  holds the digests of their tokens and never a token. At most 1 MiB waits for
  a slow operator: past it, the session ends with 1011 relay backpressure, and
  the node's other sessions go on; a node that reads slowly slows its operators
  instead, each session's frames to it a turn each. So one operator's upload
  never holds another's keystrokes behind it. A frame of the node for a session
  that ended in the last 2 seconds was on its way, and is dropped; one for an
  id never given closes the node's socket with 1003, as the contract says.
  Ctrl-C or SIGTERM first closes each socket of the reverse road with 1012. So
  each node connects again, and each session resumes once the relay is back
  with its pairs: each socket gets the frames that wait for it first, 1 second
  at most. The role waits for each answer to its Close, 3 seconds at most in
  all; a node or an operator that comes meanwhile gets 503 and tries again.
  Where nothing may listen, the node of a quick tunnel serves the same roads
  behind its tunnel, with no listener. The tunnel's name is then the relay
  host: see podssh node --relay.

  --mint keys:FILE mints tokens and makes pairs for the keys of FILE alone.
  FILE is a list in the format of podssh node --allow, read again for each
  request. A request with no key gets 401 and a challenge of the relay's, which
  lives a minute; podssh then asks once more with the key of this client
  (client.key in the cache, the key that a node's list lets in). It sends the
  challenge and the key's signature of them, of the relay's name and of the
  path. Each of these gets 403: a key that is not on the list, a signature that
  does not verify, a challenge that ended or was answered before. So does a
  request whose Host is not the name that its TLS asked for. The 403 names the
  key's fingerprint for the owner's list. podssh caches the token as any other.

  FILE of --mint keys:FILE may be an https:// URL, for a relay whose image has
  no writable volume: the list is fetched through the host's proxy with the
  trust of --ca-file, 1 MiB at most. A fetch has 20 seconds and three redirects
  at most, to https:// alone. It is fetched once before the relay takes a
  connection, which stops the start (78) when it fails. Then it is fetched
  again each --list-ttl SECONDS (300). A fetch that fails leaves the copy to
  age, and a line on stderr says so; a copy older than its TTL and --list-stale
  SECONDS (3600) lets no key mint until a fetch works. A file that cannot be
  read does the same. An answer of the server is the list, whatever it holds: a
  page that is no list lets no key mint. A key taken off the list mints until
  the next fetch, not the next request, as a file's would. Its trust is TLS
  alone; --mint net, whose document its owner signs, is the stronger way. Each
  line names the URL by its host alone, as its path may hold a secret; an
  http:// URL is refused (64), and another FILE is a file, as before. The relay
  behind a node's quick tunnel takes the same words, at the defaults.

  --mint net mints tokens and makes pairs for the members of the net that this
  host holds (see podssh net). Each member proves itself by the same signature,
  with the key that the net names for it; --mint net,keys:FILE for those and
  the keys of FILE. The document is read again, and its owner's signature
  checked, for each request: a member that a newer document removed is refused
  from that serial on. A token that it minted before lives until its end or the
  relay's stop, as a token of a list's key does. Where the net has a policy, a
  member mints only where a rule lets it reach relay:*. The rule names the
  relay so, as podssh relay serve is no member of the net; the relay behind a
  node's quick tunnel is reached by relay:NAME too, NAME the node's name in the
  net; with no policy each member mints. A host that holds no net, or one that
  ended, does not start (78). The 403 of a key that is no member names the key
  and the document's serial, never the net or its members. A member's refusal
  by the policy names them.

  With --mint keys:FILE or net, half of the relay's 4096 pairs is a reserve. It
  is in equal parts for the keys that it mints for at that moment. The other
  half goes to whoever asks first: a key makes a pair within its reserve, or
  past it while the places left still hold each other key's. Else it gets 429
  with its own count and share (this key holds N pairs, past its share of M
  while others wait). The 429 names no other key. A pair keeps the fingerprint
  of its key, also in --pairs FILE, so that the share holds across a restart; a
  pair that is stopped or expires gives its place back.

  With --mint keys:FILE or net, the relay counts what each key carried. A token
  names no key and ends at a restart. So at each mint for a key, the relay
  keeps the token's SHA-256 with the key's fingerprint. It keeps them in memory
  until the token ends, 64 live tokens a key at most. The forward road's
  sessions are /connect/, each link of /v1/layer/ and a session of the HTTP
  road. Each counts its payload each way and charges its key once, at its end;
  an empty keepalive frame is no byte, and a refusal is no session. --quota MIB
  is each key's budget for a day (UTC), both ways together: once a key spent
  it, a session gets 403 forward: this key's quota of MIB for today is spent.
  The 403 comes before its target is dialed, until the next day. A line on
  stdout says the session that spent it. A session that began under the budget
  runs to its own end. So a key may pass its budget by the sessions that it
  holds open. Under a budget, a token that the relay holds no more, past a
  key's 64, gets 403, and podssh mints another. --usage FILE keeps each key's
  totals of the day and the day before in FILE, of mode 0600, so that they
  outlive a restart. FILE is written through a file beside it and a rename each
  2 s while a count moved, and at a planned stop; a file that does not read
  stops the start (78), and a write that fails is a line. SIGHUP says each
  key's totals on stderr, the most of today first. Both flags with --mint
  anyone or nobody, which count no key, are refused (64).

  The certificate and its key are read again on SIGHUP, and when either file
  changes, which the role looks at each minute; on Windows, which has no
  SIGHUP, that is the way. The handshakes after the read take the new pair, and
  each session that is open goes on with its own. A pair that does not load, or
  whose key is not the key of its first certificate, is said on stderr. The
  pair of before then stays. The role takes SIGHUP for this, so SIGHUP no
  longer stops it.

  --acme NAME takes a certificate for NAME from an ACME CA (RFC 8555): Let's
  Encrypt, unless --acme-directory URL names another, such as a CA's staging
  directory or Pebble for a test, whose own certificate --ca-file names. The CA
  validates NAME by TLS-ALPN-01 (RFC 8737) on the role's own listener, so
  nothing else listens: NAME must resolve to this host, and the CA's connection
  to its port 443 must reach --listen. A new account agrees to the CA's terms,
  which the role names as it makes the account. The account's key, and the
  certificate with its own P-256 key in one file, are kept in the cache (acme/,
  see FILES). Each is of mode 0600, in a directory of mode 0700. So a restart
  serves the certificate kept and asks the CA for nothing;
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR=none refuses --acme (78), and so does a cache with no
  directory that can be made private (73). The role renews the certificate 30
  days before its end, or at a third of its life left for a shorter one. The
  renewal has a new key, and the next handshakes take it. A renewal that fails
  is said on stderr, and the certificate of before stays. It is asked again
  after 5 minutes, then twice as long each time up to 6 hours. When no
  certificate is kept and the first order fails, the role stops with the CA's
  reason (69). SIGHUP reads the file kept again.

  podssh relay serve is a mailbox of the pairing by code too, at /v1/mailbox:
  magic-wormhole's mailbox protocol for podssh's application alone. So the two
  ends of podssh relay pair --code and podssh relay join meet at your own relay
  with --pair-mailbox wss://HOST/v1/mailbox. A client of magic-wormhole's own
  library with podssh's application id meets them there. It keeps its
  nameplates and mailboxes in memory, two sides each (a third gets crowded). A
  mailbox holds 32 messages of 8 KiB at most each. Each is kept for 20 minutes
  at most; it learns no code. Each connection to it is braked as a request of
  /v1/pair is.

  The relay brakes /v1/mint and /v1/pair for each address, as the default relay
  does: 120 requests of one address within a minute, the two together, and then
  429 with Retry-After. Retry-After is the seconds until the oldest of them is
  a minute old, which podssh says. The address is the connection's own, never a
  header that a client sends; an IPv6 address counts by its first 64 bits. The
  relay counts 4096 addresses at most, and forgets the one heard from least
  lately first. /health, the documents and the sockets of both roads are not
  braked, and the first refusal of an address is a line on stdout.

  The relay's listener takes the cleartext road beside TLS, for a client whose
  proxy tunnels CONNECT but cuts TLS that it does not know: a connection whose
  first byte begins no TLS handshake is served with no TLS. It is served only
  with what a session needs with a token of one session, as each hop reads it:
  GET /health; POST /v1/mint?once=1, for whom --mint names and under the same
  brake, which answers a token that lives 5 minutes, with "once": true; and
  /connect/HOST/PORT with that token in X-Relay-Token, which its upgrade
  spends, whatever its end, so that a second use is refused. A token of 72 h,
  the mint of one, the reverse road, the documents and the probes are refused
  there (403), and go over TLS. --cleartext no serves TLS alone. Over TLS, POST
  /v1/mint?once=1 mints the same token of one session.

  --sshd ADDR:PORT shares the relay's port with an sshd of yours, for a host
  that lets one port in: a connection of the listener whose first four bytes
  are SSH-, the start of an SSH client's version line, goes to the sshd at
  ADDR:PORT. The sshd reads each of its bytes as they came, and each byte of
  the sshd goes back; a record of TLS goes to TLS, and another start to the
  cleartext road, as before. So the port publishes a shell to each client that
  reaches it, behind that sshd's own authentication alone: no token, no brake
  and no limit of the relay stand before it. The sshd sees each client as the
  address that the relay dials it from. OpenSSH 9.8 and later shut out a source
  of failed logins (PerSourcePenalties). So they would shut out each client of
  the port for one client's failures: give that sshd PerSourcePenaltyExemptList
  with that address. Each connection is a line on stdout, and another at its
  end. The line names the client's address and the relay's own end of its
  connection to the sshd. The sshd's log names that end in the client's place.
  A client that waits for the server's line before it sends its own reaches no
  sshd, as the relay never speaks for one; OpenSSH's client sends its line
  first. The sshd is no target of the relay's policy: it is dialed as you named
  it, the loopback and what NO_PROXY names directly, another address through
  HTTPS_PROXY where it is set. Where the sshd does not answer, the client gets
  one line that says so, before any version line. The relay's line on stdout
  names the sshd and why. ADDR is an address, not a name (64). The first line
  says that SSH goes to that sshd.

  --publish publishes a TLS site of a node by its name, for an owner with one
  port: each takes a DNS name and the name of a pair of this relay, joined by
  =. An example is site.example.org=p-0123..., the name that the pair's file
  holds. The flag is repeatable. Before its own TLS, the relay peeks at a
  connection's ClientHello, within 10 s and its one record of 16 KiB at most.
  It takes none of its bytes: one whose server name is a published name, in any
  case and with or without a trailing dot, goes to that pair's node. It goes as
  a session of the pair, each byte as it came. So the node's TLS (podssh node
  --publish-tls TARGET) answers it with its own certificate, and the relay
  holds no key of the name. Each other connection goes on as before: a client
  by address, which sends no name; another name; a record cut short or longer
  than 16 KiB, which goes to the relay's TLS after the 10 s; and what is no
  TLS. A CA's validation of a published name, which offers acme-tls/1 alone,
  goes to the node too. So the node can take a certificate of its own for it;
  the name of --acme is the relay's own and is never published (64). The relay
  reads the name and never the bytes. A line on stdout names the name and the
  visitor's address at the start and at the end of each. The session is one of
  the reverse road's, with its bounds: 64 MiB, the bound of 1 MiB for a visitor
  that reads more slowly than its node sends, and the pair's life. The node
  renews that life at this relay by its stop token. A name whose pair is not
  here, has ended, or has no node joined, closes, with a line that says why.
  Pairs are made after the relay starts: keep them with --pairs so that a name
  of --publish outlives a restart. The first line names each published name and
  its pair.

  --derp-keys FILE serves DERP at /derp, over a WebSocket of the subprotocol
  derp, as Tailscale's derper serves it to the keys that it verifies: a node of
  podssh ts in its relay mode takes it in the place of the operator's Tailscale
  relay. The flag of podssh ts that names a DERP server pins the node to this
  relay. Two nodes whose keys FILE lists meet here. FILE holds one node key a
  line, nodekey:HEX (# starts a comment); it is read at the start, where a line
  that is no key stops it (64). It is read again at each login, so that a key
  added takes no restart. A key that it does not list is closed with 1008 not
  authorized, which podssh ts reads as the refusal of its node key (77). Each
  packet goes to the key that it names, 32 of them waiting for a receiver at
  most; /derp/probe and /derp/latency-check answer an empty 200. The packets
  are WireGuard's, sealed end to end: the relay sees keys, sizes and times.
  Each login and each end is a line on stdout, with the key's first 8 hex
  digits.

  --relay-roads WORDS makes the relay the meeting point of a net, on its one
  listener. A net whose hosts let only port 443 in then needs neither n0's iroh
  relays nor Tailscale's DERP fleet. WORDS is iroh, derp, or both, separated by
  a comma. iroh serves iroh's relay protocol at /relay, with iroh-relay's own
  server code. An iroh endpoint whose relay URL is https://HOST:PORT/ meets
  other endpoints here. It admits the endpoints whose keys --mint admits:
  anyone, the keys of its list, or the members of its net. With --mint nobody
  it admits none, so the start stops (64). A refused endpoint gets iroh's
  denial, not authorized. /ping answers an empty 200, as iroh's relays answer.
  derp serves DERP at /derp, as --derp-keys does. With no --derp-keys, it
  admits each node key, and only with --mint anyone (64 otherwise). Each road
  serves /generate_204, the probe of a captive portal, with the answer to an
  iroh or Tailscale challenge. /relays.json names each road as meet, null where
  it is off. Each endpoint that comes and goes is a line on stdout. The
  datagrams are sealed end to end: the relay sees keys, sizes and times. A
  build with no iroh road refuses iroh (70).

  The relay's TLS offers h2 before http/1.1 (RFC 8441): a client that chooses
  it gets SETTINGS that offer extended CONNECT and 16 streams at once. Each
  stream has a window of 1 MiB in one of 16 MiB for the connection. So the
  sessions of a client's process are streams of one connection. A CONNECT whose
  :protocol is websocket is the upgrade of its path, with its token and its
  checks. It is answered 200 where the upgrade is answered 101; GET /health,
  /relays.json, /trace and /llms-full.txt, and POST /v1/mint, answer there too;
  another request, such as the HTTP road's, a probe's or a pair's, is asked for
  again over HTTP/1.1. The answer is HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED, which a client of
  HTTP/2 follows at once. A connection with no stream for 2 minutes ends.
  --http2 no offers http/1.1 alone, as before; the first line says which.

  --quic yes serves QUIC too, on UDP at the address and port of --listen. The
  role binds that port with its listener, before it gives up its capabilities;
  PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses it with the listener, and a port of UDP that another
  process holds stops the start (69). Its TLS is 1.3, with the certificate that
  the listener presents at that moment. It offers the ALPN podssh-relay/1
  alone, so that no client of HTTP/3 and no CA's validation gets a connection
  there. Each bidirectional stream that a client opens is one connection of
  HTTP/1.1 to the same routes, with the same tokens, checks, brake and limits;
  a connection holds 64 streams at most, and ends after 30 s with no packet.
  Each connection is a line quic on stdout. /relays.json offers it as
  forward.quic, the port. podssh's client keeps it with the offer of the
  resumable layer, and races it before its TCP roads (see THE RELAY). The first
  line says QUIC on UDP and its address.

  podssh relay pair NAME --once asks the relay for a pair whose connect token
  takes one upgrade alone: one operator's session. Its later legs take the
  tokens of one leg that its node gives, where the node gives them; else the
  session has no resume. After it the token is refused, also by the status. So
  a token that leaks from a log after its use is worth nothing. podssh relay
  serve makes one, and offers it in its /relays.json; a relay that makes none
  is said so (69), and the pair that it made is stopped. The node's token and
  the stop token stay as they are; --renew is refused with it (64).

  Beside the contract, podssh relay serve takes a node's tokens of one leg: the
  node's socket gets a hello that offers them. A text frame of the node's,
  {"type":"token", "digest":HEX,"expires":MS}, registers the SHA-256 of one
  until MS, a day at most. The same frame with an end that passed withdraws it.
  Such a token takes one upgrade of /v1/connect/NAME, never the status. It
  takes one only while the node is joined with room for a session, else 503 and
  the token waits; the node hears {"type":"spent","digest":HEX} before the
  session's open, and a token taken once is refused after, also when the node
  registers it again. A pair keeps 256 such tokens at once, and 256 spent ones,
  the ones that end first making room; they live in memory, and a node
  registers its own again on its next socket. POST /v1/rotate/NAME with the
  stop token and {"digest":HEX} makes HEX, the SHA-256 of the next stop token,
  the one to come: the first request that uses that token makes it the pair's
  stop token, and ends each one before it. So the new token crosses no wire
  before its use; --pairs FILE keeps both. /relays.json offers both, as
  reverse.leg_tokens and reverse.rotate.

  Beside the contract, podssh relay serve keeps sessions readied ahead for a
  node that asks, as podssh node --spares N asks: the node's hello offers them
  ("spares": true), and the node's text frame {"type":"spares","want":N} asks
  for N, 16 at most, 0 for none; a frame with no whole number closes the node's
  socket with 1003 invalid spares frame. A node that says nothing gets none.
  The role sends {"type":"open","id":ID,"spare":true} for each, with the node's
  sessions counted inside its 64, and takes no spare that the node has not
  readied. An operator's leg takes the youngest readied one before it opens a
  session of its own: it hears ready at once, then the bytes that the node sent
  on the spare. Those are 64 KiB at most, past which the spare closes. Its
  first byte goes to the node with no open; a leg that finds none goes the way
  of before and asks for one more, up to N. A minute in which no leg took one
  leaves one; a spare that waited 15 s closes and another is drawn; one that
  the node refused stops them until the next minute; a leg that finds no room
  closes one; a halt closes them, and a resume draws them again. A spare's
  close says why, and its id is a session's that ended, for a frame on its way.
  Each take is a line reverse spare taken on stdout, in the place of reverse
  open.

  podssh relay serve reads the dialect of the reverse road that a node's or an
  operator's upgrade states in the header X-Podssh-Proto: none is 1, the
  dialect of before, which each client of the contract speaks, and podssh's own
  clients state 1. One that it does not read gets 426 with one line that names
  both and the side to update, and its own in X-Podssh-Proto. That answer comes
  once the pair's token passed, so that a client with no token learns nothing
  of it. It comes before the pair's name is checked, or a token that takes one
  upgrade is spent; its hello to a node says its own as version. It reads 1
  alone.

  The relay also serves the probes of podssh doctor --stream, with no token, as
  go-httpbin's /drip and /anything under /v1/probe: GET
  /v1/probe/drip?duration=S&numbytes=N (&delay=S, &code=C) sends its N bytes,
  the first at once and the last after S seconds, 600 s and 64 KiB at most;
  POST /v1/probe/anything reads a body of its Content-Length, 8 MiB at most
  (413 past it, 411 with none), and drops it. It answers its length and the
  time, from the head, that each part of it came. At most 16 run together (503
  past them). /relays.json names their limits in limits.probe, and behind a
  node's quick tunnel the node's own; and the HTTP road's own in limits.http.

  A relay host outside the default's domain (ssh.relay.ajam.dev) comes from a
  signed list of deployments alone. /relays.json may carry one as its field
  signed: the document's exact text, the Ed25519 key that signed it, and that
  key's signature of podssh-relays/1, a zero byte and the text. The text holds
  its form podssh-relays 1, a serial, issued, not_after, and its deployments,
  each a name and up to 8 hosts. podssh uses it only when the key is one that
  it trusts: one compiled in, a key of PODSSH_RELAY_KEYS or of RelayKeys in the
  settings file (SHA256:... or its 64 hex digits; none trusts no key at all),
  or the key of a member of your net with the role relay. A list of another key
  is not used, nor one with one changed byte, past its not_after or living more
  than 400 days. Nor is one with a serial below the list kept of its key. The
  default list then keeps the default's domain alone. A list that holds is kept
  in the cache (relay-deployments.json, one for each key, checked again at each
  read). It comes from the pool's refresh after a mint and from podssh relay
  info. So a binary keeps the other deployments when the default's domain is
  gone. The default list is then the default host and up to 3 hosts of its
  pool, then up to 4 hosts of the other deployments. The first of each
  deployment comes first; a list that you name takes none, and neither does a
  run with PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN, as that token is the default deployment's. Each
  host of another deployment mints a token of its own and is sent no other, and
  its TLS is checked by its own name. podssh relay info says whether the first
  host's list is signed, by which key and whence it is trusted, and keeps it;
  podssh relay status names each deployment of the default list and whether its
  list was signed. So do podssh status (deployments) and podssh doctor
  (deployments). podssh relay serve --deployment, repeatable, takes a name and
  its hosts as backup=relay.example.org,relay2.example.org:8443. The key of
  --list-key FILE (relay-list.key in the cache, made when it is missing) signs
  a list of those deployments in its /relays.json. The role signs it again each
  day with a higher serial, for 90 days each time. Its first line names the
  key's fingerprint: give that fingerprint to each client, in PODSSH_RELAY_KEYS
  or RelayKeys, or name the key as a member of your net with the role relay.
  Nothing of a request goes into what the role signs.

  A relay member is a member of your net with the role relay and a host in the
  net's document (see podssh net). With no --relay-host, it is asked for its
  list: before the race of a session on the default list, and before podssh
  relay status asks its hosts. A run asks that host's /relays.json at most once
  a day for each member, whatever it answered. It waits 5 s for each and 8 s in
  all. It asks with no token, through the proxy of the environment, and with
  TLS checked by the host's name. Its list is taken only when the member's key
  signed it, by the rules above (PODSSH_RELAY_KEYS=none takes none). Its
  deployments then follow the default list in that run; a list there of another
  key is not the member's, also when another setting trusts that key. No run
  asks with PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN, nor with a list that you name, nor when the
  cache keeps no file. The asks are kept in the cache (relay-members.json).
  podssh relay status names each relay member: its host, then its list taken
  with its serial, or why not, and when it was asked; --json gives them as
  members.

  A relay member, a member of your net with the role relay and a host in the
  net's document, carries sessions too. It carries them between two other
  members that reach no common road. podssh node makes a pair at each such
  member by its own key, at most three, the relay of its own pair aside. It
  keeps a socket on each beside its own road, with the one keeper of its
  sessions. It does neither for a node with no resumable layer or no end-to-end
  channel; each pair made, or refused, is a line of the node. podssh ssh NAME,
  NAME a member with its key in the document, asks each such member for a leg
  once each road before it failed: POST /v1/leg/KEY, KEY the node's key, with
  the proof of the key of the client's end-to-end channel. Then the upgrade,
  with the token of one leg that the role drew; -v names it a member's relay
  role. No pair of the node's is needed on the client's host. A role gives a
  leg only with --mint keys:FILE or --mint net, and only to a key that it mints
  for; it sees bytes that it cannot read, and the node's allowlist, or the net,
  still decides who gets in.

  Usage: podssh relay [OPTIONS] SUBCOMMAND [NAME | HOST PORT]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        pair, join, revoke, halt, resume, status, info, trace, rank, conform,
        spec or serve.
    [NAME]...
        the label of a pair, which you choose; for info and trace, HOST PORT.

  Options:
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts, HOST[:PORT][,...]: status asks each, and pair, info and
        trace use the first; conform needs one HOST[:PORT] here (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots); with serve --acme, for the ACME
        directory, and with serve --mint keys:https://URL, for the list's
        server.
    --operator-file FILE
        pair: write the operator's part of the pair to FILE, a new file that
        only its owner can read.
    --once
        pair: ask the relay for a connect token that takes one upgrade alone,
        one operator's session with no resume, which podssh relay serve offers;
        a relay that makes none is said so (69), and its pair stopped.
    --code
        pair: give the operator's part by a short code, in place of
        --operator-file: the pair stored under NAME while it has 10 minutes
        left, else a new one, and the node's key; the code shows on this
        terminal alone, lives 10 minutes and is used once; the operator types
        it at podssh relay join NAME.
    --pair-mailbox URLS
        pair --code and join: where the two ends meet, wss://HOST[:PORT]/PATH
        or ws://, by commas, in order, such as podssh relay serve's
        wss://HOST/v1/mailbox (default: env PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX, else
        magic-wormhole's public mailbox, then Least Authority's); no turns
        pairing by code off.
    --allow FILE
        pair --code: add the operator's key to FILE, the allowlist that podssh
        node NAME takes with its own --allow, which the node reads again for
        each session.
    --client-key FILE
        join: this operator's key file, whose key goes to the node's host
        (default: client.key in the cache).
    --renew
        pair: renew the pair stored under NAME at its relay, 72 h from now, its
        tokens the same, so that each operator's file holds; podssh relay serve
        renews; a relay that renews none is said so (69), with the next pair in
        the last 24 h as the way.
    --reason TEXT
        halt: the words that each operator of the halted pair hears in the
        relay's refusal, and that relay status shows: one line of 200 bytes at
        most.
    --pair-file FILE
        status: the pair in FILE, or its operator's part, as pair
        --operator-file writes it, not the one stored under NAME; NAME, when
        given, is the label shown.
    --document FILE
        spec: check FILE, a copy of the relay's document, and read nothing from
        the network.
    --json
        status, info, trace, rank and conform: the answer as one JSON object on
        stdout, when the run ends; for a pair, its label, online, sessions,
        expires, seconds_left and halted, with halt_reason where its owner gave
        one.
    --rounds N
        rank: probe each host N times, 1 to 20 (default 3), in a new random
        order each round.
    --count N
        rank: the WebSocket pings of each probe, 1 to 20 (default 5).
    --target HOST:PORT
        rank: the target of each probe's session, which the relay dials
        (default github.com:22, never a destination of yours that would count
        the probes); conform: a target for the checks of a session that the
        relay dials, best an echo server of yours.
    --reverse
        conform: check the reverse road too, on a pair that the check makes,
        uses and stops at its end, also after a failure.
    --cached
        rank: print the rank kept in the cache, its age and whether it holds
        for this egress; connects nowhere.
    --forget
        rank: remove the rank kept in the cache; connects nowhere.
    --listen ADDR:PORT
        serve: serve the relay's forward and reverse roads on ADDR:PORT, a
        listener that you ask for (127.0.0.1:0 takes a free port);
        PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses it.
    --cert FILE
        serve: the certificate chain that the relay presents, in PEM, read
        again on SIGHUP or when it changes.
    --key FILE
        serve: the certificate's P-256 key, in PEM (EC PRIVATE KEY or PRIVATE
        KEY), in a file that only its owner reads; read again with --cert.
    --acme NAME
        serve: a certificate for NAME from an ACME CA (Let's Encrypt by
        default), in place of --cert and --key: proven by TLS-ALPN-01 on the
        listener, which the CA reaches at NAME on port 443, kept in the cache
        and renewed in the role.
    --acme-directory URL
        serve --acme: the https:// URL of the CA's ACME directory (default:
        Let's Encrypt's, https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory).
    --port-file FILE
        serve: write the port that it listens on to FILE, for --listen ADDR:0.
    --mint WHO
        serve: who may mint a token at /v1/mint and make a pair at /v1/pair:
        anyone; keys:FILE, the keys of FILE (the format of podssh node
        --allow), each by its signature of the relay's challenge; FILE is a
        file read again for each request, or an https:// URL whose list is
        fetched again each --list-ttl; net, the members of the net that this
        host holds, by the same signature, as its policy lets them reach
        relay:*; net,keys:FILE, both; or nobody (the default: 503, and tokens
        are given another way).
    --allow-private
        serve: dial private, loopback and other non-public addresses too (by
        default only public targets, as the default relay).
    --routes RANGES
        serve: dial the private ranges RANGES too, ADDR/BITS or one address,
        separated by commas, as podssh node --exit --routes reads them: a
        target whose each address is public or inside one; another is refused
        in the words of a target that is not public; not with --allow-private.
    --keepalive SECONDS
        serve: send each client an empty frame every SECONDS, 1 to 3600
        (default 25).
    --idle SECONDS
        serve: end a session after SECONDS with no payload either way, 1 to
        86400 (default 180, the default relay's); published in /relays.json as
        idle_timeout_ms. A value above the default moves this role's cut only:
        a client keeps its own lower budget.
    --session-hours HOURS
        serve: end a session after HOURS, 1 to 168 (default 12); published as
        max_session_ms. Above the default, a client still stops at its own
        budget.
    --max-session-mib MIB
        serve: end a session after MIB of payload, both ways together, 1 to
        4096 (default 64); published as max_session_bytes. Above the default, a
        client still opens a new session at its own budget.
    --connect SECONDS
        serve: wait SECONDS for the dial of a target before the upgrade, 1 to
        120 (default 10); published as connect_timeout_ms.
    --max-connections-per-address N
        serve: keep at most N connections open from one address (an IPv4
        address, or the /64 of an IPv6 one), 0 for no cap (default 256); one
        more is closed before TLS and said once a minute; a peer on the
        loopback, a proxy in front, counts in all alone; published as
        max_connections_per_address.
    --max-connections N
        serve: keep at most N connections open in all, 0 for no cap (the
        default); published as max_connections.
    --pairs FILE
        serve: keep the pairs of the reverse road in FILE, of mode 0600; this
        way, they outlive a restart (the digests of their tokens, never a
        token).
    --quota MIB
        serve --mint keys:FILE or net: each key's budget for a day (UTC), in
        MiB, both ways together, from 1 to 16777216: each session of the
        forward road is charged to its token's key at its end; once the key
        spent it, a session gets 403 before its target is dialed, until the
        next day.
    --usage FILE
        serve --mint keys:FILE or net: keep each key's totals of the day and
        the day before in FILE, of mode 0600; it is written each 2 s while a
        count moved, so that they outlive a restart; SIGHUP says them on
        stderr.
    --list-ttl SECONDS
        serve --mint keys:https://URL: fetch the list again each SECONDS, 1 to
        86400 (default 300), through the host's proxy with the trust of
        --ca-file; a fetch that fails leaves the copy to age.
    --list-stale SECONDS
        serve --mint keys:https://URL: read the copy for SECONDS more past its
        --list-ttl while its server fails, 0 to 604800 (default 3600); past
        that, no key mints until a fetch works.
    --cleartext WORD
        serve: yes (the default) or no: on the listener, a request whose first
        byte begins no TLS handshake gets the cleartext road, for a client
        whose proxy cuts TLS: /health, a token of one session (POST
        /v1/mint?once=1, as --mint says) and /connect/ with it, which its
        upgrade spends; each other request there is refused (403).
    --sshd ADDR:PORT
        serve: send each connection of the listener whose first four bytes are
        SSH- (an SSH client's version line) to the sshd at ADDR:PORT; ADDR is
        an address, not a name; its bytes go untouched, so that one port serves
        the relay and a shell: a shell for each client that reaches the port,
        behind that sshd's own authentication; each other start goes to TLS or
        the cleartext road, as before; refused with --cover (64), which an SSH
        client of the port would name.
    --proxy-protocol RANGES
        serve: the TCP balancers of the owner (haproxy's send-proxy, nginx's
        proxy_protocol), as ADDR/BITS or addresses, separated by commas. A
        connection from one of them must begin with a PROXY header of version 1
        or 2. Its source is then the client for the brake, the slots and the
        log. A connection from a balancer without the header is closed. So is
        one from any other address that begins with a header, since anyone can
        write one.
    --publish NAME=PAIR
        serve: send each TLS connection whose ClientHello names NAME, a DNS
        name, to the node of PAIR; PAIR is a pair of this relay (its name
        p-..., which the pair's file holds); the connection goes before any
        handshake, with its bytes untouched; this way, the node's own TLS
        answers it with its own certificate (podssh node --publish-tls);
        repeatable; the relay reads the name, never the bytes; a CA's
        validation of NAME (acme-tls/1) goes to the node too; NAME is never the
        name of --acme.
    --cover DIR
        serve: answer the role's own TLS name as a static site from DIR:
        index.html, the assets, robots.txt, the site's own 404 and a Server
        header (--cover-server), for each request that is not the contract's;
        an unknown name, and /health, /trace, /llms-full.txt, /relays.json and
        /v1/probe/* with it, get the site's 404, which the socket of
        --control-socket keeps instead; an authenticated client (a token at
        POST /v1/delegate) gets a temporary credential of the same chain and
        name; a wildcard leaf is refused at the start, in both modes, and each
        name of a multi-name leaf is named by --cover-name; no RFC 9345
        delegation and no TLS-level delegation.
    --cover-server VALUE
        serve --cover: the Server header of the site, 64 visible bytes that
        name no project (default: nginx).
    --cover-name NAME
        serve --cover: a name of the certificate that the role terminates
        itself and answers with the cover site, while --publish names forward
        to their pair's node; repeatable; the first is the role's name; each
        must be a name of the certificate and none may be a --publish name; a
        name not named here gets the site's 404.
    --cover-script FILE
        serve --cover: the cover script of the role, a TOML measurement with
        its date, cover_version, record_size, timing and split policy; a
        missing script, or one with no date or no cover version, is a refusal
        at the start (78); loaded and checked at the start, and its replay is
        what the tests read; the tunnel's records are not shaped by it yet,
        which the record layer's own work covers.
    --cover-issuer-key FILE
        serve --cover: the operator's Ed25519 secret that signs each cover
        credential, 64 hexadecimal digits of its 32-byte seed in FILE; the
        public half is pinned for the role and each upgrade is checked against
        it; an application-layer credential, not an RFC 9345 or TLS-level
        delegation; with neither this nor --cover-issuer-public, a key is made
        for this process, so a restart refuses the credentials of the one
        before.
    --cover-issuer-public HEX
        serve --cover: the hexadecimal Ed25519 public key that the role pins,
        for an operator who holds the secret elsewhere: each cover credential
        is checked against it, and none is issued here (POST /v1/delegate
        answers 503); with --cover-issuer-key it must be that key's public
        half, else the start is refused.
    --control-socket PATH
        serve --cover: the Unix socket, of mode 0600, that serves /health,
        /trace, /llms-full.txt, /relays.json and /v1/probe/* while the public
        listener answers the site; required with --cover; a path that exists
        already is refused. A socket's address holds 103 bytes on macOS and the
        BSDs, 107 on Linux. A longer path is bound through a short way to it
        (/proc/self/fd, else a link under /tmp or /var/tmp), which the first
        line says. A path that no short way serves is refused (78).
    --derp-keys FILE
        serve: serve DERP at /derp, over a WebSocket of the subprotocol derp,
        as Tailscale's derper does; for the node keys in FILE, one a line
        (nodekey:HEX, as the status of tailscale and of podssh's ts_echo
        example write them; # starts a comment), read again at each login; a
        node key that is not in it is closed with 1008 not authorized, as the
        operator's relay closes it; this way, podssh ts --ts-mode relay
        --ts-relay HOST:PORT pins this relay. The packets are WireGuard's,
        sealed end to end: the relay sees keys, sizes and times.
    --relay-roads WORDS
        serve: also be the meeting point of a net on this listener. WORDS is
        iroh, derp, or iroh,derp. iroh serves iroh's relay protocol at /relay,
        with /ping. derp serves DERP at /derp for the node keys of --derp-keys;
        with no such file and --mint anyone, for each key. Each serves
        /generate_204. /relays.json names each as meet.
    --deployment NAME=HOSTS
        serve: a deployment that /relays.json names in its signed list,
        NAME=HOST[:PORT][,HOST[:PORT]...], repeatable, in order; a client that
        trusts the list's key (PODSSH_RELAY_KEYS, RelayKeys, a member of its
        net with the role relay) tries those hosts after its default list; each
        with a token of its own.
    --list-key FILE
        serve --deployment: the Ed25519 key that signs the list, in a private
        file, made when it is missing (default: relay-list.key in the cache);
        the first line names its fingerprint.
    --resume-deadline TIME
