        serve: keep a session of /v1/layer/ whose link is lost for TIME, and
        tell its client so: 90s, 30m, 8h or 3d, from 1 minute to 72 h (default
        10m).
    --resume-budget MIB
        serve: the replay buffers of the sessions of /v1/layer/ in all, in MiB,
        4 for each session: from 4 to 16384 (default 256, 64 sessions), or 0
        for none, which offers no such road; a new session past it is refused
        in its handshake, and podssh's client takes /connect/ instead.
    --resume-host HOST[:PORT]
        serve: the name of this process alone, which its certificate holds,
        where several processes serve one name: /relays.json names it as
        forward.host; podssh's client sends each link of a session of
        /v1/layer/ to it; this way, each resume reaches the process that holds
        the session (a host of the name's deployment).
    --http2 WORD
        serve: yes (the default) or no: offer h2 by ALPN before http/1.1, with
        extended CONNECT (RFC 8441); this way, the sessions of a client's
        process are streams of one connection, each upgrade a CONNECT answered
        200; /health, /relays.json, /trace, /llms-full.txt and the mint answer
        there too, and each other request is asked for again over HTTP/1.1; no
        offers http/1.1 alone, as before.
    --quic WORD
        serve: yes or no (the default): serve QUIC too, on UDP at the address
        and port of --listen, a second socket that you ask for; with TLS 1.3,
        the listener's certificate and the ALPN podssh-relay/1; each stream one
        connection of HTTP/1.1 to the same routes; /relays.json offers it as
        forward.quic, and podssh's client races it before TCP (PODSSH_QUIC).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    offer a service of this host to an operator outside: a pair, with its
    operator's part in a file
        $ podssh relay pair lab --operator-file lab-operator.json

    whether the node is online; then stop the pair
        $ podssh relay status lab && podssh relay revoke lab

    on podssh relay serve, the pair renewed for 72 hours with its tokens, so
    that each operator's file holds
        $ podssh relay pair --renew lab

    whether the relay reaches a target, and the first line that the target
    sends
        $ podssh relay trace github.com 22

podssh status
  the state of this host as one line of JSON: relays, token, proxy, terminal, a
  host key.

  podssh status writes one line of JSON on stdout and exits 0: schema, podssh,
  relays (each host and port) and relays_from (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY, or
  the default and its pool); deployments (each deployment of the list, its
  hosts, and its signed list or none; see podssh relay), pool (cached, when it
  was fetched, how many hosts), token (source: PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN, cache or
  none; the relay that it is for; when it expires; whether it can be used),
  cache (from: PODSSH_CACHE_DIR, none or default; dirs: the directories in the
  order podssh tries them; passed: each usual place that is in another user's
  tree, its dir and why, see FILES); proxy (the variable, HOST:PORT and the
  kind, http or socks5), offline, attachment, stdin_tty and stdout_tty; host
  for a destination (its name in known_hosts, whether a key is recorded, the
  key types); session_log, relay_failures and relay_opened (the relay hosts
  tried last and first: road, host, ago_s, and the reason or the opens),
  relay_rank (the rank kept: age_s, this_egress, holds, named, source, relay
  rank or background, partial, first and hosts; null with none), relay_order
  (rank, samples, pool or off); relay_rank_auto (whether a setting asks for a
  rank in a session's background and which one, and when the last was made:
  asked, by, last_ms, last_age_s, partial), open_files (soft, hard, at_start,
  raised, refused: the limit of open files, which podssh raises at start; null
  on Windows), and pairs: each stored pair's label, when it expires, whether it
  expired, and next_now. next_now says whether podssh relay pair LABEL makes
  its next pair now. renews says whether its relay renews it, as its node last
  learned: true or false, and null when no node learned it of this pair.

  The line's net is the net that this host holds, read with no connection:
  name, serial, owner (its fingerprint), expires_ms, ended, file and count, the
  number of members; null when this host holds none or PODSSH_NET is no, and
  error, with why, when its file does not read. With --net, net also holds
  members: each member's name, roles, key (its fingerprint), tickets (their
  kinds, never a ticket) and routes. It also holds what the races from this
  host last found of it: reached, the road that answered first in the words of
  podssh ssh -v, with ms from the start of the race and ago_s; missed, why the
  last race found no road, with ago_s; and last, reached or missed, whichever
  came last, or null when no race to it was kept. Each race of podssh ssh, of
  the copies and of podssh ping to node://NAME, and the pair's road alone,
  keeps its end. It goes in net-roads.json in the cache (see FILES), at most
  256 nodes. Where a node takes its net from a URL (see podssh node), net also
  holds url: the URL by its host alone, serial, age_s, ttl_s and stale_s of its
  last fetch. It holds stale, true past the time between two fetches, and
  closed, true past the stale window too, when the net lets nobody in. It holds
  error, the fault of the last fetch, else null; url is null with no fetch
  kept.

  With --keys, the line's keys lists the public part of each key that podssh
  keeps on this host. It is read with no connection, and no key is made. Each
  entry has role, label, path, type, public, fingerprint, iroh and state. role
  is client, the key that reaches a node, or node, one for each label. acme is
  the account of podssh relay serve at each certificate authority; warp is the
  device of a warp:// destination. net_owner, when this host holds a net, is
  the owner's key from the net's document. Its path is the key of ~/.ssh whose
  .pub file holds that key, which podssh does not open. state is present,
  absent or unreadable, with error, which names the file and never its text.
  public is a line of OpenSSH for an Ed25519 key, the JWK of an account, and
  the base64 of a device's SubjectPublicKeyInfo. fingerprint is the SHA-256
  fingerprint that podssh keygen -l prints, or an account's thumbprint. iroh is
  an Ed25519 key in iroh's hex, the node's name on the iroh road. With
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR=none, each key is absent. --keys with a destination is
  refused (64); without --keys, keys is null.

  exits lists each exit node of this host by its label, as the node last wrote
  it: at_ms, and its callers. Each caller has key (its fingerprint), connects,
  refusals, bytes_up, bytes_down and last_ms. Bytes are counted at the
  end-to-end channel, its framing included. The list is empty when no node of
  this host is an exit.

  It shows no token and no proxy credentials, opens no connection, asks no DNS
  and writes nothing. A bad --relay-host or destination is a usage error (64),
  a bad PODSSH_RELAY a configuration error (78). podssh doctor is the report
  that measures.

  Usage: podssh status [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host]
        a host whose host key is looked up: [user@]host, host:PORT or
        [IPV6]:PORT.

  Options:
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to report, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env PODSSH_RELAY,
        else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --net
        also each member of the net held: its roles, key, tickets and routes,
        and the road that last reached it from this host, or the race that last
        found none.
    --keys
        also the public part of each key that podssh keeps on this host: the
        client's, each node's, each ACME account, the WARP device, and the
        net's owner; never a private byte.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    the state of this host as one line of JSON, and whether a host's key is
    known
        $ podssh status github.com

podssh doctor
  what this host allows and whether the relay works: ok, FAIL or ???? per
  check.

  Each line is ok, FAIL or ????, the check, and what podssh found. ok: podssh
  can work with it; a missing pty, listener, DNS or user database entry is ok,
  because podssh is made for them. FAIL: something that podssh needs is broken.
  ????: the check could not run, and it does not fail the run.

  The checks cover this host, the egress and the relay. This host: the user
  database entry, and where host keys and tokens can be written. They say
  whether PODSSH_CACHE_DIR chose the place or is none. They name each usual
  place of the cache passed over as another user's (see FILES). Then /proc, a
  pty, and a socket bind that is closed at once. Then the directories that can
  run programs, the terminal, and the sshd of a roost. The egress: the proxy
  setting, TLS and the trust store, what the proxy allows, and the system
  resolver. Then the addresses of the cache, and DNS over HTTPS with the form
  that answered; on github.com port 22 only the server's banner shows that
  plain ssh can leave, as a proxy can take the CONNECT and carry nothing. The
  relay: each relay host, with where its address came from: a pin, the system
  resolver, the cache or DNS over HTTPS; a token, a session to github.com port
  22 that must show the published host key of GitHub, and the clock.

  The line sshd is for a roost (podssh node --sshd): where this host has an
  sshd, looked for as the roost looks (on PATH, then in /usr/sbin,
  /usr/local/sbin and /sbin). It also gives what one dial of 127.0.0.1:22 reads
  first within 2 s, judged as the roost judges it: its version line (present at
  /usr/sbin/sshd; 127.0.0.1:22 answers SSH-2.0-...), nothing listening, or
  another first line. With no sshd found, it names the command that installs
  one, as the roost does; podssh runs none. The dial is of the loopback, so it
  is made with PODSSH_OFFLINE too. Each form is ok: a host with no roost needs
  no sshd.

  The sections that connect run at once by default, each into its own part of
  the report, and the report keeps its order: a section's lines go out once
  each section before it has ended. The first one that still runs goes out line
  by line. So a run takes about as long as its longest section, not their sum.
  Each section reaches its servers one at a time, as before. So a run holds at
  most one connection for each section that runs. Those are the egress, the
  relay, OpenTunnel, DERP, the public carriers, the net's member relays, and
  each road that it names. The exceptions are the one UDP socket of the line
  nat and the 6 handshakes at once of the section burst. The relay's forward
  also races its hosts as podssh ssh does. --jobs N, or DoctorJobs N in the
  settings file, starts at most N sections together, in the order of the
  report; --jobs 1 runs one after another.

  --quick checks this host, the egress and the relay alone, what each run of
  podssh ssh and podssh proxy needs. It adds the section of each road that the
  run names (--forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless). It leaves out the
  quick tunnel's edge (the lines quick tunnel roots, UDP out and edge road, so
  that --quick --full makes no QUIC handshake). It also leaves out the line
  nat, and iroh and tor in a build with them. It leaves out OpenTunnel, DERP,
  the public carriers, the pairs and the net held; its last line, sections in
  the section left out, names them, as ????: checks that did not run.

  The section burst runs after the relay's checks, and in --quick too. It opens
  6 TLS handshakes with the first relay host at once and 6 one after another,
  within 10 s. They go in two rounds whose order is swapped (burst, one at a
  time, one at a time, burst). Its line concurrency says no concurrency limit
  seen up to 6; or a concurrency limit, k/6 together and 6/6 one at a time,
  where fewer sessions at once may hold; or not shown to be a concurrency
  limit, where a handshake fails alone too. The line of a limit names the kind
  of each failure (reset, timeout, refused, refused by the proxy). Through a
  proxy, it measures the proxy's limit. In --json, its numbers are k, burst_ok,
  control_ok and each round's.

  --tier checks this host alone, with the lines of its section, and ends with
  one verdict of its capabilities in the section tier. identity is a user name,
  from the database or a variable, and the capability to bind a port below
  1024. That capability is read from the sets of /proc/self/status, which
  podssh reads and never changes. exec is the probe of the line exec: a copy of
  podssh ran from a directory, or none did. terminal is the line pty. state is
  the line token cache: a directory of the cache that can be written. resolver
  is one class of the order of the dialer: a proxy that is given the names, a
  pin, the system resolver, a fresh cached address, DNS over HTTPS, or none. It
  costs one lookup of the first relay host's name, with no proxy set, and one
  request at each DNS over HTTPS resolver at most. Each is ok, closed or ????:
  a capability that could not be read is ????, never ok. A closed capability is
  a fact and never fails the run (the exit stays 1 only for FAIL); it counts as
  nothing. Its line ends with unavailable because of this and the commands and
  flags that it closes, from one table in the code: identity (podssh ssh with
  no user@host, a listener of podssh relay serve or of podssh exit on a port
  below 1024); exec (the detached runs of session, node and pipe, update);
  terminal (session, podssh node --sshd); state (session, detached); and
  resolver (ssh, proxy and pipe, which need the relay's name). The line verdict
  counts them. The memfd and execveat route is not probed: the rung of exec is
  the path probe alone. --tier ends the run before the egress, with --hop and
  --stream. The MCP tool doctor takes it as tier.

  The line TLS reference makes TLS with github.com on port 443 by its name, its
  certificate checked. It goes straight out with no proxy, else over the
  CONNECT that the proxy took for it. It says what it met: a handshake, a reset
  or a timeout. After the counts, a line diagnosis names a case that the
  handshakes of the roads show beside it, and counts as nothing. Those roads
  are each relay host, each DERP server, and each resolver of DNS over HTTPS
  with no proxy. In a build with iroh, they are each relay of n0's too: each
  relay host reset while github.com's completed is an egress that resets TLS
  for each name that it does not list. There a road through a listed name
  serves (--forwarder, --via, a relay of your own); each handshake reset,
  github.com's too, is an egress that resets each one on port 443; each timed
  out, github.com's too, is a path that drops them, not one that lists names; a
  resolver, asked by its address with no name, that timed out says nothing of
  names. A reset and a timeout are read from the kind of the error, never from
  its words, which differ between systems. With --json, diagnosis lists each,
  with kind (tls-names, tls-reset or tls-dropped), detail and evidence, the
  names that show it.

  The line nat is in the section egress. It says whether the NAT in front of
  this host keeps one mapping for a local port whatever the destination: one
  UDP socket of port 0 asks two STUN servers in turn for the address that each
  saw. Each ask is a Binding Request of RFC 8489 with 3 tries of 1 s. An answer
  is taken only from the address asked and with the request's id. The servers
  by default: Cloudflare's stun.cloudflare.com:3478, which its Realtime TURN
  documentation names, then Google's stun.l.google.com:19302, which WebRTC's
  samples name; PODSSH_STUN names others, or no turns the line off. Both saw
  this host's own address: no NAT. Both saw one address: one mapping for all
  destinations, so a peer that learns it may reach this host directly (hole
  punching can work). Two addresses: a mapping for each destination, where hole
  punching will not work and the relays carry each session. Each is ok, a fact;
  ???? where no UDP socket binds, and with fewer than two mapped addresses. A
  server that is silent, or one that answered with none or with an error, is
  named. UDP goes straight out, as no proxy carries it, whether a proxy is set
  or not; PODSSH_OFFLINE sends nothing.

  The line ipv6, in the section relay, says whether an IPv6 target can be
  reached. Through the first relay host that answered, by what its /relays.json
  says of its host's way out: podssh relay serve says yes, none (and refuses an
  IPv6 target before the upgrade) or that it cannot tell, and how it knows; the
  default relay says nothing of it, and the line gives its egress when last
  measured, on 2026-11-03: none, as each IPv6 target upgraded and then closed
  with 1011. Direct, by this host's own probes, which send nothing: through a
  proxy, the proxy's way out decides; else an IPv6 socket made and closed, then
  this host's table of IPv6 routes where Linux gives one. The line is ok, a
  fact; ???? when no relay host answered or its /relays.json cannot be read.

  --exit NAME checks the exit NAME of your net, among the roads that the run
  names, with --quick too. It checks it as podssh proxy --exit NAME reaches it:
  exit net, what the net held says: NAME a member with the role exit, and the
  rule of its policy that lets this client reach exit:NAME. This client's key
  is --client-key FILE, else client.key in the cache; the line is ???? where
  this host holds no net; exit pair, the pair kept under NAME; exit, one
  session from the exit to --exit-target HOST:PORT (github.com:22 by default,
  identified by its published host key; another target by its first bytes),
  with the node's verdict. A refusal says whose it is: the road (the relay, or
  the pair), the channel, the net's policy, the exit's check of an address, or
  its dial.

  The line cleartext is in the section relay. It says what a request with no
  TLS meets on the way to the first relay host that answered (else the first
  host). It asks at the host's port, and at port 80 beside 443, as the
  cleartext road would meet it: the CONNECT that the proxy takes, then GET
  /health with no token and no target, and what came back, named: a reset or a
  close with no answer (a hop that expects TLS cuts cleartext); a record of TLS
  (the far end speaks TLS alone there); the edge's refusal (a 400 that says
  that a request of plain HTTP was sent to its HTTPS port); a refusal by policy
  (403), a redirect, or an answer, the relay's own /health named; then whether
  the road reaches the relay. One probe after another. The line is ok, a fact,
  as a reset is no fault where TLS answers; ???? when the proxy setting cannot
  be read. With --forwarder, the section of the forwarders has the same line
  for each one's host, at 443 and 80. It says whether a ws:// form of it can
  pass.

  The line http2, in the section relay, after cleartext, says what the same
  host offers the WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441). It sends nothing but
  HTTP/2's preface, its SETTINGS and a PING: the protocol that its TLS chose
  when podssh offered h2 then http/1.1. On h2, it says whether its SETTINGS
  offer extended CONNECT, with its streams at once; then whether the sessions
  of a run share one connection to it, by PODSSH_H2 (podssh relay serve offers
  it; the default relay's edge chooses h2 and offers no extended CONNECT). The
  line is ok, a fact; ???? when the host was not reached; FAIL for a word of
  PODSSH_H2 that is not auto, yes or no. With --h2-shape WORD (default:
  PODSSH_H2_SHAPE, else existing), a line http2 shape names the shape's
  SETTINGS and window, which podssh-ws's h2 road sends. It says that its
  PRIORITY frames and padded DATA are recorded and not sent through h2 0.4. No
  session of the run takes that road, whose default is the WebSocket upgrade.
  With --early-data 0rtt|1rtt|off (default: PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA), the
  session of each VLESS server offers that early data, and its line names the
  first write. With --trojan, the section trojan states Trojan's controls by
  name from trojan::capability(): a TCP stream is carried, and UDP associate
  (command 0x03) is refused with why; it makes no connection. With --forwarder,
  the section of the forwarders has the line for each wss:// one, whose road
  keeps the upgrade of HTTP/1.1.

  The line ech, in the section relay, after http2, says what Encrypted Client
  Hello did for the same host. It reads the connection of its /health, with no
  connection of its own: off, as by default (PODSSH_ECH, or ECH in the settings
  file, asks for it); the name went sealed, and whether with the retry configs
  that the server sent; or why its hello named it: the name publishes no list
  in its HTTPS record, or the read of the record failed. Or the server refused
  the sealed hello, or one was refused within the last 5 minutes. The line is
  ok, a fact, as a plain hello reaches the host as before; ???? when no
  connection to the host was made; FAIL when PODSSH_ECH=strict sent no plain
  hello.

  --stream URL checks this host, then what the path to URL does to a stream,
  and nothing else, one connection at a time: URL is https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
  (TLS checked with doctor's trust) or http://..., through HTTPS_PROXY as each
  road dials. The probes are under PATH, /v1/probe by default, where podssh
  relay serve serves them, and a quick tunnel of podssh node --relay;
  go-httpbin serves the same paths under its prefix /v1/probe. The section
  stream gives: stream server, the server's own limits, from limits.probe of
  its /relays.json. What is met below them is then the path's (behind a quick
  tunnel's node, the node's: a body taken whole, 32 KiB at most, and an answer
  quiet for 60 s ended); response, 5 bytes sent over 2 s, which come as they
  are sent or at once after the last, held until the end; request body, 4
  pieces of 1 KiB half a second apart, which the server says came over 1.5 s or
  at once; body cap, bodies from 64 KiB, twice as big each time up to 8 MiB or
  the server's own cap, until one does not pass. It gives the sizes between
  which the cap lies and the status that refused it; quiet stream, a response
  whose second byte comes --stream-idle SECONDS after its first (130 by
  default, 1 to 600), and when and how it ended. Where a size or a time is the
  documented default of a product, the line says that it looks like it, never
  that it is. The defaults are nginx's client_max_body_size of 1 MiB and
  proxy_read_timeout of 60 s, and an AWS Application Load Balancer's 60 s. They
  are also Cloudflare's 125 s, a Google Cloud load balancer's 30 s, and
  Heroku's 30 s. A path that holds a stream is ok: podssh works with it; a
  server that cannot be reached is FAIL, and a probe that it does not serve
  ????. With --full, the same section runs among the others at the relay that
  you named (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost). It does not run with
  --quick, which wins: --quick --full runs the login to github.com and no
  stream probe. At the default relay, which serves no probe, it holds a socket
  of its reverse road alone. The socket is for a pair made for the check and
  stopped after it, and is held quiet after the relay's hello; an end before
  the hold is the path's, or the relay's own drop of a node's socket. With
  --json, each probe's line has its numbers in samples: the times in ms, the
  sizes in bytes, the status. For a server over TLS, the body cap and the quiet
  stream are kept in the cache for the HTTP road to that host (HOST:PORT): its
  batches up are then half the first body that did not pass. Its wait down is
  two thirds of the quiet end that the path made, never more than the road's
  own; a quiet end at the server's own limit is not the path's, and is not
  kept.

  The section carriers asks each public carrier that the roads of a node try
  unasked. It makes one connection through the proxy each, one after another,
  carrying nothing of yours: the transit relay of PODSSH_TRANSIT (Least
  Authority's by default), whose WebSocket opens and closes with no line said,
  so it pairs nothing; each mailbox of PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX (magic-wormhole's
  and Least Authority's by default), which says its welcome and is bound to
  podssh's application, no nameplate claimed; and the Piping Server of
  PODSSH_PIPING (ppng.io, then piping.onrender.com, by default), each asked its
  /version; and croc's bridge of PODSSH_CROC (getcroc.com's by default, a third
  party's, which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns off too). Its WebSocket to its
  first relay opens and closes with no frame, so it joins no room. A variable's
  no asks none of its carrier, ????; a value that its road refuses is a FAIL.
  The Wisp demo server is a forwarder, which the line fallback names. The
  section net says the net held, read with no connection (FAIL for a file that
  does not read, or a net that ended). Then it asks /health of each member with
  the role relay, at most 8. It asks at the host that the net's document names
  for it, as the relay section asks the relay hosts; a member relay that the
  document names no host for is ????. With PODSSH_OFFLINE, the net's line
  comes, and no member relay is asked.

  POLICY: with --hop HOST, --policy FILE judges the hop's algorithms by an
  algorithm policy. One more connection runs the handshake to the hop's host
  key, and ends there. The file and the verdict are those of podssh ssh
  --policy. The line hop policy is ok with the policy's name on a pass. It is
  FAIL on a mismatch, naming each one as FIELD: expected A,B, got C. A FAIL
  makes the exit 1, as each FAIL of doctor does. It is ???? with no reading, or
  with a size that one exchange cannot measure. --policy goes only with --hop
  (64). A file that cannot be used is refused before any probe (78).

  Each CONNECT, and the direct TCP check, is tried nine times over a second or
  more: its line gives the best time (the path's floor), the median and the
  95th percentile. It gives the jitter (the median change from one try to the
  next), and the loss: the tries that timed out and those that broke counted
  apart. A refusal is an answer, not a loss. A first try that timed out is not
  repeated, and no try starts that could end more than 10 s after the first
  began.

  Through a proxy, the line IP CONNECT asks for an address, the first resolver
  of DNS over HTTPS. Then it asks for TLS with that address, as each other road
  asks for a name; the line egress takes names the case: names and addresses,
  names only (a road to an address, as --direct to one, cannot leave),
  addresses only, or neither. With no proxy, the same line comes of the direct
  TCP check and of DNS over HTTPS, which reaches its resolvers by their
  addresses.

  A forward session whose upgrade fails says which of three ways. One is an
  answer other than 101, with its status and its text: the relay or a hop
  refused. One is a 101 whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept is not the one of the
  request's key: something between answered in the relay's place. One is a
  valid 101 after which the connection ends with no Close: something between
  drops the stream after the upgrade.

  podssh doctor connects to the relay hosts and, through the relay, to
  github.com. The report goes to stdout; the exit codes are in EXIT STATUS. Its
  line UDP out says whether a node's quick tunnel takes QUIC: with a proxy set
  it takes HTTP/2, as no proxy carries UDP, and nothing is sent. Its line edge
  road says, with --full, which road over TCP reaches the edge, as the node
  tries them: port 7844 directly or through the proxy, else, in a build with
  the feature warp and with a device of WARP kept, inside WARP's tunnel; doctor
  registers no device, and keeps a new key of WARP's endpoint, read from WARP's
  API, as a run of warp:// keeps it.

  With --full, the relay section adds login: podssh logs in to github.com
  through the relay as git, with an Ed25519 key made for the check and never
  written, and GitHub refuses it. That shows that the handshake, the host key
  (the one that forward identified) and the authentication path work. No pty is
  asked for: GitHub refuses the key before a channel opens. With no proxy set,
  --full (not with --quick, which wins) also sends the node's probe of UDP to
  the quick tunnel's edge, Cloudflare's. The probe is one QUIC packet that the
  edge answers with a Version Negotiation, waited for 300 ms; when it is
  answered, a QUIC handshake with the edge, as the node's QUIC makes one,
  closed at once with nothing registered: UDP out then says what answered, and
  in what time, or that the node skips QUIC and takes HTTP/2. In a build with
  the feature tor, --full bootstraps Tor as a tor:// destination does, and
  opens no stream. It goes through the proxy, its first hops on the ports of
  PODSSH_TOR_PORTS or the bridges of PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES, the network of
  PODSSH_TOR_NETWORK. The line tor says how long it took, through which
  bridges' transports, or why it failed.

  With --forwarder, PODSSH_FORWARDER or Forwarder of the settings file, the
  section forwarders gives a line for each forwarder, in order: the upgrade,
  then a session through it to github.com port 22. Its host key must be one
  that GitHub publishes, as the relay's forward line asks; a forwarder that
  closes before GitHub's bytes says its code and its reason. With none named,
  its line fallback says whether a run whose relay hosts all failed tries the
  forwarders that podssh names (see podssh ssh); it asks none of them, so it is
  ???? (unknown in --json), never ok.

  With --shadowsocks FILE, the section shadowsocks gives a line for the first
  server of FILE. When the file starts with a subscription, that is the
  subscription's first (its list fetched or kept, as a run takes it): the TCP
  through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, and the server's salt and first chunk
  with their time. Then the section opens a session through it to github.com
  port 22, whose host key must be one that GitHub publishes. A server that
  stays silent names the proxy as the likely cause when one carried the TCP,
  else the password or the method.

  With --via URL or PODSSH_VIA, the section via gives a line for that forward
  proxy over TLS: the proxy of HTTPS_PROXY that carried the TCP to it, if one
  did. It gives the version of HTTP that it chose (HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1) and the
  time of its CONNECT. Then the section opens a session through it to
  github.com port 22, whose host key must be one that GitHub publishes. A 407
  says what the proxy asks for.

  With --vless FILE, the section vless gives a line for each server of FILE.
  Where its link says auto, it gives one for each mode of XHTTP (packet-up,
  stream-up, stream-one): the proxy of HTTPS_PROXY that carried the TCP to it,
  if one did, the transport that carried the session and the time of VLESS's
  answer. Then the section opens a session through it to github.com port 22,
  whose host key must be one that GitHub publishes. A server that ends the
  session before its answer refused the ID, or could not reach the target. A
  link whose mode is stream-one says, before any connection, that HTTP/2
  carries it and HTTP/1.1 refuses it (78), and which modes pass. --early-data
  and --h2-shape act as on ssh.

  With --hysteria FILE, the section hysteria gives a line for each server of
  FILE, after the roads over TCP that the run names: whether UDP reaches its
  port, the address that answered the probe and its round trip, and the time of
  the session through it. Then the section opens a session through it to
  github.com port 22, whose host key must be one that GitHub publishes. Where
  the probe gets no answer, the line says that UDP does not pass here, with no
  wait for QUIC; a server whose host has a proxy of HTTPS_PROXY, which carries
  no UDP, is not tried, and its line says so.

  With --tuic FILE, the section tuic gives a line for each server of FILE,
  after the roads over TCP and Hysteria's: whether UDP reaches its port, and
  the time of the session through it. Then the section opens a session through
  it to github.com port 22, whose host key must be one that GitHub publishes.
  Where the probe gets no answer, the line says that UDP does not pass here,
  with no wait for QUIC.

  With --turn turns:HOST[:PORT] and --turn-auth-file FILE, the section turn
  gives a line for that TURN server, after the roads over TCP that the run
  names: its software where it says it, the allocation's relayed address,
  lifetime and time, and the time of Connect and ConnectionBind. Then the
  section opens a session through it to github.com port 22, whose host key must
  be one that GitHub publishes. Where TLS fails beside HTTPS_PROXY, the line
  says that a proxy that re-terminates TLS stops this road.

  With --devtunnel TUNNEL[:PORT], in a build with the feature devtunnel, the
  section devtunnel gives a line for that tunnel. It comes after the roads over
  TCP that the run names: the road of a devtunnel:// destination with the
  credential that podssh ssh takes, and its time. The credential is the token
  of PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE, the access token of
  PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_ACCESS_FILE, or none. The line also gives the host key of
  the SSH server at the port, or why it has none. A failure names its stage:
  setup (the token file or a setting), management, websocket, ssh, channel or
  reconnect. In another build the flag is refused (70).

  In a build with the feature gsr, the section gsr says whether TLS with SRP
  builds on both sides (gsr tls, OpenSSL's version). It makes no connection for
  that. Once PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE names the road's secret, the section makes
  one round trip of the control protocol with the relay (gsr, its time). The
  round trip goes to the shard of that secret, by a secret that nobody holds,
  so that no node is disturbed; with --full, it holds such a registration with
  the relay's pings alone for 20 s (gsr idle). That says whether a proxy on the
  way cuts a quiet tunnel before the road's keepalive. With no secret named, no
  byte goes to the relay.

  With --dns-zone ZONE, the section dns asks whether a resolver passes a TXT
  query for a zone of your own, as the DNS road needs. The resolver is
  --dns-server ADDR, else the first nameserver of /etc/resolv.conf. First a UDP
  socket is opened toward it, which sends nothing. Where the host refuses UDP,
  the line dns resolver says so, and nothing is sent. Then two queries go, each
  for a random name under ZONE, so that no cache answers. The first has an OPT
  record of EDNS0 of 1232 bytes, the second none; each waits 3 s. Each line
  gives the RCODE, the time, the size and the TC bit. It says whether the OPT
  record came back, and counts records of another type. NOERROR and NXDOMAIN
  are ok: the resolver answered for the zone. SERVFAIL, REFUSED, silence and an
  address in the answer are FAIL. A portal that answers each name itself gives
  that address. A datagram that answers another query is not taken. No HTTP
  proxy carries UDP, so the queries go straight to the resolver. Nothing is
  sent without --dns-zone. The DNS road is a last resort: slow, and plain to
  the resolver's operator.

  With --json, the report is one JSON object on stdout when every check has
  run: schema (1), podssh, os, arch, checks (each with section, check, status
  and detail; status is ok, FAIL or unknown), counts (ok, fail, unknown) and
  diagnosis (each case after the counts; empty when none). A check tried
  several times adds samples: tries, connected, best_ms, median_ms, p95_ms and
  jitter_ms (null when no try connected), timed_out, broke, refused, and ms,
  the time of each try that connected. The details are the text's, the exit
  code is the same, and nothing is printed before the object.

  Usage: podssh doctor [OPTIONS]

  Options:
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to check, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env PODSSH_RELAY,
        else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the next starts after 2 s or
        a failure; the default), parallel or serial; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE (default: env SSL_CERT_FILE,
        else system and built-in roots).
    --cover NAME
        check the delegated credential of a cover relay's NAME in place of the
        relay's own checks. A token at POST /v1/delegate is answered with the
        chain, issuer, window, subject key and TLS exporter. Another issuer, a
        lapsed window and another exporter are each refused by name; /health
        and the documents are off the public listener under a cover.
    --json
        write the report as one JSON object on stdout, when every check has
        run.
    --full
        also log in to github.com through the relay with a key made for the
        check, which GitHub refuses; and, with no proxy set, make a QUIC
        handshake with the quick tunnel's edge; with --quick, which wins, the
        handshake and the stream probes do not run.
    --hop [USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        check only this host and a first hop of -J as --direct reaches it: the
        connection through HTTPS_PROXY with the server's banner, its host key,
        and the methods that it offers to a key made for the check.
    --policy FILE
        with --hop, judge the hop's KEXINIT by the algorithm policy in FILE,
        with no login; the line hop policy gives the verdict.
    --quick
        check this host, the egress and the relay alone, with the roads that
        the run names (--forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via, --vless); a line
        names the sections that it left out; it leaves out what --full adds
        besides the login to github.com: the QUIC handshake and the stream
        probes.
    --tier
        check this host alone and give one verdict of its capabilities:
        identity (a user name, the capability to bind a low port); exec (a
        directory that runs a program); terminal (a pty); state (a directory
        that keeps files); and resolver (how names resolve); each ok, closed or
        ????; and for each closed one the features that it closes; reads the
        capability sets and drops nothing; connects nowhere but for one lookup
        of the relay's name.
    --jobs N
        run at most N sections at once, 1 to 64, in the order of the report
        (default: each at once; also DoctorJobs of the settings file); --jobs 1
        runs one after another.
    --stream URL
        check this host and what the path to URL does to a stream, alone:
        whether a response and a request's body pass as they come, the largest
        body that passes, and how long a quiet stream lives; URL is
        https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH] or http://..., a server of podssh relay
        serve, the quick tunnel of podssh node --relay, or go-httpbin; its
        probes under PATH (default /v1/probe).
    --stream-idle SECONDS
        how long the probe of a quiet stream holds it, 1 to 600 (default 130),
        with --stream; or with --full, which probes a stream at the relay that
        you named, or a quiet socket at the default relay.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        also check these forwarders, templates or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp: the upgrade, then one of GitHub's published host keys
        on github.com port 22 through each (default: env PODSSH_FORWARDER, else
        Forwarder of the settings file).
    --shadowsocks FILE
        also check the first Shadowsocks server of FILE: TCP, the server's
        salt, then one of GitHub's published host keys on github.com port 22
        through it.
    --vless FILE
        also check each VLESS server of FILE, on each mode of XHTTP where its
        link says auto: the transport that carried it, then one of GitHub's
        published host keys on github.com port 22 through it.
    --early-data WORD
        the VLESS road's early data: 0rtt, 1rtt or off (default: env
        PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA, else off); a nonce repeated inside ten minutes
        is a replay, and the session continues at 1-RTT on the same connection.
    --h2-shape WORD
        the shape of the HTTP/2 road that podssh builds: existing (the
        default), browser or firefox (default: env PODSSH_H2_SHAPE); SETTINGS
        and their order and the connection's window are sent, while PRIORITY
        frames and padded DATA are recorded and not sent through h2 0.4. The
        default session road is the WebSocket upgrade of HTTP/1.1 and does not
        read it.
    --trojan
        state what podssh's Trojan road carries: the TCP stream to a target,
        and UDP associate, refused by name with why; no connection is made.
    --hysteria FILE
        also check each Hysteria 2 server of FILE: whether UDP reaches its
        port, and its round trip, then one of GitHub's published host keys on
        github.com port 22 through it.
    --tuic FILE
        also check each TUIC server of FILE: whether UDP reaches its port, then
        one of GitHub's published host keys on github.com port 22 through it.
    --dns-zone ZONE
        also ask a resolver whether a TXT query under ZONE, a zone of your own,
        gets through, as --carrier dns:FILE needs. After a probe that UDP
        opens, two queries of 3 s each go; each line gives the RCODE, the time
        and the size.
    --dns-server ADDR
        the resolver that --dns-zone asks: IP, IP:PORT or [IPv6]:PORT (default:
        the first nameserver of /etc/resolv.conf).
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        also check this forward proxy over TLS: TLS to it, the version of HTTP
        that it chose, then one of GitHub's published host keys on github.com
        port 22 through its CONNECT (default: env PODSSH_VIA).
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        also check this TURN server: its software, the TCP allocation and its
        time, the Connect, then one of GitHub's published host keys on
        github.com port 22 through it (with --turn-auth-file).
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --devtunnel TUNNEL
        also check TUNNEL[:PORT] of Microsoft Dev Tunnels (a name, or
        ID.CLUSTER; port 22 by default) with the token of
        PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE, the access token of
        PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_ACCESS_FILE, or none: the management API, the relay's
        WebSocket, its SSH and a channel to the port, whose first bytes it
        reads; a failure names its stage; in a build with the feature
        devtunnel.
    --exit NAME
        also check the exit NAME of your net: what the net held says of it and
        of this client, the pair kept under NAME; and one session from it to
        --exit-target, with the node's verdict and whose a refusal is; NAME
        auto: the exit whose route of the net holds --exit-target's address.
    --exit-target HOST:PORT
        the target of the session from --exit NAME (default github.com:22,
        identified by its published host key).
    --client-key FILE
        the key of this client for --exit NAME (default: client.key in the
        cache, as podssh proxy --exit takes it).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    what works on this host, one line for each check
        $ podssh doctor

podssh keygen
  make an SSH key pair, or print a key's public key or fingerprint.

  The keys are in the formats of OpenSSH. The private key has mode 0600, as the
  keys of OpenSSH have. On Windows it has an access list of its own that lets
  in only the user, SYSTEM and the Administrators, as OpenSSH's keys do; a new
  key never replaces a file that exists. The public key goes to FILE.pub, which
  others may read and not change. podssh prints the SHA-256 fingerprint.

  podssh keygen -p -f FILE changes the passphrase of a key: podssh asks for the
  old one, then for the new one two times. podssh keygen -c -f FILE changes its
  comment, to -C COMMENT or to one that podssh asks for, in the key and in
  FILE.pub. The file is replaced only with the same key, read back and compared
  first, and no copy of the old file is kept. A key in another format that
  podssh ssh -i reads is written in the format of OpenSSH. -P '' is for a key
  with no passphrase; a passphrase given with -P is refused.

  podssh keygen -F HOST prints the lines of HOST in known_hosts (-f FILE, else
  ~/.ssh/known_hosts), as ssh-keygen does. -R HOST removes them, and -H hashes
  each host name; a host on another port is [HOST]:PORT. -R and -H keep the old
  text as FILE.old, and the new text takes the file's place whole, with its
  mode. -R keeps a line that names the host through a wildcard, as its key is
  for other hosts too.

  podssh keygen -Y sign -f KEY -n NAMESPACE FILE signs FILE to FILE.sig, or
  standard input to standard output. This is as ssh-keygen -Y sign does for
  git; the agent signs when it holds the key of KEY (-U: the agent alone). -Y
  verify -f SIGNERS -I PRINCIPAL -n NAMESPACE -s FILE.sig checks the data on
  standard input against SIGNERS, an allowed-signers file. It says Good or
  Could not verify signature. (exit 1). -Y check-novalidate, find-principals
  and match-principals are those of ssh-keygen. A signature never replaces a
  file.

  podssh keygen -Y sign -f KEY-cert.pub signs with that certificate and the
  private key KEY (or the agent's), as ssh-keygen does; -f KEY signs with the
  plain key even with KEY-cert.pub beside it. A cert-authority line of SIGNERS
  allows such a signature when its key is the certificate's CA. The certificate
  must be a user certificate, valid at the time, that lists the principal of
  -I; a plain line of the key does not allow it.

  podssh keygen -s CA -I ID [-n NAMES] [-V INTERVAL] [-z SERIAL] [-O OPTION]
  [-h] FILE.pub certifies each key into FILE-cert.pub. This is as ssh-keygen -s
  does, and -U says that the CA is in the agent. podssh keygen -L -f FILE
  prints a certificate. -V here is a validity, such as +52w or
  20260101:20270101; the version is podssh -V. A certificate replaces the one
  that is there, as OpenSSH's does, and keeps its mode; a new one is 0644, as a
  certificate is public.

  podssh keygen -e -m FORMAT -f FILE prints the public key of FILE as RFC4716
  (the default), PKCS8 or PEM; -i -m FORMAT -f FILE prints such a key as a line
  of OpenSSH. -m PEM or PKCS8 with a new key or -p writes the private key in
  that format. An Ed25519 key has a form of RFC4716 only. -y and -l read a key
  in each format that podssh ssh -i reads. -l on a private key shows the
  comment of FILE.pub, when that is the same key, as ssh-keygen -l does: a key
  with a passphrase keeps its comment encrypted.

  podssh keygen -t ed25519-sk or -t ecdsa-sk makes a key in a security key
  (FIDO2), as ssh-keygen does: the device keeps the key, and the file holds the
  device's handle of it, in the format of OpenSSH. Each signature needs a touch
  of the device, within 30 s. -O resident keeps the key in the device, -O
  verify-required asks the device's PIN at each use, and -O no-touch-required
  signs with no touch. -O application=ssh:NAME and -O user=NAME name the key.
  On Linux podssh reaches the device through /dev/hidraw (-O device=PATH names
  one); on Windows, Windows shows its own dialog. With no device that podssh
  may reach, it says why, asks nothing and writes nothing (exit 1).
  PODSSH_SK_DEVICE set to none turns security keys off.

  podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm makes an ECDSA P-256 key in this machine's TPM
  2.0. The key never leaves the TPM, and a copy of its file is useless in
  another TPM. The key is sealed to PCRs of the SHA-256 bank: PCR 7 by default,
  the state of Secure Boot, or the list of -O pcr=LIST. The TPM signs with it
  only while those PCRs hold the values that they held when the key was made.
  After a boot that measured something else, the TPM refuses the key, and
  podssh ssh -i says so and tries the next key. The key has no passphrase: the
  TPM takes its policy and no password. The file is a TSS2 PRIVATE KEY, as
  openssl_tpm2_engine and ssh-tpm-agent read it. podssh reaches the TPM through
  /dev/tpmrm0 (-O device=PATH or PODSSH_TPM_DEVICE names another). On Windows
  it reaches the TPM through the TPM Base Services. Where the owner's hierarchy
  has a password, as Windows sets it, the key is made under the storage key
  that the TPM keeps (0x81000001). With no TPM that podssh may reach, as in a
  container or a sandbox, it says why and writes nothing (exit 69). Before the
  file is written, the new key signs once and the signature is checked. -y and
  -l read the public key from the file.

  podssh asks for the passphrase two times, on the terminal or through
  SSH_ASKPASS. -N '' makes a key with no passphrase. A passphrase given with -N
  is refused, because each process on the host can read a command line. With no
  terminal and no SSH_ASKPASS, podssh stops at once and names -N ''.

  DSA keys are refused: OpenSSH 10 removed them. The default comment is
  USER@HOST, with the local user's name as podssh ssh takes it: PODSSH_USER,
  USER, LOGNAME or USERNAME, else the user database's entry (see ENVIRONMENT).

  A key sealed to a TPM can also take signed boot states, so that a firmware's
  update needs no new key. podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O policy-key=FILE makes
  such a key. It signs in each boot state that the ECDSA P-256 key of FILE
  signed, and its file holds the first: the state of now. After an update that
  moved the PCRs, podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O add-policy -O policy-key=FILE
  -f KEY signs the state of now into KEY. The key then signs again, and -C
  names the new policy. Sign a new state only once you know why it changed: the
  key then signs in it, a tampered one too. Keep the policy key off the host,
  as whoever reads it can sign any boot state. A login tries the signed
  policies of the file, the newest first.

  -V here is the validity of a certificate, with -s. podssh -V prints the
  version.

  -n, -s, -I, -O and -U mean one thing with -Y and another with -s, as in
  ssh-keygen.

  Other names: podssh ssh-keygen

  Usage: podssh keygen [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [FILE]...
        with -Y sign: the files to sign, each to FILE.sig; with none, standard
        input to standard output.

  Options:
    -t, --type TYPE
        key type: ed25519 (the default), ecdsa or rsa; ed25519-sk or ecdsa-sk,
        a key of a security key (FIDO2); ecdsa-tpm, a key sealed to this
        machine's TPM 2.0; with -s, the signature of an RSA CA: rsa-sha2-512
        (the default) or rsa-sha2-256.
    -b, --bits BITS
        key size: ecdsa 256 (the default), 384 or 521; rsa 2048, 3072 (the
        default), 4096 or 8192.
    -f, --file FILE
        the private key's file; the public key goes to FILE.pub (default
        ~/.ssh/id_TYPE); with -Y sign the key that signs, or its certificate
        KEY-cert.pub; with -Y verify, find-principals and match-principals the
        allowed-signers file.
    -N, --new-passphrase PHRASE
        -N '' for a key with no passphrase; without -N, podssh asks (terminal
        or SSH_ASKPASS).
    -P, --old-passphrase PHRASE
        with -p or -c: -P '' for a key with no passphrase; without -P, podssh
        asks for the old one.
    -p, --change-passphrase
        change the passphrase of the key in -f FILE: the old one is asked, then
        the new one two times.
    -c, --change-comment
        change the comment of the key in -f FILE to -C COMMENT, or to one that
        podssh asks for.
    -C, --comment COMMENT
        the key's comment (default USER@HOST).
    -q, --quiet
        print nothing but errors.
    -y, --print-public
        print the public key of the private key in -f FILE; podssh's own key
        file (client.key, node.key) gives the line that --grant-to and an
        allowlist take.
    -l, --fingerprint
        print the fingerprint of the key in -f FILE, its private file or its
        .pub.
    -F, --find-host HOST
        print the lines of HOST ([HOST]:PORT for another port) in known_hosts:
        -f FILE, else ~/.ssh/known_hosts.
    -R, --remove-host HOST
        remove the keys of HOST from known_hosts; the old text stays in
        FILE.old.
    -H, --hash-hosts
        hash each host name of known_hosts; with -F, print the lines hashed.
    -Y, --signature OP
        SSH signatures: sign, verify, check-novalidate, find-principals or
        match-principals.
    -n, --namespace NAME
        with -Y: the namespace of the signature, such as git or file; with -s:
        the principals of the certificate, NAME[,NAME...].
    -s, --signature-file FILE
        with -Y verify, check-novalidate and find-principals: the signature;
        without -Y: the CA's key, which signs each FILE (a public key) to
        FILE-cert.pub.
    -I, --identity ID
        with -s: the key id of the certificate; with -Y verify and
        match-principals: the principal to look for in the allowed signers.
    -O, --option OPTION
        with -Y: hashalg=sha256 or sha512 (sign), verify-time=TIME and
        print-pubkey (verify); with -s: clear, permit-*, no-*,
        force-command=CMD, source-address=LIST, verify-required,
        extension:NAME[=VALUE], critical:NAME[=VALUE]; with -t ed25519-sk or
        ecdsa-sk: resident, application=ssh:NAME, user=NAME, no-touch-required,
        verify-required, device=PATH; with -t ecdsa-tpm: pcr=LIST (7 by
        default), device=PATH, policy-key=FILE (a key kept off the host) and
        add-policy (the boot state of now, signed into -f's file).
    -U, --agent-key
        the key is in the agent (SSH_AUTH_SOCK), which signs: the key of -f
        with -Y sign, the CA's with -s; the file may hold the public key.
    -V, --validity INTERVAL
        with -s: the validity of the certificate: +52w, or FROM:TO of +TIME,
        -TIME, YYYYMMDD[HHMM[SS]][Z], always and forever (podssh -V prints the
        version).
    -z, --serial SERIAL
        with -s: the serial of the certificate, 0 to 2^64-1.
    -h, --host-certificate
        with -s: a host certificate, not a user certificate.
    -L, --print-certificate
        print the certificate in -f FILE.
    -e, --export
        print the public key of -f FILE in the format of -m: RFC4716 (the
        default), PKCS8 or PEM.
    -i, --import
        print the public key in -f FILE, in the format of -m (RFC4716 by
        default), as a line of OpenSSH.
    -m, --format FORMAT
        RFC4716, PKCS8 or PEM: with -e and -i, the format of the public key;
        with a new key or -p, of the private key.
    -D, --pkcs11 PROVIDER
        podssh reads no PKCS#11 token. Refused.
    -r, --revocation-list FILE
        podssh reads no key revocation list yet. Refused.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    make a key where ssh-keygen does not work
        $ podssh keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

    a key with no passphrase, for a script
        $ podssh keygen -N '' -f ./deploy_key

    the public key of a private key
        $ podssh keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

    the fingerprint of a key
        $ podssh keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

    a key that signs only in this machine's TPM, while Secure Boot is as it is
    now
        $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O pcr=7 -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

    such a key that also signs in each boot state that a key kept off the host
    signs
        $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O policy-key=/mnt/usb/policy_key -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

    after a firmware's update, sign the new boot state into that key, so that
    it signs again
        $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O add-policy -O policy-key=/mnt/usb/policy_key -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

podssh ts
  the tailnet node and byte pipe, over DERP (not in this build).

  Other names: podssh tailscale

  Only a build with the feature ts has this command: a release build leaves the
  Tailscale adapter out. Each other build exits 70.

  Usage: podssh ts [OPTIONS]

  Options:
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh agent
  an SSH agent inside podssh, and add, list, remove and lock its keys.

  podssh agent serves the agent protocol on a socket of mode 0600, in a new
  directory of mode 0700 of XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or the temporary directory. On
  Windows it serves a named pipe of this user. It serves until SIGINT, SIGTERM
  or SIGHUP, which remove the socket and its directory. It stays in the
  foreground: start it with &. It prints the lines of SSH_AUTH_SOCK and of its
  pid, as ssh-agent -s does. A client of another user is closed. PODSSH_LISTEN
  set to no refuses it (exit 78).

  add FILE (with -t SECONDS for a lifetime), list, remove FILE or --all, lock
  and unlock talk to the agent of SSH_AUTH_SOCK, as ssh-add does. That agent is
  podssh's or OpenSSH's; a passphrase or a password is asked on the terminal or
  through SSH_ASKPASS. Keys live in the agent's memory only. A key that asks
  for a confirmation of each use is never used. list writes the size, the
  fingerprint and the type of each key, and exits 1 when there is none.

  The agent holds a key of a security key (ED25519-SK, ECDSA-SK) that add gives
  it, as ssh-add gives one. It signs with it in the device: it asks for the
  touch on its own stderr. It asks a PIN only through SSH_ASKPASS with
  SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE set to force, as it runs in the background. With no
  device, it refuses the signature and says why.

  The agent holds a key sealed to a TPM (podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm) that add
  gives it. add sends it as ssh-tpm-agent's ssh-tpm-add does, so only podssh
  agent and ssh-tpm-agent keep it. The agent keeps the key file, never a
  private key, and keeps it only once the key signed in the TPM. It signs in
  the TPM. With no TPM, or after the boot state changed, it refuses and says
  why on its stderr.

  add-password [USER@]HOST[:PORT] and add-passphrase FILE (with -t SECONDS for
  a lifetime) give podssh's agent a server's password or a key file's
  passphrase. It comes from stdin when stdin is no terminal, else from the
  terminal or SSH_ASKPASS, never from the command line; a passphrase must open
  its file. The agent keeps each in its memory only, and tells it only to its
  own user. podssh ssh asks the agent of SSH_AUTH_SOCK before each prompt for a
  password, a passphrase or a password of keyboard-interactive, also with
  BatchMode. The agent forgets one that a server refuses; -v names where a
  secret came from, never its value. podssh doctor says how many the agent
  keeps, never which. A locked agent tells none.

  Other names: podssh ssh-agent

  Usage: podssh agent [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        add, add-password, add-passphrase, list, remove, lock or unlock; with
        none, the agent serves.
    [FILE]...
        the key files of add, add-passphrase and remove; [USER@]HOST[:PORT] for
        add-password.

  Options:
    --socket PATH
        serve on PATH, a socket of mode 0600, or \\.\pipe\NAME on Windows
        (default: a new directory of mode 0700 in XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or the
        temporary directory).
    -t, --lifetime SECONDS
        add, add-password and add-passphrase: the key or the secret leaves the
        agent after SECONDS.
    --all
        remove: each key of the agent.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh ping
  a short check of the path: each step to the relay, pings, and with a host the
  echo and throughput; with node://NAME, each of its roads and the one that
  answered first; with --nodes or --net, those of each node.

  With no destination, podssh ping measures the relay leg of each relay host,
  one after the other: the token (from PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN, cached or minted),
  DNS and TCP or CONNECT through the proxy, TLS, and the WebSocket upgrade,
  each with its time. The relay answers the upgrade once it reached the target;
  then --count WebSocket pings, each with its send time in its payload and
  matched to its pong. They give the minimum, p50, p95 and maximum in
  milliseconds, and the pings that had no pong in time. The target is --target,
  else github.com port 22, which podssh doctor reaches too; never the
  destination, whose server would see a connection that sends no SSH bytes:
  OpenSSH's PerSourcePenalties count those against the relay's address, which
  other users share. --direct with no destination is refused (64): it has no
  relay leg to measure, and no host.

  With a destination, the run is resolved as podssh ssh resolves it
  (ssh_config, -J, -i, --direct). The relay leg is followed by the time to log
  in. Then comes the echo of one byte at a time through cat, --count times. One
  echo before them is not counted, as the first can wait for cat to start. Then
  comes the throughput down and up of --size bytes, which stay under the
  relay's limit of one session in both ways together. Down reads what head
  writes from /dev/zero, and up writes into cat > /dev/null; each line names
  the remote command that ran. These programs are an assumption about the host,
  so they run only for a destination. A program that the host lacks ends the
  run with its status, never with a hang: each step and the whole run have a
  limit. A destination that cannot be reached or logged in to ends the run with
  255, as podssh ssh ends. Its line on stdout says why, or that each try is
  said on stderr.

  podssh ping can take node://NAME, or the name alone of a member of the net
  with the role node. It then measures the roads that podssh ssh races to that
  node, as tailscale ping names the path that answered: in the order of the
  race and with its delays, each road that starts runs on to the far end's
  first bytes. A line for each says its time and when it started into the race,
  why it failed, or that it did not start. A fallback starts only when each
  road before it failed; the last line names the road that answered first, with
  its time from the start of the race. Each road that starts opens its one
  connection, as a race of podssh ssh does. Each link ends before a byte is
  sent on it. So the node opens no session and dials nothing at its TARGET, and
  nothing logs in. The exit is 0 when a road answered and 69 when none did;
  --size, --count and --target are a host's, and refused with a node (64).
  --json gives node beside schema, podssh, relays, empty, destination, null,
  and exit. node has name, roads, each with road, started, started_ms, ms,
  answered and error, then won and won_ms. The road that answered, or the race
  that found none, is what podssh status --net says of the node. With
  --under-load or --connect-runs, a node is measured as a host is, through the
  road that podssh ssh takes to it, and logged in to.

  A list of nodes. --nodes NAME,NAME,... measures the roads of each node of the
  list, and --net those of each member of the net held with the role node. Each
  node is measured as podssh ping node://NAME measures it, so a monitor of a
  fleet reads one shape. At most --parallel nodes are measured at once, 8 by
  default and 64 at most. Each node has the bound of --timeout, else
  PODSSH_TIMEOUT, else 60 s; the whole run has its own limit. A node that does
  not answer delays no other node past its bound. The lines of each node come
  in the order of the list, then how many nodes answered. With --json, one
  object holds schema, podssh, nodes and exit. Each node has name, roads, won
  and won_ms, as node of a single node, then code and error. The code of a node
  is 0 when a road answered, 69 when none did, and 75 past its bound; a refusal
  of the node keeps its own code. The exit is 0 when each node answered, 1 when
  some did not, and 69 when none did. A destination, --size, --count, --target,
  --under-load and --connect-runs are refused with a list (64). So are
  --parallel and --timeout with no list. --net with no net held, or with no
  member of the role node, is refused (78).

  What a user feels. --under-load measures the echo of keys typed as a user
  types them, 40 keys 150 ms apart. Each key is sent at its time whether or not
  the one before came back, through cat: first idle, then beside head -c
  62914560 /dev/zero, a download of 60 MiB on a second channel of the same
  connection. The keys under load start once it ran for 3 s, so that the path's
  queue is full when the first key goes. The download stops once the last key
  came back; a key whose echo came after it ended is not counted beside it. A
  download that ended within its 3 s is said, with no figure. The lines give
  the echo idle and under load (minimum, p50, p95 and maximum) and the
  download's rate while the keys ran. It replaces the echo, down and up, so
  --count and --size are refused with it (64). The plain measures beside the
  download would pass the relay's 64 MiB for one session.

  --connect-runs N (1 to 20) comes first: N cold connects, one after the other,
  each a connection of its own, the login, and true run to its exit status.
  Each is timed from the start of its own connection; the destination is
  resolved once before them. A run that fails ends the measures, with the code
  that podssh ssh would give. Both measure through a host, and are refused with
  none (64). --under-load opens no connection beside the run's own;
  --connect-runs opens one at a time, each closed before the next.

  With --json, the run writes one JSON object on stdout when it ends, and
  nothing before it: schema (1), podssh, count, size, relays (each with host,
  target, token, token_ms, connect, connect_ms, tls_ms, upgrade_ms; pings with
  min_ms, p50_ms, p95_ms and max_ms; pings_lost and error), destination
  (destination, login_ms; echo with samples_ms, the raw time of each echo;
  connect with runs, command, its summary and samples_ms; under_load with keys,
  gap_ms, warmup_ms, idle and loaded, each with its summary and samples, each
  with sent_ms, from the download's start under load, and echo_ms; and beside
  under load, and load with command, bytes, typing_bytes, typing_seconds and
  ended_ms; down and up with command, seconds and bytes or error, and error)
  and exit. The exit codes are in EXIT STATUS.

  Usage: podssh ping [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host]
        a host for the login, echo and throughput, or node://NAME for its
        roads; none: the relay leg.

  Options:
    -p, --port PORT
        the destination's port.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -4, --ipv4-only
        use IPv4 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=4.
    -6, --ipv6-only
        use IPv6 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=6.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to measure, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env PODSSH_RELAY,
        else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR.
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --target HOST:PORT
        where the relay leg goes (default github.com:22, which podssh doctor
        reaches too; never the destination).
    --direct
        reach the destination without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when
        one is set.
    --size SIZE
        bytes each way for the throughput, with K, M or G (default 8M, at most
        30M: both ways stay under the relay's 64 MiB).
    --count N
        pings of each relay host, and echoes through the destination (default
        10, at most 100).
    --under-load
        with a host, in place of the echo and throughput: 40 keys 150 ms apart
        through cat, idle, then after 3 s of a download (head -c) beside them
        on the same connection.
    --connect-runs N
        with a host, first: N cold connects, each timed from its own connection
        to the exit of true (at most 20).
    --json
        the measures as one JSON object on stdout.
    --nodes NAMES
        in place of a destination, the roads of each node of NAME[,NAME...],
        each as ping node://NAME measures it.
    --net
        in place of a destination, the roads of each member of the net held
        with the role node.
    --parallel N
        with --nodes or --net, the most nodes measured at once (default 8, at
        most 64).
    --timeout DURATION
        with --nodes or --net, the bound of each node, as a duration (30s, 2m),
        10m at most; never required (default: env PODSSH_TIMEOUT, else 60s).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    how good the path is: each step to each relay host, and the round trip of
    WebSocket pings
        $ podssh ping

    and through a host: the login, the echo through cat, and 8 MiB down and up
        $ podssh ping user@example.org

podssh health
  the far host's load, CPUs, memory, uptime, network, disks and processes, read
  over one exec.

  podssh health logs in to one host as podssh ssh does (the relay or --direct,
  ssh_config, -J, -i). It runs one command there that only reads: a fixed
  script, as sh -c, so that a login shell of fish or csh only starts sh. No
  text of yours goes into it. It reads the files loadavg, uptime, meminfo, stat
  and net/dev of /proc with the read of the shell, and counts the processes. It
  reads the cgroup of its own shell (/proc/self/cgroup, then the files of that
  cgroup under /sys/fs/cgroup, each only where it can be read). It runs sleep,
  df and uname only where command -v finds them.

  One line for each fact: the load of 1, 5 and 15 minutes and the CPUs; the
  busy share of the CPUs over one second; the memory available and the swap
  used. The memory available is MemAvailable of the kernel, else an estimate
  from the free memory, the buffers and the cache, which the line names; the
  uptime; for each network interface but the loopback, the bytes in and out
  since the start and over one second; the use of the file system of the root
  and of the home, from df; the processes. A host with no sleep gives no rate
  and no busy share; one with no df, no disk.

  CONTAINERS: /proc gives the whole host's CPUs, memory and load, also inside a
  container. Where the cgroup of the far shell limits them, under cgroup v2 or
  v1, health gives the cgroup's beside the host's: cpus N (SOURCE), M on the
  host. N is the least of the quota over its period (cpu.max, or
  cpu.cfs_quota_us of v1), the CPUs of the effective cpuset, and the host's;
  the memory available of the limit (memory.max, or memory.limit_in_bytes of
  v1), then the host's. The first is the limit less the working set, never more
  than the host's MemAvailable. The working set is the use less the inactive
  file cache, as docker stats counts it; and the load line says that it is the
  whole host's. A limit of a parent cgroup binds as the cgroup's own does. The
  cgroup's share of its CPUs over the second, the periods in which it was
  throttled, its pressure (PSI: the share of the last 10 s that its tasks
  waited), and an io.max or a pids.max that limits get their lines too. A
  cgroup with no limit, a limit at or above the host's (LXCFS), or a host that
  hides /sys/fs/cgroup gives the host's facts, as before.

  A host with no /proc gives the name that uname prints, and no facts for this
  system, with exit 0. A host with no sh, a login that fails, and an answer
  with none of the script's lines give exit 255, as podssh ssh does. A name
  that the host gives (an interface, a mount) has the controls of a terminal
  taken out.

  With --json, one JSON object on stdout, also after a failure: schema (1),
  podssh, destination, system (for a host with no /proc), load, cpus, the busy
  percent and the seconds between the samples. Then memory (in KiB, and whether
  the available memory is an estimate), and the uptime in seconds. Then network
  (each interface, its bytes and its bytes in a second) and disks (each mount,
  its file system and its KiB). It ends with processes, error and exit. Each of
  these is the host's. effective holds the facts to plan from, on any host:
  cpus (a number, as 4.0 or 1.5), cpus_from, memory_total_kib,
  memory_available_kib, memory_from, and the cgroup's cpu_used,
  cpu_busy_percent, throttled_periods and periods. cpus_from is cgroup v2
  cpu.max, cgroup v2 cpu.max of a parent, cgroup v2 cpuset, cgroup v1
  cfs_quota_us, cgroup v1 cpuset or host. cgroup, where one was read, holds its
  version, its path, and each value as it was read.

  PREFLIGHT: with --preflight, after the facts, the same login asks what the
  server allows of what a long command needs later. Each probe takes 10 s at
  most, and the lines are as podssh doctor gives them: ok, FAIL or ????, a
  name, and what came. login: the user, the hops of -J, the method that let the
  user in, and the server's version line. road: the relay's limits on a
  session, or none with --direct. In the resumable layer, a limit ends a link,
  and the session goes on a new one. The limits are 64 MiB both ways, 180 s
  with no payload and 12 h, from its /relays.json where one was read. sftp: the
  subsystem, its sizes and its extensions, and what podssh cp does without
  copy-data, posix-rename@openssh.com, hardlink@openssh.com and
  limits@openssh.com; no subsystem is ok, as podssh cp then copies by exec.
  remote forward: a tcpip-forward on the server's loopback, on a port that the
  server chooses, then its cancel at once; a refusal, or no answer, is FAIL, as
  -R cannot work there. jump: a direct-tcpip channel to the server's own
  loopback, port 22, closed at once; one that opens, or one refused as connect
  failed, is ok; administratively prohibited, an unknown channel type, or no
  answer is FAIL, as -J, -L, -D and -W through that host cannot work.

  exec tools: one exec of sh names each tool on PATH that the copy by exec,
  podssh job, podssh cp --delta and podssh ping use; a missing cat, mv, rm,
  mkdir, sleep or wc is FAIL, and each other missing tool is named with what it
  stops. A host whose login runs no sh fails it. tmux: from the same exec; a
  missing tmux is FAIL, with what could install it, as podssh job names it, and
  podssh job --no-tmux. cgroup: the CPUs and the memory to plan from, from the
  facts. keepalive, last: one keepalive@openssh.com with a reply wanted; a
  reply, a success or a failure, is ok; no reply, or a connection that ends at
  it, is FAIL, and -o ServerAliveInterval=0 is the way round it. Nothing that a
  probe asks stays: the forward is cancelled, and the channel and the SFTP
  session are closed, at once.

  With --preflight, once the login is done, the exit is that of podssh doctor:
  1 when a check failed or the facts did not come, else 0. A login that fails
  is 255, as without it, and its line is FAIL. With --json, preflight holds
  checks, each with section, check, status and detail as podssh doctor --json
  gives them, and counts (ok, fail and unknown); without --preflight it is
  null.

  POLICY: with --policy FILE, podssh health gives no facts. It reaches the host
  as podssh ssh does, and runs the handshake to the server's host key. There
  the policy judges the server's algorithms, and the connection ends. Nothing
  is sent to log in to the destination, so no key or password is needed, and
  known_hosts is not read. The file and the verdict are those of podssh ssh
  --policy. The verdict is one JSON object on stdout, with or without --json.
  The exit is 0 for a pass and 78 for a mismatch. It is 69 for no reading: no
  connection, a KEXINIT that does not read, or a size that one exchange cannot
  measure. --policy goes with no --preflight (64).

  Usage: podssh health [OPTIONS] [user@]host

  Arguments:
    [[user@]host]
        the host to read: [user@]host, host:PORT, [user@][IPV6]:PORT or
        ssh://[user@]host[:PORT].

  Options:
    -p, --port PORT
        the host's port.
    -l, --login-name USER
        user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        identity file, repeatable.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -F, --config CONFIG
        read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads no
        file.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -4, --ipv4-only
        use IPv4 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=4.
    -6, --ipv6-only
        use IPv6 only; forwarded to the relay's ?family=6.
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself, errors included.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
