        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --json
        the facts as one JSON object on stdout, also after a failure; effective
        holds the CPUs and the memory to plan from, a container's cgroup's
        where it limits them.
    --policy FILE
        in place of the facts, judge the server's KEXINIT by the algorithm
        policy in FILE, with no login: JSON on stdout; exit 0, 78 or 69.
    --preflight
        after the facts, what the server allows, from the same login: SFTP, -R,
        -J, the tools of sh, tmux, the cgroup and a keepalive, each ok, FAIL or
        ????; exit 1 when one failed.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    a host's load, memory, uptime, network and disks, from one command that
    only reads
        $ podssh health user@example.org

    and what its server allows before a long command needs it: SFTP, -R, -J,
    tmux, a keepalive
        $ podssh health --preflight user@example.org

podssh play
  play a recording of podssh ssh --record again, with its timing.

  podssh play FILE writes the output of a recording again, on stdout, with its
  timing: a file of podssh ssh --record, or another asciicast v2 file. --speed
  plays it faster or slower, and --idle-limit cuts each wait to its seconds, as
  the file's idle_time_limit does when it has one. A file of another version is
  refused (exit 1), and an event of another kind than output is passed over.

  A recording holds what the session showed, its secrets too (a key that was
  printed, a password that a program echoed). It never holds what was typed.
  Played again, its control sequences reach your terminal: play only a file
  that you trust.

  Usage: podssh play [OPTIONS] FILE

  Arguments:
    [FILE]
        the recording: an asciicast v2 file.

  Options:
    --speed FACTOR
        play this many times as fast, as 2 or 0.5 (default 1).
    --idle-limit SECONDS
        wait this long at most between two events (default: the file's
        idle_time_limit, else no limit).
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh config
  ssh_config blocks from the host list of another tool: import.

  podssh config import ansible FILE reads an Ansible inventory in its INI form,
  from FILE, or from stdin with -. It prints a Host block of ssh_config for
  each host, with a summary on stderr; it writes no file, and you add what it
  printed to ~/.ssh/config. A host's ansible_host, ansible_port, ansible_user
  and ansible_ssh_private_key_file (or their ansible_ssh_ names) give HostName,
  Port, User and IdentityFile. They are combined from all, its groups and its
  own line as Ansible combines them; host:PORT and ranges such as www[01:03]
  are read as Ansible reads them.

  The -o options of ansible_ssh_common_args and ansible_ssh_extra_args, which
  Ansible gives to ssh, follow as lines of the block, and -J as ProxyJump;
  ProxyCommand and the other keywords that run a command, and each other flag,
  are named in a comment, with no value.

  A password or a passphrase (a variable whose name holds pass) is never
  imported and never printed: the summary counts it. A host whose
  ansible_connection is not ssh gets a comment and no block. A host name that a
  Host line cannot hold (a space, *, ?, !, " or #) is refused by name. A bad
  line ends the run with its number (exit 65); a file that cannot be read gives
  66.

  podssh config import putty FILE reads PuTTY's sessions: a .reg file of the
  registry's key Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions, from regedit or reg
  export, in UTF-16 or UTF-8. It also reads the session files of PuTTY on Unix,
  a file or its directory. The session Default Settings is PuTTY's template,
  not a host. user@host in HostName gives User; a key of PuTTY's format (.ppk),
  which ssh cannot read, is a comment that says how puttygen converts it; an
  SSH proxy gives ProxyJump; ProxyPassword is counted. Environment, a proxy
  command and the other proxies are comments with no value.

  podssh config import mobaxterm FILE reads MobaXterm's sessions, an
  .mxtsessions export or the bookmarks of MobaXterm.ini: the SSH sessions, each
  with its folder in a comment; the gateways give ProxyJump; a command after
  the login, a proxy and a key path in MobaXterm's own form are comments; each
  entry of [Passwords] and [Sesspass] is counted. podssh config import remmina
  FILE reads one profile of Remmina, or each of a directory
  (~/.local/share/remmina): protocol=SSH makes a block, server gives HostName
  and Port, name the label and group the folder; each secret, in the keyring or
  encrypted, is counted; a placeholder of a template such as %Host% is no host.
  podssh config import mremoteng FILE reads mRemoteNG's connections,
  confCons.xml or an export of it: Protocol SSH2 makes a block, each with its
  folders in a comment; a field that a connection inherits comes from the
  nearest folder above it that has its own; SSHTunnelConnectionName gives
  ProxyJump through that connection; a PuTTY session other than Default
  Settings and SSHOptions are comments with no value; each password is counted,
  never decrypted; SSH1 is a comment; a file encrypted whole
  (FullFileEncryption) is refused by name (exit 65).

  A session's label becomes the name of its block, each run of characters that
  a Host line cannot hold made one -. The label itself is in a comment above
  it; a session of another protocol gets a comment and no block. The formats of
  FinalShell and Termius, and Ansible's YAML, are refused by name (exit 64).
  They wait until a real export of each is at hand to test against.

  Usage: podssh config import FORMAT FILE

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        import.
    [FORMAT FILE]...
        import: the format, ansible (an INI inventory), and the file, - for
        stdin.

  Options:
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    Host blocks for the hosts of an Ansible inventory, added to the user's
    ssh_config
        $ podssh config import ansible inventory.ini >> ~/.ssh/config

podssh mcp
  the commands as tools for an agent: a Model Context Protocol server on stdin
  and stdout.

  podssh mcp is a server of the Model Context Protocol on stdin and stdout, for
  an agent that runs it: each line of stdin is one JSON-RPC message and each
  line of stdout one answer, and podssh's own words go to stderr. It answers a
  client of the revision 2026-07-28, whose requests name their version in
  _meta. It also answers one that opens with initialize (2025-11-25,
  2025-06-18, 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05). It ends at the end of stdin, and each
  call then in flight ends with it.

  The tools: ssh_exec runs one command on a host (destination [user@]host,
  command, and stdin, timeout_seconds and host_key_fingerprint at will); its
  result has podssh's exit code, the command's status or signal, how the
  session ended and why it failed, stdout, stderr and timed_out. stdout and
  stderr are at most 1 MiB each, truncated says so, and output that is not
  UTF-8 comes as base64. status, doctor and man give what podssh status, podssh
  doctor and podssh man give, in their JSON form.

  THE RISK: an agent with ssh_exec runs commands on each allowed host, as you,
  with your keys and your ssh_config. The words of a call come from a model,
  and text that the model read can ask it for a command or a host; so ssh_exec
  reaches no host unless --allow-host names it, and is not offered with none.
  Name each host, or the fewest patterns that hold them; !PATTERN excludes, and
  a pattern with USER@ needs a destination that names that user. The host is
  matched as the call names it, before the HostName of your configuration.

  For an agent that watches and must not change: --read-only offers no tool
  that changes a host, no job_start, job_stop, cp_put or session_ tool, and
  refuses a call of one by name; ssh_exec is then offered only with
  --allow-command. --allow-command PATTERN, repeated, names what ssh_exec may
  run: a pattern is words, the program as typed and * for one word of any text.
  A command matches when its words are as many and each the pattern's. A
  command with a character that the remote shell reads as more than a word's
  text (; | & $ ` < > ( ) \ quotes, a newline, ~ # ! = %, and the globs * ? [ ]
  { }) is refused, as the shell would run more than the pattern says. The
  patterns are named in ssh_exec's description, and a pattern whose program is
  * is refused (64).

  Each call runs podssh ssh as a child, with BatchMode=yes (no prompt, ever)
  and StrictHostKeyChecking=yes. So a host whose key known_hosts does not hold
  is refused, unless host_key_fingerprint names its key, as
  --host-key-fingerprint. The child has no pty, no escape character, no
  forwarding of a port, an agent or X11, and no shared connection; these come
  before -F FILE, so a file cannot undo them. A call past its limit (60 s, or
  timeout_seconds, at most 3600) ends its session, as a cancelled call does;
  four calls run at once, and the others wait.

  With a host allowed, health and the job_ tools are offered too. Each is a
  child of its verb with the same options and the same check of --allow-host,
  and a host key that known_hosts holds: health gives podssh health --json;
  job_start runs a command in the host's tmux that outlives the call, and gives
  its id; job_list, job_log (a window of the output: offset, max_bytes, and
  more when bytes follow), job_wait (until the job ends, at most wait_seconds;
  a job that runs on is a result, ended false, to call again) and job_stop take
  that id.

  cp_put and cp_get copy with podssh cp between a path of this host and a path
  of an allowed host. Each file's SHA-256 is checked at both ends; they are
  offered only with --allow-dir DIR, as --allow-host lets an agent reach a
  host, not read the files of this one. A local path is resolved, its links
  followed, and refused unless it lies inside a DIR, before anything runs; a
  relative one is under the first DIR. A DIR that holds ~/.ssh or podssh's
  cache, or lies inside one, and the root, are refused (64). A DIR that is not
  there is 78. cp_put takes content in place of local_path, the bytes of one
  file in base64, 1 MiB at most; cp_get puts a tree (recursive) only into a
  path that is not there. A tree goes as podssh cp -r copies it, a link as a
  link. The result has the exit and the events of podssh cp --jsonl.

  --allow-session offers session_start, session_send, session_wait,
  session_capture and session_stop: a shell with a pty on an allowed host, held
  by podssh session between the calls. The server drives only the sessions that
  it started, never one of yours, and stops each as it ends; the text of
  session_send goes on the child's stdin, never on a command line.

  --client-config CLIENT (claude-desktop, cursor, vscode or gemini) prints the
  JSON entry that the client reads to start this server, and starts none: its
  command is this binary's absolute path, as a client started from a launcher
  may not have the shell's PATH. Its args are mcp and the other flags typed,
  checked as a run checks them (64, 78), each path made absolute. VS Code's
  entry is under servers with type stdio, the others' under mcpServers. A line
  on stderr says where the client's documents say that it reads the entry; the
  command writes no file of the client's. Another CLIENT is 64.

  Usage: podssh mcp [OPTIONS]

  Options:
    --allow-host PATTERN
        a host that ssh_exec, health, the job_ tools and the copies may reach:
        [USER@]HOST with * and ?, or !PATTERN to exclude; repeat it (default:
        none). A node is node://[USER@]NAME, and only a pattern that starts
        with node:// matches one.
    --allow-dir DIR
        a directory of this host that cp_put may read and cp_get may write,
        links followed and held inside it; repeat it (default: none, and no
        copy tool); one that holds ~/.ssh or podssh's cache is refused.
    --allow-session
        offer the session_ tools, a shell with a pty on an allowed host that
        outlives each call; the server stops each that it started as it ends.
    --read-only
        offer no tool that changes a host: no job_start, job_stop, cp_put or
        session_ tool, and ssh_exec only with --allow-command; a call of one by
        name is refused.
    --allow-command PATTERN
        a command that ssh_exec may run: words, the program as typed, * for one
        word; a command with a character that the shell reads (; | & $ `
        quotes, globs, redirections) is refused; repeat it (default: any
        command).
    -F, --config FILE
        the ssh_config of each session, as podssh ssh -F FILE.
    --direct
        each session over TCP with no relay, as podssh ssh --direct.
    --client-config CLIENT
        print the entry that CLIENT (claude-desktop, cursor, vscode or gemini)
        reads to start this server with the other flags typed; it is checked as
        a run checks them, with this binary's absolute path and each path made
        absolute; it starts no server and writes no file.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    tools for an agent, run by its MCP client: commands on the web hosts but
    web9
        $ podssh mcp --allow-host 'web*.example.org' --allow-host '!web9.example.org'

    the same tools with copies to and from one directory of this host, and
    sessions that end with the server
        $ podssh mcp --allow-host build.example.org --allow-dir ./artifacts --allow-session

podssh session
  a session that outlives each call, for an agent: start it, send keys, wait
  until the output stops, read the screen.

  podssh session start NAME [OPTIONS] HOST [COMMAND] starts a podssh of its own
  in the background. It logs in to HOST as podssh ssh does, with its connection
  flags and the Host blocks of ssh_config. It holds one session with a pty: the
  login shell, or COMMAND. start returns once the session is ready, with the
  path of its socket on stdout; what the session's podssh says until then comes
  on stderr. Its exit code is start's when it ends first (255 for a connection
  or a login that failed). The pty's size is that of COLUMNS and LINES, else 80
  by 24. Until it is ready, the session's podssh keeps start's terminal: a
  password, a key's passphrase and a new host key are asked there, as podssh
  ssh asks them (within --timeout), and Ctrl-C reaches it; then it leaves that
  terminal and its session. With no terminal, they come from podssh agent or
  SSH_ASKPASS, and a new host key needs StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new or a
  known_hosts that has it.

  send NAME TEXT types TEXT and Enter (a carriage return; --no-enter leaves it
  out). In TEXT, \r, \n, \t, \e (Escape), \xNN (\x03 is Ctrl-C) and \\ give the
  bytes they name; each other \ is refused. send NAME with no TEXT types stdin
  as it is: a password goes so, never in a command line, which each process can
  read.

  wait NAME returns when the output has stopped for --idle (2s by default),
  counted from the last send. So a wait right after a send waits for what it
  brings; output that stops inside an escape sequence has not stopped. With
  --match TEXT it returns when TEXT comes in the output since the last send,
  with the terminal's sequences and control bytes taken out; the echo of the
  line that send typed counts too, so match a text that only the command's
  output holds. It says idle or match on stdout, and exits 75 when --timeout
  (60s) passes first, 69 when the session ended first.

  capture NAME writes the screen as a terminal of the pty's size shows it: its
  rows, with no blank at their ends and no empty row at the end. --raw writes
  the last 64 KiB of the output as it came, from a place where a terminal can
  start to read it. It never starts inside a sequence or a character. stop NAME
  ends the session and its podssh.

  list writes a line for each session of the directories of the cache: its
  name, running or ended and the status, and its host, with a tab between them.
  A session whose podssh takes the connection and gives no answer within 2 s is
  listed with the state no-answer and no host. stderr says why: it is there,
  busy or stuck. A socket that nobody serves any more, as after a crash, is no
  session, and the next start of its name takes its place. With no session,
  stdout stays empty and one line on stderr says so and names the directories
  read; a directory that cannot be read is a line on stderr with its error; -q
  leaves out each of these lines. --json writes one object instead: sessions
  (each with its name, state, host and socket; [] for none), read (the
  directories read) and unreadable (each with its error). The exit is 0.

  The session's podssh ends at stop, or a minute after its session ended (so
  that the last screen can still be read). It also ends after an hour with no
  request, or at SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP. serve NAME [OPTIONS] HOST is that
  podssh in the foreground, for a program that keeps it itself: it writes one
  line of JSON on stdout when it is ready, and its messages on stderr; with
  --detach it writes nothing more after that line, as start runs it.

  THE SOCKET: start and serve listen on a socket of this user's: NAME.sock in
  the directory sessions of the cache (see FILES), made mode 0700, the socket
  mode 0600; on Windows a Unix-domain socket there, whose clients must run as
  this user. A path too long for the address of a socket (107 bytes on Linux)
  goes to the next directory of the cache (see FILES). That one may be under
  the temporary directory. With none that fits, start names each one and asks
  for --socket. --socket PATH names another, also \\.\pipe\NAME on Windows, and
  @NAME on Linux, which has no file. A client of another user is closed before
  it is read. No TCP: a request types into a shell. The bind is the probe:
  where this host refuses it, start exits 77 with the reason; PODSSH_LISTEN set
  to no refuses start and serve before any bind (78), and so does
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR set to none with no --socket.

  THE RISK: each program that runs as you can type into the session and read
  its screen, as it can with your keys. The socket carries no key, password or
  token: the session's podssh logs in with what podssh ssh would use. One line
  of JSON is each request and each answer, with the version first ({"schema":1,
  ...}), for a program that speaks to the socket itself: info, send (text, or
  bytes in base64), wait (idle_ms, match, timeout_ms), capture (raw) and stop,
  each with the session's name.

  Usage: podssh session SUBCOMMAND [OPTIONS] [NAME] [HOST [COMMAND...] |
      TEXT]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        start, send, wait, capture, stop or list; serve is what start runs in
        the background.
    [NAME]
        the session's name: letters, digits, _ and -, 32 at most.
    [HOST]
        start and serve: the host, as podssh ssh takes it; send: the text to
        type, with \r, \n, \t, \e, \xNN and \\; with none, send reads it from
        stdin.
    [COMMAND]...
        start and serve: the command to run on the host with a pty, in place of
        the login shell; send: more words of the text, joined with spaces.

  Options:
    --socket PATH
        the session's socket: start and serve listen there, the others connect
        there (default: NAME.sock in the directory sessions of the cache; on
        Windows also \\.\pipe\NAME).
    --timeout DURATION
        start: how long to wait for the session to be ready; wait: for what it
        waits for (default 60s).
    --idle DURATION
        wait: until the output has stopped this long, counted from the last
        send (default 2s when --match is not given).
    --match TEXT
        wait: until TEXT comes in the output since the last send, the
        terminal's sequences taken out.
    --no-enter
        send: no Enter (a carriage return) after the text.
    --raw
        capture: the last 64 KiB of output as it came, from a clean place of
        the terminal's grammar, in place of the screen.
    --detach
        serve: after the line that says it is ready, write nothing more on
        stdout and stderr (start gives it).
    --json
        list: one JSON object on stdout: each session with its name, state,
        host and socket ([] for none), the directories read, and those that
        could not be.
    -p, --port PORT
        start: port to connect to.
    -l, --login-name USER
        start: user to log in as; also user@host.
    -i, --identity-file FILE
        start: identity file, repeatable; also -oIdentityFile=.
    -o, --option NAME=VALUE
        start: an OpenSSH option, as -o Name=Value; repeatable.
    -F, --config CONFIG
        start: read this ssh_config file in place of ~/.ssh/config; none reads
        no file.
    -J, --jump-host HOSTS
        start: log in through these hosts first: [user@]host[:port][,...].
    -v, --verbose
        raise log level; repeatable.
    -q, --quiet
        quiet: no messages from podssh itself.
    --relay-host HOSTS
        relay hosts to try in order, HOST[:PORT][,...] (default: env
        PODSSH_RELAY, else the built-in relay and its pool).
    --relay-failover MODE
        how the relay hosts are tried: staggered (the default), parallel or
        serial; also env PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER.
    --relay-addr HOST=IP
        use IP for HOST instead of DNS, HOST=IP[,...]; also env
        PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (for hosts with no DNS).
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CA certificates in FILE for the relay (default: env
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else system and built-in roots).
    --direct
        connect without the relay: TCP, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set.
    --forwarder TEMPLATES
        reach the first hop through other products' WebSocket forwarders, in
        order, in place of the relay: ws:// or wss:// URLs with {host} and
        {port} once each, or neither for a first frame of JSON; or
        wisp+wss://HOST/PATH/ for a Wisp server; or the words mudlet, ssheasy,
        mudix and wisp; also env PODSSH_FORWARDER.
    --shadowsocks FILE
        reach the first hop through Shadowsocks servers, in order, in place of
        the relay: FILE is private, with ss:// lines (chacha20-ietf-poly1305,
        aes-256-gcm, aes-128-gcm; no plugin), subscription https://URL lines,
        and Outline access keys (ssconf://URL, or key https://URL), whose
        server may be in a WebSocket over TLS.
    --vless FILE
        reach the first hop through VLESS servers that you run (Xray-core,
        shoes), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is private, with a
        vless:// share link on each line; over a WebSocket (type=ws) or XHTTP
        on HTTP/2 (type=xhttp), which passes where a proxy refuses the upgrade.
    --trojan FILE
        reach the first hop through Trojan servers that you run (trojan-gfw,
        trojan-go, Xray-core), in order, in place of the relay: FILE is
        private, with a trojan:// share link on each line, in TLS alone
        (type=tcp) or in a WebSocket over TLS (type=ws).
    --tuic FILE
        reach the first hop through TUIC servers that you run (sing-box,
        mihomo, Itsusinn's tuic), in order, in place of the relay; over QUIC
        where a probe finds that UDP passes: FILE is private, with a tuic://
        share link on each line.
    --hysteria FILE
        reach the first hop through Hysteria 2 servers that you run
        (apernet/hysteria), in order, in place of the relay, where UDP passes:
        FILE is private, with a hysteria2:// share link on each line; a probe
        of UDP to each server's port goes first, and with no answer the road
        ends at once.
    --via https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a forward proxy over TLS that you run
        (Caddy's forwardproxy, squid's https_port), in place of the relay: TLS
        to it, through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then CONNECT inside, HTTP/2
        when it chooses h2, else HTTP/1.1; also env PODSSH_VIA.
    --via-auth-file FILE
        the Basic credentials of --via in FILE, a private file: one line,
        USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; never in
        the URL; also env PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE.
    --wstunnel wss://HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a wstunnel server that you run (wstunnel
        server wss://[::]:443), in place of the relay: the WebSocket to it,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, its token naming the target; ws://
        has no TLS; also env PODSSH_WSTUNNEL.
    --wstunnel-secret-file FILE
        what the server of --wstunnel checks, in FILE, a private file:
        path-prefix PREFIX, credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE,
        or the prefix alone; never in the URL; also env
        PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE.
    --chisel https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]
        reach the first hop through a chisel server that you run (chisel server
        --port 443 --auth USER:PASS), in place of the relay: its WebSocket,
        through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set, then SSH inside it and a channel
        to the target; http:// to this host alone; also env PODSSH_CHISEL.
    --chisel-auth-file FILE
        what the server of --chisel takes and shows, in FILE, a private file:
        auth USER:PASSWORD, as chisel's --auth, and fingerprint BASE64, the key
        that chisel server prints, which podssh then checks; never in the URL;
        also env PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE.
    --turn turns:HOST[:PORT]
        reach the first hop through a TURN server that you run (coturn), in
        place of the relay: a TCP allocation of RFC 6062; its control
        connection and a second connection to the same server that carries the
        bytes; each through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set (port 443 when none is
        named); turn: has no TLS and goes to this host alone; also env
        PODSSH_TURN.
    --turn-auth-file FILE
        the credential of the server of --turn, in FILE, a private file:
        USER:PASSWORD on one line, or auth-secret SECRET for a coturn of
        use-auth-secret; never in the URI; also env PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    a shell that stays between the calls of an agent: type a line, wait for 2 s
    of quiet, read the screen
        $ podssh session start work user@example.org && podssh session send work 'make test' && podssh session wait work --idle 2s && podssh session capture work

podssh serve
  an SSH server here: one connection on stdin and stdout, as sshd -i, or the
  node of a pair through the relay; with a host key kept and authorized keys.

  podssh serve --stdio is an SSH server for one connection on stdin and stdout,
  as sshd -i: OpenSSH's ssh, or podssh ssh, reaches it through its
  ProxyCommand, on this host or at the other end of any pipe. Nothing listens.
  It runs as the user that started it, with no passwd entry, setgroups or
  chroot. At its start it gives up each capability of the process, before it
  reads a file; a capability that stays is a refusal (78).

  podssh serve NAME is the node of the pair NAME (podssh relay pair NAME) whose
  sessions serve answers itself, in its process: no TARGET is dialled, and
  nothing listens. An operator reaches it as any node: podssh ssh
  node://user@NAME, podssh cp or sftp to node://NAME. That goes through the
  relay, with the node's end-to-end channel and resumable layer. A host with no
  sshd, which may not listen, gives a shell and its files this way. The keys,
  the host key and the other flags are those of --stdio; --stdio and NAME are
  one of the two (64). The node's lines say serving podssh serve, in this
  process. Whoever holds the pair's connect token reaches serve, whose
  authorized keys alone guard each login. SIGHUP reads the keys again for each
  session of the node, as with --stdio, and --revoke-ends-sessions ends a
  removed key's sessions there too.

  Only public keys log in, with a one-time code after the key where --totp asks
  for one (below). The keys are each --authorized-key, and the lines of each
  --authorized-keys file; with neither, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. A key is
  compared by its key alone: the login name selects nothing, but a name of
  --share (below). The options before a key are its rules (below); a line whose
  options serve cannot all honour, and a line that is no key, are passed over,
  and said with their number and why. A file that is a symbolic link, another
  user's, or one that others can change is refused (78). With no key at all,
  the start is refused (78): no setting lets each key in.

  podssh serve --listen ADDR is the same server on a listener that you ask for.
  PORT alone listens on 127.0.0.1. ADDR:PORT takes an address of this host, and
  [ADDR]:PORT an IPv6 one; no name is resolved. unix:PATH is a socket of mode
  0600: a client of another user is closed. --listen may be repeated; each
  address binds at the start, in order. Port 0 lets the system choose, and
  serve's line names the port. Each connection is served as one of --stdio,
  with the same keys, host key and flags. On a TCP socket, the client's address
  meets from= of a key line; on a socket of unix:, no from= matches. --stdio,
  NAME and --listen are one of the three (64).

  The bind is the probe: serve makes no other socket to test it. A bind that
  the host refuses ends the start with 77. Its line names the address, the
  system's words, and the ways with no listener: cannot listen on
  127.0.0.1:2222: Permission denied; this host refuses the listener. Another
  failure, such as a port in use, ends it with 69. A path that is not a socket
  is never removed (64). PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses --listen before any bind
  (78). Each bind comes before the drop of the capabilities, so a port under
  1024 binds where the start holds cap_net_bind_service.

  Each connection takes a place under --max-connections (64 by default) at its
  accept, before a byte is read. One more gets serve's version line and a
  disconnect, too many connections, with the cap named. OpenSSH prints it:
  Received disconnect ... 12: podssh serve: 64 connections at once already.
  Past 16 such refusals under way, a connection is closed with no word, and one
  line a second says so. A place comes back when its connection ends. SIGTERM
  or SIGINT closes each listener, and its socket's file goes. Then each
  connection stops as under --stdio, and serve exits 0. SIGHUP reads the keys
  again for each connection. A listener whose accept fails 10 times in a row
  listens no more; with none left, serve exits 69.

  Each connection must log in within --login-timeout SECS of its accept (60 by
  default, 1 to 3600). The time is counted from the accept, not from the last
  byte: a client that sends a byte now and then ends at the same time. Past it,
  serve sends a disconnect: podssh serve: no login within 60 s of the
  connection (--login-timeout). A client that sent no version line yet is
  closed with no disconnect. Each end is one line of serve's log. A login in
  time cancels the deadline. --pending-max N (16 by default) caps the
  connections that have not logged in. One more is refused as past
  --max-connections, with --pending-max named. A login gives its place back at
  once.

  The algorithms are one stated set, the same at each start, never russh's
  default of the day. Key exchanges: mlkem768x25519-sha256, curve25519-sha256,
  curve25519-sha256@libssh.org, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,
  diffie-hellman-group18-sha512, diffie-hellman-group17-sha512,
  diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, diffie-hellman-group15-sha512 and
  diffie-hellman-group14-sha256. Host key algorithms: ssh-ed25519,
  ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, rsa-sha2-512
  and rsa-sha2-256. Of those, a client is offered the ones that the host key
  serves. Ciphers: chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com, aes256-gcm@openssh.com,
  aes256-ctr, aes192-ctr and aes128-ctr. MACs: hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,
  hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com, hmac-sha2-512 and hmac-sha2-256. Compression:
  none, zlib and zlib@openssh.com. A client that offers no name of a list is
  refused in the handshake (OpenSSH: no matching cipher found, and the set as
  Their offer).

  The options of a key line are OpenSSH's (the format of the authorized_keys
  file in sshd(8)), read as sshd reads them: separated by commas, names in any
  case, a value in double quotes where a backslash before a quote is a quote.
  command="..." runs in place of each command, shell and sftp request, as SHELL
  -c, with the client's command in SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND (not set for a shell;
  internal-sftp for sftp); command="internal-sftp" serves SFTP alone, and
  refuses one with arguments. no-pty refuses a pty (OpenSSH, with -tt, ends
  with PTY allocation request failed). no-port-forwarding refuses each forward,
  and each permitopen="host:port" (an IPv6 address in brackets; * for any port)
  lets in that target alone, the host compared as written, with no lookup.
  restrict turns off the pty and forwarding, and a later pty or port-forwarding
  turns one on again. expiry-time="YYYYMMDD[HHMM[SS]]" (local time, or UTC with
  Z) refuses the key after it. from="patterns" lets the key in from a matching
  address alone: addresses with * and ?, blocks such as 10.0.0.0/8, and ! to
  refuse; serve looks up no name, so a host name matches nothing. serve knows
  an address only when its stdin is a TCP socket (as from inetd): on a pipe, as
  from a ProxyCommand or the relay, no from= matches, and the key is refused.
  no-agent-forwarding, no-X11-forwarding and no-user-rc change nothing (serve
  offers none of them). A security key (sk-ssh-ed25519, sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256)
  logs in only with a signature whose flag of presence is set (the key was
  touched), as sshd checks it: no-touch-required takes one without, and
  verify-required also asks for the flag that the key verified the user (a
  PIN); restrict changes neither, and serve's stderr names the flag that was
  missing. environment=, permitlisten=, tunnel=, principals=, cert-authority
  and any option that serve does not know make the line unused, named. Of the
  lines of one key, the first that lets it in now holds. Each refusal by a rule
  goes to the client: a forward refused as administratively prohibited, a pty
  or a command with its line on the channel's stderr. It also goes to serve's
  stderr, with the key's fingerprint and the option; a key refused at login is
  said there alone, as the client hears Permission denied.

  The host key is --host-key FILE, else serve_host_ed25519_key in the cache
  (see FILES): made at the first start, an Ed25519 key of mode 0600, and read
  at each later one, never overwritten; of two starts at once, one makes it and
  the other reads it. Its fingerprint goes to stderr at each start, with a
  warning when the file is in a temporary directory, which a reboot can empty:
  each client would then meet a new host key. A key file with a passphrase is
  refused (78). An RSA key signs through aws-lc-rs, whose RSA is constant-time,
  with SHA-2 alone (rsa-sha2-512, rsa-sha2-256), never through russh's rsa
  crate. An RSA key outside 2048 to 8192 bits, or a key that is not Ed25519,
  ECDSA or RSA, is refused (78). --host-key also takes a key file of a TPM
  (podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm): the TPM signs each key exchange, and serve
  holds no private key. Such a key must sign at the start: with no TPM, or
  after the boot state changed, serve does not start (78).

  A command (exec) runs as SHELL -c COMMAND. A shell request runs the shell as
  a login shell (its argv[0] the shell's name after a dash). Each runs as the
  user that runs serve, on three pipes: stdout comes as data and stderr as
  extended data, apart. Each child leads a session of its own (setsid), in HOME
  when it is a directory, else /; a signal request goes to its process group.
  When it ends, its pipes are read to their end, for 2 s of silence at most (30
  s in all): a job that it put in the background can hold them. Then comes
  exit-status, or exit-signal with the signal's name and the core flag, always
  before EOF and close. X11, a Unix socket's forward and each subsystem but
  sftp are refused with their answer.

  A pty request (OpenSSH's -t and -tt) is granted where a pty opens at that
  moment: serve tries /dev/ptmx, then /dev/pts/ptmx, at each request, and keeps
  nothing for the next one. The command or the shell then has the pty's slave
  as its stdin, stdout and stderr and as its controlling terminal. It runs in a
  session of its own, so Ctrl-C and the job control of a shell work as under
  sshd; TERM is the request's (xterm-256color when it is empty), and the
  variable of the slave's path is set as sshd sets it. The size is the
  request's (80x24 when it is zero) and follows each window change; the
  request's terminal modes are set where termios has them, and a mode that it
  lacks or that the kernel refuses is passed over. On a pty, stdout and stderr
  come as one stream of data, and the client's EOF ends its input alone. On
  Linux, where neither master opens, serve makes a pty of its own: a helper
  process makes a user and a mount namespace, mounts a new devpts instance, and
  gives back its master and its slave. The slave has no path, so the variable
  of the slave's path is not set; a host that refuses unshare or mount refuses
  this too (podssh doctor's line pty devpts). Where no pty opens, on Linux
  (x86_64 and aarch64), serve gives the program a tty that it answers itself:
  the program's stdin, stdout and stderr are one socket. A seccomp filter of
  the program's own, set before it starts, sends its tty calls and its opens to
  serve. The tty calls are the ioctl requests of termios, the window size and
  the foreground group. serve answers them from one termios state, and gives a
  copy of the socket for /dev/tty; each other call goes to the kernel. The
  program sees a tty: test -t 0, stty, a shell's job control, vi, less and top;
  the keys go through a line discipline in serve that follows the state that
  the program set. That state is echo, editing, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z and Ctrl-\ to
  the foreground group, and the window size with SIGWINCH. On a socket, Ctrl-D
  on an empty line ends the program's input for good. A program that reads two
  lines quickly may get both in one read. Where the host's own filter already
  holds a listener, so that a second is refused, serve answers the same calls
  by ptrace: the program's filter stops it at each tty call and open, and
  serve's thread answers from the same state. It follows each process that the
  program starts, and an open of /dev/tty becomes a copy of a descriptor that
  holds the socket. The program and its children can then use no ptrace of
  their own (gdb, strace); serve says so. A host that refuses both, or the
  program's memory to serve, refuses this (podssh doctor's lines pty notify and
  pty ptrace); --pty notify takes it with no pty tried, and refuses the request
  where it fails. Where none of these opens (a cage with no /dev/ptmx), serve
  is the line discipline itself (--pty auto): the command or the shell runs on
  pipes, and each key is echoed and edited in serve. A line goes to the program
  when Enter submits it. Ctrl-C and Ctrl-\ go to the program's process group as
  SIGINT and SIGQUIT. Its output comes around the line under edit, with each
  line ending CR LF. A login shell runs with no prompt of its own and a trap of
  SIGINT and SIGQUIT. So Ctrl-C ends the command and not the shell; serve draws
  the prompt $. A program that draws on a tty (vi, less, top) gets a line that
  says so, then runs. --pty line takes the line discipline with no pty tried;
  --pty no refuses such a request with its answer, and a command then runs on
  pipes (OpenSSH, with -tt, ends with PTY allocation request failed); podssh
  doctor's lines pty, pty devpts and pty notify say which a client meets. On
  Windows the request is refused.

  A login shell on a tty, of any of the kinds above, is shown the message of
  the day first, as sshd shows it. The file is --motd FILE, else /etc/motd
  where it is there. A command, a forced command= and a subsystem are shown
  none. A user with ~/.hushlogin is shown none; serve takes the home from HOME.
  At most 64 KiB of the file is shown, and serve's stderr says when the rest
  was cut. Each control character but tab and newline is dropped, so the file
  cannot drive the terminal. The file is read again at each login. A --motd
  FILE that cannot be read refuses the start (78); later, a login goes on
  without it, and stderr says why.

  With --shell-integration, a login shell on a tty is marked for the terminal:
  OSC 133 marks each prompt, command and output, and OSC 7 names the directory.
  A terminal then jumps between commands, and opens a tab in the same
  directory. On a pty, or a tty that serve answers, bash and zsh take the marks
  from their start. bash runs with an rc file of serve's own that reads the
  files of a login, then adds hooks. It is no login shell then, so logout
  refuses; exit ends it. zsh runs with ZDOTDIR at a directory of serve's own.
  Its .zshenv gives ZDOTDIR back, reads the user's .zshenv, and adds hooks. The
  files are in TMPDIR, else /tmp, and go when the session ends. serve never
  writes a file of the user's. Another shell gets no marks, and stderr says so.
  On the line discipline, serve marks its own prompt and each line submitted.
  It cannot see a command end, so the output's end comes at once, with no
  status. A command gets no marks.

  Where systemd is this host's service manager, each child on a pty runs in a
  transient scope of its own, as sshd moves each session. A stop of serve's
  unit then leaves each user's shell, and its memory counts against the scope.
  At its start, serve checks /run/systemd/system, busctl and systemctl on PATH,
  and that the user's manager says running or degraded within 2 s. Where that
  fails, stderr says so once, and each child starts where serve is. With
  systemd, the child waits between its fork and its exec until the user's
  manager has moved it into podssh-serve-PID-N.scope. A move that fails, or
  takes past 2 s, lets the child go on where serve is, with one line on stderr.
  No session fails because systemd is absent or slow. The user's manager lists
  each open session's scope as podssh-serve-*. On another system there is no
  probe and no line.

  The sftp subsystem is served in the process: SFTP version 3 as OpenSSH's
  sftp-server speaks it. So OpenSSH's sftp, its scp (SFTP is its mode since
  OpenSSH 9.0) and podssh cp reach a cage that has no sftp-server, scp or
  rsync. The files are reached as the user that runs serve, with no chroot:
  what that user may read and write, a client may. A path is taken as the
  client gives it, and a relative one starts at HOME (/ with none). Served:
  open, read, write, close, stat, lstat, fstat, setstat, fsetstat, opendir,
  readdir, remove, and rename (never over a name that exists). Served too:
  mkdir, rmdir, realpath, readlink and symlink, and the extensions
  posix-rename@openssh.com (a rename over a name), fsync@openssh.com and
  limits@openssh.com. Two more are podssh's own: sha256@podssh, the SHA-256 of
  a byte range of an open file, and sha256-blocks@podssh, that of each block.
  So podssh cp checks a copy with no second read and no exec; other clients
  pass them by. A digest has 20 s, and one second more for each 32 MiB of its
  range. A failure is its status code with the path and the system's words (no
  such file, permission denied, failure). Each call on the file system has 20
  s: past it the reply is a failure that says so, and the handle that it used
  is closed. The session goes on, so a FIFO with no writer or a dead mount
  cannot stop it; a session that left 8 such calls ends. At most 256 handles
  are open in a session, a read is 255 KiB at most and a request 256 KiB. A
  listing names owners by number, as serve reads no passwd entry. scp in its
  legacy mode runs scp by exec, and exits 127 in a cage that has none.
  --no-shell leaves SFTP served, as it runs no program.

  A client's forward (direct-tcpip, from OpenSSH's -W, -L and -J) is a TCP
  connection that serve opens from its own host. It goes to the host and port
  asked, any of them, as sshd allows by default: a name is resolved there, or
  given to the proxy of serve's HTTPS_PROXY. The loopback and the names of
  NO_PROXY go directly, as podssh's own dials go. The dial has 20 s. One that
  fails is refused as connect failed, with its reason in words, the system's
  error or the proxy's status and reason (OpenSSH: open failed: connect failed:
  podssh serve: could not connect to 127.0.0.1:1: Connection refused); a port
  of 0 or past 65535 too. The bytes go both ways, an end of one way keeps the
  other open, and the TCP connection ends with its channel. At most 256
  forwards are open at once on one connection, and one more is refused as a
  resource shortage. --no-forwarding refuses each forward, administratively
  prohibited, with the flag named.

  A client's -R (tcpip-forward) binds no socket. Without --publish-remote,
  serve refuses each one. With it, serve makes a pair for each at the relay
  (PODSSH_RELAY, else the default) and runs the pair's node in its own process.
  It keeps the pair in its cache under a label, rPORT-XXXXXX. podssh operator
  LABEL on serve's host then reaches the client's service: each session opens a
  forwarded-tcpip channel to the client, toward the address and port of its -R.
  Each runs the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel, with a key of this
  forward alone. A request of port 0 is told a port from 49152 to 65535, which
  names the forward and binds nothing. serve's stderr names the label, the pair
  and the key; no line holds a token. The client hears the name in a debug
  message of SSH, which OpenSSH shows at -v alone (Remote: ...), and on the
  stderr of its next session that runs a program. At most 8 are open on a
  connection. Each of these refuses one: --no-forwarding, a key's
  no-port-forwarding, the same address and port twice, PODSSH_OFFLINE, and a
  relay that takes no node within 20 s. serve's stderr says why; OpenSSH says
  remote port forwarding failed. A cancel, the connection's end and serve's
  stop each stop the node, then the pair (POST /v1/stop), and forget its copy;
  where the relay did not answer, serve's line names podssh relay revoke LABEL.
  With --remote-listen, serve listens for each -R on this host's 127.0.0.1
  instead, whatever address the client named. It takes the port asked, or one
  that the system picks for port 0, and the client is told that port.
  PODSSH_LISTEN=no refuses the flag at the start (78). Each connection opens a
  forwarded-tcpip channel to the client, 32 at once for a forward at most.
  Where the bind fails, the forward is refused with its reason, or made a pair
  of the relay where --publish-remote is on too. The forward's end closes the
  listener.

  The environment of a child is serve's own, as the cage gave it (PATH,
  HTTPS_PROXY and the rest stay). It goes without podssh's credentials:
  PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN, the secrets of Cloudflare Access, and each variable of
  podssh whose name holds TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD or PASSPHRASE. Of those, the
  ones that name a file stay. It adds USER and LOGNAME (serve's, else the uid's
  number: no passwd entry is read), HOME (/ with none), SHELL and PATH (sshd's
  /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin with none). A client's env request (OpenSSH's
  SetEnv and SendEnv) is taken when its name matches an --accept-env pattern
  (default LANG and LC_*). It is never taken for LD_*, PATH, HOME, SHELL, ENV,
  BASH_ENV, IFS, USER, LOGNAME or SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND, whatever the pattern;
  --accept-env '' takes none.

  The shell is found with no passwd entry and no /etc/shells: --shell PATH
  alone when it is given; else SHELL, then /bin/sh, /usr/bin/sh, /bin/bash,
  /usr/bin/bash, /bin/ash and /bin/dash. A candidate passes when it is an
  absolute path to a regular file that this user may execute. A real run of -c
  'exit 0' must also end with 0 within 5 s: a noexec mount, a data file with
  its mode bits set or a missing loader fail there. The search runs at the
  start and again at each session, with no cache. At the start, a candidate
  passed over is said with its reason (not executable (noexec mount), for one).
  No shell at all refuses the start (78), as does a --shell that does not run;
  --no-shell skips the search, and refuses each command and shell. In a
  session, the same line goes to the channel's stderr, and the request fails
  (OpenSSH: exec request failed). podssh doctor's line shell names the shell
  that serve would run, and each candidate passed over.

  A client that reads slowly slows the child: its output is read 32 KiB at a
  time, and read again only once that went out within the client's window. So a
  client that stops reading leaves the pipe or the pty full and the child
  waiting in its write. serve's memory does not grow; the session goes on when
  the client reads again. The other way, each channel's window (512 KiB) opens
  as the child, the SFTP server or a forward's target takes the bytes. So a
  child that reads nothing of its stdin holds its own channel alone, never the
  other channels of the connection.

  SIGTERM or SIGINT stops serve cleanly: it takes no new session or forward,
  and sends the client a disconnect with the reason podssh serve is stopping
  (OpenSSH prints it). It hangs up the process group of each command, shell and
  pty child (SIGHUP, then SIGCONT, as the kernel does when a terminal goes
  away). A group that still runs 5 s later is killed with SIGKILL; a second
  SIGTERM or SIGINT kills at once. Then serve exits 0. A client that closes its
  channel, or a connection that ends, hangs up that channel's child the same
  way. So nothing of a session that is gone runs on unless it asked to (nohup).

  SIGHUP reads the authorized keys again: each --authorized-keys file, or
  ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; each --authorized-key stays. Each line is read as at
  the start, its options its rules: a line that is not used is passed over and
  said. The next login meets the new set; a session that logged in goes on,
  under the rules it logged in with. A file that is gone or cannot be read, or
  no key at all, keeps the set before, and one line on stderr says why; a
  reload that took says how many lines are used now. The other settings are the
  command line's, and a restart changes them. Under --stdio, a SIGHUP that
  comes with the end of the input is the client's end, as OpenSSH hangs up its
  ProxyCommand when it exits: it reads nothing and says nothing. A client that
  closes the connection after its login, with or without a disconnect, ends it
  with no line.

  With --revoke-ends-sessions, a reload that takes a key out also ends that
  key's open sessions. A key whose line now refuses it (from=, expiry-time=)
  counts as out. The client gets a disconnect that names the key (OpenSSH
  prints it), and its children are hung up as at a stop. One line on stderr
  names each key. A key's expiry-time= then ends its sessions at that second
  too. A reload that keeps the set before ends nothing. Without the flag, no
  session ends by a reload.

  With --share, each login shell on a pty is shared by two names, told once to
  its owner on stderr. A name is 128 random bits in hex, after rw- (it types)
  or ro- (it watches). ssh NAME@HOST, by the same road, attaches to the shell
  with any key. A name that serve does not hold reads as a wrong key. A
  watcher's input never reaches the pty: it may send only its window size.
  Writers, the owner among them, take turns: one writer's bytes reach the pty
  until 200 ms of its silence. The pty's size is the least of each attached
  window. A seat first gets the screen so far: the program's modes and its last
  lines, from a ring of 64 KiB. Then it sees the output from its attach on, and
  one that falls behind skips ahead. A name opens no forward and runs no
  command. The names die with the shell, and each seat then exits 0. A shell on
  serve's own tty (--pty line or notify) is shared the same way: each seat sees
  the screen that serve draws. There, the EOF of the owner's channel no longer
  ends the shell's input: Ctrl-D or exit does.

  The owner deletes or rotates a name from a new channel of the same
  connection: the subsystem share@podssh reads one line. The line is rotate
  WHICH or delete WHICH, where WHICH is rw, ro or a whole name. rotate prints
  the new name, and the old one lets nobody in; delete prints what it deleted.
  Each seat that a name opened stays. A refusal is one line on stderr and exit
  status 1. Only the connection that holds the owner's shell may ask; a login
  under a name may not. With OpenSSH, open the first login with ControlMaster,
  then: echo rotate rw | ssh -S SOCKET -s HOST share@podssh.

  Under NAME, a login shell on a pty can outlive its client. podssh ssh's ~d
  keeps it under a name, and --attach NAME joins it again from a new login.
  Only the key that kept it finds it, by that name. serve's layer then names
  keep.v1, and podssh ssh offers ~d only where it does. env keep@podssh NAME
  before the shell keeps it as NAME if its client is lost with no ~d. Only a
  shell on a pty of the kernel is kept, and none with --share. A kept shell
  waits --keep-lease for a client (24 h by default, 30 days at most); env
  lease@podssh SECONDS asks for less. Its output with no client goes to a ring
  of 256 KiB, and an attach gets what came since the detach. A ring that
  dropped a part says how many bytes, and gives the rest from a clean boundary.
  One client has the shell at a time; --take takes it, and the other client's
  channel ends with a line. A key keeps 4 shells at most, and serve 32. At the
  end of a lease, serve hangs up the shell's process group, and kills it 10 s
  later. A job in a process group of its own, as job control makes, is the
  user's to leave behind, as under sshd. A shell that its client leaves with no
  ~d and no keep@podssh is hung up, as before.

  A kept shell's ticket is its key and its name: another key, or a name that
  this key does not keep, is refused alike. shells@podssh gives each shell's
  offset, the bytes of its output so far. Before an attach, env count@podssh
  OFFSET replays from the offset that the client has. An offset that the ring
  no longer holds, or env reset@podssh yes, gives a reset. serve says so on
  stderr, with the offset where it starts, then gives the last output from a
  clean boundary. serve decides the reset itself, so a gap never repeats. One
  attach at a time: a second one while the first catches up is refused with a
  line.

  An attach with no offset, or a reset, may come from a new terminal. serve
  first sends it the program's modes where the replay starts: the alternate
  screen, the keys, bracketed paste and the mouse. A reset's line goes before
  them and names an offset after them, so they never move a client's offset. An
  attach with no offset to a shell off the alternate screen also gets the
  ring's last screenful, as a reset: a shell at a still prompt draws nothing
  again. Once the client has the shell, serve sets the pty one row shorter for
  100 ms, then its size again. The program on it then draws its screen again.
  An offset that the ring holds gets the bytes alone.

  A stop or a restart of serve, or of its host, ends each kept shell: a process
  does not outlive either. serve writes the names of its kept shells to
  serve-NAME.kept beside its host key, mode 0600. The next start says which
  shells ended with the last run, and shells@podssh lists them as lost. Under
  --stdio no shell is kept: serve ends with its one connection. Under --listen
  none is kept either. --keep-lease with either is a usage error (64).

  POLICY: with --policy FILE, podssh serve judges each client's algorithms,
  before authentication. The file must say client policy = true; another is
  refused at the start (78). The policy reads the client's first KEXINIT: its
  key exchanges, host keys, and the ciphers, MACs and compressions it sends
  with. A mismatch, or a KEXINIT that does not read, ends the connection. The
  client gets a disconnect that names the policy, and no key logs in. One line
  on stderr names the client's address and each mismatch, as doctor does:
  FIELD: expected A,B, got C. A client offers no host key, so a size rule never
  refuses one.

  --audit-log FILE appends one JSON line for each event. They are serve's start
  and stop, a connection, a login accepted or refused, a session's start and
  end, and a forward opened, refused or closed. FILE is made with mode 0600;
  one that others may read, or another user's, refuses the start (78). Each
  line has the keys schema, time (UTC), level, event and fields. The fields
  name the run, the connection, the channel and the key's fingerprint. A
  session's end has its exit status or signal, the bytes each way and its
  duration. A line never holds a key, a token, a value of the environment or
  what a session sent. With --share it holds no login name, as a name of
  --share is the right to a shell. A command line is written only with
  --audit-commands, as it can hold a password. Each run's first line,
  serve.start, has a map of what it records. Each line's fields.prev is the
  SHA-256 of the line before it, so two serve processes append one chain.
  podssh serve --audit-verify FILE recomputes it, and prints the last line's
  SHA-256. It exits 0 when the chain holds, 65 when a line was changed, put in
  or removed, and 66 when FILE cannot be read. A command line in a run that
  declined to record one also fails it. The chain finds an edit, and does not
  stop one. A cut of the tail reads as a run with no serve.stop: keep the last
  hash off this host to find it. A write that fails, such as on a full disk, is
  said once on stderr, and no session stops.

  --totp FILE asks each key that passes for a one-time code too, as sshd with
  PAM asks for one. The key gets a partial success, then keyboard-interactive
  shows one prompt, One-time code:, with no echo. The code is RFC 6238's:
  HMAC-SHA-1, a step of 30 s, six digits, as authenticator apps and oathtool
  --totp -b compute it. A code of the step before or after now is taken too,
  for a clock that is off. A code is taken once: a second use, or an older code
  after it, is refused. Each failure of a key makes it wait longer before the
  next try: 1 s, then twice as long, at most 60 s. After three wrong codes on
  one connection, the client must sign with its key again. FILE holds the
  secret in base32 on one line, at least 80 bits; spaces and case do not count.
  A FILE that others may read, another user's, or no secret refuses the start
  (78). serve keeps the last step taken and each key's failures in FILE.used,
  mode 0600, under the lock of FILE. So two serve processes never take one code
  twice. A FILE.used that does not read refuses each code, and says to remove
  it. podssh serve --totp-new FILE makes a secret of 160 bits, mode 0600, never
  over a file that is there. It prints the path alone, and exits 0, or 73 when
  FILE cannot be made. Load the file's one line into an authenticator app. A
  name of --share logs in with no code, as the name alone is its right. serve's
  stderr and the audit log say a refused code and why, never the code or the
  secret.

  --gateway FILE makes serve a gateway in front of private hosts. The login
  name picks a route of FILE, a block that starts with route PATTERN (* and ?,
  case-sensitive) and gives on its own lines: upstream HOST:PORT (22 with no
  port; [IPv6]:PORT), host-key TYPE BASE64, the upstream's key, which serve
  pins; principal NAME, the user that serve logs in as there; ca-key FILE, a
  private key with no passphrase, mode 0600, beside FILE when its path is
  relative; one key TYPE BASE64 line for each key that may take the route; and
  source-address LIST where the upstream must see the gateway's address. The
  first route whose pattern matches decides; a key that it does not list is
  refused, and no later route is tried. A name that no route matches is
  refused: nothing maps to none. A key that is only offered never causes a
  dial. After the client signs with a key of the route, serve makes a fresh key
  and a user certificate of it by the route's CA. The certificate names the
  principal alone and is valid from 60 s before now to 30 s after. It permits a
  pty and port forwarding, nothing else. serve logs in at the upstream with it
  within 20 s. Its key id is podssh-gateway route=PATTERN user=NAME
  key=SHA256:..., which the upstream's log names. The upstream must trust the
  CA: TrustedUserCAKeys of a stock sshd, with the principal allowed for that
  user. An upstream whose host key is not the pinned one, or that refuses the
  certificate, refuses the login, and serve's stderr says why. Then each
  session is carried to the upstream, which answers it: pty, shell, exec,
  subsystem, env, window changes, signals and the exit status. So is each
  forward of -L, -D and -W; --accept-env and --no-forwarding hold at the
  gateway first. X11, agent forwarding and -R are refused. When the upstream's
  connection ends, so does the client's. SIGHUP reads FILE again; a file that
  does not read keeps the routes before. No private key of a user reaches the
  gateway; a copy of a route's CA key mints logins for that route's principal
  until the upstream stops trusting it. These refuse the start (78), with the
  file and its line: a FILE that others may write, that does not read, or that
  holds no route, and a ca-key that others may read. --gateway with a flag of
  serve's own sessions (--authorized-key, --authorized-keys, --shell, --pty,
  --motd, --shell-integration, --share, --keep-lease, --totp, --publish-remote,
  --remote-listen, --revoke-ends-sessions) is a usage error (64).

  --gateway net:NAME takes the routes of the gateway NAME from the net's signed
  document that this host holds (see podssh net). Its owner signs them with
  podssh net gateway set NAME FILE. FILE holds the blocks of a route file, but
  each ca-key is the CA's public key, TYPE BASE64. The CA's private key never
  leaves the gateway's host: name it with --gateway-ca FILE, repeated for each
  CA. A route whose CA is none of them is refused, with one line; the other
  routes are taken. With --net-url URL and --net-owner KEY, serve fetches the
  document as podssh node does. It fetches nothing at the start while the copy
  from URL is younger than --net-ttl. So a ProxyCommand's serve sends one GET
  each TTL, however many clients come. A fetch or a document that fails, a bad
  signature among them, keeps the routes in force, with one line. A newer
  serial that reads takes their place at the next look, each 5 s, or at SIGHUP.
  So does a section that the owner removed: nobody passes by it then. A section
  that this podssh does not read lets nobody in by it either. A document past
  its end, or a copy past --net-stale, refuses each login until a newer one
  comes. These refuse the start: no --gateway-ca (64), or a --gateway-ca,
  --net-url, --net-owner, --net-ttl or --net-stale with no net:NAME (64). So do
  no document, no route taken, or a document past its end (78). A file whose
  name begins with net: is given as ./net:NAME.

  serve NAME --print-unit prints a unit of systemd that runs serve NAME with
  these flags, each file by its absolute path, and writes nothing. It is a user
  unit; with --system --run-as USER, a system unit that runs as USER, with HOME
  and the login shell of USER's passwd entry. Its sessions run the user's
  programs, as sshd's do. So the unit leaves out each line of the node's
  hardening that would change what a session may do. A comment names each, with
  why. It keeps ProtectKernel*, ProtectClock, ProtectHostname,
  ProtectControlGroups and RestrictRealtime. serve installs nothing itself: put
  the unit in place by hand.

  The connection ends when the client leaves: exit 0, else 255 when it failed;
  a stop exits 0, as does a session that a reload ended. Without --stdio, NAME
  or --listen the run is a usage error (64). So are two of them, and --shell
  with --no-shell. On Windows it exits 70.

  Usage: podssh serve [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [NAME]
        the label of a stored pair (podssh relay pair NAME), whose node this
        serves through the relay, with no TARGET and no listener; not with
        --stdio.

  Options:
    --stdio
        serve one SSH connection on stdin and stdout, as sshd -i, for a
        ProxyCommand; nothing listens.
    --listen ADDR
        serve each SSH connection that comes on ADDR: PORT on 127.0.0.1,
        ADDR:PORT on an address of this host ([::1]:PORT for IPv6), or
        unix:PATH, a socket of mode 0600; may be repeated; never with
        PODSSH_LISTEN=no.
    --max-connections N
        with --listen: the connections at once, logged in or not; one more is
        refused with a disconnect, too many connections (default: 64).
    --pending-max N
        with --listen: the connections at once that have not logged in; one
        more is refused as with --max-connections (default: 16).
    --login-timeout SECS
        with --listen: the seconds from a connection to its login, 1 to 3600;
        past them it ends, told why, however busy the client is (default: 60).
    --host-key FILE
        the host key: an OpenSSH private key with no passphrase, made there
        (Ed25519, mode 0600) when missing, never overwritten (default:
        serve_host_ed25519_key in the cache).
    --authorized-key KEY
        a public key that may log in, as a line of authorized_keys: TYPE BASE64
        [COMMENT]; may be repeated.
    --authorized-keys FILE
        a file of authorized_keys lines; may be repeated (default, with no key
        flag: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).
    --accept-env PATTERN
        the names of a client's env requests that a session takes, with * and
        ?; may be repeated (default: LANG and LC_*); never LD_*, PATH, HOME,
        SHELL, ENV, BASH_ENV or IFS.
    --shell PATH
        the shell of each session and command, the only one tried: a start
        where it does not run is refused (default: SHELL, then /bin/sh,
        /usr/bin/sh, /bin/bash, /usr/bin/bash, /bin/ash, /bin/dash).
    --no-shell
        run no command and no shell: each such request is refused, and no shell
        is looked for.
    --pty MODE
        what a pty request meets where no pty opens: auto, a devpts instance of
        serve's own, then a tty whose calls serve answers (Linux); then serve
        as the line discipline on pipes (echo, editing, Ctrl-C to the command);
        notify, the tty that serve answers with no pty tried, else the request
        refused; line, the line discipline with no pty tried; no, the request
        refused (default: auto).
    --motd FILE
        the message of the day: shown before each login shell on a tty, never
        for a command, and not when ~/.hushlogin exists; at most 64 KiB, with
        no control character but tab and newline (default: /etc/motd, where it
        is there).
    --shell-integration
        mark each login shell's prompts and commands for the terminal (OSC 133)
        and its directory (OSC 7): bash and zsh on a pty by a start file of
        serve's own that reads the user's, which serve never writes; the
        prompts and lines of serve's line discipline (default: no marks).
    --publish-remote
        answer a client's -R (tcpip-forward) with a pair of the relay for each,
        at most 8 a connection, with no bind here (default: each -R is
        refused).
    --remote-listen
        answer a client's -R with a listener on this host's 127.0.0.1, at the
        port asked or one the system picks; where the bind fails,
        --publish-remote's pair if it is on (default: no listener).
    --no-forwarding
        open no forward: each direct-tcpip channel that a client opens is
        refused (default: each forward dials its host and port from this host).
    --revoke-ends-sessions
        a SIGHUP that takes a key out of the authorized keys ends that key's
        open sessions, and a key's expiry-time= ends them at its time; one line
        names each key (default: a session goes on under the rules it logged in
        with).
    --share
        offer each login shell on a pty by two names told once to its owner:
        one types in it, one watches it; each dies with the shell.
    --keep-lease TIME
        with NAME: how long a shell that its client detached (~d of podssh ssh)
        waits for a client, as 90s, 30m or 8h, 30 days at most; 0 keeps no
        shell (default: 24h).
    --policy FILE
        before authentication, judge each client's KEXINIT by the client policy
        in FILE (client policy = true); a mismatch ends the connection with a
        disconnect and one line naming the client and each mismatch.
    --audit-log FILE
        append one JSON line for each login, session, forward, start and stop
        to FILE, mode 0600, each line chained to the one before by SHA-256;
        never a key, a token, the environment or session data.
    --audit-commands
        with --audit-log: also record each command line, which can hold a
        password (default: a command is recorded without its words).
    --totp FILE
        after a key, ask for the one-time code of the secret in FILE (base32,
        mode 0600) by keyboard-interactive: RFC 6238, 30 s, six digits, each
        code taken once.
    --totp-new FILE
        make a new secret in FILE, mode 0600, never over a file that is there,
        print its path alone, and exit.
    --gateway FILE
        serve as a gateway: the login name picks a route of FILE, whose keys
        may take it. serve logs in at the route's pinned upstream by a
        certificate of its CA, and carries each session and forward there;
        nothing runs here. net:NAME takes the routes of the gateway NAME from
        the net's signed document that this host holds.
    --gateway-ca FILE
        with --gateway net:NAME: a CA's private key, mode 0600 with no
        passphrase, whose public half a route of the document names; may be
        repeated; a route whose CA is none of them is refused.
    --net-url URL
        with --gateway net:NAME: take the net's document from URL, an https://
        URL, as podssh node --net-url does: fetched at the start, unless the
        copy from it is younger than --net-ttl, then again each --net-ttl
        (default: NetUrl of the settings file).
    --net-owner KEY
        with --net-url: the owner that each document must have, its fingerprint
        SHA256:... or its public key (default: NetOwner of the settings file).
    --net-ttl SECONDS
        with --net-url: fetch the document again each SECONDS, 60 to 86400
        (default 300).
    --net-stale SECONDS
        with --net-url: read the copy for SECONDS more past --net-ttl while its
        server fails, 0 to 604800 (default 3600); past that, the gateway lets
        nobody in.
    --audit-verify FILE
        check the chain of the audit log FILE, print what it found and the last
        line's SHA-256, and exit: 0 when it holds, 65 when a line was changed,
        66 when FILE cannot be read.
    --print-unit
        with NAME: print a unit of systemd that runs serve NAME with these
        flags, on stdout, and write nothing: a user unit, or with --system
        --run-as USER a system unit.
    --system
        with --print-unit: a system unit,
        /etc/systemd/system/podssh-serve-NAME.service, that runs as the user of
        --run-as, with the hardening that leaves its sessions as sshd's.
    --run-as USER
        with --system: the user that serve runs as, a user of /etc/passwd other
        than root; the unit names its HOME and its login shell.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

podssh detached
  the runs that --detach and -f sent into the background, by their names: list
  them, the state of one, stop one.

  podssh detached list writes a line for each run in the background that this
  user started with -f or --detach. The runs are of podssh ssh, pipe and node,
  by their name: the name, its state (running; running, its supervisor gone,
  for a run of --restart whose supervisor ended; or ended), its pid and its
  words, with a tab between them. A run's name is its --detach-name, else its
  verb and its pid (ssh-4242), which no other running run has. So a run with no
  name is never refused. With no run, stdout stays empty and one line on stderr
  says that no run is known and names the directory read (none with -q). list
  --json writes one object instead: runs (each with its name, state, pid, a
  number or null, and words; [] for none) and dir, the directory read (null
  with no directory of the cache). The exit is 0.

  Each run holds the lock of its name, NAME.lock in the directory detached of
  the cache (see FILES), from before its connection to its end; with --restart
  its supervisor holds it, so that each restart keeps it, and the run that it
  starts holds NAME.run.lock. A second start of a name that runs refuses with
  75 before it connects, and names the pid that runs; so does a start of a name
  whose run of --restart outlived its supervisor. The system lets a lock go
  when its process ends, however it ends, so a run that crashed leaves no name
  taken. With PODSSH_CACHE_DIR set to none there is no lock: a line says so,
  and the run goes on, as a run that never starts locks its server out.

  status NAME writes the run's name, state, pid, verb, words, log and start,
  one to a line. With --restart, the pid is its supervisor's, and its run's is
  on a line of its own. A run of --restart also has the age of its last
  heartbeat (see podssh ssh); it exits 0 when the run runs, 69 when it does
  not. stop NAME sends SIGTERM to the holder of the name (a supervisor passes
  it to its run). After 10 s it sends SIGKILL to each holder still there, the
  supervisor first; on Windows it ends each at once (TerminateProcess), the
  supervisor first. It exits 0 once each lock of the name is free, and 69 when
  nothing of that name runs. It exits 75 when a lock is still held after the
  kill.

  Each reads the locks, never a pid alone: a run's record (NAME.json) stays
  after it ended, and the system gives its pid to another process, which a
  signal would reach. A pid is sent a signal only while the lock of its run is
  held, and it is the pid that the holder wrote there.

  Usage: podssh detached SUBCOMMAND [OPTIONS] [NAME]

  Arguments:
    [SUBCOMMAND]
        list, status or stop.
    [NAME]...
        the run's name: its --detach-name, else its verb and its pid, as podssh
        detached list shows it.

  Options:
    --json
        list: one JSON object on stdout: each run with its name, state, pid and
        words ([] for none), and the directory read.
    -q, --quiet
        list: no line on stderr when no run is known.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    the runs in the background, then the state of one, and its stop: each read
    from the run's lock, never a pid
        $ podssh detached list && podssh detached status lab && podssh detached stop lab

podssh update
  this binary from the newest release, its signature and its sum checked first;
  only when asked.

  podssh update replaces this binary with the release's binary for its own
  target, and only when asked: no other command looks for a release. It reads
  the newest release from GitHub's API, else from the releases' Atom feed,
  through HTTPS_PROXY when it is set: a prerelease only when this binary is
