  one, and never one older than this build. --version TAG takes that release,
  an older one too. --check stops before the binary: it names the release,
  checks its signature, and names the file that it would replace.

  Nothing is written before two checks. The release's SHA256SUMS against the
  signature that its workflow made with Sigstore (SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json):
  the certificate that Fulcio gave the workflow release.yml of this repository
  at that tag, by Sigstore's roots compiled into podssh. It also checks Rekor's
  record of the signature, with no other network. Then the binary's SHA-256
  against its line. The new binary goes beside the old one, with its mode. It
  runs there once, as podssh --version with no input, for 10 s at most: when it
  does not start on this host, or ends with another code than 0, it is removed
  and refused (65). So is one that names another version than the release's. An
  installed node would not start again with such a binary. Then the old one is
  kept as podssh.prev beside it (a hard link, else a copy). The new one goes
  over it in one rename; on Windows the running file is renamed to
  podssh.prev.exe first, else to podssh.exe.old, which the next run removes. A
  failure leaves the old binary as it was.

  --rollback puts back the binary that the last update kept, with no network:
  once podssh.prev answers --version here, it goes over this binary in one
  rename. This one is kept as podssh.prev in its place, so that a second
  --rollback goes forward again. A run that started before, as an installed
  node, goes on with its own binary until it starts again. With nothing kept
  the exit is 69; with a kept binary that does not run here, 65, and nothing
  changes; with --check or --version, 64.

  THE WAY BACK is the kept file itself: mv podssh.prev podssh puts it back with
  no podssh (on Windows, cmd /c move /Y podssh.prev.exe podssh.exe, which
  PowerShell runs too). The last line of an update names that command with its
  paths. --rollback is in 1.0.0-beta.4 and later: the line names it beside the
  move only when the binary now in place has it. The binary of an older
  release, which --version can install, refuses it as an unknown flag. The line
  of --rollback says the same of the binary that it put back.

  Once the binary is replaced, each node of --detach of this user that takes
  the signal of an upgrade is sent SIGUSR2. On Windows, its event of an upgrade
  is set. Such a node is one of each road but a carrier's, a temporary one and
  a quick tunnel's with the relay role behind it. It says so beside its record
  in the cache's detached directory. The signal goes while its run's lock is
  held and its record names its pid. The node takes the new binary with its
  sessions (see the notes of podssh node); a line names each. A node that is no
  run of --detach, as a unit of systemd, takes it by the signal USR2. kill or
  systemctl kill sends it to its process or its unit; until then, and after
  --rollback, a node goes on with its own binary.

  Exit 0 when the binary was replaced, or there was nothing to do; 69 when
  GitHub, the release or one of its files did not come; 65 when a check failed,
  the run of the new binary too; 73 when the binary could not be replaced, as
  in a directory that this user cannot write; 78 when no release has a binary
  for this system; 64 for a TAG that is no version. When Sigstore changes its
  roots, a binary of before refuses the new releases: download the release by
  hand, as its message says.

  Usage: podssh update [OPTIONS]

  Arguments:
    [ARGS]...

  Options:
    --check
        only say what an update would do: the release, its signature checked,
        and the file it would replace.
    --version TAG
        this release, as v1.0.0-beta.3, older than this build too; default: the
        newest, a prerelease only if this build is one.
    --ca-file FILE
        trust only the CAs in this PEM file for TLS to GitHub (default:
        SSL_CERT_FILE, else CaFile, else the system's).
    --rollback
        put back the binary that the last update kept beside this one
        (podssh.prev), once it ran here, and keep this one in its place; no
        network.
    --help
        Print help for this subcommand and exit.

  Examples:
    say what an update would do, its signature checked, then replace this
    binary with the newest release
        $ podssh update --check && podssh update

THE RELAY
  podssh opens a TLS connection to a relay host on port 443, and a WebSocket
  session for each connection. The relay opens the TCP connection to the
  target. Thus a host needs only one kind of egress: HTTPS to the relay hosts,
  directly or through the proxy. The default relay is tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev.

  Hosts
      With no --relay-host, no PODSSH_RELAY and no RelayHost in the settings
      file, podssh tries tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev first, then up to 3 hosts of
      its pool. The relay publishes the pool; podssh caches it, and fetches it
      again at the next token mint once it is 7 days old. Until a pool is
      cached, these hosts are the pool: tcp-us-east-1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev,
      tcp-eu-west-3.ssh.relay.ajam.dev, tcp-ap-southeast-1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev,
      tcp-azure-westeurope.ssh.relay.ajam.dev,
      tcp-us-central1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev, tcp-ap-south-1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev.
      Then up to 4 hosts of other deployments that a signed list names, each
      with its own token (see podssh relay).
  Failover
      Each host gets one attempt of 45 s or less, and each step (TCP, the
      proxy, TLS, the WebSocket upgrade) 20 s or less. An error that another
      host can repair goes to the next host. An error that each host would give
      (such as a refused target) stops each attempt at once. ConnectionAttempts
      repeats the whole round, after a random wait that starts near 1 s and
      doubles to near 30 s.
  --relay-failover MODE
      How the hosts are tried; also PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER, and the flag wins.
      staggered, the default: the next host starts when the one before it has
      not opened within 2 s, or at once when it failed; the first that opens is
      kept, and of two that opened together the earlier in the list. parallel:
      each host starts at once, and one that opened waits up to 2 s for the
      hosts before it. serial: one host at a time, each step of a host with a
      successor 5 s or less. A session that opened and is not kept is closed at
      once. One token is minted at a time for each deployment: an attempt waits
      up to 2 s for a mint in flight, then reads its token, or mints at its own
      host.
  A host that failed
      A relay host that failed with an error that another host can repair is
      tried last for 10 min. So is one that said nothing while a host after it
      opened. This holds in each run and each mode, also in a list that you
      named; a note says so, and no host is left out. So is a host whose last 2
      sessions were cut on its side within 300 s of their open, for 5 min. A
      cut on its side is the link lost, or the relay's close for it. A host
      that opened in the last 10 min, with no failure since and its last
      session not cut, is tried before the others. The record is
      relay-failures.json in the cache, for each road apart; a host that opens
      keeps its entry, with no failure. podssh status and podssh doctor show
      it.
  A process's sessions
      The sessions of one process that open against a relay host share a gate
      for it: while the host gave no failure, up to 8 attempts at once; after a
      failure that another host could repair, none for 1 s, then one probe at a
      time. Each probe that fails doubles the wait, up to 30 s. Any answer of
      the host opens the gate again: a session, a refusal by its policy, the
      relay's 502 for a target. A mint's Retry-After holds it longer, up to 300
      s. A session whose list has a next host goes on to it at once, with a
      line, HOST: waits N s after a failure of this process; trying the next
      host; at its last host it waits, which a line says too, as long as its
      ConnectTimeout lets it. The wait is no attempt, and never counts as a
      host that did not answer. Each new command starts with open gates; the
      record of failures carries what one run learned to the next.
  A dropped session
      podssh ssh tries a session again when the relay dropped it before any
      request reached the destination: during the SSH handshake or the login,
      before the command, the shell, the subsystem, -W's connection, -R's
      forwards or -N's wait. A drop of the link to the relay goes to the next
      relay host; a drop of the relay's link to the target tries once more. A
      close at the relay's limits (1001, 1009) or for a backlog (1013), and
      each drop after a request, end the run with 255. Each try says why on
      stderr; a try after the first asks nothing, so a login that needs a
      prompt then stops. The tries are at most ConnectionAttempts times the
      relay hosts.
  Tokens
      podssh mints a token from the relay (no account is needed), caches it,
      and mints a new one when the relay refuses a cached token.
      PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN replaces the mint. A token goes only into a request
      header to a relay host: never into output, a URL or a command line.
  Liveness
      podssh pings the relay every 10 s. After 3 checks in a row with no frame
      from the relay, the link is dead and the session ends. So a silent relay
      is found in 30 to 40 s. To a node, the resumable layer also sends a
      record when it sent nothing for 10 s, and the node does the same; a link
      that carries nothing from the node for 30 s is dead, and the session goes
      on over a new one.
  DNS
      Through a proxy, podssh sends host names and needs no DNS. With no proxy,
      it finds a relay's address in this order: an IP address in place of the
      name, --relay-addr and PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR, the system resolver. Next comes
      an address that carried a session to the host in the last 7 days
      (relay-addresses.json in the cache). Then DNS over HTTPS to 1.1.1.1,
      8.8.8.8, 1.0.0.1, 8.8.4.4, 9.9.9.9, 149.112.112.112 (by address), each by
      its JSON API where it has one. A server with no JSON API, or whose JSON
      does not read, is asked in RFC 8484's wire form. Last comes an older
      address that carried a session. An address of the cache that does not
      connect within 4 s hands over to the next source. TLS checks the relay's
      name at each address, so a wrong one fails the handshake; an address of
      the cache at which a host fails so, or as no relay would (the upgrade,
      another server's answer), is forgotten.
  Trust
      TLS is always verified, and no option turns the check off. With --ca-file
      or SSL_CERT_FILE, only that file is trusted. Else the trust store is the
      Mozilla roots in the binary (webpki-roots 1.0.12 of 2026-11-10), and
      podssh-ca.pem next to the binary. It also takes the roots of the system's
      stores, and the first system bundle. The stores are, on Windows, ROOT of
      the current user and of the machine. There a certificate is left out when
      a Disallowed store holds it, when it is not valid today, or when its
      usage leaves out servers. On macOS, the stores are the trust settings of
      the user and of the administrator, where security add-trusted-cert and an
      MDM profile put a root; elsewhere the roots are the bundle's. podssh
      doctor names each store with its count. A certificate that no root here
      signs ends with UnknownIssuer and what to do: a proxy that re-signs TLS
      needs its CA. Give it in --ca-file or SSL_CERT_FILE, which replace
      podssh's roots, or in podssh-ca.pem next to the binary, which adds to
      them. A certificate that has expired or is not valid yet ends with this
      host's clock and its reading: certificates are checked against it, and a
      wrong clock refuses each host. A system bundle adds roots and removes
      none: to stop trusting a root that Mozilla removed after this binary was
      built, give --ca-file or SSL_CERT_FILE with a current bundle. Else use a
      newer podssh. podssh doctor says when the roots in the binary are older
      than 12 months. podssh offers TLS 1.3 first, and TLS 1.2 with ECDHE and
      AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, for a proxy that intercepts TLS and speaks
      only 1.2; a server that speaks 1.3 gets 1.3, and a fall to 1.2 cannot be
      forced. There is no CBC suite and no RSA key exchange. Each hello names
      its host in the clear, unless PODSSH_ECH or ECH in the settings file asks
      for Encrypted Client Hello: then the name of a host that publishes a list
      in its HTTPS record goes sealed, over TLS 1.3 alone (see ENVIRONMENT).
  Idle limit
      The relay closes a session after 180 s with no traffic. podssh ssh sends
      a keepalive every 60 s. With OpenSSH, set ServerAliveInterval below 180.
      To a node, the resumable layer's records keep each link busy, and SSH
      sends no keepalive unless ServerAliveInterval is set.
  Session limits
      The relay ends a session after 64 MiB, both ways together, or after 12
      hours. podssh cp and mv count each session's bytes and age. Before 60 MiB
      or 690 minutes, they open a new session and go on at the offset of the
      copy. The new session keeps the host key and the login of the first;
      PODSSH_SESSION_BUDGET lowers the bytes. podssh ssh, whose connection is
      one, says once that a session passed 60 MiB. A link that the cap cuts
      after the remote exit status and before the output's end exits 255;
      podssh sftp says so at 80 % and at 95 % of 60 MiB (not with -q). To a
      node, the resumable layer moves the session to a new link at 48 MiB of a
      link or after 11 hours. -v prints a line for each move. A pair expires
      after 72 hours at most: podssh ssh node:// and podssh operator warn 60
      minutes before. The relay then ends each session of the pair, unless its
      owner renewed it on podssh relay serve (podssh relay pair --renew).
      --direct has no limit.
  The HTTP road
      For a proxy that ends TLS for the relay's name, refuses the WebSocket
      upgrade and still carries plain HTTPS requests. The road is taken when
      each relay host failed and the way to one of them refused the upgrade.
      That refusal is a page of the proxy's, or a 426 of a relay that got the
      request with its Upgrade taken off. podssh ssh, each command that reaches
      a server as it does, and podssh proxy then carry the session over
      requests of HTTP/1.1 to that host. podssh relay serve serves the road,
      with the same token, the same targets and the same limits as the
      WebSocket road. The split form comes first, on two connections on this
      road alone: the bytes up in numbered batches of 256 KiB at most, one POST
      after another. The bytes down come from their offset in a request that
      waits up to 25 s; the role holds 8 batches and 2 MiB down that the client
      has not acknowledged. An answer down ends a moment after nothing more
      came, or at 1 MiB. So a hop that holds an answer to its end holds a short
      one. Each request goes again, as it was, until an answer comes, for 60 s
      at most: a batch's number and an offset make it one that may come twice.
      The role names the batch that each answer stores, and the reason of each
      refusal (full, unknown session, not allowed); the last batch carries the
      count of the bytes up, and the target's end the count of the bytes down.
      A count that differs fails the session. When the second connection does
      not answer within 20 s, the serial form follows on the first: one POST
      after another, each with a batch up when one waits and the bytes down in
      its answer. A session's id goes in its paths, and its key in a header
      alone. A close of the road other than 1000 is said by podssh ssh as by
      podssh proxy: the leg that ended it, with its code and reason, before
      SSH's own line. The batches and the wait are the road's own, or smaller.
      They are smaller where podssh doctor --stream measured a cap on bodies or
      a quiet end on the path to that host (see FILES). The role's /relays.json
      names these limits in limits.http, which a client that does not know it
      ignores. podssh doctor's line forward names the road that carried its
      check: over a WebSocket, or over the HTTP road and its form, one, split
      or serial, with the road in its --json samples. PODSSH_HTTP_ROAD turns
      the road off, or names one form. Where the host's /relays.json names a
      third form, one (podssh relay serve's, over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2), it comes
      first: one POST whose body is the way up and whose answer, after a mark
      that comes at once, is the way down. It runs on one connection, for a way
      whose hops pass a body as it comes; a mark that does not come within 2 s
      means that a hop holds the body. The split form then follows, at once for
      the rest of the run. The resumable layer takes this road too. Where the
      way refuses the upgrade of a layer's link, that link and each later one
      go on the road. Each is a new session of the road, at
      /v1/http/open-layer/HOST/PORT, or /v1/http/one-layer/HOST/PORT in the one
      form. The relay gives its bytes to the layer as one link, so a cut
      session resumes on a new one. podssh says so in one line.
      PODSSH_HTTP_ROAD=no keeps each link an upgrade, and a form that it names
      is each link's form. The default relay serves no HTTP road.
  The WebSocket over HTTP/2
      Where a relay host offers it, as podssh relay serve does, a session is
      one stream of an HTTP/2 connection (RFC 8441). This holds for podssh ssh,
      each command that reaches a server as it does, and podssh proxy: podssh
      offers h2, then http/1.1, by ALPN, on a TLS connection of this road
      alone. Once the server's SETTINGS offer extended CONNECT, it asks for the
      session with a CONNECT whose :protocol is websocket. The CONNECT carries
      the path, the name and the token of the upgrade, the token in a field
      that HPACK never indexes; a 200 opens it, and another status is the
      relay's refusal, as for the upgrade. The sessions of one process share a
      connection, 16 at most. Each has a window of 1 MiB in a window of 16 MiB
      for the connection; another session opens another connection, and one
      with no session closes after 30 s. A lost connection is a lost link for
      each of its sessions. Where TLS chose http/1.1, the upgrade goes on that
      connection; where the SETTINGS offer no extended CONNECT, or HTTP/2 did
      not carry the CONNECT, that connection closes. The upgrade goes on a new
      one, and -v says why. The run then takes HTTP/1.1 to that host for 10
      minutes. PODSSH_H2 says which hosts take the road: by default a relay
      host that you named, and no host of the default relay, whose edge offers
      no extended CONNECT. podssh doctor's line http2 names what a host offers.
  QUIC to podssh's relay role
      A relay host that you named may offer QUIC in its /relays.json
      (forward.quic, as podssh relay serve --quic yes does). Where it does and
      no proxy is set for it, a session races QUIC on UDP before TCP. This
      holds for podssh ssh, each command that reaches a server as it does, and
      podssh proxy: first one packet of a version that no server speaks, to the
      host's first address of each family at that port. A server of QUIC
      answers it with its versions within 300 ms; then QUIC's handshake with
      the ALPN podssh-relay/1, checked as TLS is for the host's name. Then the
      upgrade of the session on one stream of the connection, with its path and
      its token. The relay's refusal is as on TCP. The TCP road starts 300 ms
      after QUIC, or at once where QUIC failed; the first session is kept and
      the other road is closed at once, and a refusal of the relay on either
      road ends the race. A host whose UDP failed is not tried over QUIC again
      by that run for 10 minutes. One whose QUIC answered is not probed again
      for as long. A connection keeps itself alive every 10 s and ends after 30
      s with no packet: a lost connection is a lost link, which the resumable
      layer resumes on any road. -v names the road: over QUIC. PODSSH_QUIC says
      which hosts race it: by default a host that you named and that offered
      it; no turns it off.

RETIRED VARIABLES
  A PODSSH_ variable that a release stopped reading is refused while it is set
  to a value that is not empty: podssh names it, says what took its place, and
  exits 78 before it connects; --help, --version and podssh man still answer. A
  service's file of variables (--env-file) that sets one is refused with its
  line, and --install leaves one out. A name that podssh never read is not
  refused, so a misspelt name is still ignored. Each name that a release
  stopped reading is listed below.

ENVIRONMENT
  https_proxy, HTTPS_PROXY, all_proxy, ALL_PROXY
      The proxy for each connection: an HTTP CONNECT proxy, as
      http://[USER:PASSWORD@]HOST:PORT (port 80 when none is given), with
      Basic, or Digest when the proxy asks for it; or a SOCKS5 proxy, as
      socks5:// or socks5h://[USER:PASSWORD@]HOST:PORT (port 1080), with the
      user and password of RFC 1929. The first one that is set is used, in this
      order. podssh sends host names to an HTTP proxy and to a socks5h://
      proxy, so it needs no DNS; to a socks5:// proxy it sends the address that
      it resolves, as curl does: write socks5h:// where this host has no DNS. A
      SOCKS5 proxy that takes no names gets one more try with an address. It
      never shows the proxy's credentials. SOCKS4 is refused. The iroh road and
      podssh ts take either kind, and send the host names to both.
  http_proxy, HTTP_PROXY
      Not used: they are for http:// URLs. podssh doctor says so when one of
      them is set and no variable above is.
  no_proxy, NO_PROXY
      Hosts to reach without the proxy, separated by commas: example.com also
      matches its subdomains, * matches each host, and a block ADDR/BITS
      (10.0.0.0/8, fd7a::/16) matches each address inside it, never a name. A
      loopback address never goes through a proxy.
  PODSSH_RELAY
      The relay hosts, as --relay-host. The flag wins. node://NAME and --exit
      NAME refuse it (78), saying that PODSSH_RELAY does not apply: the pair
      names its relay.
  PODSSH_RELAY_FAILOVER
      How the relay hosts are tried, as --relay-failover: staggered (the
      default), parallel or serial. The flag wins; another word is a
      configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_SSH_CONFIG
      The ssh_config file of podssh ssh, as -F: none reads no file. The flag
      wins. A process manager sets it once, also where the home cannot be
      written.
  PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR
      Addresses to use in place of DNS, as --relay-addr, after the flag's
      addresses.
  SSH_CONNECTION
      Set by sshd in a session: podssh node --temporary, which podssh ssh
      --upgrade starts there, stands in front of the server's address and port
      that it names; it is tried on the loopback first.
  PODSSH_SESSION_LOG
      A line for each session of podssh ssh and podssh proxy, at its end (see
      FILES): 1 or yes in the cache, an absolute path in that file, 0 or no for
      none; over SessionLog of the settings file; off by default. Another value
      is refused (78).
  PODSSH_ERROR_PROGRAM
      A program that gets a report when podssh itself fails, run as SSH_ASKPASS
      is: by its name, with no shell and no argument. Its stdin is one JSON
      object: schema (1), podssh, os, arch, verb, exit, messages (the last 64
      lines of podssh's own messages, 16 KiB at most); and relay (host, close
      code and reason, or null). A report never holds a token, a proxy URL or
      its password, a key, the environment, the command line or a byte of a
      session. These start no program: an exit 0, the status of a remote
      command or of a child that podssh passes on, and a stop by SIGINT or
      SIGTERM. Its stdout and stderr go to stderr; after 30 s podssh stops it.
      Its status is ignored, and the exit code stays the run's. podssh calls no
      AI service and no address for the report: the program decides.
  PODSSH_SETTINGS
      The file of podssh's own settings (see FILES), an absolute path that must
      exist; none reads none. The flags and the other variables beat the file.
  PODSSH_TIMEOUT
      The default of --timeout for each command that has the flag (podssh
      edit's with --no-terminal alone), as a whole duration such as 30s; the
      flag wins, and an empty value is no value. A bad value is a configuration
      error (78). For podssh operator, proxy and pipe, whose --timeout is
      another name of --ConnectTimeout, it bounds the session's open alone,
      held to a day; pipe reads it for a node: or relay: side where no side
      listens.
  PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN
      A relay token to use in place of one podssh mints. podssh never prints
      it.
  PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID, PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET
      A service token of Cloudflare Access, both or neither, for a cf://HOST
      destination behind Access: podssh sends them in the headers that
      cloudflared sends, never in a URL, and never prints them.
  PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_TOKEN, PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_TOKEN_FILE
      A token of Cloudflare Access for a cf://HOST destination, or the file
      that holds one: what cloudflared access token -app=https://HOST prints on
      a host where its login can run. The variable wins over the file; podssh
      never prints the token.
  PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID_FILE, PODSSH_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE
      The files that hold a service token of Cloudflare Access, its id and its
      secret, in place of the variables, which win. A file keeps the secret out
      of the environment. podssh --install carries these paths, and never the
      secret. The settings keywords AccessClientIdFile and
      AccessClientSecretFile give them too. A file that cannot be read is
      refused (78), and the line names the variable.
  PODSSH_NICK
      The nick of podssh chat, as --nick: the name that the peer sees. The flag
      wins.
  PODSSH_REPLAY_BUFFER
      With a node that offers the resumable layer, the bytes that podssh keeps
      in each direction until the node acknowledges them. They are kept so that
      a new link can send them again: a whole number of bytes, from 4194304
      (the default) to 16777216. When they are kept in full, podssh sends
      nothing more until an acknowledgement comes. Another value is ignored.
  PODSSH_PROGRESS
      line or off: the progress line of podssh cp, mv, scp, sftp and run on
      stderr, on or off whatever stderr is. With neither, the line shows when
      stderr is a terminal and -q is not given; where it is no terminal, podssh
      cp, mv and run write a plain line each 10 s once the run has passed 10 s;
      off silences that too; --jsonl gives progress objects instead.
  PODSSH_ZMODEM
      off: podssh ssh does not watch a session's output for ZMODEM (sz and rz
      of lrzsz), nor for podssh tx at the far end. The bytes go to stdout as
      they come. Else it watches in each session with a pty and a local
      terminal (see podssh ssh and podssh tx).
  PODSSH_SPARE_LINKS
      no: with a node that offers the resumable layer, podssh opens no spare
      link beside a link that went silent; it finds such a link dead after 30 s
      only (see podssh ssh). Else a spare link opens once the node has not
      answered for three round trips of the link: 1 s at least, 3 s at most.
      One opens each 10 s at most. This is not so on the iroh road, whose QUIC
      carries a session across a new address by itself.
  PODSSH_TITLE_STACK
      yes or no: whether the terminal keeps a stack of window titles (XTWINOPS
      22 and 23), where the notice of a silent node shows (see podssh ssh).
      With neither, podssh knows xterm and VTE by XTERM_VERSION and
      VTE_VERSION, and no other terminal.
  XTERM_VERSION, VTE_VERSION
      Set by xterm and by VTE: podssh ssh shows the notice of a silent node in
      the window's title of such a terminal, but inside tmux or screen. The
      title is saved first on its stack of titles.
  PODSSH_SESSION_BUDGET
      Lowers the bytes that podssh cp and mv carry in one relay session before
      they open a new one, for a relay with smaller limits: a whole number of
      bytes, 1048576 at least. It never raises the budget of THE RELAY's
      session limits; another value is ignored.
  PODSSH_SHELL_ID
      Set by a far end that keeps shells in each shell that it starts: the
      shell's id there. podssh ssh --attach sends it, so that the far end
      refuses to join a shell to a client that runs inside it.
  SSL_CERT_FILE
      Trust only the CA certificates in this file, as --ca-file. The flag wins.
  PODSSH_TS_TEST_CA_FILE
      For tests only: a PEM file of CA certificates that the node of podssh ts
      adds to its roots. With it, a test's control server of its own CA is
      reached with TLS checked. podssh ts says when it is set. Its checks
      before the start trust podssh's own roots, which take a podssh-ca.pem
      beside the binary.
  SSH_AUTH_SOCK
      The SSH agent's socket. On Windows, a named pipe; with none set, podssh
      tries the pipe of the OpenSSH agent, then Pageant when its window is
      there.
  SSH_ASKPASS, SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE, DISPLAY, WAYLAND_DISPLAY
      A program that asks for passwords and passphrases, chosen as OpenSSH
      chooses: SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force always uses it; prefer uses it when
      DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY is set; never does not use it. When
      SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE is not set, podssh asks on the terminal. It uses the
      program only when there is no terminal and DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY is
      set.
  XAUTHORITY
      The authority file of the X server of DISPLAY, whose cookie -Y forwards
      (else ~/.Xauthority).
  HOME, USERPROFILE
      The home directory, for ~ in file names (USERPROFILE on Windows when HOME
      is not set).
  PODSSH_USER, USER, LOGNAME, USERNAME
      The login name when none is given: the first of them that is set. With
      none set, the name of the effective uid's entry in the user database
      (/etc/passwd, read as a file; on macOS the system's directory), and root
      for uid 0 with no entry; -v says where the name came from. On a host with
      no name, a destination with no user is refused (64), with what was read
      and the ways to give one: user@host, -l, PODSSH_USER, USER or User in
      ssh_config. The same name is %u and Match localuser. It is also the nick
      of podssh chat when neither --nick nor PODSSH_NICK gives one, and the
      default comment of podssh keygen.
  USERDOMAIN
      On Windows, with USERNAME, the user DOMAIN\USER whose logon starts the
      task of podssh node --install.
  PODSSH_CACHE_DIR
      The directory of podssh's cache, tried before the others; none keeps no
      file, and a token is then minted on each run. A relative path is not
      used, and podssh says so. A directory that refuses a write is skipped,
      and podssh says why (see FILES).
  XDG_CACHE_HOME, LOCALAPPDATA, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, TMPDIR, TMP, TEMP
      Where podssh keeps its cache (see FILES).
  XDG_CONFIG_HOME, APPDATA
      Where podssh looks for its settings file, APPDATA on Windows (see FILES).
  PODSSH_DETACH_LOG
      podssh's own, for the run that a supervisor of --restart starts: the log
      that each of its runs writes, the supervisor's. Set by podssh; a user has
      no need to set it.
  PODSSH_SYSTEMD, DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS
      On Linux, whether a run in the background asks the user's systemd for a
      scope of its own once it is ready. With the scope, a logout does not end
      it: no asks nothing; yes asks outside a login session's scope too; unset
      asks only from a login session's scope. It asks on the user's bus that
      DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS names (unix:path= only), else on
      XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus, else on systemd's own socket there.
  PODSSH_DETACH_NAME, PODSSH_DETACH_SUPERVISOR
      podssh's own, for a run in the background (see podssh detached): its
      name, which --detach-name gives. In each run that a supervisor of
      --restart starts, also the supervisor's pid, so that the run holds its
      own lock beside the name's. Set by podssh, and removed from a run that
      --detach starts; a user has no need to set them.
  PODSSH_LISTEN
      no: podssh pipe listens on nothing, and unix-listen:, tcp-listen:,
      http-listen: and ws-listen: exit 78 before any bind; so do podssh session
      start and serve. Else they listen where the bind works.
  PODSSH_MPTCP
      yes: with --direct and no proxy, ask Linux for Multipath TCP. Where the
      server speaks it too, it can carry a connection on after one of two
      networks of this host goes. Where the kernel offers none, a proxy carries
      the connection or the server does not speak it, the connection is plain
      TCP; -v says which. no, or unset, asks for nothing; another value is
      refused before the connection, as a configuration error (78; podssh ssh
      exits 255).
  PODSSH_SK_DEVICE
      The security key (FIDO2) that podssh keygen, podssh ssh and podssh agent
      use: a path of /dev/hidraw* on Linux. none: podssh uses no security key,
      and each use says so. Unset: on Linux each FIDO device of /dev/hidraw*
      that this user may open, on Windows the one that the person chooses in
      Windows' dialog.
  PODSSH_OFFLINE
      Forbid each network connection. Test suites set it. podssh doctor then
      shows the network checks as one ???? line.
  PODSSH_IAP_TOKEN_FILE
      The file of the token of an iap:// destination, which must be private
      (chmod 600): a token that gcloud auth print-access-token printed, read
      again for each link of the session; this way, a token written there later
      serves a new link; or the JSON key of a service account (gcloud iam
      service-accounts keys create). For it podssh asks Google's token
      endpoint, oauth2.googleapis.com, for a token, with a JWT that it signs
      (RS256), and renews the token before its end; or the credentials of
      gcloud auth application-default login. The token goes in the upgrade's
      Authorization header alone; podssh never prints it. A file that cannot be
      read, or holds no token, is a configuration error (78).
  GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
      Google's own variable for the file of a key: read as
      PODSSH_IAP_TOKEN_FILE is, when that one is not set.
  PODSSH_EICE_CREDENTIALS_FILE
      The file of the credential of AWS for an eice:// destination, which must
      be private: the JSON that aws configure export-credentials writes in its
      process format, or a shared credentials file, whose profile is
      AWS_PROFILE's, else default. podssh signs a new URL with it for each
      tunnel, good for 60 s, as aws-cli signs one; the URL carries the key's
      id, the signature and a temporary key's token; it is the one URL of
      podssh that holds a credential, and podssh never prints it.
  AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, AWS_PROFILE
      AWS's own variables: the shared credentials file, read for eice:// when
      PODSSH_EICE_CREDENTIALS_FILE is not set (else ~/.aws/credentials, when it
      is there); and the profile of either file (default when it is not set).
  PODSSH_WARP_ACCEPT_TERMS
      yes accepts Cloudflare's Terms
      (https://www.cloudflare.com/application/terms/), which a device of WARP
      needs: with it, the first warp:// destination registers one device with
      Cloudflare's API, api.cloudflareclient.com, else
      api.devices.cloudflare.com (PODSSH_WARP_API first), through the proxy; it
      keeps its record in the cache (see FILES); later runs read the record and
      register nothing. Unset, no or empty, a run with no record refuses (78)
      and names it. Another word is a configuration error (78). A build with
      the feature warp.
  PODSSH_WARP_TEAM_TOKEN_FILE
      The file of a team's token of a Cloudflare One organization, which must
      be private: the device registers in that organization (its header
      CF-Access-Jwt-Assertion), not as an anonymous one. Read at the
      registration alone; podssh never prints it.
  PODSSH_WARP_ENDPOINT
      WARP's endpoint of HTTP/2 as ADDRESS:PORT, in place of 162.159.198.2:443;
      the device's pinned key stays its own. The run tries it alone, not the
      endpoints of the device's record (the one that last opened,
      162.159.198.2:443, then the peers that WARP's API gave). The record keeps
      those as they were. Another value is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_WARP_API
      Another route to WARP's API, as https://HOST[:PORT] (a path of / at most,
      no user or query). It is tried before api.cloudflareclient.com and
      api.devices.cloudflare.com, for the registration and for each read of the
      device's record again: a compatible API, or a name that this host can
      reach. A route that is not reached gives way to the next; an answer, a
      refusal too, is the API's. The device's record keeps the route that
      answered, tried first after this one. Another value is a configuration
      error (78).
  PODSSH_WARP_PROBE
      no skips the probe of a WARP tunnel that has just opened: one TCP
      connection inside it to 1.1.1.1:443, whose answer must come back through
      it within 3 s, tried twice 700 ms apart; without it, a front door that
      takes TLS and relays nothing gives a tunnel whose streams go quiet. For a
      host where that target is filtered inside WARP; -v says that the probe
      was skipped. Unset, empty or yes keeps it; another word is a
      configuration error (78). A build with the feature warp.
  PODSSH_WARP_H3
      When WARP's road goes over HTTP/3, connect-ip with each IP packet in a
      QUIC datagram on UDP port 443; where a probe of UDP (one QUIC packet,
      answered within 300 ms) found that UDP passes: auto, the default, after
      the road over HTTP/2 failed to reach the endpoint (not after a refused
      device); first, before it; no, never. UDP goes through no proxy. Another
      word is a configuration error (78). A build with the feature warp.
  PODSSH_WARP_SERVER, PODSSH_WARP_SERVER_PIN
      A server of connect-ip over HTTP/3 (RFC 9484) that the user runs, as
      https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH], in place of WARP's endpoint: a warp://
      destination then needs no device, and the server assigns the address
      inside. Its certificate is checked by the roots of the trust, or pinned
      by PODSSH_WARP_SERVER_PIN, the SHA-256 of its DER in 64 hex digits
      (colons allowed). The probe of UDP waits 1.5 s. Another value is a
      configuration error (78). A build with the feature warp.
  PODSSH_TOR_PORTS
      The ports that a first hop of a tor:// destination may have, which Arti
      reaches through the proxy: a list such as 443,80, or any. Unset or empty:
      443 alone when a proxy is set, as a cage's proxy allows little more, and
      any port when none is. With PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES it does not hold. Another
      value is a configuration error (78). A build with the feature tor.
  PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES
      The file of the bridges of a tor:// destination, a bridge line a line as
      Tor gives them out; with or without the word Bridge of a torrc; # begins
      a comment. Arti's first hops are then these bridges alone, and
      PODSSH_TOR_PORTS does not hold. A line is a plain bridge, ADDRESS:PORT
      FINGERPRINT, or one of meek_lite or webtunnel, which podssh speaks
      itself, in this process, through the proxy: meek_lite sends Tor's bytes
      in POSTs to its url=, TLS to its front= with the front's name and Host
      the URL's host; WebTunnel upgrades at its url=, then carries raw bytes.
      Each TLS is checked with podssh's trust (--ca-file, SSL_CERT_FILE,
      CaFile, else the system's), and WebTunnel's cert= after that check, never
      in its place. Arti asks each line for the bridge's fingerprint, so a line
      with none is refused, the meek_lite line of Tor Browser among them; so is
      another transport (obfs4, snowflake), which would be another program.
      These are a configuration error (78): a line that does not read, or a
      file that cannot be read, holds no bridge or is longer than 64 KiB. A
      build with the feature tor.
  PODSSH_TOR_NETWORK
      The file of arti-client's configuration of another Tor network than Tor's
      own, as chutney writes it (arti.toml): a private network, whose
      authorities, caches and rules of paths replace Tor's; the cache's
      directories, the proxy and PODSSH_TOR_PORTS still hold. Its guards and
      its directory go apart from Tor's, under the cache's tor/networks/ by a
      digest of the file. Unset or empty: Tor's network. A file that cannot be
      read, or longer than 1 MiB, is a configuration error (78). A build with
      the feature tor.
  PODSSH_EICE_MAX_TUNNEL_DURATION
      The longest life of an eice:// tunnel, aws-cli's maximum tunnel duration:
      whole seconds from 1 to 3600, which an IAM policy may require; unset, the
      endpoint's own hour. podssh cp goes on in a new tunnel a twelfth of it
      before its end, 30 s at least. Another value is a configuration error
      (78).
  PODSSH_DERP_SERVER
      The DERP servers of the DERP road in place of Tailscale's fleets, as
      --derp-server: HOST[:PORT], separated by commas, in order; the port is
      443 when none is named. The flag wins; a bad value is a configuration
      error (78). podssh node --derp calls the first whose /derp/probe answers
      home; podssh ssh tries the rest after a ticket's server when the list
      holds that server.
  PODSSH_DERP_MAIN
      no: the DERP road keeps to Tailscale's four servers for tailcat. Unset,
      empty or yes: Tailscale's main DERP fleet follows them: one server of
      each region first, in the order of the regions, then the others; its
      servers are pod-services' list, read on its date; a node calls the first
      that answers home, and a client tries them after a ticket's server of
      either fleet. Another word is a configuration error (78). With
      PODSSH_DERP_SERVER or --derp-server it says nothing.
  PODSSH_DERP
      no: no DERP road that the user did not ask for: podssh node with no pair
      refuses as before, and podssh ssh node://NAME dials no ticket that it
      kept under NAME. --derp, --derp-ticket and derp:TICKET still take the
      road. Unset, empty or yes: the fallback is on; another word is a
      configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_TRANSIT
      The transit road of a pair, which podssh takes unasked: a magic-wormhole
      transit relay, Least Authority's wss://relay.mw.leastauthority.com by
      default. There a node of the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel
      waits for the pair's operators beside the pair's road. podssh ssh
      node://NAME meets it there when each other road failed. Its token and the
      proof of the pair come from the pair's connect token; the relay sees
      ciphertext. no: no transit road; a ws:// or wss:// URL: that relay in
      place of Least Authority's; unset, empty or yes: the default; another
      word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_CROC
      croc's relay road of a pair, the last fallback: croc's public relays
      behind croc-web's WebSocket bridge, the one that podssh's list of
      services names. There a node of the resumable layer and the end-to-end
      channel waits in a room of the pair beside the pair's road. podssh ssh
      node://NAME meets it there when each other road failed. Its rooms and the
      proof of the pair come from the pair's connect token; the relay sees
      ciphertext. no: no road; a ws:// or wss:// URL: that bridge (croc-web of
      your own, its query relay=N&port=P when it names one, else relay 0 and
      port 9009), which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn off; unset, empty or
      yes: the listed bridge, none while the list names none; another word is a
      configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_ZEROTIER
      ZeroTier's road of a pair, in a build with the feature zerotier, the last
      fallback after croc's: an ad-hoc network of the pair's own through
      ZeroTier Inc.'s roots and its TCP relay, the one that podssh's list of
      services names. There a node of the resumable layer and the end-to-end
      channel waits beside the pair's road. podssh ssh node://NAME reaches it
      there when each other road failed. The node's identity and the network
      come from the pair's connect token; the roots and the relay see
      ciphertext. no: no road; IP:PORT: that relay (ZeroTierOne's tcp-proxy of
      your own), which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn off; unset, empty or
      yes: the listed relay; another word is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_TOX
      Tox's relay road of a pair, in a build with the feature tox, the last
      fallback after ZeroTier's: a TCP relay of the Tox project's public nodes:
      the one that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks among those that
      podssh's list of services names. There a node of the resumable layer and
      the end-to-end channel waits beside the pair's road, under a key of the
      pair's connect token. podssh ssh node://NAME reaches it there when each
      other road failed; the relay sees ciphertext. no: no road; IP:PORT=KEY
      (the relay's key in 64 hex digits): that relay (c-toxcore's
      tox-bootstrapd of your own, with its TCP relay), which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT
      does not turn off; unset, empty or yes: the listed relays, none while the
      list names none; another word is a configuration error (78), which does
      not echo the value.
  PODSSH_YGGDRASIL
      Yggdrasil's road of a pair, in a build with the feature yggdrasil, the
      last fallback after the Tox road: a public wss:// peer of Yggdrasil's
      network, the one that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks among those
      that podssh's list of services names. Through it a node of the resumable
      layer and the end-to-end channel joins the network beside the pair's
      road. It joins under a key of the pair's connect token. podssh ssh
      node://NAME reaches it by that key when each other road failed; the peers
      see ciphertext, and an end routes for the network while the road is up.
      no: no road; a wss:// or ws:// URL: that peer (yggdrasil-go of your own,
      with that Listen), which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn off; unset,
      empty or yes: the listed peers, none while the list names none; another
      word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_HYPERDHT
      HyperDHT's road of a pair, in a build with the feature hyperdht, where
      UDP passes, after Yggdrasil's road: the DHT that the bootstrap nodes of
      podssh's list of services reach. There a node of the resumable layer and
      the end-to-end channel announces a topic beside the pair's road; the
      topic is of a key of the pair's connect token. podssh ssh node://NAME
      connects to it by that key, a hole punched through both NATs, when each
      other road failed; the DHT's nodes see the two ends' addresses, and the
      channel keeps the bytes. no: no road; HOST:PORT[,HOST:PORT...]: the
      bootstrap of a DHT of your own, which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn
      off; unset, empty or yes: the listed bootstrap, none while the list names
      none; another word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the
      value.
  PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY
      Syncthing's relay road of a pair, in a build with the feature strelay,
      the last fallback after HyperDHT's road: a relay of Syncthing's pool on
      443, the one that the SHA-256 of the pair's name picks among those that
      podssh's list of services names. There a node of the resumable layer and
      the end-to-end channel joins beside the pair's road, under a certificate
      of the pair's connect token. podssh ssh node://NAME asks for it there
      when each other road failed; the relay sees ciphertext. no: no road;
      relay://IP:PORT/?id=DEVICE-ID: that relay (Syncthing's strelaysrv of your
      own), which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn off; unset, empty or yes:
      the listed relays, none while the list names none; another word is a
      configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_SMEE
      The smee.io road of a pair, the last fallback after the onion road, for a
      proxy that refuses the WebSocket upgrade: channels of smee.io's server,
      named from the pair's connect token. There a node of the resumable layer
      and the end-to-end channel reads its door beside the pair's road. podssh
      ssh node://NAME posts a hello there when each other road failed; each way
      of a link is a POST for each frame and a stream of server-sent events
      back, and the server sees ciphertext. no: no road;
      https://HOST[:PORT][/PREFIX]: that server (smee.io's server of your own),
      which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does not turn off; unset, empty or yes: the
      server of podssh's list of services, none while the list names none;
      another word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the
      value.
  PODSSH_ONION
      The onion road of a pair, in a build with the feature tor, the last
      fallback after Syncthing's relay road: an onion service of the Tor
      network, Arti's in podssh's process through the Tor road (its proxy,
      PODSSH_TOR_PORTS, PODSSH_TOR_BRIDGES and PODSSH_TOR_NETWORK hold). There
      a node of the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel waits beside the
      pair's road. podssh ssh node://NAME reaches it there when each other road
      failed. The service's key stays in the node's own directory of the cache,
      so its address stays; its descriptor is of restricted discovery, readable
      only with a key that both ends make of the pair's connect token. The
      node's line says its address, which a node of this host keeps under its
      NAME. no: no road; an onion address (56 letters of base32 and .onion):
      the node's, for a client on another host, which PODSSH_LAST_RESORT does
      not turn off; unset, empty or yes: the road, with the address of the
      node's record of pkarr, else the one kept under NAME; another word is a
      configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_ZEROTIER_PLANET
      A file of a ZeroTier planet (zerotier-one's planet, or one that mkworld
      made) whose roots ZeroTier's road joins in the place of ZeroTier Inc.'s.
      Then no root of a third party carries it. A file that cannot be read, or
      that is empty or over 16 KiB, is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_PIPING
      The Piping Server road of a pair (podssh node NAME, podssh ssh
      node://NAME), for a proxy that refuses the WebSocket upgrade: a POST and
      a GET of plain HTTPS for each way of a link, on paths that the pair's
      secret gives; under the resumable layer and the end-to-end channel. Unset
      or empty: the fallback that podssh takes, through https://ppng.io, then
      https://piping.onrender.com where ppng.io fails (a node waits at the
      first that answers; a client that meets no node at one tries the next): a
      node serves it alone once a probe at its start finds the upgrade to the
      relay refused on the way; a client tries it once the pair's road found
      the same. no: no such road. yes (the same servers), or
      https://HOST[:PORT][/PREFIX] of a Piping Server (that server alone): the
      road as asked, which a node serves beside the pair's road and a client
      races 250 ms after it; with --plain, --no-e2e or a udp: TARGET the node
      refuses it (64). Another word is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_OPENTUNNEL
      The OpenTunnel road, which podssh takes unasked for a node with no other
      road: a blind TLS tunnel with no account, https://opentunnel.xyz by
      default. It is the road of podssh node --opentunnel and podssh ssh
      node://NAME --opentunnel-name. It is also the road of podssh funnel
      --opentunnel, which a funnel that the quick tunnel cannot carry takes
      unasked. no: no such road, and the flags are refused (64); an
      https://HOST[:PORT] URL: that service in place of OpenTunnel's, whose
      certificates the trust of --ca-file checks; unset, empty or yes: the
      default. Another word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo
      the value.
  PODSSH_PINGGY
      The Pinggy road, a last fallback: a TLS tunnel of Pinggy's free tier with
      no account. Its node's leg is SSH on port 443, raw, else inside TLS that
      the host's trust verifies. Its client's TLS pins the node's key. It is
      the road of podssh node --pinggy and podssh ssh node://NAME --pinggy-name
      HOST#PIN, which a node with no other road serves unasked. no: no such
      road, and the flags are refused (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of
      Pinggy's protocol in place of Pinggy's, whose host key nobody names;
      unset, empty or yes: Pinggy's own. Another word is a configuration error
      (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_SERVEO
      The Serveo road, a last fallback: a private alias at Serveo with no
      account, derived from the node's key. Its node's leg and client's hop are
      raw SSH on port 443, then 22. It is the road of podssh node --serveo,
      which a node with no other road serves unasked after the Pinggy road. It
      is also the road of podssh ssh node://NAME, which a client with a key of
      the node races last but for the ssh-j road. no: no such road, and the
      flag is refused (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of Serveo's protocol,
      whose host key nobody names; unset, empty or yes: the server that
      podssh's list of services names, and none where it names none. Another
      word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_SSH_J
      The ssh-j road, the last fallback: ssh-j.com, a public SSH jump and
      forwarding server with no account on port 22. It is the road of podssh
      node --ssh-j and podssh ssh node://NAME; the node and the client derive
      the node's name there from its key; a node with no other road serves it
      unasked after the Pinggy road and the Serveo road. no: no such road, and
      --ssh-j is refused (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of the same protocol,
      whose host key nobody names; unset, empty or yes: ssh-j.com where
      podssh's list of services names it, else no server, and --ssh-j is a
      configuration error (78). Another word is a configuration error (78),
      which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN
      The localhost.run road, a last fallback: a tunnel of HTTP made by ssh -R
      with no account, SSH on port 22 as nokey with the forward of port 80. It
      is the road of podssh node --localhost-run and podssh ssh node://NAME
      --tunnel-url https://HOST. A node with no other road serves it unasked
      after the ssh-j road, before the localtunnel road. no: no such road, and
      the flags are refused (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of the same shape,
      whose host key nobody names; unset, empty or yes: localhost.run where
      podssh's list of services names it, else no server, and --localhost-run
      is a configuration error (78). Another word is a configuration error
      (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_SANDHOLE
      The Sandhole road, a last fallback: the localhost.run road's shape at
      Sandhole's public server: SSH on port 443, then 22, with a key made for
      the login alone and the forward of port 80. It is the road of podssh node
      --sandhole and podssh ssh node://NAME --tunnel-url https://HOST of a name
      under its tunnels' zone. A node with no other road serves it unasked
      after the localhost.run road. no: no such road, and the flags are refused
      (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of the same shape, whose host key nobody
      names; unset, empty or yes: demo.sandhole.com.br where podssh's list of
      services names it, else no server, and --sandhole is a configuration
      error (78). Another word is a configuration error (78), which does not
      echo the value.
  PODSSH_BARE
      The Bare hop, the last fallback of all: podssh ssh node://NAME reaches
      the tunnel's name of the localhost.run or Sandhole road through a Bare v3
      node, once each road before it failed; this way, a proxy sees the node's
      name alone; the node dials the name itself and sees it, and the
      end-to-end channel keeps the bytes. No relay token goes to it. no: no
      such hop; an https:// URL: that node; unset, empty or yes: the node of
      the kind bare-node of podssh's list of services, else none. Another word
      is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_HOSTC
      The hostc road, a last fallback, after the Sandhole road and before the
      localtunnel road: hostc's public server with no account, of podssh node
      --hostc; the node asks it for a tunnel over HTTPS and keeps one WebSocket
      to it, both on 443 by name through HTTPS_PROXY; the name is random; so a
      client takes it as a tunnel's name of the localhost.run road (podssh ssh
      node://NAME --tunnel-url https://HOST, or the node's record); this
      variable is its switch. A server that answers 426 speaks a newer version
      of hostc's protocol than this podssh: the road ends, and the next road
      goes on. no: no such road, and --hostc is refused (64); an https:// URL,
      or http:// on this host's loopback: that server of hostc's protocol;
      unset, empty or yes: hostc's where podssh's list of services names it,
      else no server, and --hostc is a configuration error (78). Another word
      is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL
      The localtunnel road, a last fallback, before the bore road:
      localtunnel's public server with no account, of podssh node --localtunnel
      and podssh ssh node://NAME; the node and the client derive the node's
      name there from its key; the node needs an egress that reaches the port
      that the server names, its client port 443 alone; a node with no other
      road serves it unasked after the localhost.run road. no: no such road,
      and --localtunnel is refused (64); an https:// URL, or http:// on this
      host's loopback: that server of localtunnel's protocol, whose tunnels are
      names under its own; unset, empty or yes: localtunnel's where podssh's
      list of services names it, else no server, and --localtunnel is a
      configuration error (78). Another word is a configuration error (78),
      which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_BORE
      The bore road, the last fallback: bore.pub, a public server of bore's
      protocol that gives a TCP port with no account. It is the road of podssh
      node --bore and podssh ssh node://NAME; the node and the client derive
      the node's public ports there from its key; raw TCP to the control port
      7835 and to the port; so a proxy that allows 443 alone leaves the node
      out; the client then reaches the port through the forwarders that the
      binary names; a node with no other road serves it unasked after the
      localtunnel road. no: no such road, and --bore is refused (64);
      HOST[:PORT]: that server of bore's protocol, at its control port (7835
      where none is named); unset, empty or yes: bore.pub where podssh's list
      of services names it, else no server, and --bore is a configuration error
      (78). Another word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the
      value.
  PODSSH_PINGGY_TRACE
      1: the Pinggy road says each visitor's bytes each way every 5 s while it
      lives, on the node's stderr. It says each link's on the client's with -v,
      with a write that waits and since when. So a run that stalls names the
      side where the bytes stop. The node says each visitor's end, why and its
      bytes each way, with or without it. Unset or another value: no such
      lines.
  PODSSH_FRP
      The file of the frp road, the user's own frps: a private file with a line
      each: server (frp://HOST[:PORT] or wss://HOST[:PORT][/PATH]), token
      (frps's) and secret (the node's STCP service's); and name where the
      service is not the node's NAME; user (frpc's user, which a visitor logs
      in as); and for a visitor alone owner (frpc's serverUser) and plain (a
      real frpc's service of an sshd; SSH reaches it on the visit itself, with
      no end-to-end channel). podssh node NAME TARGET serves the road with it
      when --frp names no file. podssh ssh node://NAME races the road once each
      road before it failed, or takes the plain service alone. Unset or empty:
      no frp road. A file that does not read is a configuration error (78),
      which names its line and never its text.
  PODSSH_RELAY_LAYER
      yes: podssh proxy and podssh ssh, and each command that logs in as podssh
      ssh does, read the /relays.json of the first relay host. Where it offers
      the resumable layer (forward.layer, which podssh relay serve gives), they
      carry the session in it to that host alone. Or they carry it to the
      process that it names as forward.host, of its deployment: the relay keeps
      the connection to the target while this host's link is lost, for 10
      minutes unless it says otherwise. A new link resumes the session, which a
      line on stderr says. A host that offers none takes the contract's road,
      with one line. So does a host with no room for a new resumable session;
      so does one whose first link fails for a reason that another host may not
      share; so does podssh ssh --no-resume. Unset or empty: the same where the
      first host offered the layer within a day, with no line where it is not
      there: each read of a host's offer is kept in the cache for a day
      (relay-offer-HOST-PORT.json). For a relay host that the user named whose
      offer is not kept, its /relays.json is read once, 1 s at most, before the
      session; the default relay's offer comes with the refresh of its pool
      alone. A kept offer whose host answers 404 for the layer is forgotten,
      with one line, and the contract's road carries the session. no: the
      contract's road, with no request more. Another word is a configuration
      error (78).
  PODSSH_RELAY_RANK
      no (or off, 0): the default relay hosts go in the order of /relays.json,
      with no rank. Unset or another word: when a rank of podssh relay rank
      holds for this egress (24 h): the default list is the default host and
      the best three other hosts of the pool, in the rank's order; the default
      host is at its place among them; where none holds, the times of each
      run's own race, the last 8 of each host, order the pool. A list that the
      user named keeps its order, and a host that failed lately goes last over
      its rank. auto: the same; and a session of podssh ssh on the default list
      ranks the hosts in its background when no rank holds for this egress;
      once a day, 8 hosts, one probe each 10 s at most, each with ?dial=lazy;
      never unless asked. The settings file's RelayRank yes, no or auto says
      the same, below the variable: a variable that is set, and not empty,
      wins.
  PODSSH_RELAY_KEYS
      More keys to trust for a signed list of relay deployments: KEY[,KEY...],
      each SHA256:... as ssh-keygen -l shows an Ed25519 key, or its 64 hex
      digits; an example is the key that podssh relay serve --deployment names
      on its first line. They add to the keys compiled in, the settings file's
      RelayKeys and the members of your net with the role relay. A list that
      /relays.json carries, signed by one of them, adds its deployments' hosts
      after the default list, each with a token of its own; a list of another
      key, with a changed byte, past its not_after or older than the list kept
      is not used. none trusts no key, those compiled in too. A word that is no
      key is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_RELAY_RANK_PACE
      For tests only, and read only by a build with debug assertions, never by
      a release binary: DELAY_MS,GAP_MS: the wait of a rank in a session's
      background after the session opened, and between the starts of two of its
      probes. They are in place of 60 s and 10 s, so that a test of the bounds
      runs in seconds.
  PODSSH_DIRECT
      no: when each relay host failed, podssh ssh ends with the relay's
      failure, as with --relay-host, and does not try the direct road. So does
      each command that reaches a server as it does (cp, each, job, health,
      containers, ping, pipe ssh:). Unset, empty or yes: with no relay named
      (no --relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost), the direct road is tried
      once, as --direct dials it. It uses the family of -4 or -6 when one is
      given, and goes through HTTPS_PROXY when one is set. It is also tried
      after a relay that closed a session to an IPv6 target before any byte.
      The server's version line must come within 10 s. The settings file's
      Direct says the same, below the variable; another word is a configuration
      error (78).
  PODSSH_CLEARTEXT
      no: no cleartext road: when each relay host failed, and the TLS of one
      failed on the way: by its certificate, a reset or a close in the
      handshake, or its bound. Then podssh ssh, each command of its road,
      podssh proxy and podssh pipe end with the relay's failure. The fallback
      to the forwarders that podssh names then tries no ws:// form of them.
      Unset, empty or yes: the road is tried last, a host of each deployment
      once, through HTTPS_PROXY as each road dials: a token of one session,
      minted in cleartext (POST /v1/mint?once=1) and never cached, then the
      upgrade with it, which each hop can read; no other token goes there.
      Another word is said in a line, and the road is not tried.
  PODSSH_HTTP_ROAD
      The HTTP road (see THE RELAY): when each relay host failed and the way to
      one of them refused the WebSocket upgrade: podssh ssh, each command that
      reaches a server as it does, podssh proxy and relay: of podssh pipe carry
      the session over plain HTTPS requests to that host. podssh relay serve
      serves these requests. Unset, empty, auto or yes: the one-POST form where
      the host's /relays.json names it (one connection, the bytes both ways in
      one request; a way that holds its body takes the split form within 2 s,
      and for the rest of the run); then the split form, then the serial form;
      split, serial or one: that form alone; no: no such road. Another word is
      a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_H2
      The WebSocket over HTTP/2's extended CONNECT (see THE RELAY), for podssh
      ssh, each command that reaches a server as it does, and podssh proxy: the
      sessions of one run to a relay host as streams of one TLS connection.
      Unset, empty or auto: offered to a relay host that you named
      (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost), as podssh relay serve offers
      it; and to no host of the default relay, whose edge offers no extended
      CONNECT; yes: offered to each relay host, where one whose HTTP/2 offers
      none costs one more connection in a run; no: the upgrade of HTTP/1.1
      alone, as before. Another word offers it to none, and podssh doctor's
      line http2 fails with it.
  PODSSH_H2_SHAPE
      The shape of this client's HTTP/2: its SETTINGS and their order, the
      window, the fields' order, PRIORITY and padding. existing is the road's
      own, browser is Chrome's, firefox is Firefox's; PRIORITY and padded DATA
      are recorded and not sent through h2 0.4. The road is podssh-ws's
      h2_road; the default session road, the WebSocket upgrade, does not read
      it.
  PODSSH_VLESS_EARLY_DATA
      Early data on the VLESS road: 0rtt announces the link's ed size while its
      nonce is new, 1rtt is the fallback from the start, off (the default)
      offers none. A nonce used twice in 10 minutes is refused and the session
      stays at 1-RTT; another word is a 78.
  PODSSH_QUIC
      QUIC to podssh relay serve (see THE RELAY), for podssh ssh, each command
      that reaches a server as it does, and podssh proxy: a session raced over
      QUIC on UDP first, then over TCP. Unset, empty or auto: to a relay host
      that you named (--relay-host, PODSSH_RELAY or RelayHost) whose
      /relays.json offered QUIC (forward.quic); that offer is kept for a day,
      as its offer of the resumable layer is; yes: to each relay host, at the
      port that it offered, else at its own; no: never. In each case only where
      no proxy is set for the host, as no HTTP proxy carries UDP; and never
      with a TLS configuration that a caller of the library gave. Another word
      races QUIC to none.
  PODSSH_FORWARDER
      The forwarders of podssh ssh, of each command that reaches its server as
      podssh ssh does, and of podssh proxy, as --forwarder: other products'
      WebSocket forwarders, templates, Wisp servers (wisp+wss://) or the words
      mudlet, ssheasy, mudix and wisp, in order, in place of the relay. The
      flag wins, and so do --relay-host and --relay-failover; beside
      PODSSH_RELAY, or with a bad template, it is a configuration error (78).
      An empty value is no value.
  PODSSH_FORWARDER_FALLBACK
      no: when each relay host failed, podssh does not try the forwarders that
      it names (mudlet, ssheasy, mudix, then the Wisp demo server, wisp); yes,
      the default, tries them, 10 s at most each, where the relay was podssh's
      own choice and no relay host answered about the target. Its 502, or its
      refusal of the target by policy, ends the run. Over ForwarderFallback of
      the settings file; another word is a configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_PROXY_LISTS
      no: podssh does not ask the public lists of proxy nodes for a node to
      carry the session of podssh ssh. That ask comes when each relay host,
      each forwarder and each ws:// form failed. The nodes are VLESS, Trojan
      and VMess's AEAD form, which anonymous operators run; the lists are the
      services of the kind proxy-list of pod-services. It is never asked for a
      pipe of podssh proxy, whose stream a node could read. yes, the default,
      tries at most 16 nodes, 12 s each, as the last fallback, where the same
      conditions as the forwarders' hold; one line names the lists' hosts and
      says that the target goes to a third party that nobody vouches for; the
      line of the node that carries names its host. SSH and its host key keep
      the session's bytes private. These nodes are never tried: a node that is
      not on 443 with TLS, or that fronts another name than its host; one that
      sits under a school's, a church's or a government's suffix; one that is
      at a private address. PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no turns this off with the other
      last fallbacks. Another word is no.
  PODSSH_LAST_RESORT
      no: turns off each last fallback that sends the target to a public
      service of a third party that nobody vouches for. These are the public
      proxy nodes, PODSSH_PROXY_LISTS; the Pinggy road, PODSSH_PINGGY; the
      Serveo road, PODSSH_SERVEO; the ssh-j road, PODSSH_SSH_J; the
      localhost.run road, PODSSH_LOCALHOST_RUN; the Sandhole road,
      PODSSH_SANDHOLE; the srv.us road, PODSSH_SRV_US; the tunnl.gg road,
      PODSSH_TUNNL_GG; the Bare hop, PODSSH_BARE; the hostc road, PODSSH_HOSTC;
      the localtunnel road, PODSSH_LOCALTUNNEL; the bore road, PODSSH_BORE;
      croc's relay road, PODSSH_CROC; ZeroTier's road, PODSSH_ZEROTIER; Tox's
      relay road, PODSSH_TOX; Yggdrasil's road, PODSSH_YGGDRASIL; HyperDHT's
      road, PODSSH_HYPERDHT; Syncthing's relay road, PODSSH_SYNCTHING_RELAY;
      the onion road, PODSSH_ONION; the smee.io road, PODSSH_SMEE; the file
      hosts' road, PODSSH_FILEHOSTS; and the roads that join them. yes, the
      default, leaves each to its own variable. Another word is no.
  PODSSH_VIA
      The forward proxy over TLS of podssh ssh, of each command that reaches
      its server as podssh ssh does; and of podssh proxy and podssh doctor, as
      --via: https://[USER@]HOST[:PORT], in place of the relay. The flag wins,
      and so do --relay-host, --relay-failover, --forwarder and --shadowsocks;
      beside PODSSH_RELAY or PODSSH_FORWARDER, or with a URL that cannot be
      read, it is a configuration error (78). An empty value is no value.
  PODSSH_VIA_AUTH_FILE
      The credentials file of the proxy of --via or PODSSH_VIA, as
      --via-auth-file, which wins: a private file, one line, USER:PASSWORD, or
      the password alone when the URL names USER (see FILES).
  PODSSH_VIA_HTTP
      1.1 or 2: the one version of HTTP that podssh offers the proxy of --via
      by ALPN; a proxy that does not take it is refused. Unset, empty or auto
      offers h2, then http/1.1, and the proxy chooses. Another word is a
      configuration error (78).
  PODSSH_WSTUNNEL
      The wstunnel server of podssh ssh, of each command that reaches its
      server as podssh ssh does, and of podssh proxy, as --wstunnel:
      wss://HOST[:PORT] or ws://HOST[:PORT], in place of the relay. The flag
      wins, and so do --relay-host, --relay-failover, --forwarder,
      --shadowsocks and --via; beside PODSSH_RELAY, PODSSH_FORWARDER or
      PODSSH_VIA, or with a URL that cannot be read, it is a configuration
      error (78). An empty value is no value.
  PODSSH_WSTUNNEL_SECRET_FILE
      The secret file of the server of --wstunnel or PODSSH_WSTUNNEL, as
      --wstunnel-secret-file, which wins: a private file of path-prefix PREFIX,
      credentials USER[:PASSWORD] or authorization VALUE (see FILES).
  PODSSH_CHISEL
      The chisel server of podssh ssh, of each command that reaches its server
      as podssh ssh does, and of podssh proxy, as --chisel:
      https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH], in place of the relay. The flag wins, and so
      do --relay-host, --relay-failover, --forwarder, --shadowsocks, --via,
      --vless, --trojan, --tuic, --hysteria and --wstunnel; beside
      PODSSH_RELAY, PODSSH_FORWARDER, PODSSH_VIA or PODSSH_WSTUNNEL, or with a
      URL that cannot be read, it is a configuration error (78). An empty value
      is no value.
  PODSSH_CHISEL_AUTH_FILE
      The file of the server of --chisel or PODSSH_CHISEL, as
      --chisel-auth-file, which wins: a private file of auth USER:PASSWORD and
      fingerprint BASE64 (see FILES).
  PODSSH_STUN
      The STUN servers of podssh doctor's line nat, in place of
      stun.cloudflare.com:3478 and stun.l.google.com:19302: HOST[:PORT], 2 to 4
      of them separated by commas, the port 3478 when none is named; asked in
      turn from one UDP socket until two gave the address that they saw. no:
      the line asks none, and says so as ????. Unset or empty: the two by
      default. Another value is a configuration error (78), before any probe.
  PODSSH_ECH
      Encrypted Client Hello. yes: the name of each host that podssh reaches
      over TLS by a name goes sealed inside the hello. It does so where the
      name's HTTPS record publishes a list (its ech parameter). The hello in
      the clear then names the list's public name instead. The record is read
      before the connection, from the resolvers of DNS over HTTPS, through
      HTTPS_PROXY as each road dials; it is read once for each name and its TTL
      (30 s at least, 300 s with none); a name with no list, or whose read
      failed, goes plain and is asked again 30 s later. A server that refuses
      the sealed hello with retry configs gets one more hello with them; any
      other refusal goes on with a plain hello, which names the host, and the
      name is left alone for 5 minutes. strict: as yes, but no plain hello ever
      goes to a name that was to be sealed; the connection fails, with why (the
      cleartext road, which PODSSH_CLEARTEXT=no turns off, still names the
      host). no, unset or empty: nothing is sealed and no record is read, the
      default. Over ECH of the settings file; another word is a configuration
      error (78). A proxy is still given the host's name in its CONNECT, and
      the address stays visible; never to an address, nor with a TLS
      configuration that a caller of the library gave. podssh doctor's line ech
      says what it did.
  INVOCATION_ID, WSL_DISTRO_NAME, TERMUX_VERSION
      Read, never set, by --detach and -f, each to say before the run goes to
      the background what may end it there: a unit of systemd that started it,
      whose stop ends it too; WSL, whose machine may stop when no terminal of
      it is open; Termux, whose processes in the background Android may end.
  PODSSH_TURN
      The TURN server of podssh ssh, of each command that reaches its server as
      podssh ssh does, and of podssh proxy, as --turn: turns:HOST[:PORT] (RFC
      7065; port 443 when none is named), in place of the relay. The flag wins,
      and so does each other road's flag; beside PODSSH_RELAY,
      PODSSH_FORWARDER, PODSSH_VIA, PODSSH_WSTUNNEL or PODSSH_CHISEL, or with a
      URI that cannot be read, it is a configuration error (78). An empty value
      is no value.
  PODSSH_TURN_AUTH_FILE
      The credential file of the server of --turn or PODSSH_TURN, as
      --turn-auth-file, which wins: a private file of USER:PASSWORD, or
      auth-secret SECRET (see FILES).
  PODSSH_FILEHOSTS
      The file hosts' road of a pair, the last of the last fallbacks, in a
      build with the feature filehost (none of a release yet): each small write
      of a link of the resumable layer is a sealed note at the public MQTT
      broker of PODSSH_MQTT. Each larger piece is one sealed upload to a public
      file host of podssh's list of services, its URL a sealed note there. One
      request goes at a time (see the notes of node and ssh). no turns it off;
      yes, or unset, takes the hosts of the list whose terms let a program
      upload unasked, in the list's order; a list of the services' ids, by
      commas, takes those alone, in that order; naming a host whose terms ask
      for its user's consent gives it; an id that the list does not hold is a
      configuration error (78). PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no, or PODSSH_MQTT=no (no
      board), turns it off too.
  PODSSH_SRV_US
      The srv.us road, a last fallback: the localhost.run road's shape at
      srv.us: SSH on port 22 as nomatch, logged in with the node's own key, and
      the forward of port 1. It is the road of podssh node --srv-us and podssh
      ssh node://NAME; srv.us derives the tunnel's name from that key. So a
      client that holds the node's whole key derives it too, and races the road
