```text
      last, with no record; a node with no other road serves it unasked after
      the Sandhole road. srv.us sees the node's public key. no: no such road,
      and the flags are refused (64); HOST[:PORT]: that server of the same
      shape, whose host key nobody names, its tunnels named under HOST; unset,
      empty or yes: srv.us where podssh's list of services names it, else no
      server, and --srv-us is a configuration error (78). Another word is a
      configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_TUNNL_GG
      The tunnl.gg road, a last fallback: the localhost.run road's shape at
      tunnl.gg: SSH on port 22 with no key, the forward of port 80 and the
      command output=json. It is the road of podssh node --tunnl-gg and podssh
      ssh node://NAME --tunnel-url https://HOST of a name under its tunnels'
      zone. A node with no other road serves it unasked after the srv.us road;
      its name is random, so a client finds it by --tunnel-url, a kept name or
      the node's record. no: no such road, and the flags are refused (64);
      HOST[:PORT]: that server of the same shape, whose host key nobody names;
      unset, empty or yes: proxy.tunnl.gg where podssh's list of services names
      it, else no server, and --tunnl-gg is a configuration error (78). Another
      word is a configuration error (78), which does not echo the value.
  PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE
      The file of your token of Microsoft Dev Tunnels, for a devtunnel://
      destination and podssh doctor --devtunnel (see FILES). Unset or empty
      with PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_ACCESS_FILE unset too, the road asks with no token,
      which a tunnel that allows anonymous access takes. A build with the
      feature devtunnel.
  PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_ACCESS_FILE
      The file of a tunnel's access token of Dev Tunnels (devtunnel token
      TUNNEL --scopes connect prints one). It is for a tunnel that its owner
      shares with you: one line, the token alone, # a comment; a private file
      as the token file is (see FILES). With PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE also
      set, the road is refused (78). A build with the feature devtunnel.
  PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_API
      Another base of the management API of Dev Tunnels, https://HOST[:PORT],
      in place of the service's global one; http:// goes to this host alone,
      for a test. Another value is a configuration error (78). A build with the
      feature devtunnel.
  PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE
      The file of the GSRN road's shared secret, as --gsr-secret-file, which
      wins: podssh node --gsr serves the road with it; podssh ssh node://NAME
      races the road last with it; and podssh doctor asks the relay at its
      shard (see FILES). Unset or empty: no secret. A build with the feature
      gsr; another build passes it over.
  PODSSH_TPM_DEVICE
      The TPM 2.0 that podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm and podssh ssh use: a device,
      or the socket of a TPM in software (swtpm socket --server type=unixio).
      none: podssh uses no TPM, and each use says so. Unset: /dev/tpmrm0, the
      kernel's resource manager. On Windows: the TPM Base Services, and a
      device or a socket is refused.
  PODSSH_NET
      The net's document of podssh net: the absolute path of its file, in place
      of net.doc in the cache's directory. no: the net is off; this way, no
      member's name, no node's door and no document of the end-to-end channel
      comes from it; podssh net refuses (78). Unset, empty or yes: net.doc in
      the cache; another word, such as a relative path, is a configuration
      error (78), and the net is off.
  PODSSH_PAIR_MAILBOX
      The mailboxes of podssh relay pair --code and podssh relay join, and of
      podssh net invite and podssh net join, as --pair-mailbox, which wins:
      ws:// or wss:// URLs by commas, in order, such as podssh relay serve's
      wss://HOST/v1/mailbox. Unset, empty or yes: magic-wormhole's public
      mailbox, then Least Authority's; no: no code, which then refuses (78)
      with the way left, the operator's file or podssh net add and take; a URL
      that cannot be read is a configuration error (78), which does not echo
      it.
  PODSSH_MQTT
      The public MQTT brokers of the pairing by code, after each mailbox: where
      no mailbox answers, the two ends meet at the code's topic of a broker of
      podssh's list of services; it is shiftr.io's public instance, over a
      WebSocket on 443. A line first says that a third party that nobody
      vouches for carries the messages; the pairing's proof keeps them secret.
      no, or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no: no broker; unset, empty or another word:
      the brokers.
  PODSSH_PAIR_NTFY
      The public ntfy servers of the pairing by code, the first place after the
      mailboxes: the two ends post the code's messages, each 4,095 bytes at
      most, to a topic that the code's nameplate gives, and poll it. A line
      first says that a third party that nobody vouches for carries them.
      ntfy.sh allows 250 messages a day for each address, and a pairing posts
      seven. An https:// URL: that server alone; no, or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no:
      none; unset or empty: the servers of podssh's list of services.
  PODSSH_PAIR_NOSTR
      The public Nostr relays of the pairing by code, after the ntfy servers:
      the code's messages go as ephemeral events tagged from its nameplate,
      over a WebSocket on 443, after the third party's line. no, or
      PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no: none; unset, empty or another word: the relays of
      podssh's list of services.
  PODSSH_PAIR_TRACKER
      The public WebTorrent trackers of the pairing by code, after the Nostr
      relays: the code's messages go as offers and answers between the peers of
      a hash of its nameplate, after the third party's line. Both trackers of
      podssh's list of services are in a filter list of piracy (hagezi's
      anti.piracy), so a network that applies it refuses them; the facts
      filter-list, filter-list-part and filter-category of each service say so.
      no, or PODSSH_LAST_RESORT=no: none; unset, empty or another word: the
      trackers.
  JOURNAL_STREAM
      Set by systemd for a service whose stderr is the journal: the device and
      inode of that stream. Where they are those of podssh's own stderr (a
      program that inherited the variable has another), each error line also
      goes to the journal's socket. It goes beside that stream as one entry, at
      its priority (3, and 2 for a fatal one). Then journalctl -p warning shows
      a refusal and why a node ended; each line stays on stderr, at the
      stream's info, as before. The SSH client's lines go too: an error at 3,
      and a warning at 4; warnings include a forward that the server refused, a
      channel that it opened unasked, and a setting that may cut the session. A
      warning shows at INFO as in OpenSSH, so -q and -o LogLevel=ERROR hide it;
      a log in a file (-E) sends nothing. The socket binds nothing, and a send
      that fails is dropped, never an exit code. No flag turns it on or off.
  PODSSH_HANDOVER
      Set by podssh alone, never by hand, between the two binaries of a node's
      upgrade in place (see the notes of podssh node). It names the descriptor
      of the memory that holds the node's sessions and what its roads keep of
      the run: a key for the run only, a quick tunnel's name. It also names the
      node's pid, so that only that process reads it, never a program that the
      node starts. probe makes podssh --version add the line podssh-handover
      and the version of the sessions that this binary takes; a node reads them
      before it hands its sessions to a binary. On Windows it names the
      inherited pipe that carries them and a nonce, and the child removes it
      once read.
  PODSSH_HANDOVER_ROOT
      Set by podssh alone, never by hand, on Windows: in a node's next binary,
      the pid of the node's first binary; that binary waits for the ones after
      it, and the run's record names its pid; the event of an upgrade and the
      mark beside the record use it.
  TERM, SSH_TTY
      Sent to the server with a pty request; xterm-256color when it is not set.
      podssh serve gives a child on a pty the client's TERM, and SSH_TTY the
      pty's name.
  COLUMNS, LINES
      The window size sent with a pty request when there is no terminal to
      measure (80 and 24 when they are not set).
  COMPUTERNAME
      On Windows, the host name in the default comment of podssh keygen.
  ProgramData
      On Windows, the directory of the system known_hosts file.
  SystemRoot
      On Windows, where an sshd of OpenSSH is looked for (System32\OpenSSH): a
      roost that the loopback refuses, and doctor's line sshd.
  SystemDrive
      On Windows, the drive whose root a detached run takes as its working
      directory (see podssh ssh -f).
  PAGER
      The pager of podssh man on a terminal. Empty, or cat, writes the manual
      with no pager.
  SHELL, BASH_ENV
      The shell of LocalCommand with PermitLocalCommand=yes: SHELL -c COMMAND;
      empty or not set, /bin/sh when it is there, else podssh ssh exits 78.
      podssh serve: the first shell it tries after --shell, when it runs; else
      it is passed over, and said (see podssh serve). podssh serve never takes
      SHELL or BASH_ENV from a client's env request: the shell would run, or
      read, the file it names.
  SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND
      Set by podssh serve for a command that a key's command="..." runs in
      place of the client's: the client's command (internal-sftp for an sftp
      request; not set for a shell). Never taken from a client's env request,
      and serve's own never reaches a child (see podssh serve).
  LESS
      Options for less. podssh man sets FRX when it starts less and LESS is not
      set.
  VISUAL, EDITOR
      The editor of podssh edit: VISUAL, else EDITOR, else vi on PATH. A
      program and its words, split at blanks with no shell, or one program
      whose path has a blank; an empty value is no value.
  PATH
      Where podssh man looks for less, podssh edit for vi, and podssh doctor
      for directories that run programs.

FILES
  ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa, ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519,
  ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk
      The identity files tried, in this order, when no -i or IdentityFile is
      given.
  ~/.ssh/known_hosts, ~/.ssh/known_hosts2
      The user's known hosts. podssh records a new host key in the first file
      (mode 0600, in a directory of mode 0700). With no home directory, a new
      key is accepted but not recorded.
  /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts, /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts2
      The system's known hosts. podssh only reads them.
  ~/.ssh/config
      The user's ssh_config, read by podssh ssh, cp, mv, scp and sftp unless -F
      or PODSSH_SSH_CONFIG names another file, or none. A missing file is no
      error. A file that another user than you or root owns (on Windows, than
      you, SYSTEM or the Administrators) is refused. So is a file that others
      can change (on Windows, as its access list says), and so is each file
      that an Include reads. The file that -F or PODSSH_SSH_CONFIG names is
      your choice, and is not checked, as OpenSSH does not check it. Match is
      read as OpenSSH 10.3p1 reads it, but for Match exec and Match
      localnetwork. These are refused by name, with the file and the line,
      where they would decide, and run nothing. Each hop of -J reads the blocks
      of its own name, as OpenSSH's jump host does; it logs in as its user@,
      its User, else the local user. The first ProxyCommand holds, as in
      OpenSSH: none, or podssh proxy %h %p, on the command line or in an
      earlier block, goes past a later block's command. So -o ProxyCommand=none
      goes past a Host * that names a jump host for OpenSSH, and keeps the
      file's other settings. A later ProxyJump is not read, as OpenSSH does not
      read it then; a command with no value before it is refused with its file
      and line (exit 78).
  /etc/ssh/ssh_config
      The system's ssh_config, read after the user's, and not when -F or
      PODSSH_SSH_CONFIG names a file. A relative Include in it starts from its
      directory.
  $PODSSH_CACHE_DIR, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/podssh (else ~/.cache/podssh; when it
  is in another user's tree, the .cache/podssh of the home of your uid's entry
  in /etc/passwd); else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podssh; else podssh-UID in $TMPDIR
  (else $TMP, $TEMP, and only then /tmp and /dev/shm); else ./.podssh
      The cache: the first of these directories that podssh can use. It holds
      one relay token for each relay deployment, with the host that minted it
      (relay-token-tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev.json for the default relay). It holds
      the relay's list of hosts (relay-pool-tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev.json). It
      holds the last addresses that carried a session to each relay host
      (relay-addresses.json), which a run whose resolver fails asks before DNS
      over HTTPS. It holds the key exchange group that each TLS server took
      (tls-groups.txt), which the next run offers first. For each host that
      took a key, it holds that key's fingerprint by a hash of its host key and
      the user (accepted-keys.txt): the next login sends that key's signature
      in its first request, with no query before it. It does so when the key is
      a file that opens with no question and is not RSA or a security key's.
      Neither holds a secret. It holds each pair of the reverse road under its
      label (pair-LABEL.json), as podssh relay pair writes it. Until a copy
      that broke is done, it holds its side file (podssh-cp-*.resume: the
      offset, the temporary file's name and the source's state, never a byte of
      the file). While podssh edit runs, a directory edit-RANDOM of mode 0700
      holds the copy of the far file; it goes after the edit, and stays, named,
      after a failure when the copy holds a change. Each file has mode 0600; on
      Windows, an access list that lets in only you, SYSTEM and the
      Administrators. podssh ignores a cache file that is a symbolic link, that
      belongs to another user, or that others can read. On Unix,
      $XDG_CACHE_HOME, ~/.cache and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR count only in your own
      tree: each of their directories that exists, up to the home (else up to
      /), is yours or root's. One in another user's tree, as when root runs
      with the HOME of another account, is passed over: podssh writes nothing
      more there, and makes no directory there, so a missing .cache stays its
      owner's to make. It still reads a key, the pins, a pair or a token that
      an earlier run kept there, after your own places; it says once of a key
      where to move it; it moves nothing. podssh status and podssh doctor name
      each place passed over, and why. Above the cache's own directory, podssh
      makes a missing one only in a directory of yours or of root.
  operator-NAME.json
      The operator's part of a pair that podssh relay join NAME took by a code,
      in the cache: the relay, the pair's name, its connect token and its
      expiry, as JSON with mode 0600, replaced by the next join under NAME.
      podssh operator, podssh ssh node:// and podssh relay status find it by
      NAME where no pair is stored under it.
  kept-offsets.txt
      The offsets of kept shells that this client has, in the cache. For each
      far end and shell name, it holds the bytes of output that a session got.
      A session to a far end that keeps shells writes it at its end, while the
      shell may still be kept. The next --attach NAME gives that offset, and
      the far end replays what this client missed. A far end is named by a hash
      of its host key and the user. The file has mode 0600, holds no secret,
      and forgets an offset after 30 days.
  node-name.key, client.key
      The keys of the ends of a road between two podssh ends, in the cache, the
      same on each road: a node's under its NAME, and this user's as a client;
      --key and --client-key name other files. Each holds the secret key in
      hex, has mode 0600, and is made when it is missing. podssh refuses one
      that is a symbolic link, another user's, or that others can read, and
      never replaces it: a new key would change the node's identity, which
      operators pinned, and its ticket. The names of an earlier podssh,
      iroh-node-NAME.key and iroh-client.key, are still read.
  relay-deployments.json, relay-list.key
      The signed lists of relay deployments, in the cache: the newest list of
      each trusted key, its exact text and its signature, as JSON with mode
      0600. It is checked again at each read, so that a run keeps the other
      deployments when the default's domain is gone; and the key with which
      podssh relay serve --deployment signs its list, in hex with mode 0600.
      The key is made when it is missing, unless --list-key names another file.
  grants-NAME/
      The grants used once that the node NAME let in, in the cache: a private
      directory with a file of mode 0600 for each grant. Each file is made
      create-new and synced before the session comes in. It is named by the end
      of the grant's window and the digest of what its issuer signed, and
      removed once that end passed. A grant whose file is there is refused; a
      directory that cannot take a file refuses each grant. It holds no secret:
      a serial and an issuer's fingerprint.
  net-roads.json
      The road that last reached each node from this host, in the cache: by the
      node's label, the road that answered first, its time and when, and why
      the last race that found no road ended so. It is JSON with mode 0600, at
      most 256 nodes, the oldest going first. Each race of podssh ssh, of the
      copies and of podssh ping to node://NAME writes it, and podssh status
      --net reads it. It holds no secret; a record that does not read is none.
  warp-device.json, warp-door.json
      WARP's road (warp://, in a build with the feature warp), in the cache:
      the device, pod-warp's identity file of mode 0600, JSON with its record
      of WARP's API, its certificate and its P-256 key. It is written once as
      it registers, and again when WARP's API gives the front door a new key;
      and the door that opened and the API's base that answered last, which a
      run tries first. A record that cannot be read is a configuration error
      (78), never a new registration: remove it to register again.
  acme/HOST-DIGEST/
      The state of podssh relay serve --acme NAME, in the cache, mode 0700, for
      each CA: HOST is the host of its directory, and DIGEST 8 hex digits of
      the SHA-256 of its URL. account.key, the account's P-256 key, made once
      and never replaced; NAME.pem, the certificate's own P-256 key and its
      chain in one file. It is replaced whole by a rename at each renewal, so
      that the key of one certificate is never read with the chain of another.
      Each has mode 0600; podssh refuses one that is a symbolic link, another
      user's, or that others can read.
  detached/
      The runs that --detach and -f sent into the background, in the cache,
      mode 0700: VERB-PID.log, mode 0600, which takes the run's stdout and
      stderr once it is ready; past 1 MiB it is renamed VERB-PID.log.1, which
      takes the lines written until the run writes the new one, so none is
      lost. NAME.lock, which the run of the name NAME (or its supervisor of
      --restart) holds for its life, with its pid in it. NAME.run.lock, which a
      supervisor's run holds: a second start of the name refuses while either
      is held, and podssh detached reads them. NAME.json, the run's record: its
      pid, the pid of a supervisor's run, its words, its log and its start.
      NAME.alive, whose time each run of --restart sets each 10 s, and which
      its supervisor reads . Each start of --detach or -f removes each of them
      older than 30 days whose run runs no more: no lock of its name is held,
      and the process of a log's PID is gone.
  node-NAME.env, ssh-NAME.env, node-NAME.env.lock
      The service of podssh node NAME --install, or of podssh ssh --install
      NAME, in the cache: the private file of the variables that it reads (the
      file of --env-file), with no token; FILE.lock beside it, which its run
      holds with its pid in it, so that a second start of the service ends at
      once; and a LaunchAgent's log, node-NAME.log, made with mode 0600 before
      launchd opens it. --uninstall removes them, with the unit, the
      LaunchAgent (~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.podssh.VERB.NAME.plist), the
      lines of the crontab or the task.
  node-NAME.shares, node-NAME.shares.lock
      The shares of podssh node NAME, in the cache beside its key, or the file
      of podssh node --shares FILE: one name=HOST:PORT on each line, which the
      node reads again for each session. podssh share changes it under the lock
      of FILE.lock beside it, the file replaced whole. Mode 0600; the node
      refuses one that others may change, as it names what the node dials.
  tor/
      The Tor road's directory (tor://, in a build with the feature tor), in
      the cache, mode 0700: Arti's state (its guards, which Tor asks a client
      to keep) in state/. Its copy of Tor's directory in cache/, which a later
      run reads to start sooner. Arti checks that no other user can write them;
      where a sandbox's mounts fail that check on a directory above, podssh
      made these private itself and tries once more without it. The same pair
      for another network of PODSSH_TOR_NETWORK goes in networks/, by a digest
      of its file. Removing it costs the next run a new bootstrap.
  known-nodes
      The node keys that an operator has met, in the cache: one line for each
      key of a label, LABEL KEY, the key as its fingerprint (SHA256:...) or
      itself. The first sight of a label's node writes its line; a node whose
      key matches no line of its label is refused, and no line is ever
      replaced: remove one, or add one for a new key. A file of the user that
      others cannot change. A member of the net is checked by the key that the
      net names, and its line is not written.
  net.doc
      The net's document (podssh net), in the cache, or the file of PODSSH_NET:
      one line of JSON, then the owner's signature as ssh-keygen -Y sign writes
      it, replaced whole by each document taken. A file of the user that others
      cannot change; a node of the net reads it again for each session.
  the file of --shadowsocks
      The Shadowsocks servers of --shadowsocks: ss:// lines, subscription lines
      and access keys (see podssh ssh). Its keys hold passwords. So podssh
      reads it as it reads a pair file: only as a regular file of yours that
      others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says); else, and for a
      line that cannot be read, the run is refused (78). podssh never writes
      it.
  the file of --via-auth-file
      The Basic credentials of the forward proxy of --via: one line,
      USER:PASSWORD, or the password alone when the URL names USER; # starts a
      comment. podssh reads it only as a regular file of yours that others
      cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says), as a pair file; else,
      and for a line that cannot be read, the run is refused (78), and no
      message shows the line. podssh never writes it.
  the file of --vless, the file of --trojan, the file of --tuic
      The VLESS servers of --vless, the Trojan servers of --trojan, or the TUIC
      servers of --tuic: a vless://, trojan:// or tuic:// share link on each
      line (see podssh ssh); # starts a comment. Each link holds its user's ID
      or password. So podssh reads it as it reads a pair file: only as a
      regular file of yours that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access
      list says); else, and for a line that cannot be read, the run is refused
      (78), by the line's number, never its text. podssh never writes it.
  the file of --wstunnel-secret-file
      What the wstunnel server of --wstunnel checks of a client: path-prefix
      PREFIX, the prefix that it restricts its clients to, as letters, digits
      and -._~!$&'()*+,;=:@; credentials USER[:PASSWORD], sent as Basic, or
      authorization VALUE, sent as it is, the Authorization that its
      restrictions match; each once, and one of the last two; or one line, the
      prefix alone. # starts a comment. podssh reads it only as a regular file
      of yours that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says),
      as a pair file; else, and for a line that cannot be read, the run is
      refused (78), by the line's number and never its text. podssh never
      writes it.
  shadowsocks-HASH.json
      The list of each subscription and access key of --shadowsocks, in the
      cache, under a hash of its URL, which it does not show: the time it came
      and its ss:// lines, with a WebSocket's URL beside each server in one;
      they hold passwords; mode 0600. Read for a day, then fetched again, and
      fetched again too when each of its servers failed.
  the file of --allow
      The operator keys that may come in to podssh node, on each road: one key
      on each line, as its fingerprint (SHA256:...) or in iroh's hex or base32,
      then routes=ROUTE,... for the routes that it may use (routes=* for each),
      then a comment if any; # starts a comment line. Read again for each
      session. A file of the user that others cannot change; others may read
      it.
  podssh-ca.pem
      CA certificates in the directory of the podssh binary, added to the trust
      store.
  $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/podssh/settings, podssh.settings
      podssh's own settings: RelayHost, RelayAddr (each line adds),
      RelayFailover, CaFile, SessionLog, Forwarder, ForwarderFallback;
      DoctorJobs (the sections of podssh doctor at once), RelayKeys (the keys
      of a signed list of relay deployments; each line adds), ECH (as
      PODSSH_ECH), AccessHost (each line adds), AccessClientIdFile and
      AccessClientSecretFile (see podssh pipe). NetUrl and NetOwner are
      --net-url and --net-owner of podssh node. They are Keyword value lines,
      below the flags and the variables. The file of PODSSH_SETTINGS, else the
      first of these that exists (~/.config/podssh/settings with no
      XDG_CONFIG_HOME; the second beside the podssh binary); never one of the
      working directory. A symbolic link, a file of another user than you or
      root, one that others can change, and a bad line are refused (78). Each
      command that reaches the relay refuses them. podssh never writes it, and
      no keyword holds a token. After a line [groups], each line is NAME HOSTS:
      a group of hosts, parted by commas or blanks (by commas alone on the
      command line), which podssh each takes as @NAME. After a line [snippets],
      each line is NAME COMMAND: a command that podssh ssh --snippet NAME and
      podssh each run, with its placeholders (see podssh ssh). A COMMAND in
      double quotes, with none inside, loses them, and a # in it is no comment.
  sessions.jsonl, sessions.1.jsonl
      The log of the sessions of this host, in the cache, when
      PODSSH_SESSION_LOG or SessionLog asks for it: a JSON line for each run of
      podssh ssh and podssh proxy that named a destination, at its end. The
      line holds its start, duration, verb, host, port, relay host or road,
      end, exit code, bytes and the relay's close code; never a command, an
      environment value, a token or a password. Mode 0600, opened to append
      with no symbolic link followed, a line in one write; at 1 MiB it becomes
      the second name, and a new file starts. podssh status shows the last
      line.
  sessions/NAME.sock
      The socket of each session of podssh session, in the cache: the directory
      sessions has mode 0700, and each socket mode 0600 (on Windows, the access
      list of the cache); it goes when its session's podssh ends. A socket that
      nobody serves is replaced by the next start of its name. Beside a
      socket's file, NAME.sock.lock, which its podssh holds for its life. So a
      second one of the name is refused (69), and it never removes the first
      one's socket.
  /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt,
  /etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem, /etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem,
  /etc/ssl/cert.pem, /usr/local/share/certs/ca-root-nss.crt
      The system CA bundles. The first one that podssh can read is added to the
      trust store.
  .podssh.update-RANDOM, podssh.prev, podssh.prev.exe, podssh.exe.old
      In the directory of the podssh binary, while podssh update runs: the new
      binary, written beside the old one with its mode and run once with
      --version. Then it is renamed over the old one, or removed when a step
      fails. The binary before the last update stays as podssh.prev
      (podssh.prev.exe on Windows, where the running binary is renamed to it);
      a move over it or update --rollback puts it back; on Windows, when that
      name is taken by a running one, the running binary is renamed to
      podssh.exe.old instead. The next run of podssh removes it.
  the file of --chisel-auth-file
      What the chisel server of --chisel takes and shows: auth USER:PASSWORD,
      the user and password of chisel's auth option (the password may hold
      colons); and fingerprint BASE64, the SHA-256 of the server's key in
      base64, 44 characters, as chisel server prints it; each once, either or
      both. # starts a comment. podssh reads it only as a regular file of yours
      that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says), as a pair
      file; else, and for a line that cannot be read, the run is refused (78),
      by the line's number and never its text. podssh never writes it.
  the file of --hysteria
      The Hysteria 2 servers of --hysteria: a hysteria2:// or hy2:// share link
      on each line (see podssh ssh); # starts a comment. Each link holds the
      server's credential, and Salamander's password where it names one. So
      podssh reads it as it reads a pair file: only as a regular file of yours
      that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says); else, and
      for a line that cannot be read, the run is refused (78), by the line's
      number, never its text. podssh never writes it.
  the file of --turn-auth-file
      The credential of the TURN server of --turn: one line, USER:PASSWORD,
      split at its first colon (the password may hold colons); or auth-secret
      SECRET, the static-auth-secret of a coturn of use-auth-secret. From it
      podssh makes a user and a password of a day, as coturn's REST API makes
      them. # starts a comment. podssh reads it only as a regular file of yours
      that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says), as a pair
      file; else, and for a line that cannot be read, the run is refused (78),
      by the line's number and never its text. podssh never writes it.
  the file of PODSSH_DEVTUNNEL_TOKEN_FILE
      Your token of Microsoft Dev Tunnels: one line, SCHEME TOKEN, as the
      management API takes it in Authorization: github with a GitHub token (gh
      auth token prints one), aad with a token of Microsoft Entra ID or a
      Microsoft account, or bearer. # starts a comment, and blank lines are
      skipped. podssh reads it only as a regular file of yours that others
      cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says); else, and for a line
      that cannot be used, the run is refused (78), in words that never hold
      the token. The token goes to the management API alone, never to a line,
      the journal or --json. podssh never writes it.
  serve_host_ed25519_key
      The host key of podssh serve, in the cache, when no --host-key names one:
      an OpenSSH private key (Ed25519) that the first start makes, mode 0600
      (on Windows, the access list of the cache); each later start reads it;
      podssh never writes over it. Remove it to make a new host key, which each
      client then sees as a changed one.
  /etc/motd, ~/.hushlogin
      The message of the day that podssh serve shows before a login shell on a
      tty, when no --motd names another file; a missing file shows none. A
      ~/.hushlogin in the user's home (HOME) shows none either.
  http-road-paths.json
      What podssh doctor --stream measured of the path to each server over TLS,
      in the cache: by HOST:PORT, the first body that did not pass, when a
      quiet answer ended, and when it was measured. It is JSON with mode 0600,
      at most 32 servers, the oldest going first. The HTTP road to that host
      sizes its batches and its waits by it for 7 days after the measurement;
      podssh ssh -v says so; with none, the road's own sizes. It holds no
      secret; a record that does not read is none.
  serve-NAME.kept
      The names of the shells that podssh serve NAME keeps, beside its host
      key: on each line, the fingerprint of the key that kept one and its name.
      Mode 0600, replaced whole at each change. The next start reads it, says
      which shells ended with the last run, and lists them as lost. It holds no
      output.
  the file of --gsr-secret-file and PODSSH_GSR_SECRET_FILE
      The shared secret of the GSRN road: its first line, without the line end,
      as gs-netcat -k reads a key file; any later line must be blank. At most
      32 bytes, the relay's limit. podssh reads it only as a regular file of
      yours that others cannot read (on Windows, as its access list says);
      else, and for a file with no secret, more than one, or a control
      character, the run is refused (78). Its words never hold the secret. It
      never goes to argv, a line or the relay: the relay sees the address and
      the shard that it gives. podssh never writes it.
  the file of --carrier s3:FILE
      The bucket of the carrier: NAME = VALUE lines; a line that starts with #
      is a comment. endpoint, https://HOST[:PORT][/PATH] of the S3 API; region,
      us-east-1 unless given; bucket; style, path or virtual. up and down, the
      prefixes of the client's way and the node's, the same at both ends.
      credentials, a file of the AWS form (aws_access_key_id,
      aws_secret_access_key, aws_session_token) for both ways. Or
      write-credentials and read-credentials, two key pairs; read-credentials
      none reads a public prefix unsigned. secret-file, at least 16 bytes that
      both ends hold. A relative path is read beside FILE. No key goes in FILE
      itself; a name that is no setting is refused (78), in words that never
      hold a key.
  the file of --carrier dns:FILE
      The DNS road of a carrier: NAME = VALUE lines. A line that starts with #
      is a comment; a # after a value is refused. zone, the zone whose names
      carry the stream: two labels at least, none that starts or ends with -.
      resolver, the client's: system (the default), IP[:PORT], or
      https://NAME[:PORT]/PATH, a resolver of DNS over HTTPS whose certificate
      names NAME. listen, the node's IP:PORT of UDP. Each end refuses a setting
      of the other end's (78). key-file, the path of this end's key file, which
      is required. podssh makes it, private, where it does not exist; a line
      then gives its key for the other end. A key in the place of the path is
      refused, and not shown. peer, the other end's key: on a client the
      node's, on a node each client's, by spaces or commas. queries-per-second,
      more than 0 and at most 20; a fraction is allowed. in-flight, 1 to 8.
      query-timeout and poll-max, in seconds, more than 0 and at most 60.
      answer, in bytes, 512 to 4096 (1232 by default). A relative path is read
      beside FILE. On Unix, FILE must be yours or root's, and nobody else may
      change it. A name that is no setting or is given twice, and a value out
      of its bound, are refused (78). A refusal of one line names that line.

EXIT STATUS
  0
      Success. For podssh ssh: the remote command exited 0. For podssh chat:
      each message was acknowledged, and the one thing of --send or --file is
      done; with --listen --linger, also when the --timeout passed, the run's
      planned end. For podssh ping: a relay host gave its measures, or with a
      destination each measure has its number. For podssh health: the facts
      came, or the host has no /proc and gave its system's name; with
      --preflight, also no check failed. podssh health --policy: the policy
      passed.
  1
      podssh doctor: a check failed. podssh relay spec: a fact of the relay's
      document disagrees. podssh relay conform: a check of the relay failed.
      podssh keygen: a key could not be made or read. podssh health
      --preflight: after the login, a check failed or the facts did not come.
      podssh play: the recording cannot be read, or its version is not one that
      it plays.
  64
      A usage error: an unknown command or flag, a bad value, a missing
      argument. podssh did nothing.
  65
      podssh agent add-passphrase: the passphrase does not open the key file,
      or the file needs none; nothing is kept. podssh pipe: the bytes of a udp:
      address are not each datagram after its length. podssh containers: a tool
      listed a name that podssh does not take, which is left out.
  66
      podssh cp and mv: a source is missing or cannot be read. podssh mv: a
      source that changed during the move, which stays. podssh chat: the file
      of --file or --sendfile cannot be read. podssh edit: the file is not on
      the host. podssh sftp: the file of -b cannot be read.
  69
      podssh proxy: no relay host could be reached, or the relay ended the
      session abnormally. podssh node, operator and relay: the relay or TARGET
      could not be reached, the node did not take the session, the pair was
      stopped, or another node serves it; with --sshd, a TARGET that sent no
      line within 10 s, or closed first; with --publish-tls and --acme, the
      first order of the certificate failed; with --run-as, no such user.
      podssh cp and mv: no connection to the server, or it has neither SFTP nor
      the sh and the tools of a copy by exec. podssh chat: the same of the
      relay and the pair, or a message went with no acknowledgement; each is
      said. podssh ping: no relay host answered, the relay refused its default
      target, or PODSSH_OFFLINE is set. podssh relay status: no relay host
      answered; podssh relay trace: the relay would not dial the target. podssh
      agent: no agent answers at SSH_AUTH_SOCK, or the agent keeps no
      passwords. podssh containers: the host has none of docker, podman and
      kubectl, one of them failed, or --exec names no container that a list
      has. podssh session: no session of that name answers, or its session
      ended (and the status that it ended with is said). podssh detached status
      and stop: no run of that name runs. podssh relay serve: the port of
      --listen is in use. podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm: no TPM that podssh may
      reach. podssh ssh and health with --policy: a KEXINIT that does not read
      gives no verdict. podssh health --policy also gives none with no
      connection, or with a size that one exchange cannot measure.
  70
      The command is not implemented yet, or podssh failed inside. podssh node
      and operator: the relay closed the node or the session for a fault (1003,
      1008 or 1009); or the end-to-end channel failed (a peer with no channel,
      a message that failed its check). podssh cp and mv: the digests of a copy
      differ, or the session broke; the destination was not changed. podssh mv:
      the copy is verified and its source could not be removed; the data is in
      both places. podssh chat: the peer broke the protocol, the channel
      failed, or the file of --file arrived with another SHA-256.
  73
      podssh cp and mv: the destination cannot be written. podssh edit: the far
      file changed since it was fetched, so nothing was sent and the copy here
      stays, or no cache directory takes the copy. podssh chat: the directory
      of --accept-dir is not there. podssh each: a file of --output-dir cannot
      be made; no host has run.
  75
      podssh cp and mv: the --timeout passed before the copy ended; a later try
      can work. podssh chat: the --timeout passed, or the peer talks with
      another peer; a later try can work. podssh session start and wait: the
      --timeout passed first. podssh job wait: the --timeout passed before the
      job ended, which runs on; podssh job fetch: the job is queued or running,
      so its output is not whole yet. podssh node --quick-tunnel:
      api.trycloudflare.com refused for now (429 or a 5xx) and asked for a wait
      past 5 minutes, which the line names, or refused for 5 minutes; a later
      run can work. --detach and -f: a run of the same --detach-name runs, and
      its pid is said. podssh detached stop: the run still holds its lock after
      it was killed.
  77
      podssh proxy: the relay or the proxy refused (a token, a blocked address,
      a proxy's 403 or 407). podssh node, operator and relay: the relay refused
      the pair, or the pair expired; for relay trace, the token. podssh
      operator and pipe node:: the node's key is not the one pinned in
      known-nodes or named by --node-key; or the node's allowlist refused this
      client's key, its grant, or its route. podssh cp and mv: the server
      refused the login, or podssh did not accept its host key. podssh chat:
      the same of the pair and of the keys, or the peer declined the file of
      --file. podssh session start: this host refuses the bind of the session's
      socket. podssh net policy check: the policy does not let FROM reach TO.
  78
      A setting of the environment cannot be used: PODSSH_RELAY or
      PODSSH_RELAY_ADDR (podssh ssh, cp, proxy and doctor). For podssh proxy
      also a proxy URL that is not http://, or a PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN that is not
      a token. The same value as a flag is a usage error (64). A line that
      podssh cannot use, with its file and line named: in the settings file
      (see FILES), or in an ssh_config file (-F, ~/.ssh/config, the system's,
      or one that Include reads). Also such a file that cannot be read or that
      others can change; the same keyword with -o on the command line is a
      usage error (64). podssh node, operator, relay and chat: no pair is
      stored under the label, the pair cannot be read or stored, or a node
      cannot connect as it is set up; podssh node and operator: the relay
      speaks a dialect of the reverse road that this podssh does not read, or
      does not read its own (its hello, or 426); the line names the side to
      update. podssh edit: VISUAL, EDITOR and PATH give no editor, the editor
      does not start, or PODSSH_CACHE_DIR is none. podssh node --sshd: a TARGET
      that sends lines and no version line of SSH 2, which is another service.
      podssh node: this host refuses UDP for a udp: TARGET. podssh each
      --interactive: the emergency stop cannot be armed. podssh session start
      and serve: PODSSH_LISTEN is no, or no directory takes the session's
      socket. podssh serve: no authorized key, or a key file or the host key
      that cannot be used, or no shell that runs. podssh ssh and health: the
      file of --policy cannot be read or used, or the server's algorithms do
      not meet it. podssh serve: the file of --policy cannot be used, or judges
      no client. podssh doctor: the file of --policy cannot be used.
  255
      podssh ssh: the connection, the host key, a node's key or the
      authentication failed; or the server refused a session or ended the
      connection before one opened (the line says which); or the session ended
      with no exit status (also when stdout closed and none came within 5 s);
      or the connection was lost after the exit status and before the end of
      the output, which may be cut (the line says the status); or the server
      ended a run of -N. OpenSSH uses the same code, but for a cut, where it
      gives the status. podssh ping: the destination could not be reached or
      logged in to, or a measure broke. podssh each: a host could not be
      reached or logged in to, or its session ended with no exit status. podssh
      health: the host could not be reached or logged in to, or it has no sh;
      or its answer had none of the lines of the script (with --preflight, the
      login alone). podssh containers: the host could not be reached or logged
      in to, or its list did not end within 60 s. podssh session start: the
      connection or the login failed. podssh job: the host could not be reached
      or logged in to, has no tmux, has no such job, or gave no answer; for
      wait, also a job that is lost. podssh run: the copy failed, and the
      command did not run.
  N
      podssh ssh: the exit status of the remote command, unchanged. When signal
      N stopped the command, 128 + N. podssh ping: the status of the remote
      program of a measure that failed, 127 when the host lacks it. podssh
      edit: the status of an editor that failed; nothing was sent. podssh each:
      the largest status of the hosts, 0 only when each gave 0; with
      --interactive, of their shells, and 130 for a host whose shell Ctrl-C cut
      after the end of the input. podssh containers --exec: the status of the
      session in the container. podssh job wait: the exit status of the job.
      podssh run: the status of the command, as podssh ssh gives it. Each code
      that no other row names.

EXAMPLES
  what works on this host, one line for each check
      $ podssh doctor

  the state of this host as one line of JSON, and whether a host's key is known
      $ podssh status github.com

  how good the path is: each step to each relay host, and the round trip of
  WebSocket pings
      $ podssh ping

  and through a host: the login, the echo through cat, and 8 MiB down and up
      $ podssh ping user@example.org

  a host's load, memory, uptime, network and disks, from one command that only
  reads
      $ podssh health user@example.org

  and what its server allows before a long command needs it: SFTP, -R, -J,
  tmux, a keepalive
      $ podssh health --preflight user@example.org

  log in to a host, through the relay
      $ podssh ssh user@example.org

  run one command; podssh exits with its exit status
      $ podssh ssh user@example.org 'uname -a'

  keys for a menu after the login, then the session; with no match in 30 s,
  exit 255
      $ podssh ssh -tt --expect 'Choice: ' --send '2\r' user@example.org

  the same command on three hosts, two at once: each line starts with its host;
  the exit is the worst
      $ podssh each --parallel 2 web1.example.org,web2.example.org,user@db.example.org -- uptime

  the containers of a host, of docker, podman and kubectl, each with the
  command that enters it
      $ podssh containers user@example.org

  enter one of them on the same connection, with bash
      $ podssh containers --exec web --shell bash user@example.org

  twelve hosts in one word, and the group db of the settings file; each host
  once
      $ podssh each 'web{01..12}.example.org,@db' -- 'df -h /'

  the command logs of the settings file, nginx as its {{1}}: shown, quoted, and
  asked first
      $ podssh ssh --snippet logs user@example.org nginx

  each line typed to the shells of three hosts; Ctrl-\ (Ctrl-Break on Windows)
  stops it at once
      $ podssh each --interactive 'web{1..3}.example.org'

  a long build that goes on after the connection, in the host's tmux: its ID,
  then each job of the host
      $ podssh job start user@build.example.org -- make all && podssh job list user@build.example.org

  the same on a host that has no tmux and cannot get it: the job runs under
  nohup
      $ podssh job start --no-tmux user@build.example.org -- make all

  a job's output as it comes, on one connection; the exit is the job's status
      $ podssh job log --follow user@build.example.org 0123abcd

  copy the project here to a stronger host, only what changed, then run its
  tests there
      $ podssh run user@build.example.org -- cargo test

  what that run would copy, only what changed, and the command; nothing changes
  there, and nothing runs
      $ podssh run --dry-run user@build.example.org -- cargo test

  queue a build on the least busy of three hosts, wait 2 h at most for its
  status, then fetch its output
      $ podssh job submit 'build{1..3}.example.org' -- make all && podssh job wait --timeout 2h build2.example.org 0123abcd && podssh job fetch build2.example.org 0123abcd

  a Unix socket on the server, on stdin and stdout
      $ podssh ssh -W /run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432 user@db.example.org

  Host blocks for the hosts of an Ansible inventory, added to the user's
  ssh_config
      $ podssh config import ansible inventory.ini >> ~/.ssh/config

  tools for an agent, run by its MCP client: commands on the web hosts but web9
      $ podssh mcp --allow-host 'web*.example.org' --allow-host '!web9.example.org'

  the same tools with copies to and from one directory of this host, and
  sessions that end with the server
      $ podssh mcp --allow-host build.example.org --allow-dir ./artifacts --allow-session

  a shell that stays between the calls of an agent: type a line, wait for 2 s
  of quiet, read the screen
      $ podssh session start work user@example.org && podssh session send work 'make test' && podssh session wait work --idle 2s && podssh session capture work

  keep what a session showed, with its timing, and show it again twice as fast
      $ podssh ssh -tt --record top.cast user@example.org top && podssh play --speed 2 top.cast

  a net of your own: sign it with your key, name a node in it, then reach the
  node by its name alone
      $ podssh net init home --owner-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 && podssh net add lab SHA256:JfDOvc6FaJOB34ANs+ou385/Kh+mMQhnUx0gHXVAfUI && podssh ssh user@lab

  the net's policy: who may reach which node and route, signed by its owner,
  then asked with no connection
      $ podssh net policy set policy.json && podssh net policy check laptop lab/web

  lend this host's egress to the members of its net, as an exit node: its owner
  gave it the role exit
      $ podssh node gw --exit

  SSH to a host from the exit gw, then a local SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy whose
  connections start there
      $ podssh ssh --exit gw git@github.com && podssh exit gw --listen 127.0.0.1:1080

  say what an update would do, its signature checked, then replace this binary
  with the newest release
      $ podssh update --check && podssh update

  a port, a key, and a new host key recorded with no question
      $ podssh ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new user@example.org

  an interactive program, from a host with no terminal
      $ podssh ssh -tt user@example.org top

  a host whose key fingerprint the operator gave: that key only, and no
  known_hosts
      $ podssh ssh --host-key-fingerprint SHA256:JfDOvc6FaJOB34ANs+ou385/Kh+mMQhnUx0gHXVAfUI user@example.org

  a shell in the server's tmux, attached again after a lost link
      $ podssh ssh --persist user@example.org

  through a jump host
      $ podssh ssh -J user@bastion.example.org user@inner.example.org

  a host from a script: -- before it, so it is never read as a flag
      $ podssh ssh -- user@example.org uptime

  an IPv6 address with a port, with no relay
      $ podssh ssh --direct 'user@[2001:db8::1]:2222'

  with no relay, on Linux: Multipath TCP, and -v says whether the server took
  it
      $ PODSSH_MPTCP=yes podssh ssh --direct -v user@example.org

  send a file with no scp
      $ podssh ssh user@example.org 'cat > notes.txt' < notes.txt

  a failure of podssh as one JSON object on the stdin of your program; a remote
  status starts none
      $ PODSSH_ERROR_PROGRAM=$HOME/bin/triage podssh ssh user@example.org uptime

  change a file of a host in an editor here; it goes back only if the host's
  file did not change
      $ EDITOR=nano podssh edit user@example.org:notes.txt

  through an HTTP CONNECT proxy
      $ HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.org:3128 podssh ssh user@example.org

  through a SOCKS5 proxy, which gets the relay's name
      $ ALL_PROXY=socks5h://proxy.example.org:1080 podssh ssh user@example.org

  on a host with no DNS: give the address of the relay
      $ podssh ssh --relay-addr tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev=ADDRESS user@example.org

  try these relay hosts, in this order
      $ podssh ssh --relay-host tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev,tcp-us-east-1.ssh.relay.ajam.dev user@example.org

  no relay: other products' public forwarders, in this order; they publish no
  limit
      $ podssh ssh --forwarder mudlet,ssheasy user@example.org

  use the OpenSSH client, with podssh as its way out
      $ ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' -o ServerAliveInterval=60 user@example.org

  another TCP protocol: here, HTTP
      $ printf 'HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.org\r\n\r\n' | podssh proxy example.org 80

  a VNC desktop at 127.0.0.1:5901 for a viewer: OpenSSH listens, podssh carries
  its session
      $ ssh -N -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5901 -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' user@desktop.example.org

  a program at the other end of stdin and stdout, as socat joins them; its exit
  status is the pipe's
      $ podssh pipe stdio "exec:sh -c 'tr a-z A-Z'"

  a descriptor that the calling program opened for podssh, on Unix
      $ podssh pipe fd:3 stdio

  a board's serial console on stdin and stdout, at 115200 baud, on Unix; Ctrl-C
  ends it
      $ podssh pipe serial:/dev/ttyUSB0,115200 stdio

  a TCP service behind an SSH server, on stdin and stdout, as -W reaches it
      $ podssh pipe stdio ssh:user@bastion.example.org,db.internal:5432

  the same service on a local port, for a client that connects: one client,
  then the port closes
      $ podssh pipe tcp-listen:5432 ssh:user@bastion.example.org,db.internal:5432

  an HTTP CONNECT proxy for pip, npm, cargo or git, with HTTPS_PROXY set to
  http://127.0.0.1:3128: each CONNECT goes through the relay
      $ podssh pipe http-listen:3128 relay:%h:%p

  the same proxy whose CONNECTs go on from an SSH server: ssh: with no target
  takes each one's %h:%p; a client: curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:3128 URL
      $ podssh pipe http-listen:3128 ssh:user@bastion.example.org

  a WebSocket of another service on stdin and stdout, by its URL, as websocat
  joins one
      $ podssh pipe stdio wss://ws.example.org/socket

  offer a service of this host to an operator outside: a pair, with its
  operator's part in a file
      $ podssh relay pair lab --operator-file lab-operator.json

  then the node, a roost in front of this host's sshd at 127.0.0.1:22: each
  operator's session reaches it
      $ podssh node lab --sshd

  from outside, log in to the node's SSH server with the operator's file
      $ podssh ssh --pair-file lab-operator.json node://user@lab

  copy a file to the node's SSH server with the same file; the path comes after
  the first : after the name
      $ podssh scp --pair-file lab-operator.json notes.txt node://user@lab:notes.txt

  or with OpenSSH, with podssh as its way to the node
      $ ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh operator lab --pair-file lab-operator.json' user@lab

  a host whose every road out is closed, but that the platform's own SSH
  reaches: its sshd through a node on that exec channel, with no relay and no
  pair
      $ ssh -o ProxyCommand="podssh operator --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' box" user@box

  or podssh itself on that channel: a copy to the node's sshd, each connection
  a session of the one stream
      $ podssh cp --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh node --carrier stdio box 127.0.0.1:22' notes.txt node://user@box:notes.txt

  or the other way: that host's programs reach the internet through this one,
  an exit of your net, by HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1080 in the sandbox
      $ podssh node gw --exit --carrier 'exec:ssh -T sandbox podssh exit gw --listen 127.0.0.1:1080 --carrier stdio'

  whether the node is online; then stop the pair
      $ podssh relay status lab && podssh relay revoke lab

  on podssh relay serve, the pair renewed for 72 hours with its tokens, so that
  each operator's file holds
      $ podssh relay pair --renew lab

  the node in the background under a name, started again whenever it ends; a
  second start of the name refuses
      $ podssh node lab --sshd --detach --restart --detach-name lab

  the runs in the background, then the state of one, and its stop: each read
  from the run's lock, never a pid
      $ podssh detached list && podssh detached status lab && podssh detached stop lab

  log in, then move the session to a node that the server's own podssh starts:
  it resumes after a lost link
      $ podssh ssh --upgrade user@example.org

  a node of a DNS server, on a host that allows UDP: each session is one flow
  of datagrams
      $ podssh node dns udp:10.0.0.2:53

  from outside, a program whose stdin and stdout are a datagram socket (Unix)
  sends each query
      $ podssh pipe 'exec:python3 query.py' udp:node:dns --pair-file dns-operator.json

  whether the relay reaches a target, and the first line that the target sends
      $ podssh relay trace github.com 22

  the relay itself on a host where nothing may listen: behind a quick tunnel,
  minting for the keys of owners.txt; its one line on stdout is the relay host
      $ podssh node relay --quick-tunnel --relay --allow owners.txt

  from anywhere, a session through that relay, with this client's key on its
  list
      $ podssh ssh --relay-host https://NAME.trycloudflare.com user@example.org

  make a key where ssh-keygen does not work
      $ podssh keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

  a key with no passphrase, for a script
      $ podssh keygen -N '' -f ./deploy_key

  the public key of a private key
      $ podssh keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

  the fingerprint of a key
      $ podssh keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

  a key that signs only in this machine's TPM, while Secure Boot is as it is
  now
      $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O pcr=7 -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

  such a key that also signs in each boot state that a key kept off the host
  signs
      $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O policy-key=/mnt/usb/policy_key -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

  after a firmware's update, sign the new boot state into that key, so that it
  signs again
      $ podssh keygen -t ecdsa-tpm -O add-policy -O policy-key=/mnt/usb/policy_key -f ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_tpm

  this manual with no pager
      $ podssh man --no-pager

  one section of this manual
      $ podssh man environment

  this manual as a man page
      $ podssh man --roff > podssh.1 && man -l podssh.1

SEE ALSO
  podssh COMMAND --help: the help of one command, its section of this
      manual

  podssh man SECTION: one section of this manual

  podssh man --roff: this manual as a man(7) page

  podssh man --json: this manual as one JSON object, for a program

  podssh doctor: what this host allows, and whether the relay works

  https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh: the source, the releases and the
      issues
```

<!-- document: README.md -->

# podssh

SSH from machines whose only way out is HTTPS.

podssh is one static binary. It is an SSH client, and it can carry any TCP
stream, through a WebSocket relay on port 443. It is for closed sandboxes:
CI runners, containers of AI agents, hosted notebooks. Such hosts have no
inbound ports and no direct outbound TCP. Often they have no working DNS, and
an HTTP proxy is their only way out. podssh needs no root, no `LD_PRELOAD`,
no installed `ssh`, and no TLS or crypto library of the system.

> [!WARNING]
> **Status: beta.** `podssh ssh`, `podssh each`, `podssh run`, `podssh job`, `podssh session`,
> `podssh containers`,
> `podssh proxy`, `podssh pipe`, `podssh funnel` (a local HTTP service at a
> public name), `podssh cp`, `podssh mv`, `podssh scp`,
> `podssh sftp` and `podssh edit` (files), `podssh doctor`, `podssh keygen`,
> `podssh agent`, `podssh man`, `podssh status`, `podssh ping`,
> `podssh health`, the reverse road (`podssh node`, `podssh operator`,
> `podssh relay`), `podssh chat`, `podssh play` (recordings),
> `podssh detached` (the runs of `--detach`, by their names),
> `podssh config` (settings), `podssh mcp`, `podssh net` (the owner's
> signed list of its nodes) and `podssh update` (this binary, from a signed
> release) work. `podssh ts`, the iroh road and WARP's `warp://` refuse with
> exit code 70 in a build without their features.
> Tests run them against OpenSSH and Dropbear servers, through the live
> relay, and in a box like the target sandbox. The measured state of `main`
> is in [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md), where a row of work after `v1.0.0`
> names the first release that holds it, or says `unreleased`.
> The plan is in [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md).

## How it works

```
podssh --TLS 1.3 + WebSocket, port 443--> relay --TCP--> sshd (or another TCP service)
   `-- through HTTPS_PROXY (HTTP CONNECT) when the host has one
```

- **The relay** ([`tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`](https://tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev/),
  a Cloudflare Worker) copies bytes between a WebSocket and a TCP socket. Its
  contract is at [`/llms-full.txt`](https://tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev/llms-full.txt).
  [docs/relay.md](docs/relay.md) gives the parts that podssh uses.
- **Encryption.** SSH encrypts the session between podssh and the server.
  The relay can see the target, the time and volume of the traffic, and the
  start of the SSH handshake. The host-key check makes a relay in the middle
  safe. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
- **Outbound only, unless you ask.** podssh opens outbound connections only
  (to the relay, or to the proxy that `HTTPS_PROXY` names). It listens only
  on an address that you name, of `podssh pipe` (`unix-listen:`,
  `tcp-listen:`, `http-listen:`, an HTTP CONNECT proxy, and `ws-listen:`,
  a WebSocket server) or of `podssh ssh -L` and `-D`, and on the socket of
  `podssh session start`, your own, after the bind shows that the host
  allows it. The iroh
  road, in each release binary and in a build with the feature `iroh`,
  binds UDP for direct paths only after a probe allows it. A node that you give a UDP target (`podssh node
  NAME udp:HOST:PORT`) sends UDP from its host, after a probe.
- **Fallbacks.** If one relay host fails, podssh tries the next one. If DNS
  fails, podssh uses pinned addresses or DNS over HTTPS. If the relay goes
  silent, podssh finds it in 30 to 40 s.
- **No local pty needed.** A remote pty (`-tt`) works when stdin and stdout
  are pipes. Full-screen programs and Ctrl-C work on a host that has no
  `/dev/ptmx`.

## First steps on a new host

1. Get a static binary for the host: a release from the
   [releases page](https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/releases) (`v1.0.N`
   is stable; each `v1.1.0-beta.N` is a prerelease of the next), or build
   one (see "Build").

   From the release after `v1.1.0-beta.3` on, one command installs it for
   this user, with no root. `podssh-install.sh` finds the host's file,
   checks it against the SHA-256 that it holds, and puts it in
   `~/.local/bin` (or `--prefix DIR`). A second run downloads nothing.
   `--offline podssh-VERSION.tar.gz` installs from the release's bundle,
   with no network:

   ```sh
   T=v1.1.0-beta.4   # the release's tag
   curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/releases/download/$T/podssh-install.sh"
   sh podssh-install.sh
   ```

   By hand, or for a release before it: check the binary against
   `SHA256SUMS`, and make it executable:

   ```sh
   T=v1.0.1; B=podssh-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl   # or podssh-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl
   curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/releases/download/$T/$B"
   curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/releases/download/$T/SHA256SUMS"
   grep " $B\$" SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c - && chmod +x "$B"
   ```

   From `v1.0.0-beta.2` on, a release also has
   `podssh-armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf` (a Raspberry Pi with 32 bits) and
   `podssh-riscv64gc-unknown-linux-musl`, both static;
   `podssh-aarch64-apple-darwin` and `podssh-x86_64-apple-darwin`
   (macOS, where the check is `shasum -a 256 -c`); and
   `podssh-aarch64-pc-windows-msvc.exe` (Windows on ARM). The Mac binaries
   are not signed with a Developer ID: fetch them with `curl`, as above,
   which marks no quarantine; after a browser's download, run
   `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine FILE` first. The Windows binaries are not
   signed either, and SmartScreen may warn about them.

   From `v1.0.0-beta.2` on, the release workflow also proves where each
   binary comes from. `podssh --version` names the commit of the tag. The
   provenance of each binary names the workflow and the commit (with the
   GitHub CLI):

   ```sh
   gh attestation verify "$B" --repo PodUtils/podssh \
     --signer-workflow PodUtils/podssh/.github/workflows/release.yml --source-ref "refs/tags/$T"
   ```

   And `SHA256SUMS` is signed by the workflow at the tag (with cosign 3.x):

   ```sh
   curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/releases/download/$T/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json"
   cosign verify-blob --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
     --certificate-identity "https://github.com/PodUtils/podssh/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$T" \
     --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com SHA256SUMS
   ```
2. Run `podssh doctor`. It tells what the host allows and whether the full
   path works: one `ok`, `FAIL` or `????` line for each check (`????` is a
   check that could not run). It exits 1 if a check failed.
3. Run `podssh man`. It is the whole manual: each command, flag, `-o`
   keyword, variable, file and exit code, with examples. The binary makes it
   from its own tables and needs nothing else. `podssh man ssh` gives one
   section; `podssh man --no-pager` writes it all to stdout.
4. If the host has no working `ssh-keygen`, make a key with podssh:

   ```sh
   podssh keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # -N '' for no passphrase
   podssh keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub             # its fingerprint; the private file works too
   podssh keygen -t ed25519-sk -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk   # in a FIDO2 security key (Linux, Windows)
   ```
5. On the far hosts, `podssh job` and `podssh ssh --persist` need tmux.
   Without it they exit 255 and name the command that installs it from
   the host's package manager; podssh runs none:

   ```sh
   sudo apt-get install -y tmux   # Debian, Ubuntu
   sudo dnf install -y tmux       # Fedora, RHEL
   apk add tmux                   # Alpine, as root
   ```

   Where tmux cannot be installed, `podssh job start --no-tmux HOST --
   COMMAND` runs the job under nohup instead (`podssh man job`).

## Usage

podssh is the SSH client, with the options of OpenSSH:

```sh
podssh ssh user@example.org                  # an interactive shell
podssh ssh user@example.org 'uname -a'       # a command; its exit status is podssh's
podssh ssh -i key -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new user@example.org true
podssh ssh -J user@bastion user@inner        # through a jump host
podssh ssh -A user@build 'git pull'          # the server may use your agent while the session lasts
podssh ssh -W db.internal:5432 user@bastion  # stdin and stdout to a TCP port; nothing listens
podssh ssh -N -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@bastion  # a local port to the database, if this host may listen
podssh ssh -N -D 1080 user@bastion           # a SOCKS proxy on 127.0.0.1:1080
podssh ssh -M -N -S /tmp/cm-%C user@host &   # Unix: later runs with -S /tmp/cm-%C share this connection
podssh ssh -tt user@example.org < script.txt # a remote pty; local stdin is a pipe
podssh ssh -tt --expect 'Choice: ' --send '2\r' user@menu  # keys for a prompt after the login, then the session
podssh containers user@example.org           # the containers of docker, podman and kubectl, each with the command that enters it
```

Files go over SFTP, or by exec where the server has no SFTP, verified by
SHA-256 before they take the destination's name; `mv` then removes the
source:

```sh
podssh cp report.pdf user@example.org:docs/  # up, into a directory
podssh cp user@example.org:logs/app.log .    # down
podssh mv user@example.org:inbox/a.csv .     # down, then the far file goes
podssh cp -r site user@example.org:www/      # a tree, several files at once
```

Through the relay each small file waits for its own round trips, so
several files go at once over the one connection: 4 by default,
`--parallel K` for K, `--parallel 1` for one at a time. A tester measured
100 files of 2 bytes in 210 s one at a time and 32 s with 8 (GitHub #100).

- On a host with no terminal (the sandbox of an agent), podssh never waits
  for input that cannot come. It refuses an unknown host key, gives its
  fingerprint, and gives `-o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` as the
  remedy. Passwords and passphrases come from `SSH_ASKPASS` (with
  `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force`), or podssh skips them with a note.
- An agent that runs one command at a time keeps a shell between its
  calls with `podssh session`: `start NAME HOST`, then `send NAME TEXT`,
  `wait NAME` (until the output stops), `capture NAME` (the screen) and
  `stop NAME`. Its socket is your own, and carries no credential.
- Keepalives are on (every 60 s), because the relay closes a connection
  after 180 s with no traffic.
- `--direct` connects without the relay.
- The exit codes are those of OpenSSH: the remote status, 128 plus a signal
  number, or 255 for a failure of podssh. See `podssh man exit-status`.
- `PODSSH_ERROR_PROGRAM` names a program that gets each failure of podssh
  as one JSON object on its stdin: the command, the exit code and podssh's
  last messages, with no credential. A remote status starts no program.
  podssh calls no AI service itself; the program decides.

If the host has an `ssh` client, podssh can be its `ProxyCommand`:

```sh
ssh -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' -o ServerAliveInterval=60 user@example.org
```

Or put it in `~/.ssh/config`:

```
Host example
    HostName example.org
    User me
    ProxyCommand podssh proxy %h %p
    ServerAliveInterval 60
```

`podssh proxy HOST PORT` is a byte pipe, so it also works for other TCP
protocols:

```sh
printf 'HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n' | podssh proxy example.com 80
```

`podssh chat` carries messages and files between two podssh ends, end to
end encrypted: one side waits as the node of a pair, the other reaches it.
Each line of stdin is a message; `/file PATH` offers a file, which the peer
writes only once it accepts it (`/accept ID`).

```sh
podssh relay pair NAME --operator-file op.json  # once, on the side that waits
podssh chat --listen NAME                       # the side that waits
podssh chat NAME --pair-file op.json            # the other side, with op.json sent over a trusted channel
```

A standard sshd gets a session that survives a lost link when a podssh next
to it owns the TCP connection to it: a roost. The roost checks that sshd
answers with SSH's version line, before it goes online and for each
session:

```sh
podssh relay pair lab --operator-file op.json   # on the server, once
podssh node lab --sshd                          # the roost, in front of 127.0.0.1:22
podssh ssh --pair-file op.json node://me@lab    # from outside; a lost link resumes the session
```

When the server has a podssh on its `PATH`, `podssh ssh --upgrade` does
these steps itself: it logs in, starts a temporary roost there in that SSH
session, and moves the session to it. With no podssh there, the session
stays as it is, with one note; podssh never copies itself to a server.

```sh
podssh ssh --upgrade me@example.org
```

`podssh man environment` lists each variable that podssh reads. The usual
one is `HTTPS_PROXY`: podssh sends the relay's name in `CONNECT`, so it
needs no DNS through a proxy. A SOCKS5 proxy works too
(`ALL_PROXY=socks5h://HOST:PORT`, with a user and a password if it needs
them).

podssh mints a relay token when it first needs one (`POST /v1/mint`, no
account), and caches it for its lifetime in the user's cache directory. Only
the owner can read the cache.

### Relay limits

| Limit | Value | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idle cut | 180 s with no payload (the relay's keepalives do not count) | Keep `ServerAliveInterval` below 180; to a node, the resumable layer keeps the link busy |
| Session length | 12 h | Connect again |
| Session volume | 64 MiB, both directions together | Use a new session for large transfers |
| Token lifetime | 72 h or less, minted with `POST /v1/mint` | podssh mints and caches tokens |
| Targets | Public hosts only; the relay refuses private, link-local and internal addresses | None |
| IPv6 targets | The default relay takes an IPv6 address, but reached no IPv6 host when measured (2026-10-08); `podssh ssh` then tries the direct road at once, also under `-6` | `--direct`, where the host has IPv6; `podssh relay serve` on a host with IPv6, then `--relay-host` |

### Other TCP protocols

`podssh proxy` and `podssh pipe` carry any TCP stream. A client that runs a
command as its transport needs no listener. A client that calls `connect()`
itself needs a local port or socket: `podssh pipe` listens only where you
ask for it and the host allows the bind (`podssh doctor` tries an AF_INET
and an AF_UNIX bind), and OpenSSH's `ssh -L`, with podssh as its
`ProxyCommand`, listens where a bind works and the user has an entry in the
user database. Through the relay, a session ends at 64 MiB, both directions
together ("Relay limits" above); `--direct` avoids the relay where the host
has a road of its own. These protocols are often not encrypted: reach them
with `ssh:`, so that the relay sees SSH only.

| Protocol | With no listener | With a local listener | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VNC (RFB, port 5900 + display) | A viewer that runs a command as its transport: SSVNC's `ssvncviewer exec=COMMAND` (its manual; not run here) | `pipe unix-listen:` and TigerVNC's `vncviewer`, which takes a socket's path, where only an AF_UNIX bind works; else `pipe tcp-listen:` or `ssh -L` | 64 MiB through the relay, 21 full screens of 1024x768 at 32 bits with no compression; [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md) has a viewer's rate |
| RDP (port 3389) | No client that runs a command was found; FreeRDP's `/proxy:` takes an HTTP or SOCKS5 proxy, a listener (`podssh ssh -D`) | `pipe tcp-listen:` or `ssh -L` (not measured) | 64 MiB through the relay |
| Telnet (port 23) | `podssh proxy HOST 23` carries the bytes, but the server's first bytes are options (IAC) that a client must answer | `pipe tcp-listen:`, then `telnet 127.0.0.1 PORT` | Plain text, the password too: use `ssh:` to a host near the server |
| USB/IP (port 3240) | None: `usbip` dials a host and port itself | `pipe --keep-listening tcp-listen:127.0.0.1:3240` to `ssh:`, then `usbip attach -r 127.0.0.1 -b BUSID`: `usbip` needs root and the kernel modules (`usbip-host` on the server, `vhci-hcd` here), podssh neither | 64 MiB through the relay, about 2 minutes of a disk read at the 0.5 to 0.7 MB/s measured through a sandbox's proxy: the session then ends (1009), and the device goes away; not encrypted: use `ssh:`, never `relay:` to a public `usbipd` |

```sh
# VNC where only an AF_UNIX bind works: TigerVNC's viewer at the socket
podssh pipe unix-listen:/tmp/vnc.sock ssh:me@desktop.example.org,127.0.0.1:5901 &
vncviewer /tmp/vnc.sock
# VNC where a TCP bind works: podssh listens ...
podssh pipe tcp-listen:5901 ssh:me@desktop.example.org,127.0.0.1:5901 &
# ... or OpenSSH listens, and podssh carries its session
ssh -N -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5901 -o ProxyCommand='podssh proxy %h %p' -o ServerAliveInterval=60 me@desktop.example.org
# no listener: the viewer runs podssh
ssvncviewer 'exec=podssh pipe stdio ssh:me@desktop.example.org,127.0.0.1:5901'
# Telnet to a device behind an SSH host
podssh pipe tcp-listen:2323 ssh:me@gateway.example.org,router.lan:23 & telnet 127.0.0.1 2323
# USB/IP: list the server's devices, then attach one (usbipd runs there; each usbip command connects once)
podssh pipe --keep-listening tcp-listen:127.0.0.1:3240 ssh:me@usbhost.example.org,127.0.0.1:3240 &
usbip list -r 127.0.0.1
sudo usbip attach -r 127.0.0.1 -b 1-1
```

A listener of `podssh pipe` takes one client, then closes; a viewer that
connects again, and `usbip`, which connects once to list and once to
attach, need `--keep-listening`. After `usbip attach`, the kernel speaks
USB/IP on the connection to podssh's listener, and the device stays while
that session lasts; `usbip detach` ends it.

## Build

podssh is a Rust workspace (`crates/`). It needs Rust 1.99 or later and a C
compiler: the SSH client uses aws-lc (through `russh`). Each released
binary is statically compiled, and the gate checks it. The crates that podssh shares with its
sibling projects (TLS, proxies, DNS, the WebSocket client, the terminal's line discipline, the
resumable layer, the record's checker and more) come from
[PodUtils/podcrates](https://github.com/PodUtils/podcrates) by a tag of that repository, so the
first build needs github.com.

```sh
export CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4
cargo build --release -p podssh-cli   # target/release/podssh
cargo test --no-fail-fast             # the default members
```

The Tailscale mode (`podssh ts`) links a fork of
[tailscale-rs](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale-rs) that needs a C
compiler and cmake. It is a feature: `cargo build -p podssh-cli --features ts`.

CAUTION: Builds use much memory. On a small machine or a VM, set
`CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4`. The static Linux binary is built in a `rust:1-alpine`
container. See [docs/development.md](docs/development.md).
